# ON MEDICINE
<sig>b 2</sig>

...Plantain, and even the Oak, and the lowliest grasses of the fields. <margin>A</margin>

Yet, they object again, "the learned doctors write such things, especially those who are considered the leaders." Then there is also the "Common Practice" (as they call it). Fine indeed. I only wish these men had learned something else, or were wise even late in the day, as their own consciences might testify. They would achieve this beautifully if they believed that the knowledge of herbs was something that concerned them, and not just the <term>druggists</term> <note>original: *seplasiarios*, sellers of ointments and perfumes who functioned as early pharmacists.</note>. Finally, if only they were not entirely consumed by—and even growing old in—the excessive mixing of compounds and <term>simples</term> <note>Medicines made from a single constituent, usually a plant.</note>, but instead studied the powers of herbs: what they are worth, and in what degrees their qualities are balanced. **Dioscorides** will teach this above all; then **Pliny** and **Theophrastus**. If someone wishes to call upon **Avicenna** and **Serapion** <note>Influential medieval Islamic physicians.</note> as well, I do not object, provided they always look back toward the original sources. For I have found, while diligently studying Dioscorides and Pliny, that Avicenna contains nothing other than what is already written in the books of the ancients. May the Muses and all Physicians be ill-disposed toward me if I cannot demonstrate every single one of Avicenna's "simples" using only Pliny and Dioscorides, should anyone curiously demand it of me.

Otherwise, what a grand "art" it is to write a note to the pharmacist: "Take of golden pills and *cochia* pills, a half-scruple of each; let them be sharpened with 8 grains of <term>scammony</term> <note>original: *diagridij*, a harsh purgative resin.</note>; let 7 pills be made with syrup of <term>stoechas</term> <note>A type of lavender.</note>." Or thus: "Take 3 drams of Electuary of Rose Juice, 1 dram each of *diaphinicon* <note>A laxative confection made with dates.</note> and Indian Electuary, as much sugar as is sufficient, and let a <term>bolus</term> <note>A large, soft pill.</note> be made," etc. Any ignorant <margin>B</margin> barber-surgeon could easily learn all of this in a month or two, since everything is so clearly prescribed and established that unless a man is a complete "Thessalian ass" <note>A classical proverb for someone remarkably stupid.</note>, he cannot go wrong. A certain **Thessalus** <note>A famous Roman-era physician who claimed he could teach medicine in six months.</note> once promised (as **Galen** says) a certain <term>therapeutic method</term> <note>original: *therapeutikēn*</note> that could be learned in the space of six months, and for that, he was driven out by every school of physicians. Yet I would stake my life that if you look at that trivial sort of medicine practiced today, it is exactly as he said; Thessalus spoke the absolute truth.

<margin>Ulrich Hutten</margin>
But since we have come upon the subject of spices, I would like to mention in passing what we have often heard from the most noble and learned knight, **Ulrich von Hutten**, and which he also included in his book on **Guaiacum** <note>Hutten wrote a famous 1519 treatise on using "Holy Wood" (Guaiacum) from the Americas to treat syphilis.</note>. He said: "The frugality of my grandfather, **Laurentius Hutten**, ought to be a great incentive for us in our pursuit of glory. Although he was of wealthy status and involved in the great affairs of our Princes both at home and in military service, he never allowed pepper, saffron, ginger, and foreign condiments of that kind into his house. Nor did he use any clothing other than what was made from our own wool, even though precious garments were occasionally given to him as rewards for his service. He did this not only himself, but he also attacked the customs of his peers with great reproach. 'As if,' he would say, 'there does not grow among us that which can season our food, if there is a need to delight the palate with pleasures.'" Thus far he spoke.

Yet why do I mention only him? Even the ancient writers of history testify that our ancestors lived on nothing but the simplest diet and very few medicines. And yet, while they lived so frugally, they possessed well-strengthened bodies, clearly hardened against hunger, thirst, and cold, and...

<summary>The author critiques modern physicians for relying on complex, pre-written formulas and imported spices rather than studying the botanical properties of local plants. He cites the frugality of Laurentius Hutten as a moral and practical example of rejecting foreign luxuries for domestic resources.</summary>

<keywords>botany, pharmacology, Dioscorides, Avicenna, Ulrich von Hutten, Laurentius Hutten, simplicity, spices, medical education</keywords>

# ENCOMIUM
<sig>b 3</sig>

<margin>C</margin>It is said that the **Crotoniates** <note>original: *Cmãtinos*, likely referring to the inhabitants of Croton in Southern Italy, famous in antiquity for their physical health and athletes like Milo.</note> rarely fell ill and lived to be old men. In contrast, we pull in our hands and feet at the very first signs of frost; and the more we use foreign medicines, the more frequently and violently we are beset by diseases. For how many are there among those delicate souls who, at the first sign of a suppressed stomach rumble or a "crepitus," <note>An old medical term for an intestinal sound or passing of gas.</note> immediately gulp down a potion, only to be tortured by pains of the stomach, the liver, gout, dropsy, the "Royal Disease," <note>original: *morbo regio*, an old name for jaundice.</note> or the "French Disease"? <note>original: *morbo gallico*, a common Renaissance term for syphilis.</note> Who, I ask, are more tormented by these evils than those who live out of perfume shops <note>original: *myropoliis*, shops selling scents, ointments, and exotic drugs.</note> and despise all simple food? On the other hand, whom do we see remaining more healthy than those who are content with a simple diet? Far from the workshops of the druggists, they mix their porridge with cheese and egg, just as is said of **Cato**. It was not our original intention to go quite this far; but since we are discussing these matters with good and fair-minded men, we trust in our liberty. In fact, seeing their fairness toward us, we should lament our own laziness and slipperiness more than condemn anyone’s trade—provided they have not distributed their goods through deceit or excessive <term>usury</term> <note>Lending money or selling goods at unfairly high interest or profit.</note>. Nor do we despise goods from across the sea so much that we do not also hold them in high price, provided they are used at the right time, with discretion, and by those who can afford to buy them.

Furthermore, if through frequent reading and diligent scrutiny, our Doctors would advance the study of our native herbs, they would not hold exotic ones in the highest place—especially since our own local and "household" plants provide so many and such great benefits. Otherwise, if it did not matter greatly, it would have been a waste for **Hippocrates** and the other ancient physicians who followed him to wander through forests and mountains at such great expense to their wealth and their small bodies, investigating and searching for herbs.

<margin>D</margin>It would have been a waste for them to travel through so many wildernesses and foreign nations, doing so on different days and at different seasons of the year—something **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) whose work *De Materia Medica* was the primary pharmacological text for 1,500 years.</note> testifies that he himself did. They did this because they considered it a plainly divine thing to "philosophize" with herbs. Instead, they could have done as our men do today in the schools: sat down and disputed over matters of no importance to life, governing the fates of men not by their own knowledge, but by relying on others. Yet how much more prudently did the **Egyptians** act in former times! They took such great care in employing physicians (*as **Herodotus** says*) that they appointed individual doctors for individual diseases. Among them, some are eye-doctors, others treat the teeth, and others treat the parts of the belly and the intestines; as a result, everything is full of doctors. They believed it was impossible for one person to have the causes and remedies of all diseases ready at hand.

---

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As for how such a great neglect of herbs crept in—and subsequently such a thick and lazy ignorance of them—no one has recorded more eloquently than **Pliny**. These are roughly his words in the *Natural History, Book 12, in the preface:*

> *I cannot wonder enough that the memory of certain herbs has perished, and even the knowledge of the names which authors have recorded has been lost. For who would not think that life has been improved by the commerce of things and the fellowship of a festive peace, now that the world has been shared through the majesty of the Roman Empire, and everything that was previously hidden has been put into common use? But by Hercules, people are not found who know much of what was recorded by the ancients: so much more fertile was the care of the men of old, or more successful was their industry. Thousands of years ago, at the very beginnings of literature, **Hesiod** <note>An early Greek poet (c. 700 BC) who wrote on agriculture in *Works and Days*.</note> began to reveal instructions for farmers, and not a few followed his care.*

<summary>The author contrasts the health of the ancients, who used simple local diets and herbs, with the sickly moderns who rely on expensive imports. He praises the field research of Dioscorides and the specialization of Egyptian medicine while citing Pliny the Elder to lament the loss of botanical knowledge despite the growth of global trade.</summary>

# OF MEDICINE
<sig>b 3</sig>

<margin>A</margin>
Our labor has grown. This is because we must investigate not only later discoveries but also those things which the ancients found, which have been lost to memory through laziness and the destruction of records. Who could find any cause for this "sleep" other than the public state of the world? Indeed, other customs have taken over, men's minds are occupied by other things, and only the arts of greed are cultivated—whereas before, the empires of nations were contained within themselves. Therefore, due to a certain sterility of fortune for talented men, it was necessary for them to exercise the virtues of the mind. Countless kings were honored for their skill in the arts and displayed them with pride, believing that their help and immortality were extended through them. For this reason, rewards and the works of life abounded. But for posterity, the vastness of the world and the magnitude of things became a loss, especially after a senator began to be chosen for his wealth, a judge to be made by his wealth, and nothing was seen to adorn a magistrate or a general more than his wealth. Once childlessness <note>original: *orbitas*. In Roman society, wealthy childless individuals were often courted by "legacy hunters" looking to be named in their wills, leading to a corrupt social dynamic.</note> began to be held in the highest authority and power, and legacy-hunting became a most fertile source of profit, and the only joys were found in possessing things, the value of life perished. All the arts called "liberal" <note>The "liberal arts" were those considered suitable for a free person (Latin: *liber*), as opposed to "mechanical arts" or servile labor.</note> fell from the greatest good into their opposite, and progress began to be made through servitude alone. One man adores greed in one way, another in another, yet the same hope of men tends toward that single vow: to possess.

<margin>B</margin>
Galen expresses the same opinion in his *Method of Healing*, book 1: "No one in our age is devoted to the inquiry of truth; instead, everyone looks up to money, civil power, and the insatiable delights of pleasure to such an extent that if anyone pursues any study of wisdom, they consider him insane." <note>original: *in Therapeu. lib. 1*. Galen’s *Methodus Medendi* was a foundational text for Renaissance medicine.</note> And so on—you may seek the rest in the place cited.

### C O N C L V S I O N.

But where do all these things, repeated from such a long introduction, point? For what purpose, finally, have we said them? Indeed, it is so that we may bring back into use those divine herbs and plants of all kinds that have been obsolete and obscured until now—finally, whatever the fields or woods produce. Let us restore antiquity and "keep it in good repair," <note>original: *sarta tecta*, a Roman legal phrase meaning a building is "roofed and repaired," or in sound condition.</note> as the saying goes, and stretch out a hand to collapsed herbal medicine. Furthermore, let this skill and knowledge not be restricted to a few, but let the whole world recognize the great works of God. These works are nowhere more readily seen than in the herbs themselves, painted so festively with so many and such various colors, adorned with so many flowers and seeds, and what is greatest of all, endowed with so many healing powers.

Finally, what they see me urging, let the modern and newer physicians pursue much more vehemently and with greater effort. If physicians will listen to me as an advisor—since they see today that a new age is beginning—they should remember the words of the Comic poet: "this matter requires another life, and even another diet." <note>A reference to the Roman playwright Terence in his play *Andria*.</note> They should leave behind so many old obscurities, the trifles of barbarians, <note>In the Renaissance, "barbarians" often referred to medieval Arabic and Scholastic authors whose translations were considered "corrupted" compared to original Greek sources.</note> so many uncertain traditions, and indeed, the most trifling nonsense. Instead, let them devote themselves to those genuine and pure medicines. I call "pure" that which is sought from **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, **Theophrastus**, **Pliny**, **Dioscorides**, **Oribasius**, and that class of ancient writers of medical matters who were the first principles of the art itself. This knowledge should be sought <margin>throughout all things</margin> <note>original Greek: *διὰ πασῶν* (dia pason), literally "through all," often used to mean a complete or harmonious understanding.</note>. They will then recognize how much they differ from those whom they have admired until now as if they were gods; from those ancients, they will learn to heal more healthfully and more effectively, and they will cease to demand so much from and plunder the poor common people, who are burdened enough already.

<vocab>Hippocrates, Galen, Theophrastus, Pliny, Dioscorides, Oribasius, medicine, herbalism, conclusion</vocab>

<summary>The author concludes his introduction by blaming the decline of medical knowledge on social greed and materialism, calling for a return to the "pure" botanical medicine of the Greek and Roman masters. He argues that studying plants is a way to witness God's handiwork and provides a more ethical, effective way to treat the poor.</summary>

# PRAISE
<header>E N C O M I V M</header>

<margin>C</margin> Through this shortcut, and with even greater delight, students will soon admire the elegance, splendor, and deep knowledge of the ancient geniuses. They will come to detest the barbarians <note>original: *barbaros*. Renaissance humanists used this term for medieval scholars who wrote in "corrupt" Latin or followed Arabic medical traditions rather than the original Greek sources.</note> once they see that whatever is found in the works of Avicenna, Rhazes, Serapion, and Mesue <note>These were famous Persian and Arab physicians whose works were the standard medical textbooks in Europe during the Middle Ages.</note> is also present in Hippocrates, Galen, and Celsus—and found there with much more clarity. It will become plain that everything the modern schools of "barbarians" boast about is merely the feathers of Aesop’s jackdaw <note>A reference to a fable where a bird disguises itself in the beautiful feathers of others; the author implies medieval writers stole their best ideas from the ancients.</note>. Aside from the fact that their ideas are borrowed and stolen from others, they have also lost their original luster, having been defiled by an insipid distortion of words. I will refrain for now from mentioning what is even more praiseworthy: to drink from the original springs rather than from murky puddles, and to gain wisdom from the masters of the art rather than from foolish and noisy jackdaws.

Now is the time for languages, which have never been more successfully studied. Now is the age that, having unmasked the pretense and detected the fraud of the past, seeks and strives for a better education. Finally, we have excellent books, which have never been easier to obtain or cheaper to buy. Indeed, it was never as easy for Germans to acquire the works of Bertruccius, Sillanus, or Bernard de Gordon <note>These were medieval "scholastic" medical authors whose complex, dense textbooks were being replaced by the newly printed classics.</note> and others of that kind, as it is now to get the complete works of Galen (in both Greek and Latin), Celsus, Oribasius, Hippocrates, and Pliny.

At the same time, I hope that good and diligent physicians, as well as the <term>pharmacists</term> <note>original: *myropolas*, referring to those who prepared and sold ointments and medicines.</note>, will forgive me; I have no wish to lecture them or to criticize them. For I will say what Christ said: "He who is for us, feels with us" <note>A variation of the biblical phrasing in Mark 9:40 or Luke 9:50.</note>. Truly, my words were directed at the stupid, the inept, and the impostors. Let it be far from us to twist the vices of men into a slander against the art of medicine itself. For there is <margin>D</margin> no profession so holy that it does not nourish its own monsters.

<summary>The author argues that classical Greek and Roman medical texts are clearer and more authentic than medieval Arabic commentaries, urging students to study original sources now that printing has made them affordable. He clarifies that his critique is aimed at incompetent practitioners, not the noble profession of medicine itself.</summary>
<keywords>humanism, medical education, classical vs medieval, Avicenna, Galen, Hippocrates, printing press, medical ethics</keywords>

->TO GOD ALONE BE THE GLORY<-

# INVOCATION OF DIVINE AID.

<image-desc>The text is enclosed within a highly ornate rectangular woodcut border. The border features symmetrical scrollwork, acanthus leaves, and floral motifs. Embedded within the left and right margins of the border are eight circular medallions (four on each side), each containing a profile portrait of a male figure, likely representing famous ancient physicians or philosophers. Some figures wear laurel wreaths, others crowns or scholarly caps. At the top and bottom centers of the frame, there are decorative elements including grotesque masks and foliage.</image-desc>

I see that it was the custom among ancient Physicians that when they were about to write concerning the Medical Arts <term>Medical Arts: *Res Medica*, the holistic study and practice of medicine</term>, they would, before all else, implore the aid of the most high God or some divine power. The Poets did the same once—Homer and Virgil—a practice held as much in high renown as it was pious and sacred. For this reason, I wonder all the more how, after this most religious custom was long ago abolished, there was finally accepted in its place that feigned and fawning "securing of goodwill" <note>original: *benevolentiae captatio*. A standard rhetorical technique used in introductions to win over an audience; the author here considers it shallow compared to prayer.</note> used by orators. While I do not entirely condemn it, I am plainly moved to pity by our own follies and ingratitude. 

For since in all human affairs we stand in great need of divine help and mercy, we need the deity most especially when dispensing medicines <term>medicines: *pharmacis*, a term derived from the Greek *pharmakon*, meaning both a remedy and a poison</term>, and in the ongoing investigation and curing of diseases. Indeed, even the great and truly "divine" Hippocrates <note>Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE) is the Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine." Renaissance scholars called him "divine" to signal his unmatched authority.</note> agrees with this, for in his book *On the Instruction of the Novice Physician* <note>original: *De medici novitij institutione*</note> he says the following: "It is certain that a Physician possesses many things beyond mere physical tools. Indeed, the knowledge, contemplation, and fear of the Gods dwell within his mind. For in most diseases or symptoms, Medicine yields a great deal to the Gods, and is found to honor them. For Physicians yield most things to the Gods, because Medicine does not claim for itself the power to do everything; nor does such a power exist within it." Furthermore, Mesue <note>Johannes Mesue was an influential name associated with several major Arabic medical texts. His *Canons* were essential reading for pharmacists in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> begins his *Canons* in this manner: "In the name of God, the merciful, by whose will speech receives grace." And likewise in his book, *The Cure*...

<meta>catchword: The Cure</meta>

<summary>This page serves as a formal invocation, arguing that the practice of medicine is a sacred duty that requires divine guidance. The author cites both the Greek "father of medicine" Hippocrates and the Arabic authority Mesue to prove that medical success depends on God rather than just human skill.</summary>

...nesses. God alone heals illnesses, and in His bounty, the blessed, glorious, and exalted one has produced Medicine from the leaf of nature <note>original: *frugalitatis folio*. This suggests that medicine springs from simple, natural things provided by divine providence.</note>. In this matter alone I disagree most widely with Galen <term>Galen: Claudius Galenus (129–216 AD), an influential Greek physician whose humoral theory dominated medicine for over a millennium. The author here critiques Galen's secular focus.</term>, who impiously imagines that no diseases are inflicted or cured by God, deriving their causes solely from the temperament of the body and the humors. 

Since, therefore, we ourselves are contemplating a similar work and intend to make visible the magnificent works of God, which He performs daily and wonderfully in **PLANTS**, we judge it a Christian duty that, before we gird ourselves for the description, we first appoint the Creator himself, **GOD**, the Best and Greatest <note>original: *D E V M opt. max.*, an abbreviation of *Deo Optimo Maximo*, a phrase originally used for Jupiter but adopted by Renaissance Christians for God.</note>, as the leader of our work. We pray that He may kindly favor our undertakings and deign to protect this most laborious business once it has been undertaken; and furthermore, that He might look favorably upon these gifts of ours which we bring into His temple. Our hope is that those reading these writings of ours may also sometimes experience and attain the same effects—those which the first writers of Medicine observed and which we have partly learned through our own experience. 

Let us therefore also cry out with the most religious Poet <note>The author is quoting the Roman poet Virgil from his work on farming, the *Georgics*.</note>:

->O GOD,<-

> Grant an easy course, and nod favor to our daring undertakings,
> Pitying with me the rustics who are ignorant of the way;
> Advance, and even now become accustomed to being called upon in prayers.

¶ We have taken our beginning, therefore, from the **Plantain** <term>Plantain: *Plantago*, a common weed. In the Renaissance, it was highly valued for its ability to stop bleeding and heal wounds.</term>, not only because this little herb is common and very well known, but also because nothing else so clearly reflects the divinity of **GOD** within itself. It repeatedly rouses and animates us toward the recognition of Himself and His works; He who always performs wonders in the smallest things, yet disregards whatever appears high and admirable to men.

## THE OPINIONS OF AUTHORS

### The View of DIOSCORIDES concerning Plantain, Book 2.
<note>Pedanius Dioscorides was a 1st-century Greek physician whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical authority for 1,500 years.</note>

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring figures that appear to be a physician or scholar seated and gesturing toward others, possibly in a garden or consulting room.</image-desc>The Plantain is of two types: the Greater and the Lesser. The Lesser Plantain has narrower, smaller, softer, thinner, and smoother leaves than the Greater; it has angular stalks that lean toward the ground, pale flowers, and seeds at the tops of the stems.
The Greater, by contrast, is thicker and more stately, with a broader leaf and the appearance of a garden vegetable. The stalk of this Plantain is also angular, slightly reddish, a cubit <note>An ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm.</note> in height, and is covered with small seeds from the middle all the way to the very top.

<margin>Where the Plantain grows.</margin>
Its roots are tender, hairy, white in color, and as thick as a finger. The Plantain grows in damp places, near lakes, hedges, and marshy areas. The Greater variety is more effective and better for use.

### The View of PLINY, Book 25, Chapter 8, concerning Plantain.
<note>Pliny the Elder was a Roman naturalist whose "Natural History" compiled vast amounts of ancient knowledge.</note>

There are two kinds of Plantain: the Greater and the Lesser. The Lesser has narrower and darker leaves, very much like the tongues of sheep, an angular stalk that is sometimes leaning, and it grows in meadows.

<margin>D</margin>
The other is the Greater, with its leaves enclosed as if on sides; because there are seven of these, some have called it <term>Heptapleuron</term> <note>original: "ἑπτάπλευρον" — Greek for "seven-ribbed."</note>.
Its stalk is also a cubit long and resembles that of a Turnip. It grows in damp places and is much more effective. Its power is wonderful for drying and thickening the body, serving in the place of a cautery <note>A medical treatment involving heat or caustic agents to sear tissue.</note>.

### The View of APULEIUS concerning Plantain, Chapter 1.
<note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Apuleius, the author of a highly influential 4th-century herbal.</note>

The Greeks call it <term>arnon</term> <note>original: "ἀρνὸν" — meaning "lamb," likely referring to "lamb's tongue."</note>, but for its tongue-like shape they call it <term>heptapleuron</term> <note>seven-sided</note>. Again, because it often has sprouting buds that resemble seven sides in length, the Greeks named it <term>heptapleuron</term>. Furthermore, there are two species of it. For what is named <term>Heptapleuros</term> is the larger form, with more ornate, broader, and veined leaves. It grows in valleys and gardens, as well as very much in marshes and in meadows, and it is more constrictive. The other is truly smaller and darker, smoother, and thinner. It grows in papery <note>original: "chartarijs" — this may refer to waste places or dry, thin soil where the plant looks "parched."</note> places, but is used in various ways.
Serapion says almost the same things.

### The View of HERMOLAI BARBARI concerning Plantain.
<note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493) was an Italian scholar famous for correcting errors in the Latin translations of ancient scientific texts.</note>

Plantain is sometimes called <term>Septineruia</term> <note>Seven-nerved</note>. Yet <term>Heptaneruia</term> seems to be a different herb than Plantain. This is clearly evident in a certain copy of a work titled <term>Botanicon</term>, which argues against collections of recipes. Indeed, in that work, three herbs are requested: three ounces of Plantain, six ounces of <term>Septineuron</term> <note>Seven-nerved plant</note>, and also three ounces of <term>Leoneuron</term> <note>Lion-nerved plant</note>. I do not understand what <term>Leoneuron</term> might be. Its flower is downy, like wheat, breaking out bit by bit like <term>Aphaca</term> <note>Yellow Vetchling</note> and <term>Intybum</term> <note>Chicory or Endive</note>. Plantain is among the spiked plants, but the Lesser has darker leaves and is like the tongue of sheep...

It emphasizes the plant's physical characteristics, growth habits, and medicinal "drying" properties.</summary>

<header>Volume One.</header>

...very similar, from which it gets the name *Arnoglossos* <note>Greek for "Lamb’s Tongue"</note> among the Greeks. <margin>A</margin>
->Jerome the Herbalist on the Plantain.<-
<note>Likely referring to Hieronymus Brunfels, a key figure in the transition from medieval to modern botany.</note>

Plantain is said to be three-fold. The **Greater**, which is also called **Seven-nerved** and **Lamb’s Tongue**. The **Lesser**, which is called the **Broad Lance**, because it is shaped like a lance. And the **Aquatic**, upon which frogs frequently sit. For this reason, it is called <term>frog’s spoon herb</term> <note>original: "frösch leffel krut"</note> by the Germans.

### T E M P E R A M E N T [Qualities]

It cools and dries in the second degree <note>Galenic medicine categorized plant properties on a scale of one to four</note>. However, it possesses something of a harsh or astringent quality. Therefore, it is suitable against malignant ulcers, fluxes, and rot. It dries, however, without causing irritation, and partakes of bitterness. Both the fruit <note>meaning the seed-head</note> and the root itself possess nearly the same power, except the root is drier and less cold. The fruit consists of very fine parts, while the roots consist of coarser parts. Furthermore, the leaves of the herb itself are drying, consist of finer parts, and are of a less cold power.

### P O W E R S & Benefits of it according to Dioscorides.

The leaves have a drying and constricting power. For this reason, they are beneficial when applied to all malignant ulcers and those prone to fluid-leakage, as well as to <term>elephantiasis</term> <note>a term used in the Renaissance for various severe, scaly skin diseases</note> and filthy sores. They restrain the flow of blood, creeping ulcers, <term>night-rashes</term> <note>original: "epinictidas," pustules that appear at night</note>, carbuncles, and <term>corrosive sores</term> <note>original: "nomas"</note>.
They cover old and uneven ulcers with a scar.
They heal <term>Chironian ulcers</term> <note>original: "Chironia," referring to deep, stubborn ulcers named after the centaur Chiron</note>. <margin>B</margin>
They knit together deep wounds.
Applied with salt, they are beneficial for dog bites, burns, inflammations from fire, <term>bread-like swellings</term> <note>original: "panis," likely refers to a type of abscess</note>, swellings of the parotid glands, <term>scrofula</term> <note>original: "strumis," swelling of the neck lymph nodes</note>, and <term>tears in the corner of the eye</term> <note>original: "ægylopijs," lachrymal fistulas</note>.
The herb, cooked with vinegar and salt and eaten, helps those with dysentery and <term>abdominal ailments</term> <note>original: "cœliacis"</note>.
It is also given in place of Beet, cooked with lentils.
In cases of <term>leucophlegmatia</term> <note>a type of dropsy or edema</note>, the decocted herb is given among dry meals.
The juice of the leaves, when given, benefits those with the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: "comitialibus," meaning epilepsy</note> and those who are short of breath. Rinsing with it repeatedly cleanses ulcers of the mouth.
With <term>Cimolian earth</term> <note>a medicinal clay</note> or white lead, it heals <term>Saint Anthony’s Fire</term> <note>original: "igni sacro," likely erysipelas</note>.
Poured into fistulas, it is beneficial.
The same juice is instilled for bleary eyes and ear pains.
It is also added to <term>eye-salves</term> <note>original: "collyria"</note>.
Drunk, it assists gums soaked in blood and the spitting up of blood.
It is used as a clyster <note>enema</note> for those with dysentery.
It is given in a drink against <term>wasting disease</term> <note>original: "tabem," often tuberculosis</note>.
Against <term>contractions of the womb</term> <note>original: "strangulationes uuluæ"</note>, it is applied on a piece of wool, even if the womb suffers from a discharge.
The seed, drunk in wine, stops fluxes of the bowels and the spitting of blood.
The decocted root, both by chewing and by rinsing, soothes toothaches.
The same, with the leaves, is given in wine for ulcers of the kidneys and bladder.
They say that three roots, with three measures of wine and an equal amount of water, help with <term>tertian fevers</term>, and four roots for <term>quartan fevers</term> <note>fevers that recur every three or four days, typical of malaria</note>.
There are some who use the wearing of the root as an amulet to disperse scrofula.

<header>S I M P L E Medicines</header>

<margin>C</margin> The Syrians report that the juice of Plantain and calamint <note>a mint-like aromatic herb</note> with honey cures those whose strength has failed, when given on the second and fourth day, and on the *Parasceue*—that is, Friday. Receive this as a secret, for it has been proven by true experience.

## F R O M  A P U L E I O S .
<note>Attributed to Pseudo-Apuleius, the author of a highly influential 4th-century herbal.</note>

The root of the Plantain herb suspended from the neck wondrously takes away a headache.
The juice, also warmed, removes pain of the belly by fomentation <note>applying warm, moist substances to the body</note>; and if there should be swellings, the crushed herb applied as a poultice removes the tumor.
The same juice given as a drink both heals the internal organs and cleanses the chest <note>original: "thoracem"</note> wonderfully.
For those who cough up pus mixed with blood, give them the juice of the Plantain herb to drink, and they shall be healed.
The seed, crushed and occasionally sprinkled into a wound, heals wounds quickly.
And the crushed herb itself, when applied, cools those places which are distressed by excessive heat, and heals them thoroughly.
To stop the bowels <note>to treat diarrhea</note>, it is drunk cooked with vinegar in undiluted wine, in the measure of one cup <note>original: "cyathi," a Roman liquid measure roughly equal to 0.045 liters</note>.
For the bites of serpents, it is beneficial when ground and taken with wine.
To purge worms <note>original: "lumbricis," specifically intestinal roundworms</note>, you shall crush the Plantain herb and give a spoonful of its juice to drink; apply the crushed herb itself daily to the navel.
Pounded with lard <note>original: "axungia," specifically unsalted pig fat</note>, without salt, made into the form of a softening plaster <note>original: "malagmatis"</note> and applied, it dissipates hardness.
In a quartan fever <note>a fever where paroxysms occur every fourth day, often associated with malaria</note>, give the juice in honeyed water to drink two hours before the onset, and you will marvel at the effect.
Do the same in a tertian fever <note>a fever occurring every third day</note>; crush three roots and let the patient drink them while fasting, with wine or water, just before the onset.
It is certain that for gout <note>original: "podagrae"</note> and for the pain and swelling of all the nerves <note>the term "nervus" in this period often included tendons and ligaments</note>, the leaves crushed or pounded with a small amount of salt and applied work best.
For the pains of the afterbirth, the crushed seed is believed to be beneficial.
For fresh wounds, crushed leaves are applied with old lard without salt, and the sufferer will be made healthy.
If anyone’s feet have swollen from a journey, Plantain crushed and applied with vinegar removes the swelling.
If an ulcer should grow near the eye or the nostrils, the juice of the Plantain herb, pressed and crushed, applied with a soaking of soft wool for nine days, cures it.
With old lard, it heals parotid swellings <note>swellings of the salivary glands, often associated with mumps</note>, all ulcers of the mouth, and sores <note>original: "alcolam," likely referring to aphthous ulcers or thrush</note> wonderfully.
Crushed and applied, it heals the bite of a mad dog.
Against all difficulties of the bladder, the leaves or roots of the Plantain herb in raisin wine <note>original: "passo," a sweet wine made from dried grapes</note> are a powerful remedy.

## F R O M  P L I N Y .
<note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the "Natural History."</note>

Nothing stops "fluxes"—which the Greeks call rheumatisms <note>original: "ῥευματισμοὺς," referring to any abnormal flow of fluids in the body</note>—quite so well.
It has a wondrous power in drying and thickening the body, acting in the place of a cautery <note>a tool or substance used to burn or sear tissue to stop bleeding</note>.
Plantain in honeyed water makes mild cold fevers easier, if taken two hours be-

The juice of the root, either soaked or crushed, or
The ground root itself, in water heated with iron <note>original: "ferro calefacta." In pre-modern medicine, water in which red-hot iron had been quenched was believed to take on the "astringent" properties of the metal.</note>.
Plantain corrects phlegm and eruptions, and heals superficial tumors <note>original: "panos," referring to small inflammatory swellings of the glands, often in the groin or armpit</note> when mixed with salt.

### FROM ORIBASIUS
<note>Oribasius (c. 320–403 AD) was a Greek medical compiler and the personal physician to the Emperor Julian.</note>

Plantain dries without any stinging sensation, even those parts that are not yet numb. For both the seed and the root are of similar power, although the seed thins [the humors] more effectively.

### FROM MACER’S HERBAL
<note>Macer Floridus is the pseudonym for the author of *De viribus herbarum*, a very popular medieval poem on the properties of herbs.</note>

They say, however, that the Greater [Plantain] 
Has greater power;
Which, with egg white <note>original: "lachryma," literally "tear," but used in medical recipes to mean the clear part of an egg or a plant's gummy exudate</note>, treats burns,
And it disperses cramps <note>original: "strophas," referring to twisting abdominal pains or colic</note> when crushed and applied with salt.
Cooked like a vegetable, it benefits those with dropsy <note>term: "hydropicis," people suffering from edema or fluid retention</note>.
Thus it helps the asthmatic, and it is said to help the falling-sick <note>a historical term for epileptics</note>,
And by this, ear pain shall be soothed.
Swelling is driven from the eyes by this [herb].

### EXPERIMENTAL HERBALISTS.

Arnoglossa <note>the Greek name for Plantain, meaning "lamb’s tongue"</note> strengthens the liver if it is applied externally as a compress <note>term: "epithimetur," an epitheme or local medicinal application</note> with endive water and white sugar.
<sig>B</sig>
It extinguishes "holy fire" <note>a common name for erysipelas, a painful skin infection</note> when mixed with the juice of Houseleek and vinegar.
It removes hemorrhoids when mixed with the powder of Cuckoo-pint <note>original: "Aron," the Arum maculatum</note> root.
And it cools all flesh that has been burned by fire.
It restrains the menstrual flow <note>stops excessive bleeding</note>.
It is also effective for those spitting blood <note>original: "hemopthoïcis"</note> and those suffering from ulceration of the lungs.
The root cooked with water and pellitory <note>original: "piretro," a root used to stimulate saliva and ease toothache</note> is effective for toothache if applied while warm.
The juice with vinegar is effective for clearing away spots and freckles.
For quartan fever <note>a malarial fever that recurs every four days</note>, it is used with theriac <note>term: "theriaca," a famous "universal" herbal jam or antidote containing dozens of ingredients</note> before the onset.
Both the seed and the root open the obstructed passages of the liver and kidneys.

### BENEFITS OF THE LESSER [PLANTAIN], FROM MACER.

The aforementioned Lesser Plantain can assist in all these things,
Although it may not seem to possess such great powers.

<header>VOLUME One.</header>

# Opinions of the Authors concerning HELLEBORE.
## Description of White Hellebore, according to DIOSCORIDES.

<margin>A</margin>
It bears leaves similar to those of Beet or Plantain, but shorter, darker, and reddish. The stem is hollow, about nine inches tall <note>original: "quadrantalem," a measure roughly the span of a hand</note>, and wrapped in layers like tunics when it begins to dry. It relies on many thin roots that emerge from an oblong head, fibrous in the manner of onions. It grows in mountains and rough places. The roots are to be gathered during the harvests. The best variety is white, easily crumbled, fleshy, and moderately long—yet not pointed like a Rush. When broken, it releases a fine dust and has a thin pith. To the taste, it is not excessively burning, nor does it immediately induce saliva. However, a specimen of this [inferior] kind causes a sensation of choking <note>original: "strangulat"</note>.

<gloss>Hellebore <note>original Greek: ἑλλέβ.</note></gloss>
### [Description] of the Black.

Its leaves are green, similar to those of the Plane-tree but smaller, very close to the leaves of Cow-Parsnip <note>original: "Sphondylij"</note>, somewhat rough, and cut with several divisions. The stem is rough, and the flowers are purple, clinging together in clusters. The seed is like that of the Safflower, which in Anticyra <note>A Greek city famous for its high-quality Hellebore</note> they call *Gesamoides*; it is used to move the bowels. It is attached to black, thin roots, fibrous and stemming from a small head like an onion; these roots are the part used in medicine.

<margin>Location.</margin>
It grows on hills and in rough, parched places.
<margin>Selection.</margin>
The best is that which is sought from Anticyra. It should be chosen for being thick and full, with a thin pith, and it should be sharp and burning to the taste.

## Concerning the discoverer and demonstrator, from PLINY.

MELAMPUS is famous for his arts of divination. They say the plant called Black Hellebore was named after him <note>The Greek name for Black Hellebore is sometimes "Melampodium"</note>. Others relate that a shepherd of the same name discovered it when he noticed that his goats were purged after grazing on it. By administering their milk, he is said to have healed the raving daughters of King Proetus in their presence.

<margin>B</margin>
## Time of Collection for the WHITE.

They say the White Hellebore is ready for harvest during the summer harvests. However, it is not easily gathered. Indeed, it causes a heavy feeling in the head <note>likely referring to toxic fumes or intense scent</note> unless garlic is eaten beforehand, wine is sipped occasionally, and the plant is dug up quickly.

### The Superstitious Collection of the Black, from
## THEOPHRASTUS.

The Black Hellebore is collected with a solemn preparation and a certain religious ritual, as Theophrastus says. First, it was circled with a sword. Then, the person about to cut it looks toward the east and prays for a good omen—that he might be permitted to do this by the gods, specifically Apollo and Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine</note>. Finally, he observes the flight of the eagle. For an eagle was usually present during the cutting; if it flew too close, it was an omen that the person who cut the plant would die within that year. Finally, it was extracted, and the inner pith was removed just as it is from the White.

## THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO.

The Black Hellebore purges the "melancholic humor" <note>Black bile, associated with depression and madness</note> primarily through the lower belly <note>as a laxative</note>. The White, however, expels thick and sticky humors through the upper belly <note>as an emetic, causing vomiting</note>.
Occasionally, horses, oxen, and pigs avoid the Black variety, even though they may eat the White with impunity. Nevertheless, the White is said to be more violent in its effects than the Black.
The seeds of both are very pleasing to quails, as Aristotle writes.

<margin>C</margin> The reason why the ancients condemned these for use at the table is now being investigated.

->Potency of **WHITE HELLEBORE**.<-

They say the power of the White variety lasts for thirty years.

->The Qualitative Nature of Both.<-

It possesses the power of cleansing and warming, which is why it is placed in the "third order" of substances that heat and dry <note>In ancient medicine, drugs were categorized by four degrees of intensity; the third order indicates a very strong effect</note>.

->Preparation and Administration.<-

The ancients chose the meatiest bark and the root so that the thinner pith could be removed. They covered this pith with moist sponges, and when it swelled, they split it lengthwise. Then they dried the fibers in the shade for use. Now, they give the small branches themselves from the root, which has a very heavy bark. It is also kneaded into bread and roasted. Some offer it in a broth of porridge or spelt. Some give it after a small amount of food has been eaten previously.

Mesue <note>A famous Persian physician, likely Mesue the Younger</note> believes it should be corrected in this way: namely, that it should first be macerated in honey and raisins, or in the broth of chickens and other meats, and then the root itself should be discarded.

There are those who, having hollowed out a radish root, insert Hellebore for a day and then pull it out again; they say the radish then possesses the power of purging the bowels.

Others infuse it in oxymel <note>A mixture of honey and vinegar</note>, or sweet wine, or syrups, or "rob" <note>original: "robob," a thickened fruit juice concentrate</note> as they call it, and administer it thereafter. Perhaps a small amount of barley or rice is also added.

Its operation is strengthened by Indian salt, Epithyme <note>Dodder of thyme</note>, and Polypody fern. It is also balanced by Wild Carrot, Parsley, Long Pepper, Hyssop, Calamint, and Oregano.

<margin>D</margin>
->Powers and Benefits of **WHITE HELLEBORE** according to **DIOSCORIDES**.<-

It purges by inducing vomiting, drawing out diverse and manifold substances.
It is mixed into eye-salves which can clear away obstructions to the clarity of the eyes.
It likewise draws out the menstrual flow.
It kills the fetus in the womb.
It provokes sneezing.
Furthermore, when soaked in honey with pearled barley, it kills mice.
When cooked with meats, it reduces them <note>suggesting it acts as a tenderizer or breaks down the fibers</note>.
It is given to those who are fasting, either by itself or with Sesame, or juice of the Thapsia plant, or spelt, or honey-water, or porridge, or lentils, or some other broth.
It is also kneaded into bread and roasted.

Its measurement and dispensing were handed down by those whose primary study was to teach concerning it. For some give White Hellebore <note>original: "Veratrum album"</note> in a broth of porridge or spelt. Some give it after a little food has been provided, especially to those in whom a suspected or feared choking <note>original: "strangulatio"</note> or weakness of the body might cause an impediment. For the purging is completed more safely this way, because it does not come upon the body at an inopportune time.

Even when applied to the seat <note>the rectum</note> as suppositories <note>original: "balani," literally "acorns"</note> with vinegar, they cause vomiting.
It is also used for old suppurations <note>internal collections of pus</note>.
By the same means, lice infestations <note>original: "phthiriasis"</note> are cured.
Likewise, it treats scabies, skin eruptions <note>original: "impetigo"</note>, and hardened ulcers <note>original: "fistula callosa"</note>.

<margin>A</margin>
When boiled in vinegar and used as a mouthwash, it soothes toothaches. 
Flies are also killed by it if it is soaked in milk. 
It cures the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>, vertigo, melancholy, insanity, those possessed by delusions <note>original: "limphaticis"</note>, those with gout, those in the early stages of dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note>, those with bloating <note>original: "tympaniticis"</note>, stomach ailments, spasms, those confined to bed, those with sciatica, white elephantiasis <note>a severe skin disease or form of leprosy</note>, leprosies, tetanus, tremors, and quartan fevers <note>fevers that return every four days, often associated with malaria</note> which do not otherwise cease, as well as chronic coughs with inflammation and recurring abdominal pains. 
The Gauls, as Pliny says, dip their arrows in Hellebore when hunting; they claim that if the area around the wound is cut away, the meat is found to be more tender.

### RAZES <note>Abū Bakr al-Rāzī, a 10th-century Persian physician and philosopher</note>

Black Hellebore cures "black bile" <note>one of the four humors thought to cause melancholy</note>. 
The White variety induces vomiting. 
However, drinking it directly is not safe.

### The Benefits of BLACK HELLEBORE from Pliny and Dioscorides.

It is beneficial for those with epilepsy, melancholy, insanity, joint pains, and paralysis. 
It draws out various types of bile and phlegm through the bowels. 
By drinking the decoction, dimness of vision is driven away. 
It ripens and cleanses suppurating hardnesses when a poultice <note>term: cataplasm — a soft, moist mass of material, typically of plant affairs or flour, applied to the body to relieve soreness and inflammation</note> is made from it.

<margin>B</margin>
It restores hearing if it is placed in deaf ears and removed after two or three days. 
Poultices made from it remove spots, leprosies, scabs, and finally all skin eruptions. 
It even heals the itch: for this use, it is applied as an ointment with frankincense, wax, pitch, and cedar oil. 
When applied by itself like a plaster with vinegar, it corrects skin discolorations, eruptions, and leprosies. 
It purges the upper stomach, drawing out phlegm and bile: it is given either by itself or with scammony <note>term: scammony — a purgative resin obtained from the root of Convolvulus scammonia</note> and salt, in the weight of a drachma <note>about 4 grams</note> or three obols <note>about 1.5 grams</note>. 
Vinegar in which Hellebore has been boiled, when held in the mouth for a long time, soothes pain. 
It is mixed into all plasters used for eating away <note>corrosive or caustic</note> tissue. 
Against water gathering under the skin <note>edema</note>, it is usefully applied as a plaster with barley flour and wine. 
It is planted at the roots of grapevines, and a wine is made from them which is used for purging. 
It draws out the menstrual flow when applied as a suppository. 
It kills the fetus in the womb. 
It cleanses fistulas <note>abnormal passages in the body</note> when inserted and removed after the third day.

### The Benefits of Black from MESUE <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a Christian physician in Baghdad</note>.

We have said that the White variety should be avoided because it causes suffocation, but the Black variety ought to be taken, as all authorities agree—and specifically when prepared correctly according to the medical art. It is suitable only for those with strong constitutions <note>original: "animosis corporibus"</note>, and only in the springtime. 
Therefore, when it is given at the right time and to the right person, it causes them to revive and restores a balanced constitution. For this is its property according to Hippocrates. And...

<header>SIMPLE MEDICINES</header>

<margin>C</margin> It truly cleanses the whole body and every individual limb, and through purging <note>original: "solutione"</note> it easily draws out bile mixed with phlegm <note>In the theory of the four humors, bile and phlegm were bodily fluids that caused illness if unbalanced</note>. It also purifies the blood. It draws out superfluities <note>excess or waste fluids</note> mixed with the blood from the veins—indeed, from the entire body, from the cavities of the limbs, and from any remote parts. It is among the most celebrated substances for cleansing the brain and the entire head, as well as the organs of the senses, the nerves, and the internal organs, along with the bladder and the womb. It brings manifest relief to their ailments, such as headache <note>original: "sedę," likely a variant of "soda," a term for a heavy headache</note>, migraines <note>original: "hemocraneæ"</note>, mania, melancholy, vertigo, epilepsy, and paralysis. It is likewise used for abscesses of the limbs, scrofula <note>a swelling of the lymph nodes, often tubercular</note>, cancer, and shingles <note>original: "herpeti"</note>. Vinegar from its decoction may be dripped into the ear; it helps with ringing and whistling in the ears and strengthens the hearing. It is beneficial for ailments of the spleen and for ancient, long-lasting fevers, such as quartan fever <note>a fever that recurs every four days</note>, and for bile-induced or melancholic fevers that are difficult to eradicate. It also provokes the flow of urine and menstruation. Frequent use of it even brings a healthy color to the body, purifies the skin, and wipes away every kind of mange or scab.

->Regarding the purging of VERATRUM <note>The Latin name for Hellebore</note>, or Helleborism, Hippo-<-
->crates to the philosopher Democritus.<-

<margin>D</margin> THOSE who are not easily purged through the upper parts <note>i.e., by vomiting</note> should soften their bodies with much food and rest before taking the potion. However, when they have drunk the Veratrum, they should move their bodies more and stay awake. That agitation and movement disturb and stir the body is demonstrated by the experience of sailing <note>referring to seasickness</note>. When you wish the Veratrum to act more powerfully and purge more thoroughly, move the body more. However, Veratrum is dangerous for those who have healthy flesh. Furthermore, it is dangerous for those who do not feel thirst after the purging potion. A spasm occurring after taking Veratrum is fatal. If such spasms occur during a great purging, it is a bad sign. If they are purged through movements of the belly, and through purgings and vomitings that happen naturally as they ought, it is beneficial and they bear it easily; if not, the opposite is true. Furthermore, as we said in the *Prognostics* <note>A famous medical work by Hippocrates</note>, an upper purging is suitable for those who reject food without having a fever, who suffer twinges or shocks, whose vision is dim, or whose mouth is distressed by bitterness. To speak briefly and generally: it is beneficial for all pains located above the midriff <note>term: praecordia — the region of the body around the heart and diaphragm</note>. It purges through the lower parts, however, when griping pains distress them without fever, or when there is pain in the loins, heaviness of the knees, when the menses do not flow easily, or when pains are below the diaphragm. When you provide the potion in this way, be very cautious and observant of city-dwellers, the idle, and those of a lazy constitution; especially those of a dark complexion, those having moist or somewhat dry flesh, and those who stutter or lisp. Those who strive to disperse and dissolve phlegmatic humors through a potion at the very beginning of a disease gain nothing while the phlegm is increasing, just as we said in the booklet on barley-water <note>term: pitisana — a medicinal porridge or drink made from barley</note>. For when a disease is "raw" <note>undigested or in its early, acute stage</note>, it yields to nothing. Indeed, those things which resist the disease and are life-saving waste away. For if the body is weakened, the disease triumphs and makes the sick incurable. Give Veratrum or Helleborism to those from whose head a rheum <note>a watery discharge</note> drips, or to those who are purulent, or of a sickly color; but not to those who are becoming hoarse <note>original: "raucescentibus"</note>, nor those with spleen ailments, nor those suffering from snakebites, nor those laboring under windiness <note>flatulence or gas</note>, nor...

<meta>The text cuts off with the catchword "centibus," which completes the word "raucescentibus" (becoming hoarse) from the final line.</meta>

Volume One. 35

<margin>A</margin> For those with a dry cough, nor for those prone to thirst, nor for those troubled by pain in the belly, nor those with a distended stomach, nor with the precordia <term>the region over the heart or upper stomach</term>, the flanks, or the shoulder blades distended or suffering from pain in the side; nor for the listless, nor those with dim vision, nor those suffering from ringing in the ears, nor those unable to hold their urine, nor those with jaundice <term>original: "arcuatis," literally "the rainbow disease" due to skin discoloration</term>, nor those with a weak stomach or gullet, nor those with tumors <note>original: "ficosis," referring to fig-like growths or hemorrhoids</note>, nor those prone to boils. 

But if it seems fit to purge with Veratrum <note>White Hellebore</note>, you shall purge more safely through the upper parts <note>by inducing vomiting</note>, but by the lower parts <note>as a laxative</note> least of all: these patients you shall nourish and replenish with hearty foods. As we had said in the *Prognostics* <note>original: "predictorio," likely referring to the Hippocratic work</note>, do not give the potion to those who have an aversion to food, those who vomit black bile, or those who are delirious. For those who sleep little due to pain, who have bold and wide-open eyes, or eyes that are rolled back or twisted, swollen, clouded, of a bad color or variegated, and for those burning with fever and exhausted: as we said in the little book on *Ptisana* <note>barley water</note>, sesamoid <note>likely *Reseda phyteuma* or a similar purgative plant</note> mixed with sesame purges conveniently through the upper parts. 

The dose for the drink is one drachm <term>a unit of weight, roughly 3.5 grams</term>, or half of that, with honeyed vinegar; mix a third part of this with Veratrum, and it is less likely to cause choking or strangulation <note>a common and dangerous side effect of Hellebore overdose</note>. This also clears up long-lasting quartan fevers <note>fevers recurring every four days</note>, and helps those troubled by long and tiresome fevers, and those who do not feel thirst nor cough up phlegm—treat these not before three weeks <note>original: "tria trinudina," a Roman period of three market-intervals</note>—and sometimes those suffering from pain in the sides or from intestinal blockage <term>original: "conuoluulo," a twisting of the intestines</term>. Furthermore, as we said in the books on the *Diseases of Women*, if the womb <note>original: "locelli," literally "little places" or compartments</note> requires cleansing, then cleanse it.

## H A R M F V L &nbsp; E F F E C T S .

<margin>B</margin> White Hellebore is more violent than Black. For this reason, it is not in common use today. Even in former times, it was denied to the elderly, children, women, the weak, the envious <note>or those with a sensitive/grudging constitution</note>, and those whose internal organs were ulcerated. Likewise, it was refused to those coughing up blood, or those suffering in their sides or throats.

> Black [Hellebore] kills dogs, mice, and pigs,
> And the dung itself kills chickens that drink it.

## S V B S T I T V T I O N

In its place today, they commonly use Scammony <note>a strong purgative resin derived from a species of bindweed</note>.

## D O S A G E

Themison used to give two drachms, no more. Those following him gave as many as four, with the famous praise of Herophilus, who compared Hellebore to a very brave general: for once everything inside has been stirred up, he himself is the first to exit. 

Macer says: "It seems to me that Pliny signifies that only half the weight of White Hellebore should be given, that is, because one drachm or two scruples <term>a smaller unit of weight</term> is the dose of Black, the dose of White should be half." Mesue <note>an influential 9th-century Persian physician</note> says otherwise. Its dose, he says, is from six grains <note>original: "charitis," likely referring to carats or grains</note> up to a third of a drachm, or even up to one full drachm.

### White Water-Lily <note>original: "Nymphaea alba"</note>

This plate illustrates the White Water-Lily in full anatomical detail, demonstrating the scientific precision of early modern herbals. C

## ON THE WATER LILY,
### Third Rhapsody.
<note>The term 'Rhapsody' here refers to a collected volume or a miscellaneous grouping of botanical writings.</note>

->NAMES OF THE WHITE VARIETY<-

Greek: Nymphaia <note>original: "νυμφαια"</note>
Latin: Nenuphar, Venus’s Nail, Venus’s Finger, Marsh Algae, Marsh Poppy.
German: **Hay-root / Cabbage-root / Lake-flower / Hair-string.** <note>original German: "Howurtz / Kollerwurtz / Seeblüm / Horstrang." These are archaic folk names for the water lily.</note>

->The Origin of the Name.<-

**N**enuphar is said to have been born, as Pliny writes, from a nymph who died of jealousy regarding Hercules. For this reason, some call it *Heraclion* <note>meaning 'the plant of Hercules'</note>. Others call it *Rhopalo* <note>from the Greek word for 'club'</note> because the root resembles a club. Or, as Dioscorides prefers, it seems to have claimed the name *Nymphaea* because it loves watery places. Indeed, it is found most abundantly in Elis, in the Anigrus river, and in Haliartus in Boeotia.

->Its Kinds according to DIOSCORIDES.<-

It is of two kinds. One has a black root, the other a white root. One has a white flower, and the other a yellow flower.

->APPEARANCE OF THE WHITE VARIETY.<-

<margin>D</margin> The leaves are broad, emerging somewhat above the water; they are solid, tough, leathery, and strong-smelling. Sometimes, however, they are even found under the water, with many springing from a single root. The flower is pure white, similar to a Lily, having in the center what appears to be saffron <note>referring to the yellow stamens</note>. After it has finished blooming, the fruit is round, and in its roundness resembles an apple or a poppy head, and is black in color. The root is large, rough, and knotted like a club.

->LOCATION.<-

It grows in swamps and stagnant waters.

->TIME.<-

It is dug up in Autumn.

->The Opinion of THEOPHRASTUS (Book 9, Chapter 13) on the Nymphaea.<-

**R**oot differences can be perceived both by their juices and their odors. Some are sharp, others bitter, others sweet; some are sweet-smelling, others more pleasant. The so-called "Sweet Nymphaea" usually grows in lakes, such as in the fields of Ormenium, at Marathon, and on the island of Crete. The Boeotians call this *Madonaim* and eat the fruit. It bears large leaves on top of the water.

->PLINY on the Nymphaea.<-

The Nymphaea grows in watery places, with large leaves on the surface of the water and others emerging from the root; the flower is like a Lily, and when it has finished blooming, it has a head like a Poppy. It is cut at the stalk in autumn. The black root is dried in the sun and is effective against diarrhea <note>original: "aduersaturq; aluinis," literally "opposes the bowels"</note>. There is also another Nymphaea in Thessaly, in the Peneus river, with a white root and a yellow head, the size of a Rose.

->The Opinion of APULEIUS on the Nymphaea (Chapter 68).<-

In Greek it is called *Nymphaia*, *Cacabon*, *Lothonietram*, or *Rhopalon*; others call it *Androgomos*, others *Hydrogogos*, others *Heracleos*. The Latins have called it Hercules' Mother, Marsh Algae, Marsh Poppy, Venus's Nail, and Venus's Finger.

# SIMPLE Medicines

<margin>C</margin> It is similar to the flowers of violets, but is colder and moister than them; it is beneficial for hot headaches <note>original: "sodæ calidæ"</note> and induces sleep, especially its oil. When applied over hot abscesses, it is helpful.

->FROM PLATEARIUS<-
<note>Matthaeus Platearius was a 12th-century physician from the famous medical school at Salerno</note>

Collected in September, it retains its great efficacy for two years. The flower found in hot regions is better than that which is found in cold ones.

A syrup is made from its flowers, which is used in acute fevers and for an overheated liver.

Against headaches caused by heat, the Saracens <note>A term used by medieval writers to refer to Arab or Muslim physicians</note> place the flowers in water overnight and drink that water and the flowers in the morning, or apply them to the nostrils.

->FROM GIOVANNI DI VIGO<-
<note>A famous 16th-century Italian surgeon to the Pope</note>

The water lily <note>original: "Nenufar"</note> is of a cold and moist temperament in the second degree. Therefore, its flower boiled in violet oil, unripe olive oil <note>original: "oleo omphacino"</note>, and a little pomegranate wine until the wine has evaporated, extinguishes erysipelas <note>a painful, red skin infection</note>.

->FROM AVICENNA on the powers of the heart<-
<note>Avicenna, or Ibn Sina, was a Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries</note>

The water lily is close to Camphor in its effects, except that it is moister. Its moisture causes a certain laziness and sluggishness in the substance of the spirit <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to the subtle vital force that flows through the nerves and brain</note> that exists in the brain, unless it requires moistening to be balanced. However, the spirit in the heart does not seem to suffer this harm that the brain suffers; rather, it provides a strong benefit. For the property of its aromatic scent strengthens the spirit which is in the heart. The harm from its coldness and moisture is only relative. It is balanced with saffron and cinnamon.

<margin>D</margin> ->HARMFUL EFFECTS<-

Pliny is the authority for the claim that those who drink it for twelve days are deprived of sexual desire and the ability to procreate; it is said to nourish the body and the voice instead. However, it is also written by Avicenna among those things which strengthen the heart.

# ON HORSE-HOOF,
# Fourth Rhapsody.

->NOMENCLATURE<-

Greek: *arktion* <note>ἄρκτιον</note>.
Latin: *Personatia*, *Lappa* <note>Burr or Burdock</note>, *Vngula caballina* <note>Horse-hoof</note>.
German: **Roſſzhub** <note>Modern German: Huflattich</note>.

->OPINIONS OF THE AUTHORS<-

### The Opinion of DIOSCORIDES, on the Mask-Plant. <note>original: "de Personata"</note>

It has leaves even larger than those of a gourd, and they are hairier, darker, and thicker, with a whitish stem. Sometimes, however, it is found without a stem, with a root that is white on the inside and black on the outside.

### The Opinion of PLINY on the Mask-Plant.

<margin>Pliny’s Error regarding the Mask-Plant.</margin>
Some call the plant *Arcion* by the name *Personata* <note>The "Mask-Plant"</note>, which has the widest of all leaves and bears large burrs.

### THE DECREE OF HERMOLAUS BARBARUS in the Corollary on the Mask-Plant.

<sig>D</sig>
<margin>
Butterbur <note>Petasite</note>
Burdock <note>Bardana</note>
Book 25, chapter 9.
*Perfolata*.
*Perfoluta*.
*Perfolyton*.
*Persona* <note>Mask</note>.
</margin>
*Arcion*, or *Prosopites*, sounds like *Personata* in Latin, yet it is taken for Butterbur <note>Petasite</note> by Pliny, who says that no leaf is wider than that of the Mask-plant <note>original: "Personatæ"</note> and that it bears large burrs <note>original: "lappas"</note>, which we see not on the *Arctium* <note>Coltsfoot</note>, but on the Butterbur. I interpret Butterbur as that which is commonly called Burdock <note>Bardana</note> and Great Burdock; whereas *Arction* is that which is called Horse-hoof <note>Vngula caballina</note>. Pliny established a thin distinction in the name by calling Butterbur "*Personata*" and calling *Arction* "*Perfolata*." He says that *Perfolata*, which everyone knows and the Greeks call *Arction*, has leaves even larger than gourds, hairier, darker, and thicker, with a white and large root. Almost all of these features agree with Dioscorides' *Arction*. Pliny also mentions *Perfoluta* or *Perfolyton*, a type of Egyptian herb usually sown in gardens for making wreaths; there are two kinds, male and female, and it is said that when placed under a man, it hinders his sexual desire by greatly cooling it <note>original: "Venerem uirorum maxime prodendo"</note>. I would remind the reader that the leaves of the Mask-plant (that is, Butterbur and Burdock) are larger than those of *Perfolata* (that is, *Arction* and Horse-hoof). The root of the Mask-plant is white, a finger's width thick, and has a loathsome smell; the root of *Perfolata* is the thickness of an arm and is fragrant, with a purple flower on a spike. Galen calls both this one and the former by the same name, *Arction*. However, I do not doubt that this is the same plant Lucius Columella writes is called *Persona* <note>Mask</note>, because he records it is useful for cattle bitten by a viper when placed over the scarification—a fact Pliny also proves; for that reason, some report it is called *Echion*, as if it were the "Viper-plant."

### The Inscription of Marcellus Vergilius on the Mask-Plant.

In former times, they used this Mask-plant throughout Greece and Italy to make masks <note>original: "perſonas"</note> whenever they wanted to perform in theaters or other places where they did not wish to be recognized by the people. These masks were easily prepared from plants gathered from uncultivated and fertile places, though they were not available all year round. It was most frequent in the months of May and June...

<meta>This page continues the botanical discussion of the Mask-plant (Personata), transitioning from its physical description to a scholarly debate—a "calumny" and an "apology"—regarding the plant's identification in the works of Pliny the Elder, as critiqued by the Renaissance scholar Niccolò Leoniceno and defended by Pandolfo Collenuccio.</meta>

<header>VOLUME First.</header>

<margin>A</margin>
At the festivals of the Parilia and Floralia <note>Parilia and Floralia were ancient Roman festivals; the former celebrated the founding of Rome and the latter honored Flora, the goddess of flowers and spring</note>, it is likely that they used three plucked leaves: one to cover the forehead and two others to cover the cheeks on either side, leaving open spaces between them for the passages of seeing, breathing, and speaking. For the size of the Mask-plant <note>original: "Personatæ"</note> leaves is so great that a space much larger than a human face can be covered by three of them. Nor did he undeservedly compare these to the leaves of gourds, for their shape corresponds to them. If they grow in a richer soil, they even surpass them in size. This is also the reason why the Greeks, from the same use for masks <note>original: "personarum"</note>, called it *Prosopis* <note>original: "Prosopida"</note> and *Prosopion* <note>Greek terms related to 'prosopon', meaning face or mask</note>. <margin>Why the Mask-plant is called a Burr <note>original: "Personacia, quare Lappa dicta"</note>.</margin> It is called a Burr <note>original: "Lappa"</note> because it is of the same kind. The Mask-plant grows everywhere, and since Christians have ceased to use it for masks for the reason we mentioned, and it has no other uses for health, it is now little known by this name.

### THE CRITIQUE OF PLINY’S OPINION regarding the Mask-plant, by Niccolò Leoniceno in his book on the Errors of Doctors.

But our business now is not with Avicenna, but with Pliny; therefore, let us return to him. In Book 25, regarding *Arctium*—though I believe it reads *Echion* <note>Leoniceno suggests 'Echion' is a scribal error for 'Arctium' in the ancient manuscripts</note> due to an error in the manuscript—he writes as follows: "Some call *Arctium* the Mask-plant <note>original: "Personaciam"</note>." Not many lines below, Pliny writes: "The Mask-plant, which no one is ignorant of." Although previously and here it is incorrectly written as *Persolacia* or *Persolata*, what follows proves that it should be read as *Personacia*. For he adds: "The Greeks call it *Arctium*; it has leaves even larger than gourds, hairier, darker, and thicker, with a large white root." This is drunk in wine, <margin>B</margin> at a weight of two denarii <note>A Roman silver coin used here as a unit of weight, roughly 3.4 grams or 1/24th of an ounce</note>. Indeed, he seems to have thought there were two kinds of *Arctium*, both of which were called the Mask-plant: one to be drunk in vinegar against serpents, the other in wine. However, Dioscorides, Galen, and Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note> wrote of only one *Arctium*, *Prosopite*, or Mask-plant. That it is indeed the same *Arctium*, or the same Mask-plant, which Pliny describes in the first and second place, is most clearly shown by Pliny’s own words. For of the first he writes: "Some call *Arctium* the Mask-plant, of which no leaf is wider, bearing large burrs <note>original: "lappas"</note>." Here, Pliny undoubtedly hints at that which is called by our people both *Bardana* and Great Burdock <note>original: "Lappa maior"</note>. The ancients called it the Mask-plant <note>original: "Personatã"</note> because, due to the breadth of its leaves, they used it to make masks <note>original: "Personatos"</note>. This same plant, for the same reason, was called *Prosopite* (that is, Mask-plant) by Dioscorides, Galen, and Paul, who recorded that it consists of leaves like gourds, though darker and hairier.

### THE APOLOGY OF PANDOLFO COLLENUCCIO for Pliny, against Leoniceno.

Do you wish to see another argument from an unobservant man concerning the Mask-plant? He censures Pliny because he believed it to be two-fold. Yet, to prove that this is true, so that nothing is left intact for Pliny’s defense, he says for no reason that *Echion* was placed instead of *Arctium* by a fault of the manuscript. But he understands neither Pliny nor himself in this way, which you will soon recognize to be true. After Ar...
