<meta>This page continues the scholarly defense of Pliny the Elder against the criticisms of Niccolò Leoniceno. The previous page discussed the physical characteristics of the Mask-plant (Personata) and its large leaves used for masks; this page focuses on distinguishing it from the Viper-herb (Echion) and clarifying Pliny's botanical classifications.</meta>

# THE MEDICINES OF THE SIMPLES

<margin>C</margin> Immediately following the description of the agaric mushroom <note>original: "Agarici"</note>, Pliny added the Viper-herb <note>original: "Echion"</note> in his twenty-fifth volume. Because this plant has small heads similar to vipers, it is therefore named *Echios*, as if it were called "the viper-like." He describes two kinds of this plant, similar to Pennyroyal <note>original: "Pulegio"</note>, crowned with flowers. He depicts a third kind distinguished by prickly down. He adds, moreover, that some call the Viper-herb the "Mask-plant" <note>original: "Personatam"</note> (and not *Arction*, as Nicolaus <note>Niccolò Leoniceno</note> perversely wished to suggest); however, Pliny then rejects their opinion because of the great difference in the leaves and the flower. Of this Mask-plant, he says no leaf is <margin>What the true Viper-herb is.</margin> wider, and it bears large burrs. It is as if he were saying: "We have said there are three kinds of Viper-herb similar to Pennyroyal, which has small leaves and is crowned with flowers. Those are mistaken who say that the Viper-herb is the Mask-plant, which bears large burrs and has the widest leaves of all; for all these features differ greatly from the likeness of Pennyroyal." Leoniceno, hasty in his biting criticism, did not understand Pliny’s words, which appropriately rejected the opinion of those who said the Viper-herb was the Mask-plant. For in that section where Pliny wrote, "Of which [plant] no leaf is wider," Leoniceno referred that "of which" to the Viper-herb, and not to the Mask-plant, as Pliny and the rules of grammar required. Nor indeed did Pliny believe there were two kinds of Mask-plant simply because he wrote that some people call the Viper-herb the "Mask-plant" and give the root in vinegar. For here he was not dealing with the Mask-plant, but with the Viper-herb; and so that he might reveal whatever he had found written by other authors, he wrote that some call the Viper-herb "the mask-plant" and give it in vinegar. For it does not follow logically (as we have often said) that "Certain people say this, therefore Pliny believed it"—especially since he depicted the Viper-herb as being of three kinds and clearly perceived, from the difference in the leaves and <margin>D</margin> flowers, that the Mask-plant was not the Viper-herb. Therefore, after a few lines, he speaks specifically not about the Viper-herb, but about the very well-known Mask-plant, calling it by both its Greek and Latin names, *Arction* and *Personata*. He said that no one is ignorant of it, clearly so that he might also rebuke those who previously thought the Viper-herb, a plant with small leaves, was the Mask-plant, which consists of the broadest leaves. Thus, everything fits together well. Let Nicolaus know hereafter that Pliny explained this most elegantly in this passage and believed that the Viper-herb, similar to Pennyroyal, is one thing, and the Mask-plant, with leaves larger than a gourd, is another—though some have thought them to be the same herb.

But since the subject of *Arction* <note>Burdock</note> has arisen, and because we write both for Pliny's sake and for students—so that those reading our works (however small they may be) may always seize upon something they can apply to the common good (which we have taken care to do in passing throughout this entire defense as much as we could, though Leoniceno avoided it)—it seemed right to add this: the Greeks have handed down that *Arction* is of two kinds. One, indeed, which is also called *Arcturion*; they said its <margin>*Arction* is two-fold.</margin> leaves are similar to *Phlomos* (which we call Mullein <note>original: "Verbascum"</note> in Latin), yet <margin>Mullein is another species of the Mask-plant.</margin> thicker and rounder. Its seed is similar to tiny cumin, and they said both the seed and the root are effectively given to those suffering from sciatica <note>original: "Ischiadics"</note> and difficulty urinating <note>original: "dysuriam"</note>. The other kind they call *Arction*, *Prosopiten*, *Prosopion*, and *Aparine*; we call it the Mask-plant and the Burr <note>original: "Lappam"</note>, which we have already discussed. Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> depicted both in his fourth book; Pliny recorded the first in his twenty-seventh volume, and the other in the book we have mentioned.

It also details the two Greek varieties of Arction, identifying one as similar to Mullein and the other as the common Burr.</summary>

<margin>A What Cleavers is:</margin>

### The Opinion of S I M O N O F G E N O A regarding
## Horse-hoof.

<margin>I suspect it should read: Burdock <note>original: "Bardana"</note>.</margin>
Horse-hoof <note>original: "Vngula Caballina"</note>, also called Coltsfoot <note>original: "Farfara"</note>, or as some say, *Dardana*, has two species. The smaller kind grows in fields, dry places, and vineyards. The other, larger kind, is always found at the water's edge; it has a larger leaf with less distinct angles, and its small root is fragrant—some call this the "little vessel of the heart" <note>original: "Cassula cordis"</note>.

### The same author on the M A S K - P L A N T.

<margin>Dronega:</margin>
The Mask-plant <note>original: "Personatia"</note>, he says, is used in the preparation of the lesser Mithridatum <note>An ancient "universal" antidote and tonic named after King Mithridates VI of Pontus</note>. It is explained in the ancient lists of synonyms as being Burdock <note>original: "Bardana"</note>, Great Burdock <note>original: "Lappa major"</note>, or *Dronega*. This is also what Pliny seems to say; he states that the Mask-plant is called *Echion* by some, and that no leaf is wider than its own, bearing large burrs. But *Echios* <note>Viper-herb</note> is a different plant entirely.

### The Opinion of the A U T H O R O F T H E P A N D E C T S <note>Matthaeus Silvaticus, a 14th-century botanical encyclopedist</note>

In the *Antidotarium* <note>A book of prepared medicines</note>, the Mask-plant used in the composition of the lesser Mithridatum is explained in ancient synonyms as being Great Burdock, *Bardana*, *Dronega*, and *Persolita*.

<margin>Coltsfoot is a species of Horse-hoof according to Matthaeus Silvaticus:</margin>
Regarding Horse-hoof, Galen writes thus in the sixth book of *On Simples*, in the chapter on Coltsfoot <note>original: "Tussilagine"</note>: It is Horse-hoof, or "earthy water-lily" <note>original: "Nenuphar terrenum"</note>, or *Farfara*. However, it is named *Tussilago* <note>from "tussis," meaning cough</note> because it is believed to help those with a cough and those suffering from shortness of breath <note>original: "orthopnoicis"</note>.

<margin>B Mullein and Ground-white:</margin>
And again: Coltsfoot, *Chamaeleuce* <note>Ground-white</note>, and Horse-hoof are species of Mullein <note>original: "Tapsus barbatus"</note>.

### Our J U D G M E N T.

It appears clearly that both Simon of Genoa and the writer of the *Pandects* were ignorant of the true Horse-hoof, having been misled by Pliny, who in some places calls the Burdock a "Mask-plant." Nor do I believe they have read Dioscorides’ description of *Arction*. To me, in such an obvious matter, it seems we torment ourselves needlessly, since the description of *Arction* in Dioscorides fits Horse-hoof perfectly <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail," meaning precisely</note>. The "Barbarian" <note>Likely referring to the scholar Hermolao Barbaro, who worked to "purify" classical texts from medieval errors</note> agrees with us, being a man of very sharp judgment himself. As for Pliny’s role in this, let Collinucius <note>Pandolfo Collenuccio, a scholar who defended Pliny against certain critics</note> see to that.

### Benefits according to D I O S C O R I D E S.

Taken in the weight of one drachm with pine nuts, it helps those coughing up pus.

Crushed and applied with tight bandages, it soothes pains in the joints.

The leaves are usefully applied to old ulcers.

### From A P U L E I V S <note>Referring to the "Herbarium" of Pseudo-Apuleius</note>.

The juice of the Mask-plant herb, given in a drink with old wine, miraculously heals all bites of serpents or snakes.

Likewise, if you wrap the leaves around someone suffering from a fever, it drives the fever away.

As for a wound, even if it becomes cancerous, bathe it with the water of the Mask-plant herb. Then grind the herb itself with soda, lard, and a little pitch with vinegar, and in a cloth...

# ON THE BIRTHWORTS
## Fifth Rhapsody.

### ¶ Nomenclature of the Round Birthwort.
In Greek, *aristolochia strongyle* <note>original: "αριστολοχία στρογγύλη"</note>.
In Latin, *Aristolochia*.
In German, **Hollow-root / Beaver-root / Deer-herb.** <note>original: "Holwurtz / Biberwurtz / Hinſchkrut"</note>

### ¶ Nomenclature of the Long or Greater Birthwort.
In Greek, *long aristolochia, finger-herb, apple-fruit, teuxinon*. <note>original: "μακρὰ ἀριστολοχία, δακτυλίτις, μελόκαρπον, τευξίνον"</note>
In Latin, *Aristolochia longa*.
In German, **The long Hollow-root.** <note>original: "Holwurtz die lang"</note>

# OPINIONS OF THE AUTHORS ON THE BIRTHWORTS.
## ¶ The opinion of DIOSCORIDIS on Round Birthwort.

Round Birthwort <term>Aristolochia</term> <note>The name comes from the Greek "aristos" (best) and "lochia" (childbirth), reflecting its ancient use in aiding labor.</note> adopted its name from the fact that it is thought to be the best aid for women in childbirth. Three types are handed down to us. One is called the female; it has ivy-like leaves, an excellent but sharp scent, and soft, somewhat round leaves. Many sprouts come from a single root with very long shoots. The flower is white, shaped like a small red cap, and has a heavy smell.

## ¶ The same author [DIOSCORIDES] on Long Birthwort.

Long Birthwort, the male, is called *Dactylitis* <note>original: "Dactylitis"; meaning "finger-like," referring to the shape of the root.</note> by some. It has a longer leaf than the round variety, with thin branches about nine inches <note>original: "dodrantalibus"</note> long. The flower is purple and heavy-smelling; as it withers, it takes on the shape of a pear. The tubers of the roots are round, like a turnip. However, the root of the Long variety is the thickness of a finger and reaches the length of a palm. Sometimes it grows a little larger. Both are the color of boxwood on the inside, with a bitter and heavy taste. <margin>Climbing Birthwort <note>original: "Ariſtolochia Clematitis"</note></margin> There is also a third long variety called *Clematitis* <note>original: "Clematitis"; from the Greek "klema," meaning a vine-twig or climbing plant.</note>, which has thin branches filled with roundish leaves, similar to the Lesser Houseleek. Its flowers are fuller than those of Rue, and its roots are longer and thinner, covered in a thick and fragrant bark, which is suitable for thickening ointments.

## ¶ The opinion of PLINY on Birthworts, from book 25, chapter 8.

Among the most noble plants, the Birthworts <note>original: "Ariſtolochiæ"</note> seem to have been named for pregnant women, because it is "best for those in labor." <note>original: "ἀρίστη λεχούσαις" (aristē lechousais)</note> Our people call it the Earth-apple. <note>original: "Malum terræ"</note> They recognize four kinds. One has round root-tubers and leaves somewhere between mallow and ivy, though darker and thicker. The second is the male, with a long root four fingers in length and the thickness of a walking stick. The third is of extreme thinness, like a young vine, and possesses the greatest power; this is called *Clematis*, and by others, the Cretan variety. All have the color of boxwood, small stems, and purple flowers. They bear small berries like those of a Caper. They are effective only by their roots. <margin>Pistolochia <note>original: "Piſtolochia"; likely refers to Aristolochia pistolochia, a smaller species.</note></margin> There is also one called *Pistolochia*, the fourth kind, which is thinner than the one just mentioned, with dense, hair-like roots as thick as a sturdy rush. Some call this *Polyrrhizon*. <note>original: "Polyrrhizon"; Greek for "many-rooted."</note> The scent of all these is medicinal, but that of the long, thinner root is more pleasant, for it has a fleshy bark. It is also suitable for nard ointments. They grow in rich, flat lands. It is seasonal to dig them up during the harvests; they are preserved once the soil is scraped off. However, the most praised is the Pontic variety, and whichever is heaviest is best suited for medicines.

# PHARMACOLOGY OF SIMPLES

<margin>C</margin> The round variety is used against serpents. The long variety is held in the highest esteem, even now.

->The Opinion of APULEIUS, Chapter 19.<-

The Greeks call Birthwort <term>Aristolochia</term> "Ararezam," others "Ephasion" or "Hephasian," others "Lestitin," others "Pixionice," others "Melacarpon," others "Teuxinon," others "Dardanon," others "Iontitim," others "Chamaimilon," others "Opetin." The Italians call it "Apple of the Earth" <note>original: "Malum terrae"</note>, the Dacians call it "Wild Wormwood" <note>original: "Absinthium rusticum"</note>, and the Scardians call it "Scardian." It grows in mountainous, solid, warm, and cultivated places.

->The DISPUTE of Nicolaus, concerning Pliny’s error regarding Cyclamen and Birthwort.<-

Similarity, not only of names but also of the things themselves, occasionally deceived Pliny. For he seems to have believed that the root of the Cyclamen <term>Cyclamen</term>—which is called "Earth-turnip" <note>original: "Rapum terrae"</note> because of its roundness—was the same as the root of the Round Birthwort, which also took its name from the roundness of its root. For in Book 25, in the passage where he distinguishes four kinds of Birthwort, he writes that the root of the variety called "Round" is called "Poison of the Earth" <note>original: "Venenum terrae"</note> by the fishermen of Campania. He claims that when it is crushed in his presence, mixed with lime, and scattered in the sea, the fish immediately swim toward it with wonderful greed and are instantly killed and float to the surface. This same thing, as I have learned from men of great authority, is done in our own age by those same fishermen—not with the root of the Round Birthwort, but rather with the root of the Cyclamen, for the purpose of luring and killing fish. Pliny himself also attributes these same effects not to the Round Birthwort,

<margin>D</margin> but to the root of a certain Cyclamen in Book 25. Therefore, one must either admit that there are two roots which produce the same effects (though it is neither found written by any author nor proven by experience that one of these is the Round Birthwort), or it must be said that the Cyclamen, which has a round root, is the fourth kind of Birthwort. Nothing could be said that is more contrary to the nature of things than this. Indeed, the name Birthwort <term>Aristolochia</term> is used among the Greeks, as Dioscorides and Pliny himself testify, because it is the best aid for pregnant women. However, the root of the Cyclamen is so hostile to pregnant women that if a woman with child should even step over it, she would suffer a miscarriage; as Dioscorides and many other distinguished physicians have reported, and Pliny himself confirms.

->THE DEFENSE BY COLLENUCCIO.<-

Pliny writes most appropriately of three kinds of the herb Cyclamen—which the common people and physicians now call "Sowbread" <note>original: "Panis porcinus"</note>—and of four kinds of Birthwort, and he describes them. But here, our accuser <note>referring to Nicolaus Leonicenus</note> says that Pliny thought the root of the Cyclamen appeared to be the root of the Round Birthwort because he ascribed the power of killing fish to the Birthwort root. He brings forth this argument: "I myself," he says, "have learned from men of great authority that the same thing is done in our age, not with the root of Birthwort, but with Cyclamen." Does it not seem that Leonicenus has used a remarkable testimony or syllogism against Pliny? Because Nicolaus Leonicenus says "I have heard" that fish are killed by the root of Cyclamen, he concludes Pliny is deceived, even though Pliny says *he saw it himself* when he recorded that fish are killed by the Birthwort root. Oh, inexcusable slander! Just because the Cyclamen root does this, it does not mean the Birthwort root does not. Because Nicolaus heard about the Cyclamen root from unknown persons, Pliny...

<meta>This page continues the debate between the author and the scholar Nicolaus Leonicenus regarding the botanical accuracy of Pliny the Elder. The author is defending Pliny's claim that Birthwort can be used to stun fish, arguing against Leonicenus's assertion that Pliny confused Birthwort with Cyclamen.</meta>

### ...of Physicians, VOLUME First.

<margin>A</margin>
...lied in his earlier testimony regarding <term>Aristolochia</term> <note>Birthwort, a plant used historically in childbirth and as a medicine</note>. Behold the argument of the illustrious Logician: because by "Earth-truffle" <note>original: "Tubere terrae"</note> (that is, the root of the first kind of <term>Cyclamen</term>) it happens that fish are killed, it cannot be that by "Earth-apple" <note>original: "Malo terrae"</note>, that is, the root of Round Birthwort, the same can happen. Is Pliny mistaken, who writes that he himself saw it? And is Nicolaus not mistaken, who says he only heard of it? "But," says Leonicenus, "Pliny also writes that the root of Cyclamen achieves this." That is indeed true, Leonicenus: but he says it of the *third* kind of Cyclamen, nicknamed "Ground-ivy" <note>original: "Chamaecissi"</note>, whose root is not round, but spreading. Thus, you must finally acknowledge that you are out of your mind to try to persuade yourself of this regarding the "Earth-turnip" <note>original: "Rapo terrae"</note>. Do you think Pliny was blind, or a liar, Nicolaus, when he writes that he saw the Campanian fishermen mix lime with "Earth-apple" and kill fish? Did Pliny seem to you to have said something impossible, or something beyond belief? 

But Pliny himself also records in Books 6 and 20 that the <term>Tithymalus</term> <note>Spurge</note> nicknamed "Cluster-spurge" <note>original: "Corymbiten"</note>, and in Book 20 that "Goat-lettuce" <note>original: "Lactucam caprinam"</note>, provide the same effects in killing fish. Aristotle also writes in Chapter 7 of his *History of Animals* that both river and lake fish are destroyed by the <term>Verbascum</term> <note>Mullein</note> herb, and that sea fish are also caught in this way by the Phoenicians. We too have learned by experiment and by sight that both "Squirting Cucumber" <note>original: "Cucumerem asininum"</note> and the crushed green shells of walnuts can achieve the same thing. Since, therefore, fish are killed by Cyclamen, and Cluster-spurge, and Goat-lettuce, and Mullein, and Squirting Cucumber, and walnut shells, is Pliny in error because he said the root of Birthwort also kills them? Do these seem like "Carneadean" arguments to you <note>Referring to the skeptical philosophy of Carneades, suggesting the logic is flimsy</note>, or Aristotelian demonstrations from which an unassailable truth must necessarily follow? 

Then, concluding, you proceed and speak in this manner: "Either it must be confessed that there are two roots which provide the same effects, or it must be said that the Cyclamen with the round root is a fourth kind of Birthwort." From where, I pray, comes this necessity of "confessing" or "saying," Nicolaus? 

<margin>B</margin>
First of all, we have brought forward not just two herbs that kill fish, but six; and we do not doubt that many others can do the same. Do you think it is a great or miraculous thing if two or more herbs possess the same power? Furthermore, just because Cyclamen kills fish, will it be a fourth kind of Birthwort? You should have said a *fifth* kind, for Pliny enumerates four kinds of Birthwort already. By that same reasoning, Cluster-spurge, Spurge, Goat-lettuce, Mullein, Squirting Cucumber, and walnut shells—because they kill fish—would be placed among the kinds of Birthwort; as if a single effect could only be provided by a single kind of herb! Not even an old woman would say such a thing, nor any of the empirics <note>Historical medical practitioners who relied on experience rather than theory</note>. 

"But," you say, "it is found written by no author that Birthwort kills fish." Have you read all authors, Leonicenus? Did I not warn you regarding the "Tripolium" <note>Sea-starwort</note> that he who argues in such a way must have read, understood, and held in memory all the authors who ever wrote, so that the formula and reasoning of this argument might hold firm? But is not the evidence of the thing itself more powerful than all authors? Even now, the people of Campania commonly call this root "melum terragnun" <note>A regional dialect version of the Latin "Malum terrae"</note>, which is "Earth-apple": and they use it everywhere in fishing. This fact was reported to us by that illustrious man of sharpest judgment, Sigismondo d'Este, your brother, O renowned Duke (at the time we were producing these writings). But what is this persistence, what is this hardness of brow, what is this impudence? To say "written by no author..."

<sig>d 2</sig>

The author cites several ancient authorities and contemporary testimony from the nobility of Campania to defend Pliny’s observations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the heated defense of Pliny the Elder against the criticisms of the scholar Nicolaus Leonicenus. The author is particularly incensed by Leonicenus's suggestion that Pliny fabricated his observations about fishermen using "Earth-apple" (Birthwort) to stun fish, further debating the correct botanical terminology for Cyclamen and Birthwort species.</meta>

->PHARMACY of SIMPLES<-

<margin>C</margin> ...you say it was [written?], since Pliny writes it? And because you found no one else writing of it—since you have read so few—is Pliny, who asserts that he saw it with his own eyes, therefore not to be believed? You, who think you should be believed when you say you merely heard of it! To whom I would fear to concede as a witness in these matters, even if you were sworn under oath. O unhappy Pliny! O hollow studies of letters! O vain labors and wretched late-night toilings of a most upright man! Behold, after one thousand four hundred years, a single sophist <note>A term used here to describe a scholar who uses clever but fallacious arguments</note> has finally erupted into such a kind of madness that he suggests Pliny did not merely err, deceived by a similarity of things or names (which is only human), but that Pliny actually lied, because he affirms he saw something that <term>Nicolaus Leonicenus</term> <note>A famous Italian physician and humanist (1428–1524) known for correcting errors in Pliny's natural history</note> found written by no one else. Thus, it is no longer a matter of Pliny's learning, but of his honesty. By Hercules, it is a fine thing for scholarship! It irks and shames me to deal in words against this man, who now (as <term>Aristotle</term> says) needs not words but punishment. 

Now we can understand the man by this alone: who, even while playing the Greek scholar, added (so that we might weigh his own merits in passing) that the root of the <term>Cyclaminum</term> <note>Sowbread or Cyclamen</note> is called the "Earth-turnip" <note>original: "rapum terrae"</note>. This is more according to the opinion of <term>Dioscorides</term> than the authority of Pliny—a Latin man—who calls it the "Earth-truffle" <note>original: "tuber terrae"</note>. It is as if the garden turnip were not a vegetable of the earth, but of the water, and only the Cyclamen deserves to be called "Earth-turnip." Furthermore, this illustrious man of letters pronounces it not "Cyclaminum" (as <term>Celsus</term> and Pliny, Latin men, and the reasoning derived from the Greeks require) but "Cyclamen." But perhaps it is not worth the effort to chase these trifles; now we shall proceed to the rest, and discuss <term>Endive</term> <note>original: "Intibo"</note> and <term>Heliotrope</term>.

<margin>D</margin>

## THE OPINION OF THEOPHRASTUS, Book 9, Chapter 13.

The "Earth-apple" <note>original: "Malum terrae", referring here to Round Birthwort</note> is fragrant to the smell, violently bitter to the taste, and black in color. The best grows in the mountains, and it consists of a leaf similar to a mouse's ear, though rounder.

## SERAPION ON BIRTHWORT.

There are two species of <term>Aristolochia</term> <note>Birthwort</note>: male and female. The male is "Long" and the female is "Round"; and the part which is more useful in medicines is their root.

## THE OPINION OF MACER.

> We say there are three species of Birthwort.
> The first is called "Long," whose root is long.
> The following is called "Round," because it has a round root.
> The third is called "Clematis" <note>meaning "vine-like"</note> in the Greek tongue.

## THE OPINION OF AVICENNA, Book 2, Chapter 50. And the author of the Pandects, and Mesue.

There are three species of Birthwort, namely Long, and Round, and another whose root runs along the path of vine shoots.

## THE OPINION OF THE MODERNS. From Hermolaus Barbarus.

The color of Birthwort <note>original: "Aristolochiae"</note> is black; its leaf is like <term>Chickweed</term> <note>original: "Alsine"</note>, as <term>Theophrastus</term> says, but rounder. It grows especially in the mountains. The rest of the details are in Pliny, in the place we cited. Finally he adds: there is a fourth named "Pistolochia," thinner than the third. <margin>Satyrion.</margin> Some call this "Polyrrhizon" <note>Many-rooted</note> and say it is <term>Satyrion</term> <note>A name applied to various orchids or aphrodisiac plants in antiquity</note>.

### ITS HUMORAL TEMPERAMENT FROM Mesue & Galen’s *Method*, Book 3.
<margin>A</margin>
All varieties are hot in the beginning of the third degree, and dry in the second <note>In Galenic medicine, drugs were classified by "degrees" of intensity from 1 to 4; the third degree indicates a potent, active medicine</note>. Although the **Long** variety appears more rounded than others, it is nevertheless dominated by an "earthy" quality. The **Round** variety is finer and more penetrating. All types are also "aperient" <note>opening</note> for clearing blockages, as well as being resolutive and attractive. Indeed, they draw out thorns, fish bones, splinters, and whatever else has been fixed into the flesh.

### POWERS AND BENEFITS OF THE Long Birthwort, from Dioscorides.
The **Long** variety is drunk in wine or applied as an ointment, in the weight of a drachm <note>An ancient unit of weight, roughly 3.5 grams</note>, against snakes and poisons.

When drunk with pepper and myrrh, it drives out menstruation, aids in childbirth, and clears all the burdens of wounds.

It achieves the same effect when applied as a pessary <note>A medicinal plug used internally</note>.

### BENEFITS OF THE ROUND Birthwort.
The **Round** variety is powerful for the same purposes.

Furthermore, when drunk with water, it is uniquely helpful for hiccups, labored breathing, chills, ailments of the spleen, and the pains of side-convulsions.

It extracts stingers and arrows.

Applied as an ointment, it removes all skin scales.

It consumes putrid ulcers.

It purges away filth.

Combined with iris and honey, it fills up hollow sores.

It cleanses the gums and teeth.

<margin>B</margin>
### BENEFITS OF THE CLEMATITIS <note>A specific variety of Birthwort, *Aristolochia clematitis*</note>.
It is effective against severe fevers.

If a person suffering from fever is fumigated by the scent of the plant placed over glowing coals, the fever is relieved.

It heals wounds when applied to them.

It is useful for "carcinoma of the nostrils" <note>Likely referring to erosive sores or polyps</note> when mixed with Galingale, the seed of Dragon-wort, and honey.

Cooked in oil or pig fat and applied, it cures stiffness and chills.

### FROM THEOPHRASTUS.
The **Earth-apple** <note>original: "Malum terrae," a common synonym for the Birthwort root</note> is very useful for the head, for various ulcers, for serpents, for inducing sleep, and for other things.

For ulcers, they instruct to apply it worked into water; for other things, use it scraped into honey or wine, or crushed in oil. It may also be drunk in tart wine and sprinkled on bites. To induce sleep, it should be thoroughly crushed in a dark, dry wine.

If the womb should prolapse, it will be helpful to wash it with a decoction of this plant.

### FROM APULEIUS <note>Referring to the "Herbarium" of Pseudo-Apuleius, a widely used late-antique medical text</note>.
The root of the **Birthwort** inserted into fistulas <note>Deep, narrow infected tunnels in the flesh</note> quickly purges them and leads to healing. Indeed, physicians can successfully cure almost nothing without it.

->**FROM GALEN, *On Simple Medicines*, Book 6, Chapter 53.**<-

If you have need of a cleansing or flesh-forming medicine <note>An "incarnative" medicine is one used to promote the growth of new flesh in a wound</note>, it is better to apply the **Round Birthwort**. It is used for ulcers of the womb, for the thinning of thick humors, and the opening of pores. It is also beneficial for asthmatics, those with gout, those suffering from hiccups, and epileptics when drunk; it is applied as a poultice for bruises.

->**FROM MESUE.**<-

Through its loosening property, it draws out phlegmatic fluids. Some have said it also draws out choleric ones <note>Mesue refers here to the "Four Humors": Phlegm and Yellow Bile (Choler)</note>.
And it is among the substances that most effectively cleanse the lungs and the chest of phlegm and decay.
It offers a clear and helpful remedy for asthma and coughs regardless of how it is administered.
This includes its use as a fumigation <note>incense</note> through a funnel.
Taken with honey-water <note>hydromel</note>, it cures ulcers of the ears and strengthens the sense of hearing.
Vinegar in which it has been boiled tightens the gums and removes decay from them. And if the teeth are rubbed with it, it cleanses them.
<margin>D</margin> It is also a good medicine for the chills of fevers. Its dose is from one drachm <note>about 3.5 grams</note> up to one aureus <note>original: "aureum." A weight based on the gold coin, roughly 4.5 grams</note>.

->**FROM PLINY.**<-

The **Long** variety, if applied to the womb with beef after conception, is said to ensure the formation of male children, according to tradition.
The fishermen of Campania call the root of the **Round** variety "Poison of the Earth." In our presence, they have crushed it, mixed it with lime, and scattered it into the sea: the fish flock to it with marvelous greed and immediately float to the surface, lifeless. The variety called *Polyrrhizos* <note>Greek for "Many-rooted"</note> is said to be most useful for those with convulsions, bruises, or those who have fallen from a height, when the root is drunk with water. Its seed is said to warm the body and strengthen those with pleurisy and nerve ailments. See below under Satyrium <note>Another plant entry in this volume</note>.

->**FROM AVICENNA.**<-

When Birthwort is administered with pepper, it cleanses the superfluities of the brain, especially the **Round** variety.
It benefits pleurisy when drunk with water.
It provokes menstruation and brings forth the fetus.

->**FROM MACER.**<-

> It greatly soothes the pain of the belly.

> Therefore, if the **Round** is ever lacking,

### Researcher and Herbalist.

Aron has leaves like the Dragon Plant <note>original: *Dracunculus*</note>, only they are smaller and not quite as spotted. It has a stem nine inches long <term>dodrantalem: a measurement of three-quarters of a Roman foot, roughly nine inches</term>, purplish in color, in the shape of a pestle <note>original: *pastilli*; referring to the central spike or spadix</note>, in which there is reddish, saffron-colored seed. The root is white, appearing similar to the root of the Dragon Plant, which—because it possesses less acrimony <note>sharpness or stinging quality</note>—is eaten boiled.

f
<meta>Section markers 'A' and 'B' are printed in the outer margin. A later hand has added a brief note in cursive in the bottom right margin.</meta>

### The Pronouncement of **THEOPHRASTUS** on Arum, <margin>A</margin> from Book 7 of the *Enquiry into Plants*, Chapter 11.

The root of the Arum, in order to increase in size, grows luxuriously with its leaves, which spread out quite broadly. It is common practice to bend the leaves down and bury them around the plant; this ensures the plant does not expend its energy on sprouting new shoots, but instead draws all its nourishment into its own "head" <note>referring to the tuberous root</note>. This is a technique that some also apply when cultivating various bulbs.

### The Opinion of **PLINY** on Arum, from Book 24, Chapter 16.

<margin>The controversy between Dragonwort, Arum, and Friar's Cowl.</margin>
There is a great dispute regarding the Arum and Dragonwort <note>original: *Dracontio*</note>. Indeed, some have said they are the same plant. Glaucias distinguished them by their stature, pronouncing Dragonwort to be the "wild Arum." Some have called the root "Arum" and the stem "Dragonwort," considering it an entirely different plant—if indeed this is the same plant we call *Dracunculus* <note>Little Dragon</note>. For the Arum has a black root, rounded in width, and much larger—large enough to fill a hand. The *Dracunculus* has a reddish root, coiled in the manner of a sleeping dragon, which is where it gets its name. Furthermore, the Greeks themselves have established an immense difference, stating that the seed of the *Dracunculus* is burning and biting, and that it possesses such a strong stench that the mere smell can cause pregnant women to miscarry.

### The Synthesis of **HERMOLAO BARBARO** on Arum.

Theophrastus says that the roots of Arum become plump and nourished when germination is inhibited—specifically by burying the leaves in the earth. These roots grow very large. Likewise, they are hollow and shaped like a cucumber. The root is bare of bark and can be eaten. Indeed, he says the leaves are also eaten when boiled in vinegar, making a pleasant meal, though he attributes no stem to the plant. It differs from Dragonwort if we follow Pliny: because it has a black root, round in width, much larger, and enough to fill a hand; <margin>B</margin> whereas the Dragonwort is reddish and twisted. Its seed is burning and biting, while the Arum's is milder. Galen also confirms this. When used for food, the female Arum is preferred, <margin>Two species of Arum.</margin> since it is sweeter than the male and slower to cook <note>or perhaps softens more gradually in the pot</note>. They claim that cheese can be preserved from rotting if kept in Arum leaves; though this quality is attributed by Dioscorides to the Greater or Lesser Dragonwort.

### The Annotation of **VIRGILIO** on Arum.
<note>Marcello Virgilio Adriani (1464–1521) was an Italian humanist and scholar known for his commentary on Dioscorides's medicinal plants.</note>

Pliny confuses the Arum with Dragonwort. In his 19th book, he counts Arum among the garden plants of Egypt in these words: "There is among the types of bulbs one which they call Arum in Egypt; it is very close to the Squill <note>original: *Scyllae*; a sea-onion</note>, with the leaf size of a Sorrel <note>original: *Lapathi*</note> (which is the *Rumex*), with a straight stem of two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> and the thickness of a staff, and a root of a softer nature which may be eaten even raw." However, leaves like Sorrel, a straight stem, a height of two cubits, and the thickness of a staff—all these features belong to the description of the Greater Dragonwort, and they do not fit the Arum, whose stem is only half a foot long and shaped like a pestle. This form can be seen daily in the Arum of our own region. We believe there was no greater cause for confusing these diverse species than, first, their similarity, and later, the history of the ancients; in which this entire genus was sometimes called "Arum," whereas now this specific one is called Dragonwort and that one Arum. Nevertheless, Nature has distinguished one from the other, making the former taller and the latter shorter. In the former, the shape is as we described in the previous chapter; in the latter, it can be recognized everywhere.
<margin>The most learned and true words of Virgilio on Arum.</margin>

<header>Pharmacology of SIMPLES</header>

<margin>C</margin>Dioscorides also left us a description of that sheath and hood in which the enclosed seed is wrapped; it is more pale than grassy-green in color, and not purple as it is in the Little Dragon <note>referring to *Dracunculus* or Dragonwort</note>. In former times, Arum was numbered and sown among the garden vegetables, which seems hardly believable, as the root (which was used for food) possesses such sharp pungency. We must consider one of two things: either a milder variety was brought in from elsewhere, or it can even now be made better through some method of cultivation and human skill.

### **GEORGIUS VALLA** on Arum.

Arum, which some call *Serpentaria* <note>Snakeweed</note>, has a root belonging to the first order of heating substances, and it possesses the power of cleansing, though not as strongly as Dragonwort <note>original: *Dracontion*</note>. What he means by these words, I do not clearly understand.

### **SIMON JANUENSIS** on Arum.

Arum is described by Dioscorides as follows: It is the *Larus*, which is called the Lesser Snakeweed.

And again: *Iarus* is called Aaron’s Beard, which is also called Calf’s Foot <note>original: *Pes vituli*</note>, and Lesser Snakeweed, and Lesser Dragonwort.

### The **AUTHOR OF THE PANDECTS** on Arum.

Arum is an herb with leaves similar to Dragonwort, but smaller and flat, not variegated. It has a stalk of two palms’ length <note>approximately 6 to 8 inches</note> and is purple in color. Its seed is saffron-colored, and it has a white root with the roundness of a bulb, similar to Dragonwort. This can be eaten raw or cooked, because it is not very bitter. Its leaves are eaten after being preserved in salt.

<margin>D</margin>### OUR JUDGMENT.

You see, reader, that authors and physicians—otherwise of great reputation—do not agree, even on a matter that is well known and familiar to even the oldest herbalists. They speak of the most famous herbs no differently than if they were "fighting like blindfolded gladiators" <note>original: *Andabatae conpugnant*; an ancient proverb for arguing without seeing the facts</note>. One might suspect that they are either hallucinating, or the manuscripts are corrupt, or (as I would readily believe) that the plants grow quite differently—with a different stature, color, and sometimes even a different taste—in foreign lands than they do in our Germany. In such great disagreement among the most learned physicians, I have no way to decide the matter myself, nor do I see why I should condemn anyone. Therefore, we have provided an illustration of the Arum as it was shown to us by our own herbalists. Although it does not match the descriptions in some respects (for instance, it is not considered edible today), it corresponds in most details. We have done the same for the Dragonworts that follow, being ready to yield if anyone can demonstrate more certain and trustworthy evidence.

### TEMPERAMENT.

It is of a hot and dry temperament in the first degree; it dissolves, relaxes, and thins <note>referring to its ability to thin thick humors or fluids in the body</note>.

### Its Powers and Benefits from **DIOSCORIDES**.

The leaves are prepared as food, and when dry, they are eaten after being boiled by themselves.
The root, seed, and leaves have the same medicinal powers as the Little Dragon <note>Dragonwort</note>.
Specifically, the root is smeared on gouty joints when mixed with cow dung, and it is stored away in the same manner as Dragonwort.

### FROM THEOPHRASTUS <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was the successor to Aristotle and is often called the "Father of Botany."</note>

The root of Arum is suitable for food, and its leaves can be eaten when boiled in vinegar.
It is also useful for fractures.

### FROM PLINY <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note>

They have extolled Arum with wonderful praises. First, they sought it out for the diet of women: since the "male" <note>In ancient botany, "male" and "female" usually designated different varieties or related species rather than biological sex; the "male" was often considered the more robust or sweeter version</note> variety was sweeter and slower to cook, and it would purge ailments of the chest.
The dried root, sprinkled into a drink or taken as an electuary <note>a medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note>, stimulates urine and menstruation.
Likewise, when drunk in oxymel <note>a traditional mixture of honey and vinegar</note>, it is good for the stomach; for ulcerated intestines, it should be drunk with ewe’s milk. For a cough, they gave it cooked in ashes with oil.
Others boiled it in milk so that the decoction could be drunk.
For watery eyes <term>epiphora</term> <note>original: *epiphoris*</note>, they applied it boiled.
Mixed with oil, they infused it for the vice of hemorrhoids; for freckles, they smeared it on with honey.
Cleophantus <note>A Greek physician of the 3rd century BC</note> praised it as an antidote against poisons, and for those suffering from pleurisy, pneumonia, and also for those with coughs.
Dieuthes <note>An ancient physician mentioned by Pliny</note> infused the seed, crushed with oil or rose oil, for ear pain.
Cleophantus gave it mixed with flour in baked bread for those coughing, or for those gasping and suffering from <term>orthopnea</term> <note>a condition where one can only breathe comfortably while standing or sitting upright</note>, and for those spitting up pus.
<margin>B</margin>
Diodotus <note>A physician cited by Pliny for his knowledge of herbs</note> applied it as a honey electuary for the consumptive and for lung ailments; he also applied it to broken bones.
It extracts the offspring of all animals <note>i.e., it aids in difficult labor or veterinary births</note> when smeared around the birth canal.
The juice of the root with Attic honey <note>Attic honey, from Mt. Hymettus in Greece, was considered the highest quality in antiquity</note> clears dimness of the eyes and settles stomach ailments.
For a cough, the broth of the decoction with honey is used.
It cures ulcers of all kinds wonderfully, whether they be eating sores <term>phagedenas</term>, cancers, spreading ulcers, or polyps in the nostrils.
The leaves are beneficial for burns when boiled with wine and oil.
They purge the bowels when taken with salt and vinegar.
Boiled with honey, they are also beneficial for dislocations.
Likewise, for gouty joints, the leaves are used with salt, whether fresh or dried.
Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – c. 370 BC)</note> applied it with honey for any kind of abscesses or fluid collections.
To draw out the menses in women, two drachms of the root in two cups <note>original: *cyathis*</note> of wine are sufficient.
The same drink, if women are not cleansed after childbirth, also draws out the afterbirth <note>original: *secundas*</note>.
Hippocrates also applied the root itself as a pessary.
They say it is also a healthy food to eat during a pestilence.
It dispels drunkenness.
When burned, the smell drives away snakes and specifically puts asps to flight, or intoxicates them so that they are found sluggish; they also flee from those anointed with Arum or laurel oil.
Cheese is preserved best when wrapped in Arum leaves.

### FROM PLATEARIUS <note>Matthaeus Platearius was a 12th-century physician from the medical school of Salerno, known for his work on medicinal plants.</note> Chapter 32.

The leaves of the Cuckoo-pint <note>original: *Iari*, that is, *Aronis*</note>, when mixed with cow dung and applied as a poultice <term>cataplasm</term>, help to relieve gout.

### FROM THE AUTHOR OF THE PANDECTS <note>Matthaeus Silvaticus, a 14th-century physician who wrote the *Pandectae Medicinae*, a massive medical dictionary.</note> AND FROM GALEN.

To stimulate menstruation, its juice is applied by means of a pessary.

It dissolves tumors of the ears when the root is cooked in wine and oil and used as a medicinal steam-bath <term>encatisma</term> <note>a type of sitz-bath or steaming treatment where the patient sits over the vapors</note>.

Applied in this same manner, it also thoroughly heals hemorrhoids.

It dissolves all "cold" abscesses <note>in ancient medicine, swellings caused by an excess of "cold" humors like phlegm</note> when ground together with aged lard.

It resolves scrofula <note>a swelling of the lymph nodes, usually in the neck</note> when mixed with squill <note>the sea onion</note> and bear grease.

Its powder, infused and macerated in rose water, cleanses the face and removes bumps and swellings from it.

### FROM HIERONYMUS THE HERBALIST <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), one of the "fathers of German botany."</note>

<margin>D</margin>
The water of this plant, when drunk, is the most effective remedy of all for ruptures <note>hernias</note>.

If any thick phlegm or other filth should cling to the interior of the stomach—which provokes nausea and reduces the appetite for eating—it is beautifully cured by either the herb or the crushed root, boiled in wine and drunk while fasting.

->**Good Henry**<- <note>original German: *Gůt Heinrich*; commonly known today in English as Good King Henry.</note>

[Detailed Botanical Illustration]

This woodcut illustrates the plant *Chenopodium bonus-henricus*, a perennial herb historically valued as a "pot-herb" (a leaf vegetable) and for its medicinal properties in treating skin inflammations.

The artist has captured the specific features used to identify the plant in the wild:

1.  **The Root:** At the base is a thick, fleshy, and somewhat contorted root system. Unlike the previous page's "twice-twisted" bistort, this root is sturdier and more vertical, providing the energy for the plant to return year after year.
2.  **The Foliage:** A single, strong stem rises from the base, bearing large leaves arranged alternately. These leaves are described as <term>hastate</term> <note>shaped like an arrowhead with the basal lobes pointing outward</note>. Their margins are slightly wavy, a detail clearly rendered in the woodcut.
3.  **The Flower:** The plant is topped with a terminal, spike-like <term>inflorescence</term> <note>a complete flower head including stems and bracts</note>. It consists of many small, crowded flowers that, in nature, are typically a greenish color and lack petals.

Historically, this plant was often found growing near human habitations and ruins, leading to its "Good Henry" name—distinguishing it from "Bad Henry" (various poisonous weeds like Mercury). In the 16th century, it was frequently used in poultices to cleanse sores and as a spring tonic to "purify the blood."

## OPINIONS OF AUTHORS regarding the Dragon-plant.
### The opinion of DIOSCORIDIS regarding the Greater Dragon-plant.

<margin>
Habitat of the Dragon-plant.
</margin>
The Greater Little Dragon <note>The author uses *Dracunculus*, literally "Little Dragon," for plants we now know as *Dracunculus vulgaris* or *Arum*</note> GROWS in shady places around hedges. It has an upright stem, two cubits <note>roughly 3 feet</note> high, as thick as a staff, and of many colors; it has an innate smoothness so that it seems similar to a snake. Purple spots are abundant and dominant on it. It bears leaves like those of the Dock <note>original: *Rumicis*</note> folded over one another. It produces seeds in a cluster at the top of the stem, which are ash-colored at the start; then, when they have matured, they are the color of saffron threads and reddish. The root of the Greater Little Dragon is large, round, white, and covered with a thin bark. The herb is harvested
<margin>D</margin> when the seed is already ripening; the juice is pressed out of it and dried in the shade. The root is dug up during the harvest, and once washed, it is cut into small discs <note>original: *taleolas*</note> which, being threaded on a string, are dried in the shade.

### ->Description of the LESSER by the same author.<-
The other Little Dragon has leaves like Ivy, large, and with whitish spots on the leaves. It has an upright stem, two cubits high, of varied color, spotted in the manner of snakes, with purple streaks running through it, and the thickness of a staff. The seed at the top is in a cluster, grassy-green at first; however, when it has matured, it is the glowing red color of saffron threads and has a biting taste. Its root is round, bulbous, similar to a Radish, and covered with a thin bark. It grows in shady places around un-fenced hedges.

### Pliny says almost the same, as we cited under Arum.
<margin>Pliny's opinion on Arum.</margin>

## Depiction of the DRAGON-PLANT from APVLEIVS.

It grows on the tops of mountains where there are lakes, especially in sacred places. In the land of Apulia it grows upon rocks, with a sweet taste, like a green chestnut; the very bottom of the root has the flavor and the "head of a dragon" <note>likely referring to the bulb's appearance</note>.

<header>...of the [Medicines], VOLUME ONE <note>original: *corum TOMVS Primus*</note></header>

Book 9, Chapter 22.
Four types of Snake-root <note>original: *Colubrinæ*</note> according to Dioscorides.
What is Serpent-plant <note>original: *Serpentaria*</note>?
</margin>
...is slender, and coiled in the manner of a twisted dragon. Authors differ somewhat regarding this genus. Some separate the "Little Dragon" <note>original: *Dracunculum*</note> from the Cuckoo-pint <note>original: *Aro*</note>, while others consider them the same. Glaucias called the wild Little Dragon "Arum." Phaenis called it "Aron" and "Aronia." Others called the root "Aron" and the stem "Dracontion" <note>literally "dragon-stem"</note>. Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> thought *Aron* was a broad genus under which many species were contained. Dioscorides seems to have established four types: Greater Little Dragon, Lesser Little Dragon, *Aron*, and *Arisaron*. However, in his description of *Aron*, he differs from Pliny. They also agree very little regarding the Little Dragon. The Little Dragon is dug up when the barley is ripening, during a waxing moon. There are those who call it "Serpent-plant" <note>original: *Serpentariam*</note>. I find in the works of Hippocrates that the "Snake-herb" <note>original: *Ophim herbam*</note> is approved, as its seed is useful for women’s medicines. It is not entirely clear whether this is the same as the Dragon-plant <note>original: *Dracontio*</note>, even though it takes its name from a serpent. When this same Hippocrates names a "white root," he means the root of the Dragon-plant, as Galen <note>the famous Roman physician</note> maintains.

<margin>
B
Pellitory <note>original: *Pyrethrum*</note>.
</margin>
And again: Dioscorides lists two Little Dragons, the Greater and the Lesser, as we said before. Pliny lists three. One has leaves like a Beet, not without a stalk <note>original: *thyrſo*</note>, a purple flower, and is similar to the Cuckoo-pint. The second has a long root, appearing as if marked and jointed, with exactly three small stems. The third has a leaf larger than a Dogwood <note>original: *Cornus*</note>, a reed-like root with as many jointed nodes, so they say, as it has years of age, and just as many leaves. Aetius describes the seed of the Little Dragon as being hidden in the earth and similar to pepper. Gardeners also report a plant called the "Dragon" <note>original: *Draconem*</note>, which is entirely different from this genus: they claim it is born in a miraculous way from flax seed enclosed within radishes or squill bulbs and buried in the earth. This is a tiny herb with black, minute seeds and a thin, oblong, sharp leaf that betrays both of its supposed origins. It burns the tongue with both leaf and root, tasting of vinegar and salt; some falsely think this was the plant called "Pellitory" <note>original: *Pyrethrum*</note> by the ancients—it is the most pungent among the salad herbs.

## ->A genuine explanation of all Dragon-plants, by<-
# ->MARCELLVS VERGILIVM.<-
<note>Marcellus Vergilius (1464–1521) was a humanist scholar known for his commentary on Dioscorides.</note>

<margin>
Paulus Aegineta <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note>
</margin>
The ancients confused the Cuckoo-pint <note>original: *Aro*</note> with the Dragon-plant <note>original: *Dracunculum*</note> to such a degree, and those types of Dragon-plants were described by them with so many sometimes identical, sometimes differing characteristics, that they made this otherwise well-known subject extremely difficult, both for themselves and for those reading them. The thing that has long kept us anxious, and still does, tossing us between various opinions, is the text of Dioscorides. It is like the description by Apollonius <note>referring to Apollonius of Rhodes, author of the *Argonautica*</note> of Medea’s love: like the flickering of sunlight reflected from water onto the ceiling of a house, never stable, but in constant motion, flitting in every direction. Although one reads in all the Greek copies two chapters on the Greater and Lesser Dragon-plant, their history and medicinal use are nowhere varied enough to justify a significant distinction; even though he says here that one has leaves like Dock and the other like Ivy. This writer frequently uses multiple points of comparison: color, shape, size, potency, and the like. For this reason, it often happens that because a plant is said to be similar in its parts, the whole is wrongly believed to be identical; or because it is said to differ in parts, the whole is falsely considered different, even when it is similar in every other way. This could easily have happened with both of this author’s Dragon-plants: in one, the leaves could be compared to Dock in size and shape, and in the other, to Ivy in color. Indeed, after diligently examining both chapters, we found nothing so different or distinct that it should have been necessary to compose such a long history of the plant and its medicine using the exact same words. Our suspicion was increased because neither Galen, nor after Galen, Paulus Aegineta—the most diligent authority on Greek medicine...

It features a commentary by the scholar Marcellus Vergilius, who critiques the lack of clarity in these ancient botanical descriptions.</summary>

# SIMPLE MEDICINES <note>original: *SIMPLICIVM Pharma.*</note>

<margin>C</margin> ...everywhere he [Dioscorides] reported his findings in good faith, yet others recognized this second and "Lesser" Snake-root <note>original: *Dracunculum*</note>. Neither the Latin writers after the Greeks—such as Apuleius or Johannes Serapion—nor the very ancient Latin manuscripts (which are numerous among us) show more than a single chapter for the Snake-root; no trace of a second one is found. Because of this, I have believed, and still believe, that only one Snake-root was described by Dioscorides in this passage. For it is not likely that if that other Snake-root existed in nature and had been described by this author, it would have been entirely omitted by those later writers. Nevertheless, in all the oldest Greek manuscripts, both chapters are still read. But, people argue, the history and medicinal use of each are not the same. We grant that; however, we warn that this is more a diversity of words than of things, and it is not enough to establish a separate genus. Yet, some quality is attributed to the "Lesser" Snake-root which is not read of the "Greater," such as the fact that cheese wrapped in its leaves is preserved from spoiling. But even that does not necessitate a difference in species. For that detail could have been added in a new description of the same plant. Indeed, Pliny does not attribute this power to the Snake-root, but to the Cuckoo-pint <note>original: *Aro*</note>; and whatever other details are found added to the "Lesser" rather than the other may have the same explanation. This is what we have observed, and it has been compared with the ancient writers with no small diligence on this very point. The primary powers and nature of both are the same; once these were grasped, they easily persuaded us that one Snake-root is being described in two chapters—that there is not a double genus, but a double history of it. For each is described with a round root, a thin bark, and a straight stalk two cubits high <note>a cubit is roughly 18 inches</note>, as thick as a walking-stick, spotted like a snake with purple marks running through it. The seed at the top is like a cluster of berries, first green and pale in color (which is why one text reads "ash-colored" and the other "grassy-green"), and soon, when it has ripened, it becomes a glowing saffron-red. Both grow around hedges and in shady places. What contradicts this in the history of each are only the leaves, which in one are said to be like Dock <note>original: *Rumicis*; a common leafy weed</note> and in the other like Ivy <note>original: *Hederæ*</note>. This is a great discrepancy, unless it happened for the reason we have stated. Those who wish may do for the medicine what we have done for the history: by comparing so many remedies of both at once, they may come to think that Dioscorides once had not two, but only one Snake-root. Our mind inclines toward this view, even though we have translated both chapters. For in such a variety of ancient writers and manuscripts, having sought the thing itself more diligently, we find that only one Snake-root grows in this world of ours. Having found the plant in two locations, we were permitted to contemplate it with our whole soul, and it was entirely and everywhere similar to the "Greater" type in this writer. And what should not have been omitted: before the seed is conceived, by a clever artifice of nature, it brings forth at the very summit among the leaves a wrapping, like a hood <note>a botanical spathe</note>, the maximum length of which was a cubit. That hood rose gradually from the beginning, increasing daily with a grassy-green color on the outside. Then, gaping open, it spread itself out, showing a purple color within. Fading, it would lean toward the ground, leaving another purple hood in the shape, length, and point of a goat’s horn <note>the spadix</note>, which would never open; but as the seed (which was enclosed by it in the lower part) grew, it would wither bit by bit as the seed increased, and the seed could not be seen unless this hood was broken apart. So diligent is nature in conceiving and preserving the seeds of things. The rest of the plant corresponded excellently to this writer’s description, especially the leaves, which reflected the entire shape of the Sharp Dock <note>original: *acutæ Rumicis*</note>, and as he says here, six or seven of them were entwined together, hanging from a single petiole <note>leaf stalk</note>. Not unlike the way the five fingers are divided from the wrist on a human hand—though it is still one hand—so in the Snake-root the same leaf was divided into as many parts as we have said, arranged among themselves so that one seemed to climb and stand above the other. All those leaves hung from one very thick and long stalk. It was the thickness of a human pinky finger, and its length was a little less than a foot. This leafy arrangement at the top of a bare and smooth stem presented the image of a branch, such as children in our nation are accustomed to carry around on the Calends of May <note>May Day</note> to signal the joy of the new year. We are eyewitnesses of this Snake-root; but of the "Lesser" (provided it is different from the Greater), we are not witnesses to others, nor have others been witnesses to us. We leave the plant of this "Lesser" type to be sought and found by more diligent searchers. Regarding this, it will not bother me to warn everyone again not to yield so much to the histories of the ancients that they do not think it more useful to have seen and observed the things themselves. For who would think there was another Snake-root distinct from the Cuckoo-pint <note>Arum</note>, upon hearing Theophrastus <note>the Greek "Father of Botany"</note> discussing edible roots in his eighth volume on plants in these words: "The root of the snake-root (for they call a certain Arum 'snake-root' because its stem has a certain variegation) is inedible and medicinal." <note>original Greek: ἡ δ’ τοῦ δρακοντίου, καλοῦσι γάρ τι δρακόντιον ἴρον, διὰ τὸ τὸν καυλὸν ἔχειν τινα ποικιλίαν, ἄβρωτος καὶ φαρμακώδης.</note> It seems by these words that Theophrastus makes Arum the genus of all Snake-roots, so to speak. Who could also gather a certain history of Snake-roots from Pliny, who openly testifies that he does not know them well enough himself, and says that Arum is in "great dispute" with Snake-root? We, as we said a little while ago, know only one Snake-root, and of the kind that Dioscorides describes in both chapters (except for the leaves). We also know Arum, as we shall soon say, which is easy for everyone to recognize, being so common in shady places...

<margin>
Dracunculus is only one.
</margin>

<margin>
D
</margin>

...of those things, that plant and vegetable grow in their respective places. Many names for the Snake-root <note>original: *Dracunculi*</note> are listed by Dioscorides, derived from the Arum <note>original: *Aro*</note> due to their similarity and relationship; several are also taken from the genus of dragons and serpents. For where he says the Romans call it *Luremon*, in some Greek texts it is read in such a way that one might easily guess the true reading was *Colubram* <note>meaning "Snake" or "Adder"</note>. Indeed, because of the similarity of its root to the fragrant, square-stalked Rush <note>original: *Iunci*</note> called Galingale <note>original: *Cyperis*</note>, it was called *Dracunculus*, as it resembles it with its bulbous root.
<margin>A</margin>

## The Opinion of JOHANNES SERAPION on Arum and the Snake-roots.
<note>Johannes Serapion was a 9th-century Syrian Christian physician whose works were foundational in bridging Greek and Arabic medicine.</note>

*Luff*, that is, *Dragantæa* <note>Snake-root</note>, and it is *Dracontion*.
There are two species of it. One of them is called *Aron* <note>Arum or Cuckoo-pint</note> in Greek, and the second is *Dragantæa*. But *Aron* has leaves similar to the leaves of *Dragantæa*, except they are smaller and without spots; it has a stalk about one palm in length. Its color is purple. In it is a likeness of a pestle <note>the spadix, or fleshy spike of the flower</note>, the color of which is lemon-yellow or saffron. It has a white root, similar to *Dragantæa*; it is cooked and eaten, and it is less hot <note>referring to the "humoral" heat in Galenic medicine</note> than the root of *Dragantæa*.
<margin>Arum.</margin>

The second, *Dragantæa*, has large leaves similar to the leaves of Ivy <note>original: *Cuffus*, likely a corruption of the Greek *Kissos*</note>. It has tiny white spots. Its stalk is smooth, two cubits in length, and resembles a snake’s horn, since its color is purple, spotted with various colors. In thickness, it is like a rod. At the top of its "tongue" <note>the spathe</note> it has something like a cluster of grapes, the color of which, when it first appears, is like the color of a poppy <note>red</note>; when it matures, it is like the color of a lemon. It stings the tongue. Its root is round, like a bulbous root, similar to the root of the herb called *Luff* <note>Arum</note>; it is covered by a thin skin. It grows in shady, damp places and in fields. Its roots should be gathered at harvest time, washed, cut, and dried in the shade.
<margin>Dragantæa.</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Location and collection.</margin>

### The opinion of SIMON OF GENOA on Snake-weed.
<note>Simon of Genoa was a 13th-century doctor and chaplain to the Pope, famous for his medical dictionary.</note>

*Viperina* <note>Viper-weed</note> is the same as *Aragontæa* or *Serpentaria* <note>Snake-weed</note>; they are the same according to some. However, in an ancient book, I saw another plant depicted, similar to Plantain but with broader leaves, which grows near rivers or grain fields, having soft leaves and a sharp taste.

### DESCRIPTION of Snake-weed by JOHANNES MESUE in his book on simple laxatives.
<note>Mesue the Younger was an influential (though perhaps legendary) Arabic medical author whose works on "simples" (single-ingredient drugs) were standard university texts.</note>

*Luff*, that is, *Serpentaria* <note>Snake-weed</note>, is a plant called "Dragon’s Neck." Among these, one is flat-leaved and the other is curly-leaved. The root of the flat-leaved type tends toward black on the outside but is white inside; the root of the curly-leaved type is ash-colored on the outside and white inside, though it inclines toward a lemon-yellow. Above the roots of both, stalks <note>original: *thyrsi*</note> rise up, having spots in the manner of a serpent.

### SELECTION and testing of the plant from the same MESUE.

The best part of the whole plant is the root. The best root is thick, full, and grown in open spaces. The best time for collecting it is Spring and the beginning of Summer.

## OUR JUDGMENT.

<margin>C</margin>
We owe much gratitude to the Ancients, who first handed down to us the powers and names of Herbs; we also owe much ignominy and perpetual reproach to those who, in later centuries, wonderfully and monstrously corrupted and confused everything. I speak especially of the author of the *Pandects* <note>Matthaeus Silvaticus (c. 1280–1342), author of the *Pandectae Medicinae*, a massive but often confusing medical encyclopedia.</note> and Simon of Genoa <note>Simon Januensis (13th century), a famous medical lexicographer.</note>, who, besides mixing everything up, seem to have exerted themselves only in how they might pile up massive volumes, rather than performing useful work for those who follow or searching for true knowledge of things. If this was the result of their labors, it would have been better had they never set hand to the task. For it is not the job of just anyone to record the names of things, but only of a man thoroughly practiced in all languages and letters. If their books have been corrupted—which I do not find likely, as they are very recent—then such treacherous corrupters would be worthy of perpetual darkness. From this comes the greatest evil: that we know so few Herbs. From this come so many myriads of barbaric, obsolete, and most foolish names, while they have corrupted or neglected all the old ones; today, every old woman <note>original: *Anus*</note> gives them names, and every unlearned ointment-seller <note>term: *seplasiarius* — a vendor of perfumes and medicines, often used disparagingly for those lacking formal medical training</note> does the same. Even those who ought to be held as Masters of the art think of nothing less than philosophizing about Herbs and the knowledge of things. 

Thus recently we could have been exhausted in depicting and sketching the Snake-root <note>original: *Serpentaria*</note> herb, of which the herbalists and old women showed us so many species that even the ancient Lernaean monster of Hercules did not have more heads. Therefore, I think we deserve forgiveness if we have not painted everything with perfect precision <note>literally "with a needle," meaning with extreme detail</note>. We have added only two species, which are commonly found more clearly in gardens and cultivated places. Furthermore, we have also painted that which is commonly called **Good Henry** <margin>D</margin> <margin>Good Henry</margin> <note>original: *Gut Heinrich*; the plant *Blitum bonus-henricus*</note> or **Schwerbel** <note>A vernacular German name for certain weeds, possibly a type of goosefoot</note>. For so the old women persuaded us. Regarding the description and how everything corresponds, let others see to that.

### THE TEMPERAMENT ACCORDING TO MESUE.
<note>Mesue the Younger was a pseudo-author whose 13th-century Latin texts on purgative medicines were standard in European pharmacy.</note>

The curled variety <note>original: *Crispa*</note> is hotter, as Dioscorides says, than the red variety <note>original: *Ruffa*</note>. And he said: the flat red is hot in the first degree, the curled in the second <note>In Galenic medicine, "degrees" measured the intensity of a plant's primary qualities—heat, cold, moisture, or dryness—on a scale of 1 to 4.</note>. And Galen said: the flat is hot at the beginning of the second degree, the curled at its end; and this is perhaps more true. In both, there is heat and sharpness; which, if applied to the surface with an earthy substance, prevails. Both are cleansing, cutting, penetrating, opening, and capable of thinning the humors. The curled variety, however, is stronger in all these effects.

### ITS HARMFUL EFFECTS.

Both varieties hurt the liver and the stomach by their sharpness, drawing to those organs whatever harmful humors exist throughout the little body. Furthermore, the scent ruins tender conceptions <note>embryos</note> by causing miscarriage.

### THE CORRECTION ACCORDING TO MESUE.

Truly, whatever harm <note>original: *malicię*</note> there is, it is corrected with *Rob* <note>term: *Rob* — a thickened fruit syrup or conserve</note>, or honey of raisins, or *alefangine* species <note>pills containing aloes and aromatics</note>. Accordingly, by mixing into it something from the stomach-strengthening simples or styptics <note>astringents that contract tissues</note>—such as quinces <note>original: *Citonia*</note> and mastic <note>original: *Mastiche*; a resin from the Pistacia lentiscus tree</note>—it is administered; and *Diarhodon* lozenges <note>rose-based medicinal tablets</note> are given after it is used. It is also prepared thus: Clean the root of the curled variety and wash it in wine, then...

<margin>A</margin>
...boil it in water; or if that is not pleasing and is more useful (since boiling sometimes diminishes its strength), take two pounds of its powder, and six pounds of rob <term>rob: a thickened, boiled-down fruit juice or syrup</term>, or three pounds each of honey and rob, along with two drams each of pepper, cinnamon, ginger, mace, and cloves.

### POWERS and Benefits according to DIOSCORIDES.

When taken as a diluted drink, whether raw or cooked, or licked with honey, it is beneficial against orthopnea <term>orthopnea: a form of severe shortness of breath where the patient can only breathe while standing or sitting upright</term>, ruptures, convulsions, coughs, and catarrh <note>original: *destillationes*, referring to the "dripping" of excess bodily fluids or mucus</note>.

Drunk with wine, it stimulates sexual desire <note>original: *Venerem stimulat*, literally "stimulates Venus"</note>.

It cleanses those ulcers called "evil-natured" <term>cacöethe: a medical term for a malignant or stubborn sore</term> and spreading sores <term>phagedenic: from the Greek for "to eat," referring to ulcers that spread rapidly and consume tissue</term>, especially when used with white bryony <note>original: *uite alba*</note>.

From the plant and honey, medicated plugs <term>collyria: here referring to shaped medicinal inserts or pessaries rather than eye drops</term> are composed for fistulas <note>abnormal tunnels in the body tissue</note> and for inducing labor.

It is effectively smeared on with honey for skin patches <term>vitiligines: white or discolored patches on the skin</term>.

It consumes polyps and cancers <note>original: *carcinomata*</note>.

The juice provides an effect for eye medicines, likewise against "clouds," dimness, and white spots <note>original: *albugines*, referring to white opacities on the cornea</note>.

The scent of the herb and root causes a miscarriage in early pregnancy. It has the same effect if thirty of its seeds are drunk in a paste.

There are some who pour its juice with oil into the ears for ear pains.

Furthermore, the leaves—being astringent—are applied to fresh wounds, and when boiled in wine, they are applied to chilblains <term>pernionibus: painful, itchy swellings on the hands or feet caused by poor circulation in the cold</term>.

They claim that anyone who rubs their hands with the leaves or has handled the root cannot be bitten by a viper.

### BENEFITS of the Lesser [Dragon Plant] from the same DIOSCORIDES.

The juice of the seed, dripped in with oil, mitigates ear pain.

When applied to the nostrils on wool, it consumes polyps.

Applied as a salve, it stops cancers.

Thirty of its seeds, if drunk in a paste, bring about an abortion.

They say that the scent, after the drooping flowers have withered, kills a fetus that is still tender.

The root has a strong smell.

It heals those with orthopnea, convulsions, ruptures, coughs, and catarrh.

It makes the humors of the chest easy to cough up, whether it is eaten cooked, roasted with honey, or by itself, or if its flour is licked with honey.

It drives out urine.

Drunk with wine, it excites sexual desire.

Ground with honey and white bryony, it cleanses spreading ulcers and those called "evil-natured," and leads them to form a scar.

Medicated plugs are usually made from it for fistulas and for expelling the fetus.

Those who rub their hands with its root are said not to be bitten by vipers.

Smeared on with vinegar, it clears away skin patches.

The leaves are conveniently applied to fresh wounds in place of linen bandages.

It is beneficial to apply the plant, boiled in wine, to chilblains.

The root of the Dragon plant, made into a softening plaster <term>malagma: a topical poultice or plaster used to soften tissues or draw out substances</term> with animal fat <term>axungia: rendered lard or grease used as a medicinal base</term>, extracts broken bones from the body, and even stones if they are present.

->### FROM PLATEARIUS, chapter 35<-

To whiten and cleanse the face, grind its powder with rose water; then, after the water has been dried again in the sun and the powder is dry, add one dram of white lead <term>ceruse: basic lead carbonate, used historically in cosmetics for its whitening effect despite its high toxicity</term> with rose water, and apply it.

## The Eighth Rhapsody on ASARUM.

### NOMENCLATURES.

**Greek:** *Asaron* <note>original: ἄσαρον</note>, *Wild Nard* <note>original: νάρδος ἀγρία</note>, *Blood of Ares* <note>original: αἷμα ἄρεως</note>.
**Latin:** *Perpensa*, *Asarum*, *Rustic Nard*, *Wild Nard*, *Vulgago*, *Blood of Mars* <note>original: *Sanguis Martis*</note>.
**German:** **Hazelwort.**

---

## OPINIONS OF THE AUTHORS regarding Asarum.

### The Judgment of DIOSCORIDES on ASARUM.

<margin>υναρ</margin>
Asarum is a fragrant herb used for garlands <note>original: *coronaria*</note>. It has leaves like ivy, and at the root it has purple, scented little vessels <note>referring to the small, jug-shaped flowers</note> similar to those of the Apollinaris herb <note>likely Henbane, *Hyoscyamus niger*</note>; within these is the seed, similar to the stones of grapes, which has thin, somewhat rough, and angular points. It grows upon numerous roots that are jointed, hot in taste, and stinging <note>original: *erodentis*, literally "gnawing"</note> the tongue; they are thin, slanting, similar to grass, but much more slender than grass and more fragrant.
