# PHARMACY OF SIMPLES
<note>A "simple" is a medicinal herb used on its own, rather than as part of a complex compound.</note>

### Description of ASARUM from PLINY, Book 12, Chapter 13.

Asarum also possesses the power of Nard <note>original: "Nardi uim"</note>, and for this reason, some call it Wild Nard <note>original: "syluestrem Nardum"</note>. It has the leaves of Ivy, though rounder and softer, with a purple flower and a root like that of Gallic Nard. The seed is like a berry, with a warm and wine-like flavor. It flowers twice a year in shady mountains. The best variety is found in Pontus <note>the southern coast of the Black Sea</note>, the second best in Phrygia, and the third in Illyricum. It is dug up when it begins to put forth leaves and is dried in the sun, though it quickly gathers mold <note>original: "situm"</note>. And in Book 21, Chapter 6, I find it is called Asarum because it is not added to floral crowns <note>original: "quoniam in coronas non addatur"; the name is derived from the Greek *a-* (not) and *sairo* (to adorn/sweep), implying it was excluded from festive garlands</note>.

---

### The Opinion of MESUE on Asarum.
<note>Mesue the Younger was a major, though semi-mythical, figure in medieval Arabic medicine whose works were standard in European pharmacies.</note>

Asarum is the root of a mountain herb whose leaves are angular like the leaves of Ivy; its flowers are like the flowers of Henbane <note>original: "hyoscyami"</note>, and the entire plant is aromatic and biting to the taste.

---

### The Compilation of HERMOLAU BARBARUS on Asarum.
<note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493) was an Italian scholar famous for correcting errors in the manuscripts of Pliny the Elder.</note>

Asarum, among other differences, also has softer leaves than Ivy, a root like Gallic Nard, and seeds with a warm and wine-like flavor. It flowers twice a year, in Spring and Autumn. There is an error of the scribes in Pliny, who in one place seems to order it to be dried in the sun, and in another in the shade. Unless one reads the latter passage this way: not that it *should* be dried in the shade, but that it most quickly perceives <note>meaning "suffers from"</note> mold in the shade.

<margin>
The controversy regarding Baccar and Asarum, similar and related herbs. This passage is in Book 21, Chapter 6.
</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
One must not ignore that Baccar <note>likely *Conyza squarrosa*, or Ploughman's-spikenard</note> is entirely different from Asarum, even if Pliny, in our version, attributed many of the medicines to Baccar which <term>Dioscorides</term> <note>A 1st-century Greek physician</note> assigned to Asarum. This is not surprising, since their nature is very close in power and effect. Furthermore, our "Secundus" <note>Pliny the Elder, whose full name was Gaius Plinius Secundus</note> wished for *Perpensa* or *Perpresa* (for both are read, as I explained more fully under Baccar) to be understood as Baccar, not Asarum as Dioscorides did. Conversely, the description of Asarum made by Dioscorides agrees with Baccar in many parts. First, because it yields a scent close to Cinnamon, as does Asarum. Second, because it grows in thin, non-moist soil, like Asarum. Otherwise, those who called the root of Baccar "Rustic Nard" are rebuked by Pliny, because "Rustic Nard" is properly Asarum. However, where Dioscorides says that the herb Asarum is suitable for garlands <note>original: "coronamentariam"</note>, that fits Baccar better than Asarum; for they write that it is called *Asaron* because it is *not* added to crowns and wreaths. It was once read in Dioscorides that the Romans call Asarum *Peritresa*, but we have corrected this to *Perpensa* or *Perpresa* based on Pliny. That author, I believe, names the same herb *Perpensa* in Book 21 and *Perpresa* in Book 26. There are still manuscripts in which one reads *sparsa* instead of *Perpresa*, which I consider a corruption. One also reads *Asarus*, not for Asarum, but erroneously for *Arifarum* <note>possibly *Arisarum*, or Friar's Cowl</note>. For what has the ignorance of doctors left unharmed?

---

### SELECTION of the plant according to MESUE.

The best part of the plant is the root; and the best root is that which is thicker and denser, with a subtle odor and a sharp taste with a moderate <term>astringency</term> <note>the quality of shrinking or constricting body tissues</note>.

---

### TEMPERAMENT.
<note>In Galenic medicine, the "temperament" or "complexion" of a plant describes its primary qualities (Hot, Cold, Moist, Dry) on a scale of one to four.</note>

It has a heating power, and the same degree of dryness, in the "third degree," as they call it. There are those who categorize it as hot in the second degree and dry in the third. It thin—

<meta>Catchword: It thin— [referring to "thinning" or "reducing" humors]</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
...and it opens, dissolves, and drives forth <note>original: "aperit, resoluit, & impellit"</note>.

### PREPARATION

To loosen the bowels, the herb is strengthened with whey <note>original: "aqua casei"</note>, with spikenard <note>original: "spica"</note>, and with honey-water.
It withstands moderate crushing and boiling <note>original: "concoctionem"</note>.
Some soak it in grape juice <note>original: "musto"</note> and preserve it for three months.
They use that drink for dropsy <note>an old term for swelling caused by excess fluid, or edema</note> and for ailments of the spleen.

### How Asarum appears to the author of the PANDECTS.
<note>The "Pandects" here likely refers to the *Pandectae Medicinae* by Matthaeus Sylvaticus, a 14th-century medical encyclopedia.</note>

Asarum is known as *Vulgago*, or Wild Avens <note>original: "Gariofilata agrestis"</note>, *Centuneruia*, or *Cenucerria*.

### POWERS and Benefits according to DIOSCORIDES.

It warms the body and stimulates the flow of urine.
Therefore, it is well-suited for those with "water under the skin" <note>edema or dropsy</note>.
It is also useful for long-lasting pains of the hips <note>sciatica</note>.
Its roots, when seven drachmas <note>an ancient unit of weight</note> are drunk with honey-water, induce menstruation and purge the body in the same manner as White Hellebore <note>original: "Veratri albi"; a potent and dangerous purgative</note>.

### FROM MESUE.

It induces vomiting and draws out both bile <note>original: "cholera"</note> and phlegm.
It draws back harmful humors <note>bodily fluids believed to control health</note> from the remote parts of the body.
A decoction of it is beneficial for all obstructions <note>original: "opilationibus"</note> of the liver, the spleen, and all the internal organs.
Because of this, it is given to those suffering from dropsy, jaundice <note>original: "ictericis"</note>, spleen issues, and fever.
It is among those substances that increase the production of sperm and seed.

### D O S A G E

<margin>B</margin>
The dose of its infused drink is from two *aurei* <note>a weight equivalent to a gold coin</note> up to four ounces; and in powder form, from one drachma up to two *aurei*.

### FROM MACER AEMILIUS.
<note>This refers to a famous medieval medicinal poem often attributed to "Macer," though actually written by Odo of Meung.</note>

*Asarum* in Greek is called *Vulgago* in Latin.
This herb is said to be of a hot and dry nature,
And it is assigned, as they say, the third degree in both qualities.
Taken internally, it heals the pains of the liver,
And its decoction aids in the diseases of the womb.
It is said that, when drunk, it drives away the disease of jaundice,
And it purges the chest by vomiting, just like Hellebore;
But its purging is not so violent,
Nor indeed should it be feared, if administered in this way:
<margin>A general rule for administering Simples.</margin>
First, observe the age and the strength
Of the person you wish to purge, and what time of year it is,
And if the region is burning hot or very cold,
Or if it holds a temperate middle between the two.
For it is permitted to give but little to the old and to children:
Those of middle age require more, and the youths as well:
More should be given to the stout and the strong than to the thin,
Or to weak men: and more is required in a frozen region...

PHARMACEUTICALS of SIMPLES

<margin>
C

A laxative made from Asarum.
</margin>
It should be given warm to those hardened by any labor; you shall grant more to those whom leisure has made soft. Observing these things and handling other such matters, you will safely administer not only this, but any herbs that purge by vomiting, or those that loosen the belly and the stomach. But what I have said of all herbs in common, I shall now teach specifically regarding how *Vulgago* <note>A common folk name for Asarum; original: "Vulgago"</note> is to be given. Taking thirty of its fresh leaves, add enough pure wine so that they may all be submerged. Let them be soaked in that wine for an entire night. In the morning, grind them in the wine in which they were soaked and dissolve them. Then, first give the patient enough cooked vegetables with fresh fatty pork. Let him also drink as much strong white wine as he wishes; then, provide the strained juice of Asarum to be drunk. This number of leaves is sufficient for those who are strong and large; for others (as we have said), it must be reduced according to what their strength, age, and other factors require.

### ->FROM JOANNES VIGONIUS.<-
<note>Jean de Vigo (c. 1460–1525) was an influential Italian surgeon and physician to Pope Julius II.</note>

<margin>
D
</margin>
The root, soaked in lye <note>original: "lixiuio"; an alkaline solution made from wood ashes used for washing</note>, and the head washed thereafter with it, greatly strengthens the brain.

### ->FROM SERAPION.<-
<note>Likely Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century Arabic author whose work on "simples" (individual medicinal ingredients) was widely used in Europe.</note>

When it is mixed with wine and oil and the body is anointed with it, it warms the person.

Also, seven drachmas <note>an ancient unit of weight</note> or seven *aurei* of it, taken with honey-water, purge in the same manner as Hellebore <note>a potent and often dangerous medicinal plant used as a radical purge</note>.

It is also mixed into aromatic medicinal confections.

Mixed into eye-salves <note>original: "collyrijs"</note>, it thins that membrane which is called the cornea and clears the vision.

### ->FROM PLATEARIUS.<-
<note>Matthaeus Platearius, a 12th-century physician from the school of Salerno, author of the famous herbal "Circa Instans."</note>

It cleanses wounds.

And it purges dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note> through the urine.

For this purpose, one and a half weights of *Acorus* <note>Sweet Flag</note> may be substituted for it.

### ->FROM AVICENNA.<-
<note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook for centuries.</note>

It opens and soothes all internal pains, especially when used as an infusion.

### ->From the noble herbalist HIERONYMUS.<-
<note>Likely Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), also known as Tragus, a German botanist and physician.</note>

Asarum-water, or its decoction when drunk, expels the fetus, whether living or dead; for this reason, it must not be administered to pregnant women.

It cools erysipelas <note>a bacterial skin infection often called "St. Anthony's Fire"</note> and an excessively burning liver.

# ON ALL Comfreys. Ninth Rhapsody.
<note>Latin: *Consolida*, from *consolidare* "to make solid." This refers to a group of plants used in historical medicine to mend broken bones and "consolidate" or heal wounds.</note>

## ¶ Nomenclature of Rock Comfrey.
Greek, Symphyton Petraion <note>original: *συμφύτον. πετραῖον.*</note>.
Latin, Rock Comfrey. Lesser Comfrey.
German, **Wall-root. Bone-well.** <note>original: *Walwurtz. Beinwel.*</note>

## ¶ NOMENCLATURE of Greater Comfrey.
Greek, Symphyton. Pekton <note>original: *συμφύτον. πηκτὸν.* The word *pekton* implies something "fixed" or "congealed."</note>.
Roman, Solidago <note>Meaning "the wound-sealer."</note>. Greater Comfrey. Greater Anagallis.
German, **Wall-root. Black-root.** <note>original: *Walwurtz. Schwarzwurtz.*</note>

## OPINIONS & pronouncements of the ANCIENTS regarding Comfreys.

### DIOSCORIDES Book 2, on Rock Comfrey.
Rock Comfrey <note>original: *Symphyton Petræon*</note> grows on rocks. It has branches similar to Oregano, and heads like Thyme. The whole plant is woody and fragrant, with a sweet taste and it provokes saliva. It has a long root, reddish in color, about the thickness of a finger.

### ON THE SECOND TYPE OF COMFREY.
The other Comfrey, however, sends up from itself a stem two cubits <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches or 45 cm.</note> high; it is smooth, thick, angular, and hollow in the manner of a Sow-thistle <note>original: *Sonchus*</note>. Around the stem are leaves spaced at small intervals—hairy, narrow, and oblong, approaching the shape of the leaves of Ox-tongue, which they call Bugloss. Along the angles of the stem, protruding from the hollow "armpits" of the narrow leaves, it has certain growths where the flowers are yellow, similar to Rue, and seeds like those of Mullein <note>original: *Verbascus*</note>.
<sig>B</sig>

### PLINY Book 27, Chapter 6.
We call it Alum <note>original: *Alum*, a plant name used by Pliny, likely distinct from the mineral.</note>, the Greeks call it Rock Comfrey; it is similar to Ox-tongue with small leaves, three or four branches from the root, and tips like Thyme. It is woody, fragrant, sweet to the taste, and provokes saliva, with a long, reddish root. It grows on rocks, and for that reason, it was named "Rock-dwelling" <note>original: *Petræum*</note>.

### APULEIUS.
Comfrey grows in stony and woody places; it has a pleasant smell and provokes saliva. Its branches are like Oregano or the heads of Thyme. The root is long and tawny, a finger's width in thickness. It has a stalk two cubits high, jointed and empty. On this are hairy leaves, narrow and long, with additional growths. It has a black flower and fruit without seed, similar to the fluff of bark, causing itching. The roots are clay-like on the outside, and possess a thickening <note>original: *densabilis*, referring to its ability to bind wounds</note> power.

### AUTHOR OF THE PANDECTS.
<margin>Tormentil is a species of Comfrey.</margin>
Besides Comfrey <note>original: *Symphytum*</note>, there is another "Healer" <note>original: *Consolida*</note>, called "Red," or Bistort, or Tormentil: and it has the power of consolidating.

### HERMOLAUS BARBARUS, on Rock Comfrey.
Rock Comfrey we call *Alum* in French; it has small leaves and three or four branches from the root. It grows on rocks. The Greeks gave it the name *Symphyton* because it consolidates <note>The Greek *symphyein* means "to grow together."</note>. <margin>Quince-herb.</margin> The Venetians call this *Cotonea* <note>original: *Cotonea*, likely referring to the fuzzy, "quince-like" texture of the leaves.</note>; as Pliny says, it has a root like a rose, in some places white, in others black.

->SIMPLE Medicines<-

<margin>C</margin>
## THE SAME AUTHOR ON GREATER COMFREY.

Galen names this *Symphyton mega* <note>original: "Symphyton mega," meaning Great Comfrey</note>, that is, the Great variety. It is neither sweet to the taste nor fragrant like the one mentioned above <note>Referring to Rock Comfrey</note>. More recent herbalists establish three types of Comfrey, besides the Rock variety, which they do not even recognize. First, the **Large**. Second, the **Smaller**, but with a root that is white inside and out, shaped almost like a round bulb. Third, the **Smallest**, with a purple flower spike; its leaf is not like Oregano (as the Rock variety is), but it grows in damp places with a woody, useless root that is neither fragrant nor sweet, nor does it provoke saliva—all of which are traits found in the Rock variety.

### MARCELLUS VIRGILIUS.
<note>Marcello Virgilio Adriani (1464–1521) was a Florentine scholar known for translating Dioscorides.</note>

The herbalists of our age boast that they have discovered many other types of *Consolida* <note>Comfrey or "Wound-knitter"</note> beyond those described by Dioscorides; we leave these to be judged by the physicians and those scholars.

### THE ERROR OF AVICENNA CONCERNING COMFREY and "Sucutum," which Manardus discovered. From the 6th Book of Letters, Letter 6.
<note>Giovanni Manardi (1462–1536) was a physician who criticized the errors in medieval Arabic-to-Latin translations of medical texts.</note>

<margin>
The Error of Avicenna.
D
</margin>
Regarding the third point you ask about, *Sucutum* <note>A corrupted name in medieval Latin translations of the Persian physician Avicenna</note>: no one who compares Avicenna’s chapter on *Sucutum* (Book 2, Chapter 642) with Dioscorides’ chapter on Comfrey can doubt that Avicenna’s *Sucutum* and Dioscorides’ *Symphyton* are the same thing. It happened through an error, either by the translator or by Avicenna himself, that it was called *Sempervivum* <note>Houseleek</note>. It is clear that Avicenna erred, or rather did not know what it was, from the fact that he offers various opinions on it in both his second and third books, yet adheres to none of them above the others. In the second book, he says some thought it was Houseleek, others the seed of a certain Mandrake, and others something else. In the third book, in the chapter on coughing up blood, he offers two opinions on it. For after <margin>Jacques Despars.</margin> he had said it was Houseleek, he adds another opinion from a certain "Aggregator" <note>Referring to a compiler of medical texts, likely Serapion the Younger</note>. He is not speaking of a different medicine, as Jacques Despars <note>original: "Iacobus de Partibus," a 15th-century French physician</note> believed, but says of the same *Sucutum* that a certain man wrote in his compilations that it is a species of *Calamentum*—that is, a type of Oregano—meaning it resembles it. It is clear that Avicenna calls Oregano "*Calamentum*" in his second book, chapter 158, where he treats all species of Oregano under that name. Then he adds that the same man said it grows among stones. Dioscorides ascribes both traits to the first species of Comfrey: namely, that it grows among rocks and bears a resemblance to Oregano; thirdly, along with these, that it is useful for coughing up blood. Therefore, you have guessed better than Avicenna: both that *Sucutum* is Comfrey, and that both its species are commonly called *Consolida*. The **Greater** variety grows everywhere <margin>Lucanica Ala</margin> among us, and from the likeness of its root, they call it *Lucanica*; those in Mirandola call it *Ala*, meaning (or rather, they ought to say) *Alum*. For Pliny so names the first species in his 26th and 27th books: growing on rocks, with thin Oregano-like branches, thyme-like heads on the tips, bushy, fragrant, with a sweet taste that provokes saliva, and a long, reddish root the thickness of a finger. If you have seen it (as you write) and have it with you, know that you would do me a great favor if you sent it to be seen.

## OUR CRITIQUE.

No one doubts that the name *Solidago* <note>Woundwort or Comfrey</note> was given because of its effect—namely, from "gluing" and "fixing" [wounds] together, which it does better than many other plants. Therefore, nothing prevents the name from being applied to other herbs that have equal power and the same temperament. If we grant this, then those who today show four or five species of it—namely the greater, smaller, middle, and royal—do not seem to me to be entirely hallucinating. We therefore willingly permit the author of the *Pandects* <note>A medical encyclopedia</note> his *Tormentilla*; the common herbalists their "Royal Comfrey" (commonly called **Larkspur** <note>original: "Rittersporen"</note>); and others their *Anagallis* <note>Pimpernel</note>. <margin>Theobald Fettich</margin> We also recognize under that name the tiny *Solidago* that spreads on the ground, which Master Theobald Fettich showed us, and which he calls **Daisy** <note>original: "Maßlieb"</note> or **Little Meadow Saffron** <note>original: "Zeitlößlin"</note>. I would prefer his evidence over that of a hundred "dreamers" who, lacking both learning and experience, pronounce judgment on any herb they please.

<meta>This page continues the medical and botanical profile of Comfrey (Consolida/Symphytum), shifting from the botanical descriptions of the previous page to the medicinal "temperament" and specific therapeutic applications cited by classical and Renaissance authorities.</meta>

...of the First VOLUME.

### TEMPERAMENT.
<margin>A</margin>
According to Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of the Roman Empire; his "temperament" theory dominated medicine for 1,500 years</note>, it consists of contrary powers. For it has a cutting power, by which it purges pus trapped in the chest and lungs. At the same time, it has the property of assisting with the drawing out of blood. Because of its moist nature when chewed, it soothes thirst and heals roughness in the windpipe. Therefore, it is applied to inflamed intestines, and is drunk with honey for ruptures and convulsions.

### JOHN OF VIGO.
<note>Giovanni da Vigo (1450–1525) was an Italian surgeon famous for his work on wounds and surgery.</note>
Comfrey is warm and dry, with a temperate heat and a viscous moisture.

### POWERS AND BENEFITS FROM DIOSCORIDES.
<note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD) wrote 'De Materia Medica,' the primary source for herbal medicine in the West.</note>
Crushed and drunk, it is beneficial for spitting up blood and for internal ruptures.
Applied as a salve, it glues together fresh wounds.
It is usefully applied with leaves of Groundsel <note>Senecio</note> for inflammations, especially of the seat <note>the rectum</note> and the intestines.
It restrains hernias <note>term: enterocelas (hernias of the intestine)</note>.

### FROM PLINY.
<note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the encyclopedic 'Natural History.'</note>
If it is ground between two stones, it miraculously extinguishes carbuncles <note>term: antraces (malignant skin ulcers or boils)</note> and checks dysentery.

### FROM APULEIUS. <gloss><unclear>Suth way Grey</unclear></gloss>
<note>Pseudo-Apuleius, the author of a 4th-century herbal frequently cited in the Middle Ages.</note>
For the excessive flow of women <note>menstruation</note>, give the powder of the Comfrey herb, very finely ground, to drink in wine, and it will stop the flow.
Boil the warm ash of the root and give it with honey on an empty stomach; it will heal those with convulsions, internal ruptures, or those suffering in the chest.
<margin>B</margin>
For stomach pain, if you eat it with vinegar-garum <note>term: oxygaro (a mixture of vinegar and fermented fish sauce used in ancient medicine)</note>, you will feel a great benefit.
Against a cough, boil the roots of the Comfrey herb in a cauldron with honey, pepper, and castoreum <note>term: castoreo (a secretion from beaver glands used as a stimulant and antispasmodic)</note> until reduced by a quarter; give this in old wine to drink on an empty stomach.
This herb has such a power of binding that if beef is chopped up and put into a pot, and you add two drachms <note>A drachm was roughly 3.9 grams</note> of this root, the cooked meat will stick back together into one mass.

### JOHN OF VIGO.
All types of Comfrey have the power of consolidating and "gluing" together fresh wounds.

### EXPERIMENTS.
It miraculously restores mouth ulcers, cracks in the skin, and condylomas <note>term: condylomata (wart-like growths or swellings)</note>.
Likewise, it heals fresh wounds when its water or juice is sprinkled on a cloth; taken daily at a weight of 15 ounces, it heals internal wounds and ruptures.
It checks burning convulsions, as well as any other burns and inflammations.
The juice, mixed with oil, stops blood.
In short, it is most conveniently applied to all wounds.

VOLUME One
A, h

# ON SANICLE.
## Tenth Rhapsody.

### NOMENCLATURE.
Latin names: <term>Diapensia</term> <note>Derived from the Greek "dia pason," suggesting a medicine that acts through all parts of the body as a "cure-all."</note>, <term>Sennicula</term>, <term>Sanicula</term> <note>From the Latin "sanare," meaning to heal.</note>.
German name: <term>Sanickel</term>.

### OPINIONS OF THE WRITERS.
#### The Opinion of ERMOLAO BARBARO concerning Sanicle, from his commentary on DIOSCORIDES, Book 2, in the entry for *Peplis*.
<note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493) was a Venetian scholar famous for correcting errors in ancient scientific texts.</note>
There are some among the Greeks who take <term>Peplium</term> <note>A type of spurge.</note> for <term>Senna</term>; Isaac <note>original: "Isacius"; likely the 10th-century physician Isaac Judaeus.</note> is among them. I believe it to be a different genus, since Senna bears pods and seeds within them, whereas <term>Peplis</term> does not. It is a transalpine herb with leaves like those of a <term>Grapevine</term> or <term>Wild Celery</term> <note>original: "Apij"</note>, which turn reddish. At the ends of the leaf segments, there are certain spots and also red stems at the root, which is composed of many fibers; it has tiny, blackish heads at the top of the stalk. They recommend its juice as a drink for the wounded.

### THE OPINION OF PANDOLFO COLLENUCCIO concerning Sanicle, from his book defending Pliny, in the entry for *Pentaphyllon*.
<note>Pandolfo Collenuccio (1444–1504) was an Italian humanist who wrote a famous defense of Pliny the Elder against contemporary critics.</note>
<margin>B <image-desc>A hand icon (manicule) pointing right to highlight an important passage.</image-desc></margin> In Venice, in the street they call the Apothecaries’ Row, there is the shop of a notable pharmacist which has for its title and sign "The Ethiopian’s Head." In that shop is a herbal book painted with such skill and diligence that you would believe the plants were born on those pages, not merely depicted. In it, we saw a plant painted with exactly the same characteristics we have mentioned here: having five leaves—which themselves had longer, curved angles as we have depicted—but also fruits that you might call strawberries. Beside the herb itself, the Latin name <term>Sanicula</term> and the German <term>Sanickel</term> were written. Cited therein as writing about Sanicle are Galen in his *Dynamidia* <note>A medieval medical text on the powers of herbs attributed to the ancient physician Galen.</note>, and Peter of Spain—the man who later held the Papacy and was called John XXI; he wrote the book on medicine titled *The Treasure of the Poor* <note>original: "Pauperum thesaurus"; a popular medical manual for those who could not afford expensive doctors.</note>. Also mentioned are a certain Bishop of Cervia <note>Theodoric Borgognoni (1205–1298), a pioneering surgeon.</note>, Mapheus of Lodi, and Gilbert the Englishman, a surgeon. Whether this Sanicle is the same as <term>Pentaphyllum</term> <note>Cinquefoil or Five-leaf.</note>, I have no reason to affirm, nor do I see why I should deny it.

### According to the common opinion of the Herbalists.
<term>Diapensia</term> in Greek; in Latin, <term>Greater Ferraria</term> <note>original: "Ferraria maior"</note>, or <term>Lesser Consolida</term> <note>original: "Consolida minor"; "Consolida" refers to plants that "consolidate" or knit wounds together.</note>, or <term>Sanicle</term>.

### The Noble Herbalist JEROME.
<note>Likely referring to Hieronymus Brunschwig or Hieronymus Bock, influential early German botanists.</note>
<term>Sanicle</term> is called by the Latins <term>Greater Ferraria</term> or <term>Lesser Consolida</term>; it is a wound-healing herb about the height of a palm, or a little more. There is also another wild species, rarer and less examined by herbalists, which appears and flowers only in May with white, quite elegant blossoms; from then on, it gradually disappears and hides itself.

### OUR JUDGMENT.

<margin>C</margin>
I do not find more about Sanicle among approved authors, nor have I discovered what it was called in Greek, or even in the works of Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD, author of "De Materia Medica."</note>. We have conjectured much back and forth, but since such divination is vain when not confirmed by some certain authority of a writer, we have not wished to pronounce anything rashly. Rather, may the gods punish those lazy and ungrateful herbalists of the previous century, who neglected it so much in their descriptions, or rather changed its genuine and true name into a barbarous one. Meanwhile, I strongly approve of the opinion of common herbalists, who establish this as the lesser <term>Solidago</term> <note>From the Latin "solidare," meaning to make solid or to fasten; a name given to plants believed to "knit" wounds or bones back together.</note>. 

<margin>,,</margin>
We say this along with Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,300 years.</note>: let names and words depart, let us hold fast to the thing itself <note>original: "facessent nomina & uerba, rem teneamus"</note>. Therefore, regarding the plant and its effects, since much experience is already established, we leave its Greek nomenclature—and the names under which it is read in Dioscorides and Pliny, and whether it is a true <term>Penthaphyllon</term> <note>Literally "five-leaved," usually referring to Cinquefoil.</note> or rather a species of it—to those with leisure and to those more skilled than us.

### CONSTITUTION.

It is found to be hot and dry, with a delicate and most pure juice.

### POWERS AND BENEFITS.

It provides all the same benefits as <term>Consolida</term> <note>A general term for "healing" or "knitting" herbs, often Comfrey.</note>.
Practitioners and herbalists add that its juice, applied as an ointment or decoction, represses tumors, both in humans and in livestock.
<margin>D</margin>
Also, its powder mixed with honey and licorice juice, drunk while fasting, cleanses all inflamed intestines and those covered in phlegm. 
The same effect is achieved by its decoction with rose honey and added sugar. Its primary use is in wound-healing drinks, alongside <term>Solidago</term> and <term>Periwinkle</term> <note>original: "Peruinca"</note>.

### HARVESTING.

It is gathered in the month of May and is either ground into a powder or dried in the shade.

# CONCERNING ROYAL CONSOLID,
### Eleventh Rhapsody.

## NOMENCLATURES.

In Latin, Royal Consound <note>original: "Consolida regalis," known today as Larkspur</note>.
In German, **Knight’s Spurs** <note>original: "Rittersporen"</note>.

## POWERS AND BENEFITS.

Its flowers, when crushed and steeped in rose water, clear away redness of the eyes; indeed, it is an "eye herb" through and through, which easily cures whatever ailments of the eyes occur, and which may even heal them simply by being gazed upon frequently.

It is held in high esteem by scholars, along with Rue <note>original: "Ruta," a bitter herb also used to improve eyesight</note>. For they believe that by looking at it frequently, they will never suffer from eye strain. For this reason, they should hang it in their studies <note>original: "musaeis," referring to a place of study or a library</note>.

Practitioners <note>original: "experimentatores"</note> use its distilled water or a decoction of the flowers against the "black plague" <note>likely referring to dark skin discolorations or severe infectious illness</note>, fevers and inflammations, coughs, tumors, poisons, vomiting, and "choleric passion" <note>an imbalance of the yellow bile humor, often causing digestive distress</note>, as well as against difficulty in urinating, kidney stones, sciatica, and hip pain. It is likewise used to move the bowels.

<margin>D</margin>
Furthermore, for one who has fallen into a faint <note>original: "syncopin," a loss of consciousness</note> because of the heat, if you offer one ounce of Royal Consound water with three drams of Borage and Bugloss flowers, they will be immediately revived.

## TEMPERAMENT.

Of a hot and dry temperament <note>In the Galenic system, plants were classified by these qualities to balance the "humors" of the body</note>.

# **Tormentil.**

## On TORMENTIL, and the true Cinquefoil.
### Twelfth Rhapsody.

## ¶ NOMENCLATURES.
**Greek**: Seven-leaf <note>original: "ἑπτάφυλλον" (Heptaphyllon), referring to the number of leaflets</note>.
**Latin**: Tormentilla <note>derived from "tormentum," referring to the relief of abdominal pain</note>, Bistort <note>original: "Bistorta," though usually a different plant, here associated by the author</note>.
**German**: **Tormentil. Red-root. Blood-root.** <note>original: "Rotwurtz. Blůtwurtz," referring to the red interior of the rhizome and its use to stop bleeding</note>.

## OPINIONS OF THE WRITERS.
### The Opinion of HERMOLAUS BARBARUS regarding Tormentil

<margin>Book 2 of Dioscorides, under the entry for "Saxiphagon" <note>Stone-breaker</note>.</margin>
SOME have said that the shape of the leaves of the Saxifrage <note>original: "Saxifragae," plants believed to break up kidney stones</note> is like that of wheat; others say it is similar to the Sea Bramble <note>original: "marinae Bati"</note>, and others to what is commonly called Tormentil. However, as they would have it, Tormentil is similar to the herb Cinquefoil <note>original: "Quinquefolio," or Five-leaf</note>, except that it has nearly seven leaves, not five.

<margin>C</margin>
### IN THE SAME BOOK under the term Cinquefoil <note>original: "Pentaphyllon," from the Greek for five leaves</note>.

Hippocrates seems to have known two types of Cinquefoil <note>original: "Quincq;folia"</note>. One is the white variety, which is more herb-like and grows taller from the ground. The other is the black variety, which is lower to the ground. There is also the plant commonly called Tormentil, which is very similar to Cinquefoil, except that it has seven leaves instead of five. We may call it the Seven-leaf <note>original: "Heptaphyllon"</note>; it is from its root that apothecary shops—if it pleases the Gods!—substitute for viper’s flesh in the production of theriac lozenges <note>Theriac was a famous ancient "universal antidote" that traditionally required the flesh of vipers; the author is skeptical of this herbal substitution</note>, because, as they believe, the plant is sometimes seen to behave in the manner of a viper.

->SIMON OF GENOA <note>Simon Ianuensis, a 13th-century medical lexicographer</note> on Tormentil.<-

Tormentil, Potentilla, Red Comfrey <note>original: "Consolida rubea"</note>, a species of Seven-leaf <note>Heptaphyllon</note>, similar to Cinquefoil, except that it has seven leaves where the other has five, and it has a red root.

->The Opinion of GIOVANNI MANARDI on Tormentil<-
->and Cinquefoil, from the 6th book of his Letters. In a Letter<-
->to Francesco Graballo.<-

<margin>Tormentil is the true Cinquefoil according to Manardi.</margin>
Regarding Cinquefoil, I would gladly understand whether you have accepted this common plant that grows everywhere even on paved roads. I do not think its root should be used, but rather the root of the plant they call Tormentil. Although we see it mostly as a Seven-leaf plant in Italy, here—that is, in Pannonia <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary and surrounding regions</note>—I have more often seen it as a Cinquefoil <note>having five leaves</note>.

->The Opinion of the Author of the PANDECTAE <note>Mattheaus Silvaticus, author of a 14th-century medical encyclopedia</note>.<-

<margin>D</margin>
Bistort <note>original: "Bistorta," meaning "twice-twisted"</note>, or Red Comfrey in Latin, or Tormentil; in Arabic, *Busereke*. It is a herb similar to Cinquefoil, except it has seven leaves that are hairy on both sides; and therefore it is called Seven-leaf <note>Heptaphyllon</note>. Its root is red and twisted, similar to Galangal <note>a ginger-like medicinal root</note>, but it lacks the sharp taste. Its flower is golden-yellow.

But it should be noted that there is a species of Bistort having leaves similar to Sharp Dock <note>original: "Lapatho acuto"</note>, except the color of the leaves is sky-blue on one side and green on the other. Its flower is red, and the root is red; this is called Greater Burdock by some, and Lesser Burdock by others. Its medicinal power in all respects is like the first species, but weaker.

->OUR JUDGMENT.<-

I have nothing to answer, except this: if Tormentil were not the Seven-leaf plant, I would easily allow myself to be drawn to the opinion of Barbarus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus, mentioned on the previous page</note>, believing it to be a relative of the Cinquefoil. Indeed, the descriptions of Theophrastus and Pliny fit the plant so well that no painter could have depicted it more elegantly or carefully with a needle.
<margin>Pliny, Book 25, Chapter 9</margin>
Pliny says: Cinquefoil, when dug up, has a red root; as it matures, this turns black and becomes angular. It takes its name from the number of its leaves. The herb itself begins and ends its life cycle with the Grapevine. These details Pliny borrowed from Theophrastus. Indeed, Tormentil is twisted; then it is red; and it does not appear early, but when the vines are already flowering. This is perhaps why the herbalists also called it "Bistort" <note>Twice-twisted</note>. And because it is also a wound-herb, they added the name "Comfrey" <note>original: "Consolida," from the Latin to make whole or solid</note>. Although there is a controversy regarding the leaves, it can be easily cleared up because in certain places it is found not only as a Seven-leaf, but even...

It dries and heals cancers, fistulas, and **carcinomas** <note>malignant tumors or spreading ulcers</note>.
In short, in whatever way and for whatever diseases you apply it, it is believed to be healthful.

VOLUME One.
<sig>A</sig>

# CONCERNING BETONY, Twelfth Rhapsody. <note>The author uses "Rhapsody" in the classical sense of a "miscellany" or "collection of texts" regarding a specific subject.</note>

## ¶ Nomenclatures. <note>The names of the plant in various languages.</note>
**Greek**, *kestron* <note>original: κέστρον</note>, *psychotrophon* <note>original: ψυχότροφον; literally "soul-nourishing" or "growing in the cold"</note>, <gloss>divine root <note>original: θεία ῥίζα</gloss></note>
**Latin**, *Vetonica*. Betony. Divine root. *Chiron* <note>Named after Chiron the Centaur, a legendary healer</note>. *Serratula* <note>literally "the little saw," referring to the leaf edges</note>.
**German**, **Betonien kraut** <note>Betony herb</note>. **Brun Betonien** <note>Brown Betony</note>.

# OPINIONS OF AUTHORS, regarding the herb Betony.

### The Description of DIOSCORIDES on Betony, Book 2. <note>Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD) was a Greek physician and the primary authority on herbal medicine in the Renaissance.</note>
Betony is a herb having a four-angled, thin stem, a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in height, and sometimes smaller: the leaves are long and soft, similar to those of an Oak, divided by notches around the edges, and fragrant. Among these, the larger ones are those that grow at the root. At the top of the stems is the seed, spiked in the manner of Savory. The leaves are gathered and dried: their use is very frequent. It has slender roots, like those of Hellebore <note>original: *Veratri*</note>, which induce phlegmatic vomiting when drunk in sweet water.

### The Portrayal of BETONY according to PLINY. <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of Natural History.</note>
<margin>On the discoverers of Betony.</margin>
The Vettones in Spain discovered it; it is called *Betonica* in Gaul, but in Italy *Serratula*, and by the Greeks *kestron* or *psychotrophon*; it is highly praised above all others.

It grows with an angular stem, two cubits high, spreading from the root leaves almost like those of Dock <note>original: *Lapathum*; a common broad-leafed weed</note>, serrated, with a purple seed.

### CRITIQUE OF PLINY by Niccolò Leoniceno. <note>Leoniceno (1428–1524) was a famous Italian physician known for correcting errors in Pliny's natural history.</note>
<sig>B</sig>
<margin>Pliny’s slip regarding Betony.</margin>
Pliny describes Betony (called so by the Romans and *Cestrum* by the Greeks) as having the leaf of a Dock. Dioscorides, however, with whom the senses <note>observation</note> better agree, says it has the leaf of an Oak. Dioscorides records that the *other* Betony, which is called by the other name *Britannica* <note>identified as Water Dock</note>, has leaves like Dock: so it is likely that Pliny described one for the other.

### DEFENSE OF PLINY by Pandolfo Collenuccio against Leoniceno. <note>Collenuccio (1444–1504) was a humanist who defended Pliny against the "corrections" of Leoniceno.</note>
With equal impudence it is claimed that it is "likely" Pliny erred in describing Betony, because he described the leaf not as an oak (as Dioscorides does) but similar to Dock; and because that description seemed to fit the herb *Britannica* better in Dioscorides' opinion. But it is truly strange how this man—otherwise not unlearned—appeared as a careless accuser, who neither weighs nor reports Pliny's words. "Betony," says Pliny, "is called *Serratula* by our people, spreading from the root leaves almost like Dock, serrated." Who, recognizing Dock itself and Betony (for there is no one who does not know both), would not say Betony was graphically described by Pliny? Seeing that it is called *Serratula* [the little saw], and has leaves "almost like Dock" and "serrated," is it not described somewhat better than by Dioscorides' comparison to an oak? For it is not Betony itself (which is entirely unlike an oak) but rather *Trixago* <note>Germander</note> and *Hierabotane* <note>Vervain</note> that are described with the leaf of an oak. Therefore, Pliny did not simply say "leaves of Dock," but added "serrated," which Niccolò kept silent about or ignored. Since in the description of the very well-known herb *Britannica*, Pliny thought it sufficient to say in the same book that the leaves were "black and oblong," and did not add "serrated," because they are not distinguished by those notches by which Betony is. What could be said more coldly or unfairly than to say Pliny erred because he did not use Dioscorides' words and comparisons in describing herbs, but applied other signs that seemed more appropriate?

### THE WONDER OF ERMOLAO BARBARO concerning Betony. <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493) was another humanist scholar who worked on Pliny's texts.</note>
It is a wonder to some that Pliny writes that the leaves of Betony are like *Rumex* <note>Dock</note>...

<summary>This page lists the various Greek, Latin, and German names for Betony and documents a scholarly Renaissance debate over whether Pliny the Elder or Dioscorides provided a more accurate botanical description of the plant's leaves.</summary>

# PHARMACY OF SIMPLES
<meta>catchword: propin- (continuing to "propinquis" on the next page)</meta>

C similar things, which Dioscorides assigns to Britannica: <note>original: "Britannicæ"</note> since they are seen rather as Oak Betony. <note>original: "Betonicæ quernæ"</note> Nor is it less a matter of wonder why it deserved two mentions. Unless someone contends that two kinds of Betony were demonstrated to us by Dioscorides: even Paulus Aegineta <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note> recognizes two appearances of Betony, with equal effect, as we have said before.

## THE OPINION OF APULEIUS
## regarding Betony.

<margin>The power of Betony is excessively superstitious.</margin>
The Greeks have called Betony, or Britannica, *Cestron* <note>original: κέστρον</note>, and *Prionites* <note>original: πριονίτης; "saw-like"</note>, others *Pyrine*, others *Alianthon*, and others *Psychotrophon* <note>original: ψυχότροφον; "soul-nourishing" or "growing in the cold"</note>. Likewise they have called it *Thyarizon*, *Seropodion*, and *Pandiona*; the Prophets <note>Refers to a traditional list of mystical or esoteric plant names attributed to Egyptian or "prophetic" sources</note> call it *Hierathiorine*. The Romans call it Betony, some *Serrata* <note>Serrated</note>, and *Ruszmarina* <note>Though usually meaning Rosemary, here used as a synonym for Betony</note>. This herb grows in meadows, mountainous places, and shaded spots around thickets. It guards the souls and bodies of men, and protects and defends against spells, dangers, and even terrifying visions during night walks, and is holy in every respect. It is called *Cestron* and *Psychotrophon* because it is found in cold places. It has thin and reddish roots, a very slender stem, over a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in length and four-angled, with leaves similar to the Oak, of a good scent, and with seed at the top of the stem in a spike, in the manner of Savory <note>original: "Thymbræ"</note>.

D These are mostly the words of Apuleius, or perhaps Antonius Musa <note>The personal physician to the Emperor Augustus; authorship of these texts was often debated in the Renaissance</note>. For those who recently appended the volume on the praises of Betony to Apuleius from the Basel edition are in doubt about the author. However, Dioscorides does not differ much in his description of the second Betony <note>original: "Vetonitæ"</note>: yet everyone considers that chapter to be adulterated and spurious.

## CONFUTATION of the Apuleian description, and
## the chapter in DIOSCORIDES on Betony, by
## MARCELLUS VERGILIUS. <note>Marcello Adriani (1464–1521), a Florentine humanist known for his commentary on Dioscorides.</note>

<margin>Against herbal superstitions.</margin>
In nearly all the Greek manuscripts, a second chapter on Betony has been added to the chapter on Britannica, superstitiously and imprudently. For in the most ancient Greek and Latin manuscripts of Dioscorides that we possess, it is read nowhere. Nor is it likely that this writer, after having treated the whole of Betony once, would have to act on the same subject again after another chapter intervened. Add to this that nothing is more unworthy of his majesty, nor should be less believed, than when some superstitious thing pertaining to our religion <note>A reference to folk-religious or magical practices often found in Pseudo-Apuleius</note> is taught by him. Readers will be able to judge what we say from those things which other interpreters have rendered. It did not please us to mix religion with nature, and to make those things the same which are distant from this writer by such a long interval. The vain mortality of men introduces these things first: soon imprudence and a zeal for health take them up, and once taken up, they are carried through many hands for a long time.

## IMAGE of Betony from SERAPION. <note>Serapion the Younger, an influential 12th or 13th-century Arabic author on medicinal simples.</note>

*Kastara*, that is, Betony, is a herb which grows every year, having a subtle stalk, the length of which is one arm’s length or more, and it is square: and it has long, soft leaves, similar in their shape to the leaves of acorns <note>referring to Oak leaves</note>, and in their notches, having a good scent: and the leaves which are near- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "propinquis" for the page break.</note>

VOLUME the First.

<margin>A</margin>
The leaves near the ground are larger than the other leaves; and at the top of the stalk, the seed is gathered together, much like the cluster of an ear of grain. It is similar to Savory <note>original: *Satureia*</note>, which is called *Thymbra*, and it has roots like Hellebore. Only the leaves are used.

### ITS TEMPERAMENT.

It is hot and drying in the third degree <note>Galenic medicine categorized drugs into four "degrees" of intensity for their primary qualities—hot, cold, wet, or dry. The third degree indicates a potent medicinal effect.</note>, as Platearius <note>Johannes Platearius, a 12th-century physician from the famous medical school at Salerno</note> says. Its power is to cleanse wounds and encourage the growth of new flesh.

### ITS POWERS & Benefits

#### FROM DIOSCORIDES.

Betony leaves should be administered to those with ruptures or convulsions, and to women suffering from ailments of the womb or to ease uterine contractions <note>original: *uteri strangulatus*</note>, in the weight of one drachm <note>An ancient unit of weight, roughly 3.5 grams</note> mixed with hydromel <note>A mixture of honey and water</note>.

Three drachms in a sextarius <note>Roughly a pint or half-liter</note> of wine are drunk to counter the bites of serpents. The herb is applied as a plaster with great benefit to wounds inflicted by a serpent. It is also effective against poisons when one drachm is drunk with wine. If it is taken beforehand, it will ensure that any poison swallowed does no harm. It promotes the flow of urine. It moves the bowels. It treats the "falling sickness" <note>original: *comicialibus*; epilepsy</note> and the insane when drunk with water; it also treats ailments of the liver and spleen when a drachm’s weight is taken in oxymel <note>original: *acetum mulsum*; a syrup of vinegar and honey</note>.

<margin>B</margin>
It aids digestion if one swallows a portion the size of a bean with cooked honey after dinner. It is administered in a similar way to those suffering from acid reflux. For those with stomach trouble, it is beneficial to chew it and swallow the juice, provided that a draught of wine diluted with water is taken afterward. It is given to those spitting blood in doses of three obols <note>A smaller unit of weight, roughly 0.5 to 0.7 grams</note> with a cup of diluted wine or milk. It is used with water for sciatica and pains of the kidneys and bladder. For "water under the skin" <note>original: *aquae inter cutem*; dropsy or edema</note>, two drachms are taken with hydromel. It restores those laboring under the "royal disease" <note>original: *regio morbo*; jaundice</note>. It brings on the menses when a drachm’s weight is drunk with wine. Four drachms drunk in ten cups of hydromel purge the bowels. Taken with honey, it helps with consumption <note>original: *tabem*</note> and the coughing up of pus. The leaves are dried, ground, and stored in an earthenware vessel.

#### FROM PLINY.

A wine and a vinegar are made from Betony for the stomach and for clarity of vision. It holds such great glory that a house in which it is planted is considered safe from all manner of misfortunes <note>original: *piaculis*; often referring to religious stains or the need for atonement</note>. It is believed that such power resides in Betony that if serpents are enclosed in a circle of it, they will lash themselves to death.

### FRACTURES OF THE HEAD.

The herb Betony, crushed and placed upon a blow to the head, heals the wound with wonder...

[When] given, it will move the belly.

### For pain of the LOINS.
Let the patient drink, while fasting, three drachms <note>A unit of weight roughly equal to 3.5 grams.</note> of Betony with three cyathi <note>A small cup measure, approximately 45ml.</note> of Aminean wine <note>original: "uini Amynæi"; an ancient high-quality white wine, often praised by Roman authors like Virgil.</note> and seventeen grains of crushed pepper, warmed; he will be cured.
Betony given in a drink of mead <note>original: "mulso"; honeyed wine.</note>—or in warm water for one suffering from fever—is believed to heal pains of the loins <note>The lower back or lumbar region.</note>.

### For COLIC.
The herb Betony is equally effective when taken with a dry wine.

### For a COUGH.
Let the patient take two ounces of the herb Betony with honey for eight days.

### For the pattern of DAILY FEVER.
Administer two drachms of the herb Betony and one of Lamb's Tongue <term>Arnoglossa: the herb commonly known today as Broadleaf Plantain (Plantago major), used for its cooling and astringent properties</term> in four cyathi of warm water to be drunk at the onset of the fever fit.

### For the patterns of TERTIAN and QUARTAN FEVERS.
You shall mix together three drachms of the herb Betony, one ounce of Attic honey <note>Honey from the Attica region of Greece, historically considered the finest and clearest.</note>, and three cyathi of warm water; give it to drink before the onset of the fit, and the patient will be wonderfully healed.

### For pain of the BLADDER.
Boil down four drachms of Betony and three scruples <note>A small weight, about 1.3 grams.</note> of celery root: let the celery roots be boiled in a sextarius <note>Roughly equivalent to a pint or 500ml.</note> of water until reduced to half, then finally the Betony should be mixed in and offered as a drink. They drive out the pain so effectively that it never returns to its former place.

### For the STONE.
It is beneficial to drink three drachms of Betony in the best vinegar, along with eight cyathi of honey and warm water.

### For curing DROPSY, likewise for women laboring in CHILDBIRTH, and also for those who suffer from FEVER.
One drachm of Betony drunk in one cyathus of warm water provides a remedy.
Likewise, two drachms of Betony in four cyathi of warm water if there is no fever; if fever is present, administer it in two cyathi of wine; it brings relief.

### For PARALYSIS.
Betony, crushed and applied as a poultice, is believed to glue together even severed nerves and to heal them thoroughly.

### Against the SHIVERS.
Give two drachms of Betony in two cyathi of dry wine to drink; likewise in an equal measure of warm water, at the onset of the chills <note>original: "horrores"; referring to the shivering fits or "rigors" that signal the start of a malarial fever.</note>.

### For women who are troubled by coldness of the womb.
Give four drachms of Betony in warm water, to be drunk in as many cyathi for three days. <note>original: "loci"; literally "the places," a common euphemism in historical medical texts for the uterus or female reproductive organs.</note>

### Against DRUNKENNESS.
If Betony is taken beforehand, drunkenness does not follow the wine.

### For curing the ROYAL DISEASE.
We have learned through experience that the herb Betony is beneficial when taken frequently in wine. <note>original: "Morbo Regio"; a traditional name for Jaundice, so called perhaps because it was thought to require expensive "royal" remedies or because the patient's skin turned the color of gold.</note>

### For healing a CARBUNCLE
<note>A carbuncle is a severe, painful cluster of boils under the skin, often caused by bacterial infection.</note>
Betony drunk in two cups <note>original: "cyathis"; a small cup measure, approx. 45ml.</note> of warm water cures a carbuncle.
For those who suffer from sores or skin abrasions:
Betony ground with lard, applied to the wound, is surely beneficial.

### For those WEARY from travel.
Let the person weary from a journey drink one ounce <note>approx. 28 grams.</note> of Betony in three cups of wine for three days.

### For the sick who REJECT FOOD.
Give two drachms <note>approx. 3.5 grams each.</note> of Betony in three cups of mead <note>original: "aquę mulsę"; honeyed water.</note> for the patient to drink.

### So that one might easily DIGEST.
Take three drachms of Betony and one ounce of boiled honey; boil the honey in warm water until it hardens; give two cups to drink. It is also suitable to make lozenges <note>original: "Pastillos"</note> from it and swallow them with warm water.

### For the bite of SERPENTS.
Dilute three drachms of Betony in three cups of wine and give it to drink; indeed, it heals the bites of all serpents. Also, grind Betony in three cups of dark wine and smear it upon the wound.

### For expelling POISONS that have been given.
Three drachms of Betony drunk immediately disperse the poison.

<margin>a</margin>
### For the bite of a mad DOG.
Ground and crushed Betony is applied to the bite.

### For FISTULAS.
<note>A fistula is an abnormal tube-like passage in the body, often caused by infection.</note>
Make small plugs <note>original: "turundulas"; small wicks or rolls of lint/herb used to keep a wound open or deliver medicine.</note> from crushed and ground Betony, insert a little salt, and bind the fistula; it cleanses it.

### For driving away GOUT.
The roots of Betony with the leaves, boiled down to one-third in water and drunk—or the herb itself ground and applied—are affirmed by experience to wonderfully soothe the pain of Gout <note>original: "Podagrę"; a form of inflammatory arthritis.</note>.

### For the PURGATIONS.
A drachm of Betony in wine expels "stuck" purgations <note>referring to delayed or blocked menstruation.</note>.

VOLUME ONE.

<insert>Ajuga reptans, L. C. B. 268 Sm. ft. 3.65</insert> <note>These are later botanical citations added by a reader or librarian, referencing Carl Linnaeus and other taxonomic works to identify the plant as "Bugle."</note>

### ON THE MIDDLE COMFREY, <margin>A</margin>
#### Fourteenth Collection.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a botanical specimen, identifiable as Ajuga reptans (Bugle), showing a basal rosette of leaves and a single vertical flowering stalk with whorls of small flowers. To the right of the roots is a pencil annotation: "1537. 95".</image-desc>

### NAMES
#### In German, **Golden Bugle** / **Brown Bugle** / or **Great Bugle**.

<margin>Folio 78.D.</margin>
<margin>A</margin>
As we stated above in the section on the Healing Herb <note>original: "Solidagine"; referring to a group of plants thought to "consolidate" or heal wounds</note>, there are many species of Comfrey. Among these is the present one, which they call "Middle" or "Lesser Comfrey," commonly known as **Golden Bugle** <note>German: "Guldē Guntzel"</note>, according to the herbalist **Hieronymus [Bock]**. He also identifies three varieties of this herb. To the first, he gives the German name **Brown Bugle** <note>German: "Brumel"</note>, which has a purple flower. To the second, **Golden Bugle**, which has a blue <note>original: "blaw"</note> flower. And to the third <margin>B</margin>, he gives the name of the **Great Bugle** <note>German: "Großß guntzel"</note>, which has no flowers and the shape of a beet, though with slightly more slender leaves. As to what name it might have in the works of Dioscorides <note>The primary ancient Greek authority on medicinal plants</note> other than "Healing Herb," I frankly confess that I do not know.

### POWERS AND BENEFITS.

Like the species of Comfrey mentioned above, it knits wounds together.

It breaks up and dissolves blood clots in the body caused by falls or bruises.

It is a ready remedy for canker sores <note>original: "alcolæ"</note> and spreading ulcers of the mouth.

A decoction of it, or the water applied to swellings, disperses all tumors.

Its water is given to those in desperate states of apoplexy <note>A historical term for a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness</note> and to those suffering from a burning of the tongue, if several seeds of basil <note>original: "ozimi feminis"</note> are occasionally soaked in it.

The use of the "Great Bugle" is for chafing <note>original: "intertrigines"; skin irritation caused by friction</note>, for ulcers of the penis and genitals, for hemorrhoids <note>original: "marifcas"</note>, and for all tumors and abscesses.

There are some who, when suffering from nerve pain, smear themselves with its water, and from this they begin to feel better.

I have seen those who have prescribed it as a drink for colic and for those suffering from the erosion of the intestines.

### NOMENCLATURE.

In Latin: *Herba paralysis* <note>Literally "Herb of Paralysis," so named for its use against strokes and tremors</note>, *Margarita* <note>meaning "The Pearl," an old medieval name for these spring flowers</note>.
In German: **St. Peter’s Keys / Keys of Heaven / Key-flowers / White Betony.**

We have subsequently tracked down many things among various authors regarding the "Palsywort," and we have compared many notes with other herbalists, but as yet we have found nothing that satisfies our judgment <note>original: "ad stomachum fecerit nostrum," literally "made for our stomach," an idiom meaning to satisfy one's taste or intellectual requirements</note>. The name was unknown to ancient writers. The "barbarians" <note>the author's typical term for medieval medical writers who lacked the polish of classical Greek or Latin</note> mix everything together so ignorantly, ineptly, and confusedly that they have created even more work for us. I do not understand what he means by those remarks. For today, herbalists have pointed out a far different plant to us, [appearing] at the start of spring, somewhat white and translucent, with leaves breaking out almost like the flowers of Betony <note>original: "floribus Betonicae fere folijs erumpentem"</note>. It is so similar to it that "no milk is more like milk" <note>A Latin idiom, *lac lacti similius*, meaning they are virtually identical</note>. This leads me to suspect that it is a certain species of Betony, specifically the white variety—even though Hieronymus the herbalist <note>Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), also known as Tragus, a pioneering German botanist and contemporary of the author</note> disagrees. However, let that remain a conjecture; it carries no weight of logical proof. I find nothing more in reputable authors, except in the *Corollarium* <note>A "corollarium" is a supplement or appendix; Hermolaus Barbarus wrote this as a commentary on the ancient botanist Dioscorides</note> of Hermolaus Barbarus. In his section on the Wild Cucumber, he mentions a certain plant for "Paralysis" <note>The Palsywort</note> as follows:

<margin>Hermolaus Barbarus on the Palsywort.</margin>
"There is also another flower, named *Bellis* <note>The Daisy</note>, a meadow flower, both white and somewhat reddish, which is effective against scrofula <term>strumas|A swelling of the lymph nodes, historically known as the 'King’s Evil'</term>, as Pliny believes. Whether this *Bellis* is the same as the *Bellius* or *Bellio*—also a meadow flower—which Pliny writes is crowned with fifty-five little fringed petals <note>original: "barbulis pastillicantibus," a term used by Pliny to describe the fine, ray-like petals of the daisy</note>, is something I believe we must consider. For although *Bellio* seems to be described as yellow by Pliny in his first and second volumes, and *Bellis* as white in the twenty-sixth, we do not find it written as 'yellow' in all copies of Pliny's works."

<summary>The author expresses confusion over previous descriptions of the Palsywort, comparing it to White Betony and citing the Renaissance scholar Hermolaus Barbarus and the Roman naturalist Pliny. The text highlights the difficulty early botanists faced in distinguishing between similar species like the Cowslip and the Daisy using ancient manuscripts.</summary>

-> Medicines of SIMPLES <-

C Some report that it has yellow seed, rather than the flower itself, and they commonly interpret it as being called *Paralysis* <note>Palsywort, a name for the Cowslip (*Primula veris*), used because it was believed to cure "palsy" or paralysis</note>. It is the first flower of spring and is nicknamed *Margarita* <note>The Pearl</note>; it also grows throughout the entire winter and was brought into Italy from the West, as some believe. However, I find that it has fifty-three "little beards" <note>original: "barbulas." Likely referring to the small petals or stamens that form a fringe</note>, not fifty-five. It is praised for paralysis—from which it takes its name—and likewise for Gout <note>original: "Podagras"</note> and Sciatica <note>original: "Ischiada"</note>. It has a flower similar to the one called *Paralysis*, though with fewer "little beards." The flower, because it is conspicuous from a distance, is commonly called *Paradelis*. Its leaf is not very different, except that this one is serrated, unlike the *Paralysis*.

<margin>Antipater, the Ox-eye herb.</margin>
There are those who call it *Buphthalmos* <note>Greek for "Ox-eye"</note> and "Eye of the Ox." For those who think it is the plant commonly called *Antipater* are clearly mistaken, since *Antipater* is twiggy and has a yellow flower, like a smaller variety of Savory <note>original: "Cunilaginis"</note>. Its leaves are like those of Rosemary, but wider and shorter.

<margin>
Herb Christopher.
Consul's Eye.
</margin>
Some call it *Christophoriana* <note>Herb Christopher</note> and "The Eye of the Consul." It has this unique property: the flowers born later rise higher than those born first. Based on this evidence, it might seem to some that this is the plant which Pliny records as being called the *Impia* <note>The Impious or Unfilial Herb</note>.

<margin>The Impious Herb.</margin>
The *Impia* herb, he says, is so called because it is hollow, has the appearance of Rosemary, is dressed like a staff <note>original: "thyrsi modo," referring to the Thyrsus or wand of Bacchus</note>, and has heads. From there, other small branches rise up, bearing their own little heads. They called it "Impious" for this reason: because the children extol themselves above the parent. Others believed it was so named because no animal will touch it. This herb, he says, when ground between two stones, seethes <note>original: "feruet," meaning it foams or reacts</note>; its juice is especially effective against quinsy <note>Severe inflammation of the throat</note>. No one who tried it ever died from that disease. There are also those who think that if some of it is placed in birds' nests, the chicks will not choke even when devouring food greedily. These are the words of Pliny.

D However, although there is a similarity in that specific property, there are many differences between the two. First, the *Impia* is a hollow herb, while *Antipater* is not. Second, when ground, it does not seethe. Third, it bears neither "heads" nor "staves," but only flowers. These are the observations of Barbarus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493), a scholar who worked to correct errors in ancient scientific texts</note>.

### L O C A T I O N

It grows of its own accord in green meadows.

### H A R V E S T I N G

It is gathered at the beginning of May; part is distilled in an alembic <note>A chemical still used for making medicinal waters</note>, and part is dried in the shade.

### P O W E R S  A N D  B E N E F I T S

#### From HIERONYMUS the Herbalist.

A decoction of it, or its water applied to an aching head, suppresses the pain.
It warms the stomach, the liver, and the womb.
For this reason, it is suitable for women in labor and provokes the menses.
It also heals the bites of serpents and all venomous creatures.
It calms and repels tumors of the head if a linen cloth is soaked in its water and applied, or if used as a poultice.
Its flowers are steeped in olive oil to make an ointment for paralysis and for nerves relaxed by cold or ill humors.
It wipes away skin eruptions <note>original: "Vitiligines"</note> on the face and the rest of the body.
It dissolves the humors that cause Sciatica, expelling them and drawing them out through the urine.

# Pigeon’s Crop.
### ON CAPNOS, that is, the herb Fumaria, or Earthsmoke: The Fourteenth Discourse.

-> NOMENCLATURES <-

**Greek names:** <note>original: καπνός [Kapnos]</note> Smoke; <note>original: καρυδάλλιον [Karydallion]</note> Crested Lark-herb; <note>original: κόριον [Korion]</note> Coriander-like; <note>original: κορυδάλιον ἄγριον [Korydalion agrion]</note> Wild Lark-herb; <note>original: καπνίτις [Kapnitis]</note> Smoky; <note>original: μαρμαρίτις [Marmaritis]</note> The Glistening one; <note>original: καπνογόργιον [Kapnogorgion]</note> Smoke-Gorgon; <note>original: χελιδόνιον μικρόν [Chelidonion mikron]</note> Lesser Swallow-wort; <note>original: περιστέρεον [Peristereon]</note> Pigeon-plant; <note>original: κασθαρὶσ [Kastharis]</note> Kastharis.
**Latin names:** The herb Fumaria; Earthsmoke; Capnitis; Parsley-herb <note>original: "Apium." While Apium usually refers to celery, in this historical context it was occasionally used for Fumitory due to leaf shape</note>.
**German names:** **Earth-smoke. Pigeon’s Crop. Cat’s Chervil-herb.**

-> THE OPINIONS OF AUTHORS regarding Fumitory. <-

<margin>
<note>A description of the herb Fumitory from DIOSCORIDES.</note>
</margin>
**F**umitory is a shrubby little herb, very tender, similar to Coriander, with numerous pale, ash-colored leaves everywhere, and a purple flower. <note>Dioscorides was a 1st-century Greek physician whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical authority for 1,500 years</note>

-> A description of the same from PLINY. <-

<margin>
Two types of Capnos.
</margin>
The first type of Capnos <note>Greek for "smoke"</note>, which he calls *Crow’s Feet* <note>original: "Pedes gallinaceos"</note>, grows on walls and hedges, with very thin and spreading branches and a purple flower; it is green. Its juice dispels dimness of vision; therefore, it is added to medicines for the eyes. <note>Pliny the Elder (1st century AD) noted that the plant was called "smoke" either because its juice makes eyes water like smoke, or because it appears to rise from the earth like smoke</note>

PHARMACEUTICS OF SIMPLES

<margin>C</margin>
Another bushy Fumitory <note>original: Capnos</note> is similar in both name and effect; it has, moreover, leaves like Coriander, of an ash-grey color, and a purple flower. It grows in gardens and in barley fields.

### THE PARAPHRASE OF HERMOLAUS BARBARUS
->What the non-classical authors say about the herb Fumitory.<- <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493) was a Venetian scholar known for his corrections to the texts of Pliny the Elder. "Barbari" refers to medieval or non-Greek authorities.</note>

<margin>
Cocksfoot is a relative of Fumitory.
What the Cymbalaria herb is.
</margin>
*Capnos*, or *Capnion*—that is to say, Smoke—is of two kinds. One is described here, growing in gardens and barley fields. The other is similar in name and effect, which they call Cocksfoot <note>original: Pedes Gallinaceos</note>; it grows on walls and hedges, with very slender and scattered branches and a purple flower, as Pliny says. Some people commonly identify this latter plant as *Cimbalaris* <note>Cymbalaria, likely Ivy-leaved Toadflax</note>, though I do not know how correctly they interpret it; it has a very thin leaf like Ivy, as we mentioned in the section on *Cotyledon* <note>Navelwort</note>. However, it is the custom of Aetius <note>Aetius of Amida, a 6th-century Byzantine physician</note> to call this *Capnos* that grows in hedges "Hedge Swallow-wort" <note>original: Chelidonia phragmitem</note>; he says it is useful for purging the curved parts of the liver. This is, I believe, because its juice clears away "mistiness" <note>likely cataracts or blurred vision</note> just as Swallow-wort <note>Chelidonia</note> does; for this reason, it is added to eye medicines, such as the eye-salve <term>Collyrium<gloss>a topical medical preparation for the eye, often shaped like a small stick</gloss></term> of Marcianus, who gave it the surname "Smoky Swallow-wort" <note>original: Chelidonia Capnitida</note>. If this plant is proven to be the same as *Cimbalari*, as some suspect, then that similarity will also hold true: that it had an Ivy-like leaf, just as occurs with Lesser Celandine <note>original: Chelidonio minori</note>. Therefore, I wish it to be considered whether this *Capnos* is not just similar to, but entirely the same as, Lesser Celandine. I certainly find many points of agreement. Furthermore, because Pliny writes that *Capnos* is called Cocksfoot <note>original: Pedes gallinaceos</note> by our people, a great error has seized most writers; they think the *Capnos* shown by Dioscorides is no different from the genus commonly called *Sanguinaria* <note>Bloodwort</note> and Cock's-leg. This is a shameful and regrettable ignorance—unless one’s pride has been worn down by many mistakes. For indeed, that which is called Cock's-leg is so similar to Grass <note>original: Gramini</note> that it perhaps cannot be easily distinguished from it, except that its leaf is seen to be smaller and it relies on fibers rather than a root. Moreover, the part at the top of both shrubs that is divided into three <note>original: Trifarin</note>, imitating a chicken's foot, is seen more clearly in this plant than in the Grass.

<margin>D</margin>
### Why it is called Fumaria, according to MARCELLO VIRGILIO. <note>Marcello Virgilio Adriani (1464–1521) was an Italian humanist and translator of Dioscorides.</note>

The well-known fact of "smoke" gave the herb *Fumaria* its name in the past. It is certainly not because, when brought inside to walls or their vaulted ceilings, it causes harm with its blackness, nor because (as the Poet sang) it "tests the suspended material and hardens the wood for building" <note>a reference to using smoke to season timber</note>. Rather, it is because its power makes a man’s eyes water, just as happens in smoke. For this reason, Flaccus <note>The poet Horace</note> called smoke "tearful" in his poem; and a servant of Aristophanes said he returned to the stage forced by smoke, and could not be in the house with the others <note>original: ὅτι ἔδακνε τὰ βλέφαρ' αὐτοῦ [hoti edakne ta blephar' autou]</note>, which is to say, "because it was biting his eyelids and eyes." This is the greatest annoyance that smoke causes to this part of the body; the same potency in the juice of the herb *Fumaria* was indicated by the Greeks through the name "Smoke." Not only did they call it *Capnos* with a name equal to "Smoke," but they also called it *Capnitis*, that is, *Fumaria*. Similarly, they named it *Coriandrum* from its resemblance; this word grew in many ways in this writer, with some calling it simply Coriander, others Wild Coriander, and others using the diminutive form *Coriandron*. It grows here...

<summary>This page explores the botanical identification and naming of Fumitory (Capnos), comparing it to other plants like Cocksfoot and Lesser Celandine. It explains that the name "Fumaria" or "Earthsmoke" derives from the plant's juice causing the eyes to water, similar to the irritation caused by actual smoke.</summary>

## SERAPION’S **Description**, concerning Fumitory.
<note>Serapion the Younger was a 12th or 13th-century author of a celebrated work on medicinal "simples" or single-ingredient drugs. "Description" translates the Greek ὑπογραφὴ (hypographē).</note>

*Scehiterig* <note>An Arabic-derived name for Fumitory, shahatraj</note>, that is, Earth-smoke, is an herb similar to wild Parsnip: except that it is smaller and more bitter, and has a root whose color leans toward white.

## Praise of Fumitory according to MESUE.
<note>Mesue the Younger (11th century) was a highly influential authority on pharmacy in the medieval West.</note>

Earth-smoke is among the blessed medicines, yet its exuberance and excessive abundance have removed it from the list of precious medicines. For while it loosens the bowels, it also strongly strengthens the other organs. Nor is there any visible harm in it. There is another species of it, whose flower is whitish and ash-colored; and another whose color is pale and violet.

### **S E L E C T I O N**

The better kind is the one that is green, with tender, flat leaves and a violet flower. The crispier kind is of lower quality.

### **T I M E  O F  C O L L E C T I O N**

The herb should be gathered from the beginning of Spring, and the seed from the end.

### **T E M P E R A M E N T**
<note>In Galenic medicine, "temperament" or "complexion" refers to the balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>

It is of a hot and dry complexion in the second degree. It is of a quality both sharp and bitter, and is not entirely without acridity. It thins [bodily fluids] and allows them to penetrate, opens blockages, and dissolves [congestions].

<margin>
**Rectification**
</margin>

### **R E C T I F I C A T I O N**
<note>"Rectification" refers to the process of balancing a medicine's effects or making it more effective.</note>

It contains nothing harmful, yet it requires a means of evacuation to work more vigorously. Mesue therefore believes that, for loosening the bowels, whey <note>original: "aquam casei", literally cheese-water</note>, myrobalans <note>a dried fruit used as a laxative</note>, or senna should be added to it. Also raisins and honey. Its juice is compared to the juice of Wormwood. And if bottles with narrow mouths are filled with its juice and olive oil is poured over the top, it lasts for a whole year.

## **P O W E R S** and its benefits according to DIOSCORIDES
<note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD) was a Greek physician and the primary authority on herbal medicine for 1,500 years.</note>

The juice of this plant brings clarity and tears to the eyes: from which it takes its name <note>The Greek name "Capnos" means smoke; the juice was thought to irritate the eyes like smoke, thereby clearing the vision.</note>.

Smeared on with gum, it prevents eyelashes that have been plucked out from growing back.

When the herb is chewed, it promotes bilious urine.

### **F R O M  M E S V E**

It makes for easy elimination and draws out bile and burnt humors <note>In humoral theory, "burnt" or "adust" humors were considered a cause of many skin diseases and fevers.</note>. Its power extends even to the veins and purifies the blood. It is a blessed medicine, by every method of its administration, for illnesses and infections involving bile and burnt humors—such as leprosy, scabies <note>a general term for itchy skin eruptions</note>, and impetigo <note>a contagious skin infection</note>. It is also a healthy medicine for all types of obstructions. It benefits the stomach, liver, and intestines. Its use is also effective in bilious and obstructive fevers.

### **O N  T H E  D O S E**, and its administration.

A drink of its juice is from 5 drachms up to 2 [ounces] <note>The text likely refers to ounces (℥ij) as the upper limit</note>. And of its decoction...
