PHARMACY of SIMPLE Medicines

<margin>C</margin> from 10 ounces up to 15, and of its powder from 3 drams up to 5.

->FROM GIOVANNI DA VIGO<-
<note>Giovanni da Vigo (c. 1450–1525) was a famous Italian surgeon and physician to Pope Julius II.</note>

Its juice, thickened with the juice of Sharp Dock <note>original: "Lapathi acuti"</note> and a little oxymel <note>A medicinal mixture of honey and vinegar</note>, cures every kind of skin spot <term>morphea</term>.
Likewise, a decoction of Earth-smoke, mallows, violets, and Sharp Dock, with barley bran and catmint <note>original: "nepita"</note>, most powerfully cures and cleanses every kind of scabies <note>original: "scabiem"</note>.

->FROM AETIUS<-
<note>Aetius of Amida was a 6th-century Byzantine Greek physician known for his vast medical encyclopedia.</note>

Fumitory worked and mixed with wine strengthens the stomach; and it may be given, says Aetius, in any amount to those suffering from fevers.

->FROM PLATEARIUS<-
<note>Matthaeus Platearius was a 12th-century physician from the School of Salerno, author of "Circa Instans."</note>

Against dropsy <note>original: "hydropisim"</note>, and especially against "white phlegm" <term>leucophlegmasia</term> <note>A condition involving pale swelling of the body</note>, its juice is used with two drams of Spurge <note>original: "Esulæ"</note> powder added, in warm water. Or let a syrup be made from the juice of Earth-smoke, celery, boiled fennel, and spurge powder, with sugar added.
Against joint pain <term>arthritis</term> <note>original: "artethicam"</note>, let two drams of Meadow Saffron <term>hermodactyls</term> <note>original: "hermodactylorum"</note> be given with the juice of Earth-smoke.
Moreover, the herb itself, boiled in wine and applied as a poultice over a gouty area <note>original: "locum podagricum"</note>, is very effective.
For melancholy, or phlegm, and nausea at the mouth of the stomach, its juice is given with warm water, with sugar added.
<margin>D</margin> Note that some administer it in the morning, some in the evening, some on its own, and some with an additive.
In the evening it is always offered with something that restrains and dissolves wind <note>flatulence</note>, such as fennel seed or mastic; for it agitates the humors of the belly and thereby causes griping pains <note>original: "tormina"</note>.

->FROM HIERONYMUS the Herbalist<-
<note>Likely referring to Hieronymus Bock (Tragus), a pioneer of modern botany, or Hieronymus Brunschwig.</note>

A potion of Fumitory heals the plague and ulcers of the mouth; applied as an ointment, it suppresses tumors, clears the menses, and brings about beauty.

# CONCERNING SATYRIONS, Collection XVI.
<note>In this context, "Satyrion" refers to various species of orchids. The name is derived from the Satyrs of Greek mythology, reflecting the plant's historical reputation as a potent aphrodisiac due to its twin, testicle-shaped tubers.</note>

## NOMENCLATURES.

**Greek:** *orchis*, *orchis kynos* <note>original: ὄρχις, ὄρχις κυνός — literally "testicle" and "dog's testicle."</note>.
**Latin:** *Satyrion*, *Leporium* (Hare-plant), *Testiculus vulpis* (Fox’s testicle).
**German:** *Stendelwurtz* (Orchid), *Knabenkrut* (Boy’s-herb), *Kreutzblumen* (Cross-flowers), *Ragwurtz* (Ragwort).

## OPINIONS OF THE AUTHORS, regarding Satyrion.

### THE JUDGMENT OF THEOPHRASTUS on Satyrion, Book 9, Chapter 19.
<note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC) was a Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle; he is often called the "father of botany."</note>

Regarding human bodies, they claim that herbs can provide other powers beyond those concerning health, disease, and death: for instance, the power of fertility in women, and also sterility. They say some plants are able to produce both effects from the same source, such as the one called "Testicle" <note>original: *Testiculus*</note>. Since there are twin roots, one large and the other small, they report that the larger one, given in goat's milk, is effective for encouraging sexual intercourse, while the smaller one actually hinders and inhibits it. It has a leaf like Laserwort <note>original: *Laseris* — likely referring to a plant from the *Ferula* genus</note>, but smoother and smaller, and a stem very much like the thorn-bush which they call "pear-thorn." It is a marvel, then, as has been said, that such a diversity of powers proceeds from one and the same nature.

### The Judgment of DIOSCORIDES, Book 3, on Satyrions.
<note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40 – 90 AD) was a Greek physician and botanist whose work *De Materia Medica* was the primary pharmacological text for 1,500 years.</note>

### Regarding the first SATYRION, which is called *kynos orchis*, that is, Dog's Testicle.

The Dog's Testicle, which the Greeks call *Orchis* or *Cynosorchis*, has soft leaves around the stem similar to those of the Olive, spread out on the ground, but longer, narrow, and smooth. The stem is nine inches high <term>dodrantali</term><note>A *dodrans* is a Roman unit of length approximately equal to 9 inches or the span of a hand.</note>, with purple flowers and a bulbous, oblong root, narrow in the manner of an olive. The root is of a double order: the upper part is fuller, while the lower part is softer and more wrinkled.

### The Explanation of HERMOLAUS BARBARUS.
<note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493) was an Italian Renaissance scholar known for his translations and commentaries on ancient botanical texts.</note>

The *Cynosorchis* is usually found in vineyards, having three small leaves about half a foot long, and a root shaped like human testicles, swelling and receding in alternating years. There is both a male and a female of the same name: they are distinguished by the segments of the stem and by the more branched growth of the female, which has a root shaped like a phallus <note>original: *fascini*</note>. It grows mostly near the sea and is called "Satyrion," though less properly. For there is another genus which is properly called Satyrion.

### Regarding the second SATYRION of DIOSCORIDES.

The "Testicle" which is called by another name, *Serapias* (according to Andreas), because the root is useful for few things, has leaves broader than a Leek, oblong, fleshy, and bent from the base of the stalks. It has a stem the length of a palm <term>palmeo</term><note>A "palm" (palmus) is about 3 inches.</note>, flowers that are almost purple, and a root similar to testicles.

### Regarding the Third SATYRION.

The third Satyrion is three-leaved <note>original: *trifolium*</note>, bearing three leaves bent toward the ground, similar to Dock <note>original: *Rumex*</note> or a Lily, yet smaller and reddish. It has a naked stem a cubit long <term>cubitalem</term><note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches.</note> and a white flower in the shape of a Lily. The root is bulbous, the size of an apple, yellow inside like an egg and white on the outside, sweet to the taste and not unpleasant to the mouth.

### Regarding the Fourth SATYRION, the Erythronion.

The Erythronion Satyrion, called by others *Erythranicon*, by others Water *Melion*, and by others...

[Medicines] from SIMPLES [Pharmacology]

<margin>C</margin> Some call it **Staticon**, others **Priapicum**, or **Satyriscon**, and some call it the **Satyress’s Testicle** <note>original: *Satyri Testiculum*</note>. The Romans call it **Venus's Little Mill** <note>original: *Molorticulum Veneris*</note>; it has a seed like linseed but larger, hard, smooth, and shining, which is said to excite sexual desire no differently than the Skink <note>original: *Scincus* — a type of lizard whose flesh was historically used as an aphrodisiac</note>. It has a slender root with reddish bark. Inside, however, it is white, with a sweet taste not unpleasant to the mouth. It grows in mountainous and sunny places.

### HERMOLAUS BARBARUS on this Fourth SATYRION in his *Corollarium*.
<note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493) was a Venetian scholar who sought to correct errors in the Latin translations of ancient botanical texts.</note>

This Satyrion is well known to shepherds, for it is given in drink to sluggish rams and he-goats, and in Sarmatia <note>An ancient region of Eastern Europe</note> to horses that have become too lazy for mating due to constant labor; this defect they call *Prosedamum* <note>A term for sexual exhaustion or sluggishness in livestock</note>. Indeed, the Greeks, wanting to signify this overall state of excitement, call it **Satyrion**, **Satyrismon**, and **Satyriasis**. For this reason, I believe one type of Birthwort <note>original: *Aristolochiæ*</note>, which they call "many-rooted" <note>original: *Polyrrhizon*</note>, is actually named Satyrion because of its effects. I would also call that plant "Indian Satyrion" which was brought to Theophrastus from India; he recorded that by touching it, sexual desire could last through seventy acts of intercourse, though he gave neither its appearance nor any other name. Even today, the Syrians have a plant with a similar effect which they call **Bucheides**, and also **Indian Satyrion**; perhaps it is the same one mentioned by Theophrastus, with a white, hard root—more highly valued the thicker, more wrinkled, and whiter it is—and it is useful for those suffering from gout.

<margin>D</margin> ### APULEIUS on Satyrion.
<note>This refers to Pseudo-Apuleius, the author of a famous 4th-century herbal manual.</note>

By the Greeks it is called **Satyrion**, by others **Dog's-testicle** <note>original: *Cynosorchis*</note>, by others **Eutaceon**, **Eraten**, **Panion**, **Serapion**, and by others **Orchis**. The Egyptians call it **Menem**, the Gauls **Vram**, the Italians **Priapistum**, some **Torminalis** [Colic-herb], and others **Hare’s-testicle**. It grows in the mountains, in firm and cultivated places, as well as in meadows and coastal areas. Gather it in the month of July.

### The Opinion of PLINY on Satyrions, Book 25, Chapter 8.
<note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD) was a Roman naturalist whose *Natural History* compiled the scientific knowledge of antiquity.</note>

Satyrion has a stimulating power. There are two kinds. One has leaves longer than those of the Olive, a stem four fingers high, a purple flower, and a twin root shaped like human testicles, which swells and subsides in alternating years. The other is named **Satyrion Orchis** and is believed to be the female; it is distinguished by its joints and its more branchy shrub-like form, with a root useful for the sexual organs <note>original: *fasciinis* — referring to the *fascinum*, an amulet or representation of the phallus</note>. It grows mostly near the sea.

The Greeks report a Satyrion with leaves smaller than those of the red Lily, with no more than three emerging from the ground: a smooth stem a cubit high, bare of leaves, and a twin root. They say the lower and larger part produces males, while the lower [smaller] part produces females. There is also another kind of Satyrion they call **Erythroneon** [Red-root], with a seed larger than that of the Chaste-tree, smooth, with a hard root and red bark, though it is white inside and has a somewhat sweet taste. It is said to be found in mountainous regions.

### The Opinion of SERAPION on Satyrion, Chapters 90 & 91, under the heading *Chafialehel*.
<note>Serapion the Younger was a 12th-century Arabic physician whose work on "simples" (single-ingredient medicines) was a standard medical textbook in Europe.</note>

There are two kinds of Satyrion. One has a white root or "testicles" and is called **Chafialchel** <note>A Latinization of the Arabic name for orchid</note>. The first kind of Satyrion is called **Dog’s-testicle**, or in Greek **Cynosorchis**; it is a plant that has leaves spread out upon the ground and near to it, arising from the root of a single stalk. Its leaves are similar to those of the Olive, except they are thinner and longer, spread out over the earth...

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Types of Satyrion.</margin>
Its length is roughly the span of one palm, and it has a purple flower. Its root is similar to a bulb, except that it tends toward being long and thin. It is double, shaped like two olives: one below, the other above; one is full, and the other is empty and wrinkled. This root is eaten boiled just like a bulb; this is the **Satyrion** that is commonly used. The second type of Satyrion also has two species: one is called *Chasiaalbabel* in Arabic, which means "Fox’s Testicle" <note>original: *Testiculus vulpis*</note>. In Greek, it is called "Three-leafed" <note>original: *Trifolium*</note> because it mostly grows with three leaves leaning toward the ground; these resemble the leaves of Great Sorrel <note>original: *Acetosa majoris*</note> or Lily leaves, though they are smaller. In its "testicle" <note>The anatomical term for the orchid's underground tuber</note> there is a redness leaning toward the color of blood. It has a slender stalk, one arm's length long. It has a flower similar in shape to the flowers of the White Lily. Its root is shaped like an onion bulb. It is the size of an apple, red on the outside and white like an egg on the inside; the part used for medicine is the root.

## FROM THE AUTHOR OF THE PANDECTS.
<note>The "Author of the Pandects" likely refers to Conrad Gessner, who compiled the *Pandectarum sive partitionum universalium* in the mid-16th century.</note>

<margin>Female Satyrion.</margin>
It should be known that there is another species of Satyrion, which is called the "Royal Herb" <note>original: *herba Basilica*</note> in Greek, "Citron-colored Fingers" <note>original: *Digiti citrini*</note> or *Bucheidem* in Arabic, and in Latin, "Christ’s Palm" <note>original: *Palma Christi*</note>. Its leaves are like those of the first species of Satyrion, but more slender and with black spots. Its root resembles the branch of a hand or the palm of a hand, with a saffron-colored flower. When ground with wine or water, it turns a saffron-yellow.

### TEMPERAMENT
<note>In traditional medicine, "temperament" describes the inherent qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) of a substance that determine its effect on the body.</note>

<margin>B</margin>
It is moist and warm in temperament in the first degree; therefore, it also tastes sweet to those who sample it. It possesses an abundant and wind-producing <note>original: *sufflantem*</note> moisture. Thus, because of this "inflation" <note>the production of gas or air within the body</note>, it excites lust.

## POWERS and benefits of the first type from DIOSCORIDES.
<note>Dioscorides was a 1st-century Greek physician whose work *De Materia Medica* was the primary pharmacological text for 1,500 years.</note>

<margin>On that which is called "Dog’s Testicle."</margin>
If men eat the larger root, they are said to father males; if they eat the smaller, females.
They add that in Thessaly <note>A region in Greece</note>, women drink the soft root in goat’s milk to stimulate sexual desire; they drink the dry root, however, to inhibit it, and the effect of one is neutralized by drinking the other.

### OF THE SECOND TYPE.

Applied as a poultice, it disperses tumors.
It cleanses ulcers and does not allow them to spread.
It removes fistulas. And when applied, it soothes inflammations.
The dried roots inhibit spreading ulcers <note>original: *nomas*</note> and heal rotted areas of the mouth and stubborn or malignant ulcers <note>original: *Cacöethe*</note>.
They stop the bowels <note>diarrhea</note> when drunk in wine.
Regarding this type, the same things are reported as for the "Dog’s Testicle" <note>original: *Testiculo canis* or *Cynosorchis*</note>.

### OF THE THIRD TYPE.

It is appropriate to drink this in dark, harsh wine against *opisthotonus* <note>A condition involving severe muscle spasms where the body arches backward.</note>.
It should be used whenever a desire for intimacy arises.

### OF THE FOURTH TYPE.

As they report, if the root is simply held in the hand, it stimulates sexual desire; even more so if it is drunk in wine.

110 PHARMACY OF SIMPLES

<margin>C</margin>
## FROM PLINY.
It is given in drink to sluggish rams and goats by the Sarmatians <note>The Sarmatians were a large confederation of Iranian people in classical antiquity</note>. 
It is given to horses in their drink when they have become too sluggish for mating due to constant labor; its power is neutralized by honeyed water <note>original: *aqua mulsa*</note> or by eating lettuce.

## FROM ORIBASIUS.
The roots, when ground, remove black scars.

## FROM APULEIUS.
For difficult ulcers, apply the crushed roots of the Priapist herb <note>original: *Priapisti* — a name for the orchid referring to Priapus, the god of fertility, due to the root's shape</note>; it both cleanses them and closes the scars. 
Anoint the eyes with the juice of the Priapist herb, and it will remove inflammation and pains without delay. 
If any man is unable to satisfy a woman, he should take the root of the Priapist herb—specifically the right "testicle" <note>The anatomical term for the orchid's tuber</note>, because it is larger—and 27 grains of white pepper and 4 ounces of honey. Let him dissolve these in the best wine, and take a dose of 9 scruples <note>term: scruple — an ancient measurement of weight, roughly 1.3 grams</note> of this medicine for three days.

## FROM GIOVANNI VIGO.
A wine made from its decoction, or the root boiled in chicken broth, greatly excites sexual desire.

## FROM THE HERBAL AGGREGATOR.
The women of Italy administer the crushed root with goat's milk to stir desire. It dissolves swollen abscesses <note>original: *apostemata*</note>. 
With rose honey, it cleanses wounds.
<margin>D</margin>
It cures Erysipelas <note>term: Erysipelas — a bacterial skin infection, historically known as "St. Anthony's Fire"</note>, which is a disfigurement of the skin caused by a defect of "choleric blood" <note>This refers to the ancient theory of the Four Humors, where an excess of yellow bile was thought to cause heat and redness</note>. 
Because it possesses a slight astringency, a drink of Satyrion "holds the belly" <note>original: *retinet ventrem* — acts as a treatment for diarrhea</note>. 
The variety that has purple flowers, when used with salt, opens hemorrhoids. 
And when it is administered dry, it prevents the spreading of ulcers and cuts away rot. It heals sores of the mouth.

## FROM HIERONYMUS THE NOBLE EMPIRIC.
A decoction or water of the male Satyrion strengthens the stomach when drunk in a weight of one and a half ounces. It also dispels Jaundice <note>original: *Ictericiam*</note> and promotes urination. 
It heals all wounds, both external and internal, when drunk in a weight of one and a half ounces.

Pharmacy of SIMPLES

# ON BORAGE AND BUGLOSS,
## The Seventeenth Rhapsody.
<note>In this context, a "Rhapsody" refers to a collected miscellaneous discussion or a "patchwork" of commentary on a specific subject.</note>

### NOMENCLATURE
**Greek:** Ox-tongue <note>original Greek: βούγλωσσος (*bouglossos*)</note>, Cat’s offspring <note>original Greek: γόνος αἰλούρου (*gonos ailourou*), an obscure synonym found in ancient plant lists</note>.
**Latin:** Ox-tongue <note>original: *Lingua bubula*</note>, Joy-bringer <note>original: *Euphrosynum*</note>.
**German:** **Borage / Ox-tongue / Alkanet.** <note>original German: *Burretsch / Ochsenzung / Gegenstraß*. "Gegenstraß" is an archaic German name for plants in the bugloss family.</note>

### The Problems of Marcello Virgilio, Hermolaus Barbarus, and Niccolò Leoniceno concerning Borage and Bugloss.
<note>These three men were titan figures of Renaissance humanism who sought to correct medieval medical errors by re-examining original Greek texts.</note>

### The Opinion of MARCELLO VIRGILIO in the Chapter of Dioscorides on *Cirsion*, Book 2, Chapter 120.

<margin>Bugloss and *Cirsion* differ little in form. *Cirsion* is Borage. The exchange of names between Borage and Bugloss.</margin>
Some have called the "Great Bugloss" (which we shall discuss shortly) by the name *Cirsion*. There is no small debate between this plant and the other as to which is the true Bugloss and which is its relative, *Cirsion*. Indeed, *Cirsion* and Bugloss share many similarities; however, the former is named for its resemblance to an ox’s tongue, while the latter is named for its effect on varicose veins <note>The Greek *kirsos* means a swollen or varicose vein, from which *Cirsion* is derived</note>, of which we spoke a little earlier. Nowadays, Bugloss is known to everyone. If it is the plant that is dug up in gardens and fields, it follows necessarily that it is actually *Cirsion*, which our age calls "Borage." 

Indeed, as Niccolò Leoniceno has already commented on this very matter, one might reasonably suspect that the names of these two herbs have been swapped. He suggests that the ancient "Bugloss" is actually our "Borage," and that this "Cirsion" is the new name for our "Bugloss." This makes sense because the characteristics and medicinal powers attributed to them fit better if the names are exchanged. For example, the purple flower-tops described here for *Cirsion* belong more properly to what is now called Bugloss, rather than Borage, which has blue flowers. Furthermore, what is attributed to Bugloss a little later—that it brings joy and cheer when dipped into cups of wine—is everywhere attributed to Borage. Our people boast daily that Borage should be eaten often for its cheering effect. Moreover, the rough and darker leaves described in that same passage fit Borage better than Bugloss, which has a much whiter leaf. There are other signs by which this might be indicated, but let these suffice for a matter already well-treated.

<margin>D</margin>

### AND AGAIN in Chapter 129 on Bugloss, in the same Second Book of DIOSCORIDES.

<margin>The common Bugloss is Borage. M. Cato.</margin>
We promised that under the entry for Bugloss we would add some points which lean toward the conclusion that what the ancients called Bugloss is actually the Borage of our time. We also use this conjecture: in the 40th chapter of his work *On Agriculture* <note>original Latin: *De Re Rustica*</note>, Marcus Cato, while teaching the grafting of trees and how one ought to insert and bind the shoots, added: "Moreover, cover it with Ox-tongue <note>original Latin: *Lingua bubula*</note> if it rains, so that water does not soak into the bark; tie that 'Tongue' over the bark so it does not fall," etc. It is likely that for covering the round cut of a grafted trunk, rounder leaves are more suitable than long ones, which are less fit for covering a round stem. We know, of course, that one does not *have* to use it, since any covering would defend the graft from rain—be it mud, straw, or similar things found at hand. However, readers should not neglect this clue in hunting for the truth: they should know that the ancient Bugloss (which everyone else called "Ox-tongue" because it mimics the shape) also had this use in rural affairs. 

In city life, however, its chief use—and the final point made by this writer—is that the leaves of Bugloss dropped into wine increase the soul's delight and joy. Ancient writers do not attribute much else to Bugloss beyond this use. Pliny, in Volume 25, Chapter 8, wrote of it thus: <margin>The primary power of Bugloss. Pliny.</margin> "To this is joined the Bugloss, similar to an ox's tongue; its primary trait is that, when thrown into wine, it increases the soul’s delights, and it is called *Euphrosynon* (The Cheerful One)." Later, in Chapter 26, Section 12, he says: "If someone catches the juice of Bugloss as it is drying, they say they are freed from fever." This, however, belongs more to the realm of amulets than medicine. <margin>Paulus Aegineta.</margin> Paulus Aegineta, in his sixth book, only notes this about Bugloss: <note>original Greek: βούγλωσσον ὑγρόν τε καὶ θερμόν ἐστι τῇ κράσει, ὅθεν τοῖς οἴνοις ἐμβαλλόμενον εὐφροσύνην ποιεῖν λέγεται.</note> Which is to say: "Bugloss is moist and warm in temperament. For that reason, when cast into wine, it is said to produce joy in the soul." <margin>Galen.</margin> Nor did Galen pass down anything beyond what was said by others; he added—

<summary>This page discusses the historical and linguistic confusion between Borage and Bugloss, citing ancient authorities like Dioscorides, Pliny, and Cato to argue that Borage is the true "Bugloss" of antiquity. It highlights the plant's famous association with wine and its ability to "bring joy to the soul."</summary>

<keywords>Borage, Bugloss, Cirsion, Dioscorides, Pliny the Elder, Marcus Cato, medical humanism, botanical nomenclature, Euphrosynon, herbal medicine</keywords>

--- Page 122 ---
<meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the identities of Borage and Bugloss. It completes the sentence from page 112 regarding the medicinal uses of the plant described by Marcello Virgilio, specifically its utility for respiratory issues.</meta>

...[he added] that it is useful for coughs and roughness of the throat. Every ancient writer offers readers the hope of joy and pleasure from the use of Bugloss: which is now everywhere said of Borage. It is likely that this has reached us, and is still preserved, as a tradition or a rumor handed down from hand to hand. We do not rely entirely on the common perception or the judgment of the common people in this matter; however, we do not ignore it completely. 

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>A silent objection.</margin>
<margin>Pliny.</margin>
What presses us further is the history of *Cirsion* <note>a plant often identified as a type of thistle or related to Borage in old texts</note>, in which the flowers are described as <term>purplish at the tip</term> <note>original Greek: ἀκροπόρφυροι (*akroporphyroi*)</note>. This is the proper color of the flower of that plant which people now everywhere call Bugloss. The longer leaves also provide evidence, whereas in Borage they are of a shortened roundness. 

<margin>B</margin>
But someone will say: the Bugloss of our age is more similar to "Ox-tongue" <note>the literal meaning of the Greek name *bouglossos*</note> than Borage is. We do not deny that. However, we also remind you that we do not know the reasoning behind this comparison for the ancient Greeks: exactly what they compared to an ox's tongue—for example, its roughness, width, color, or length. For the Bugloss of our age, length and color are the primary features; for Borage, on the other hand, many indicators have been listed so far which others will also examine more diligently. For the sake of uncovering the truth, we propose these things only for others to consider. 

<margin>Another distinction between Borage and Bugloss.</margin>
<margin>Virgil's opinion in this controversy.</margin>
We do not struggle for the sake of the thing itself (for it is known to all), but for the ancient names and history of the medical material—which has been poorly handled by later Greeks throughout this entire chapter. We believe, based on what has been observed so far, that the parts read at the beginning of the chapter—up to the phrase "it has leaves similar to Mullein" <note>original: *Verbasco*</note>—are not by Dioscorides. For whatever is attributed to this Bugloss by Serapio <note>an influential 9th-century Arabic medical writer</note>, the ancient translation of this writer, and several Greeks, are nothing other than having leaves similar to Mullein; having a leaf that falls to the ground; and that leaf being rough and darker, similar to an ox's tongue; and that it is believed to increase joy when cast into wine. 

There is nothing else in the older Greek manuscripts or Latin writers. And Pliny <note>the Roman encyclopedist</note> attributes what is now read in this writer—namely, that this Bugloss which produces three stalks should be given for tertian fevers, and that which produces four stalks for quartan fevers—not to Bugloss, but to *Cynoglossum* <note>Hound's-tongue</note>. His words in Book 25, Chapter 8 are: "There is also joined *Cynoglosson*, imitating dogs' tongues; and they say that its root, drunk in water, benefits tertian fevers if it sends out three stalks, and quartan fevers if it sends out four." 

Added to this is the instruction that this Bugloss should be harvested in the month of July; this writer calls it <term>July</term> <note>original: ἰούλιον (*ioulion*)</note> using the Roman word, which is never, or rarely, found in ancient Greek writers. I mean "ancient" in the sense of the time before the Greek state was entirely obliterated; for after the Roman Caesars, everyone used Latin names for the months rather than Greek ones, prompted by the fortune and majesty of that nation. Related to this is the fact that Dioscorides was not accustomed to taking time markers from the months, but from the seasons of the year; for example, the solstices, spring, autumn, winter, and summer. 

We know these things contribute little or nothing to medicine. But we are treating herbalism: we are attempting in this writer to at least render it less corrupted for Latin readers, since it is impossible to restore it entirely given the great neglect and ignorance of those who followed. We almost missed one point that still pertains to Bugloss, Borage, and their identifying marks. It is this: he said the leaves of *Cirsion* were similar to Bugloss here, moderately hairy, longer, and whitish, prickly at the extremities. Of Bugloss, however, he says: <term>a leaf falling to the ground, rougher and darker</term> <note>original Greek: φύλλον χαμαιπετές, τραχύτε καὶ μελάντερον (*phyllon chamaipetes, trachyte kai melanteron*)</note>. 

Now let the history of each be compared with nature's examples, and let us more diligently contemplate the Bugloss and Borage picked from the garden. To me indeed, that first description of *Cirsion* seems to correspond to the Bugloss of our age, while the latter seems to correspond to Borage. For the leaves of Bugloss are longer than those of Borage. The former are whitish, while the latter are darker. The former rise and stand tall by themselves; those of Borage lie on the ground. It is characteristic of Borage what he says here: <term>falling to the ground</term> <note>original: χαμαιπετές (*chamaipetes*)</note>, that is, a leaf spread on the soil.

### THE JUDGMENT OF NICCOLÒ LEONICENO on Bugloss and Borage, from his book *On the Errors of Physicians*.
<note>Leoniceno was a pioneer of the "medical humanism" movement, which used philology to correct medieval mistranslations of Greek medicine.</note>

<margin>The modesty and judgment of Leoniceno.</margin>
<margin>Simon of Genoa on Borage.</margin>
<margin>The Pandectarius.</margin>
Concerning Bugloss, about which you ask whether that which we use as Bugloss is the true Bugloss: if I respond with what I feel, I fear that just as you have very learnedly doubted, I might seem to insolently overturn the entirety of the medicine of our time. For if I strive to prove that the Bugloss which younger physicians employ for medical use is not the true Bugloss, "Why then," someone will say, "do you not also deny that the Lettuce we eat is the true Lettuce?" 

However, we are not so minded. Far be such rashness from us that we should wish to demolish all the decrees of the younger physicians; but just as we judge many of their views should be approved, so there are more in which we judge the ancient authors are more to be followed, especially in those matters where the younger physicians seem to disagree with one another. Concerning Borage, Simon of Genoa <note>a 13th-century doctor and lexicographer</note> writes as follows under the letter B: "Borage is a known herb, fit for food and medicine, both flower, leaf, and seed; Bugloss is said to be its wild species. I do not find any authentic author making a chapter on both: if he writes of one, he does not write of the other." So says he. However, the *Pandectarius* <note>Matthaeus Silvaticus, author of a massive 14th-century medical encyclopedia</note> feels otherwise. For in the eleventh chapter he writes one section on Borage, in which he alleges Dioscorides, and another on Bugloss, in which he cites Serapio from the same Dioscorides...

The author cites discrepancies in leaf shape, growth patterns, and historical month-naming conventions to distinguish the two plants and questions the accuracy of later medical interpretations.</summary>

# THE PHARMACY OF SIMPLE MEDICINES

<margin>
Bartholomew of Montagnana <note>A famous 15th-century Italian physician known for his medical "Consilia" or case studies.</note> in his *Medical Advice*.
More is believed about Bugloss than is actually true.
Conflicting views of the Modern physicians regarding Borage and Bugloss.
Two herbs similar to "Ox-tongue."
</margin>

**C** ...on the authority of Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*.</note> speaking of Bugloss, Montagnana writes these words in a certain piece of advice: "Borage, however, does not please me, because it is a very windy and gas-producing plant; this is shown by the multitude of belches it causes. And although it is considered temperate—because it is a species of Bugloss, which is temperate—little is written about it by the authorities, and more is believed about it than can be verified by reason or authority. Avicenna <note>The 11th-century Persian "Prince of Physicians."</note>, however, said nothing of it." See how great the discord is among these authors! One says no author speaks of both—that is, of Borage and Bugloss; another cites Dioscorides for both herbs; one makes Bugloss a species of wild Borage; another subjects Borage to Bugloss as if to its genus. Avicenna also, in the second book of his *Canon*, in the chapter on "Ox-tongue," notes that the physicians of his time did not use true Bugloss, but another plant which does not have the same benefits. Therefore, in the midst of such controversy among physicians—both Latin and Arabic—regarding the herb Bugloss, I will reveal what I think. First, it is accepted as a fact that "Bugloss" is the Greek translation for "Ox-tongue." However, there are two herbs known as "Ox-tongue" and thus they are similar to one another: one we call "Ox-tongue" <note>likely *Anchusa officinalis*</note>, the other "Borage" <note>*Borago officinalis*</note>. But there are also two herbs similar to "Ox-tongue" celebrated by Greek names among the Greeks: one called *Buglossum* and the other *Cirsion* by those same Greeks. Thus, I have no doubt that those two herbs—one of which we call Ox-tongue and the other Borage in our language—ought to be referred to two chapters in Dioscorides: one of which is

<margin>Explanation of Dioscorides.</margin>

on *Buglossum*, the other on *Cirsion*. For the latter, because of the great similarity it has with Bugloss, is likewise called "Great Bugloss" by the Greeks. But to those considering more diligently, the description of *Buglossum* in Dioscorides fits Borage better; however, the description of *Cirsion* (or Great Bugloss) fits the other plant better, which we commonly name Bugloss or Ox-tongue. Indeed, the same Dioscorides says the leaves of *Cirsion* are longer than the leaves of *Buglossum*. This is despite what is written in Pliny <note>The Roman natural historian.</note>, who describes *Cirsion* in Book 27, Chapter 8, in almost the same way as Dioscorides, yet says that *Cirsion* has leaves *not* longer than Bugloss (or as he translates it, "Ox-tongue"), but rather smaller. I think this error occurred due to the similarity of the Greek words and a flaw in the manuscript Pliny possessed: because instead of <term>makrotera</term> <note>original Greek: μακρότερα</note>, which means "longer," he found written <term>mikrotera</term> <note>original Greek: μικρότερα</note>, that is, "smaller." I, however, in many Greek manuscripts—not only printed ones but also handwritten ones—have found in Dioscorides the word <term>makrotera</term>, that is, "longer," and not <term>mikrotera</term>, that is,

**D** "smaller." Furthermore, it is obvious to the senses that the leaves of that herb which is commonly called Bugloss are longer than the leaves of Borage. Likewise, the same Dioscorides says that at the top of the stalk of *Cirsion* there are small purple heads which dissolve into downy fluff; this is also observed by sight in the herb we call Bugloss. In contrast, in Borage, blue heads are seen, not purple ones. In the author of *On Simple Medicine*, these words are read: "The Romans call Bugloss 'Ox-tongue,' the Lucanians call it 'Corago'." It grows in cultivated and sandy places. Perhaps, however, the word "Corago" is erroneously written for Borage; or the name *Corago*, by changing one letter, has been turned into Borage. As for 

<margin>The Pandectarius is noted.</margin>

Pandectarius <note>Referring to Matthaeus Silvaticus, author of a massive medical dictionary.</note> (if this man has any authority), under the letter L, he lists *lisinaltaur* <note>An Arabic name for Bugloss, meaning "tongue of the bull."</note>. Regarding the Bugloss of which Dioscorides, Galen, and the Arabic authors (citing both) speak, and which we use in the practice of medicine: it is better to accept Borage than that plant which is everywhere called Bugloss.

<margin>Error of Montagnana. Laziness of Simon.</margin>

And thus, what Montagnana thought will be false: that Avicenna said nothing about Borage. For, unless my opinion deceives me, the chapter on Bugloss (or Ox-tongue) in Avicenna is actually the chapter on Borage, just as it is also in Serapion <note>A name used for two influential medieval medical authors, likely the younger Serapion here.</note>. It will also be false what Simon <note>Simon of Genoa, a 13th-century medical lexicographer.</note> writes, who thought that no author had written about both herbs at the same time. Indeed, Dioscorides among the Greeks and Pliny among us made mention of both Bugloss and *Cirsion*. It cannot be denied that Borage is one of the two in Dioscorides—either *Cirsion* or *Buglossum*—especially by those who admit that Borage is a species of Bugloss or Bugloss a species of Borage. For even Dioscorides himself testifies that *Cirsion* has leaves similar to Bugloss and is called "Great Bugloss." If, however, Borage is the *Cirsion* of the Greeks, it will be true what is written by Montagnana: that so many things are recklessly proclaimed about Borage by the younger physicians. For Dioscorides reported only this about *Cirsion*: that if its root is bound over a painful spot, it soothes the pain. Pliny [wrote the same]. Let the Moderns choose which they prefer: either that Borage is the true Bugloss (as we believe), or that the use of that herb is not beneficial for those things for which they judge it to be.

## HERMOLAUS BARBARUS <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493) was a Venetian scholar famous for his "Castigationes Plinianae," where he corrected thousands of errors in Pliny the Elder’s natural history based on his knowledge of Greek.</note> in the Chapter on Cirsion.

<margin>*Ixias* <note>original: "Ixiae"; a term for varicose veins.</note>.

<term>Cirsion</term> <note>Likely a species of thistle, possibly *Cirsium vulgare*.</note> rather than, as some read, <term>Crifion</term>, is named after varices [swollen veins], for which it is considered useful. ## OUR JUDGMENT.

Now the judgment rests with you, Reader, whoever you are. We have depicted both for you: both <term>Bugloss</term> and <term>Borage</term>. You also have the judgments of learned men and the words of Dioscorides written below; and it seems likely to me that as they agree in their flowers and appearance, so they also agree in their medicinal benefits.

### TEMPERAMENT <note>In ancient medicine, the "temperament" of a substance refers to its balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>.

Both are hot and moist in the first degree.

# SIMPLE Medicines

<margin>C</margin>
->From GALEN.<- <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was a Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a millennium.</note>

Bugloss cooked in mead <note>original: "mulsa"; a mixture of honey and water.</note> is beneficial for those coughing due to a roughness of the throat.

->From GIOVANNI DA VIGO.<- <note>Giovanni da Vigo (1450–1525) was a famous Italian surgeon and physician to Pope Julius II.</note>

Bugloss generates good blood and possesses powers similar to Borage.
And its root, cooked under hot coals and pounded with soaked bread, along with an equal portion of apple pulp (also cooked under coals) and a little butter, soothes the pain of a whitlow <note>original: "panaricij"; a painful infection of the fingertip or nail bed.</note>.
It also ripens all boils.
Held in the mouth—if it has first been soaked and infused in pomegranate wine—it relieves the roughness and dryness of the tongue in those with fever, and it quenches thirst, being not unpleasant even to the sick.

->From APULEIUS.<- <note>Referring to "Pseudo-Apuleius," the anonymous author of an influential 4th-century herbal text.</note>

The herb Bugloss, pounded with honey and bread, works wonderfully to break [abscesses] in the manner of a poultice <note>original: "malagmatis."</note>.

->From SERAPION.<- <note>Likely Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century Arab physician whose work on "simples" (individual medicinal ingredients) was a standard textbook.</note>

If its leaf is ever burned, it helps with the looseness of teeth and gums, and with thrush <note>original: "alcolam"; from the Arabic al-qula, referring to mouth sores or aphthae</note>, particularly that which occurs in the mouths of children, and for all inflammations that arise in the mouth.
Its specific property is to purge yellow bile <note>original: "cholerā."</note>; but it must be taken with Armenian bole <note>original: "bolo armeno"; a reddish medicinal clay used as an astringent.</note>. And its dose is from 3 to 5 drams <note>drachmas</note> with sugar, and with one dram of Armenian bole.

->From JEROME the herbalist.<- <note>Likely Hieronymus Brunschwig (c. 1450–1512), a German surgeon and botanist known for his works on distillation.</note>

<margin>D</margin>
Bugloss water dissipates Jaundice, cleanses leprosy and scabies, and soothes discharges from the head.

->From GIOVANNI DA VIGO.<-

Its virtue is to generate good blood.
And it is universally granted to the wounded in their meals, with parsley and mint, especially cooked in chicken broth.

->From PLATEARIUS.<- <note>Matthaeus Platearius, a 12th-century physician from the School of Salerno, author of "Circa Instans."</note>

It is helpful to those recovering from illness.
Likewise for those suffering from fainting, heart conditions, and melancholy, when eaten with meat or prepared with beech-oil <note>original: "fagimine."</note>.
Against fainting, the usage is as follows: from the juice of Borage with sugar, let a syrup be made, with the addition of the bone from a stag's heart <note>original: "osse de corde cerui"; a piece of heart-cartilage once highly prized as a cardiac tonic.</note>.
Against the affliction of melancholy and epilepsy, let a decoction be made in its juice with senna <note>original: "de sene"; a common purgative</note>, and let a syrup be made from the strained liquid. If the herb is missing, let its seed be cooked in water, and a syrup made from that strained liquid. And note, that the seeds can be kept for two years with great efficacy.
The root is suitable for medicinal use. Against Jaundice, it is eaten cooked with meat and its juice; and for the juice of endive <note>original: "scariolæ"</note>, let it be used in a drink.

This vervain produces stalks a cubit long <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of measurement, roughly the length of a forearm (18 inches).</note>, sometimes even larger and angled, around which there are leaves at intervals, similar to those of an oak, but narrower and smaller, yet cut around the edges, with a somewhat grayish-blue color. ...of the VOLUME One.

<margin>A</margin>

### The Praise of Vervain from PLINY,
#### Book 25, chapter 9.

<margin>The superstitious herb Vervain.</margin>
No herb possesses more Roman nobility than *Hierobotane* <note>original: *Hierobotane*, Greek for "holy herb"</note>. Some call it *Peristerion* <note>original: *Peristerion*, meaning "pigeon-plant"</note>, while our people call it *Verbenaca* <note>Vervain</note>. This is the plant which we have indicated that envoys carry to the enemy. With this, the table of Jupiter is swept, and houses are purged and purified.

There are two kinds of it. The leafy one, which they consider the female. The male has fewer leaves. The branches of both are numerous, thin, a cubit <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches</term> long, and angular. The leaves are smaller and narrower than those of the Oak, with larger divisions. The color is sea-green <note>original: *glaucus*</note>, and the root is long and thin. It grows everywhere in flat, watery places. Some people do not distinguish between them, but make them one genus entirely, since both have the same effects. The Gauls use both for casting lots and prophesying answers. But the *magi* <term>magi: ancient practitioners of ritual and herbal magic</term> rave about this plant. They claim that those anointed with it obtain what they wish, drive away fevers, win friendships, and cure every disease. They say it must be gathered around the rising of the Dog Star <note>Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky</note>, so that neither moon nor sun is seen, with honeycombs and honey given to the earth beforehand as an atonement. After being circled with an iron tool, it is to be dug up with the left hand and raised high; it should be dried in the shade, with the leaves, stem, and root kept separate. And they say if the dining room is sprinkled with the water in which it was soaked, the banquet becomes more cheerful. Against serpents, it is crushed in wine. There is a herb similar to Mullein <note>original: *Verbascum*</note> that often deceives those who take it for Vervain, though its leaves are less white, its stems more numerous, and its flower yellow. This discarded plant attracts cockroaches <note>original: *blactas*</note>, and therefore in Rome, they call it *Blactaria* <note>Moth Mullein</note>.

<margin>
Terence in *The Lady of Andros*.
"Take some Vervain from the altar here for yourself."
Virgil, *Eclogue 8*.
"Burn rich Vervain and male incense, that I may try to turn my husband's sane mind with magical rites; nothing is missing here but the songs."
</margin>

<margin>B</margin>
The same author [Pliny] in book 22, chapter 2: The authors and founders of the Roman Empire took something immense from this plant: for the *sagmina* <term>sagmina: sacred tufts of grass uprooted with their earth</term> used in public rituals and sacred embassies were nothing else but Vervain. Certainly, both names signify the same thing: that is, grass from the citadel, uprooted with its own earth. This was always used by envoys when they were sent to the enemy for *clarigatio* <term>clarigatio: a formal Roman ritual for demanding redress or declaring war</term>, that is, to clearly demand the return of stolen property; the envoy was specifically called the *Verbenarius* <note>the Vervain-bearer</note>.

### The Depiction of Vervain from APULEIUS.

Vervain grows everywhere in flat and watery places. It has whitish leaves that appear as if incised, a simple root and a stalk <note>original: *thyrso*</note>, with a counteracting power they call *Stypticen* <note>astringent</note>. It is a plant that glues wounds together and wipes away decay. Moreover, it is a pleasant food for pigeons.

### The author PANDECTARIUS on Vervain.

<margin>
Cock's Spur.
Chicken-herb.
Upright.
</margin>
A species of *Hierobotanos* <note>holy herb</note> is "Cock's Spur" <note>original: *Centrum galli*</note>, and it is prostrate <note>lying flat on the ground</note>. The second is Vervain, which is called *Gallinacea* <note>chicken-herb</note>, and it is upright, and therefore called *orthos* <note>original: *ὀρθός*, Greek for "straight" or "upright"</note>.

### From where Vervain was so named, from HERMOLAUS BARBARUS.

<margin>
Pigeon-herb.
Bird-food.
All-colored.
</margin>
It was called *Peristereon* by the Greeks because pigeons often stay in it. Hence it is called *Columbaris*. Also *Lucinia*, and *Lustrago* <note>purifying herb</note>, and *Militaria* <note>military herb</note>. There are those who name it *Petonomon* from the feeding of birds, and *Panchronon* <note>all-colored</note> from the variety of its colors. By our people it is called *Verbena* and *Verbenaca*, or (as I believe) corruptly *Verminaca*. Also *Ferraria* <note>Iron-herb</note>, not *feria*, even if Dioscorides seems to have named it so. Since the second genus of this herb, by him...

<margin>Verminaca.</margin>

OF SIMPLE MEDICINES

<margin>C</margin> According to Dioscorides, it is called *Sideritis* <note>original: *Sideritis*, from the Greek for "iron," referring to herbs used to heal wounds caused by iron weapons</note>.

## CONSTITUTION

It has the power of drying and joining wounds together.

### POWERS AND BENEFITS
### of it according to DIOSCORIDES

The leaves, when applied with fresh pig fat or rose oil, are thought to end the pains of a wound. 
They repress "sacred fire" <note>original: *Ignem sacrum*, a historical term for skin infections like Erysipelas or "St. Anthony's Fire"</note> when applied with vinegar. 
They check rotting ulcers, 
bind wounds together,
and for old wounds, they bring about a scar when used with honey.

### From AEMILIUS MACER <note>A Roman poet whose work *De Viribus Herbarum* (On the Powers of Herbs) was a standard medical text in the Renaissance</note>

<margin>The powers of Vervain.</margin>
The Greeks call it *Verbena*, *Hierobotane* <note>holy herb</note>, and *Peristereon* <note>pigeon-plant</note>; this species is said to have two forms, though the effect of the two is nearly the same. 
Taken often with wine, it helps those with jaundice <note>original: *ictericos*</note>. 
Crushed and applied, it cures venomous bites: 
this medicine should indeed be renewed with wine over four days. 
It cleanses mouth wounds well if its warm juice is swished in the mouth. 
A freshly made decoction of the herb also provides this benefit.
<margin>D</margin>
Any rot of the mouth is also repelled by this, if it is swished for a long time in the resonant throat. 
The fresh herb joins a wound when crushed and applied. 
Taken with wine, it counteracts all poisons. 
The fever that comes on alternating days <note>likely referring to "ternary" or "tertian" malaria-like fevers</note> is driven away by this, using three of its roots. 
When drunk in water with an equal number of leaves, the sufferer should take it before feeling any chill. 
In this same way, it cures quartan fevers <note>fevers occurring every four days</note> if four leaves and four roots are consumed in a wine decoction. 
It is said to make guests cheerful when scattered among the festivities, just as was previously prescribed for Bugloss <note>original: *Buglossa*, a plant historically added to wine to "drive away sadness"</note>.
<margin>Superstitious</margin>
By holding this herb in your hand, if you ask the sick person: 
"Brother, how are you?"—if the patient answers "Well," he will 
live; if indeed he says "Badly," there is no hope for health. 
Some have ordered a crown made from this to be 
placed on the head for whatever cause of pain; 
thus they say it brings a swift remedy. 
Pliny affirms that this is healthy for all the 
internal organs, for pains of the side and complaints of the liver, 
for ailments of the chest, and especially to be used as medicine...

<summary>This page catalogs the medicinal uses of Vervain (Verbena) as recorded by Dioscorides, Aemilius Macer, and Pliny, focusing on its ability to heal wounds, treat fevers through specific numeric dosages of roots and leaves, and its use in folk-prognosis.</summary>
<keywords>Vervain, Verbena, Dioscorides, Aemilius Macer, wound healing, jaundice, fevers, medical superstition, Sideritis, ancient pharmacology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the herbal lore of Vervain (Verbena), finishing the poetic verses attributed to Aemilius Macer before transitioning to a series of practical medicinal recipes from Pseudo-Apuleius. The text bridges the gap between folklore—such as using the plant to win the favor of the powerful—and clinical applications for physical ailments like kidney stones and liver pain.</meta>

First VOLUME of Medicines.

<margin>A</margin>
He asserts this herb is for lung conditions and consumption <note>original: *phthisis*, a historical term for a progressive wasting disease, usually tuberculosis</note>.
It suppresses parotid swellings <note>swelling of the glands behind the ear</note> when mixed with old fat.
Join the herb which they named for its "thousand leaves" <note>original: *Mille*, referring to Milfoil or Yarrow (*Achillea millefolium*)</note>,
and Betony with an equal weight of Vervain;
if these are mixed and drunk with water, they believe no medicine
is more useful for those whom the stone <note>original: *calculus*, referring to kidney or bladder stones</note> tortures.
Pliny asserts that the Magi <note>ancient Persian priests or magicians</note> praise this herb significantly;
they say it resists all diseases,
and that whoever is anointed with it shall obtain whatever they seek.
They even imagine that the friendships of the powerful can be won this way,
and fevers driven away, and many such things.
Although nature's power could potentially grant such things,
to us they rightly seem vain and like old wives' tales.

## FROM APULEIUS, chapters 3 & 66. <note>Referring to the *Herbarium* of Pseudo-Apuleius, a widely used late-antique medical text</note> For in two
## chapters, he treats almost the same matter.

## For ULCERS and PAROTID SWELLINGS.
The root of the Vervain herb tied around the neck is highly beneficial.

## For SCROFULA and Parotid Swellings.
The Vervain herb, crushed and applied, heals wonderfully.

## For those who have HARDENED VEINS
## and cannot keep food down.

<margin>B</margin>
The juice of the Vervain herb is given to drink, but it must be cooked; afterward, it is mixed with wine, honey, and water, and it heals immediately.

## For pain of the LIVER.
The Vervain herb, gathered at the solstice and reduced to powder; for a strong person, you shall give five spoonfuls taken as a drink with three small cups <note>original: *cyathis*, a Roman liquid measure</note> of the best wine; it is believed to be wonderfully beneficial. For others, give according to each person's strength.

## FOR THOSE WITH STONES.
<image-desc>A manicule (pointing hand icon) in the right margin points toward the heading "FOR THOSE WITH STONES."</image-desc>
The root of Vervain crushed in the best honey-wine <note>original: *mulso*, a mixture of wine and honey</note> and given warm, helps those with stones incredibly; and not only those with the stones themselves, but whatever it might be that impedes the urine, it will quickly clear it.

## For HEADACHE.
A crown made of the Vervain herb and placed on the head will take away the headache.

## For the bites of SERPENTS.
Whoever carries the Vervain herb with its leaves and roots tucked away and girded about them will be safe from all serpents.

## FOR THE BITE OF SPIDERS,
## which the Greeks call Phalangia. <note>original: *Phalangios*, referring to venomous spiders</note>
Twigs of the Vervain herb boiled in wine and crushed; then you shall apply the sour part to the wound and it will open it; afterward, a reliable author affirms that the raw herb crushed with honey and boldly inserted into the ulcer leads surely to health.

Medicines of SIMPLES

<margin>C</margin>
# FOR THE BITE OF A MAD DOG, and the water-snake. <note>original: *hydroſa hydri*, referring to a water-snake or perhaps the dropsy associated with its bite</note>

Apply the herb Vervain <note>original: *Verbenaca*</note> to the wound; also place whole grains of wheat into the wound until they are softened and filled by the fluid: then throw those swollen grains to a hen. If she does not eat them, throw in other grains in the same way; if they then begin to be eaten, it will be a sign that the danger has been removed. <note>This is a diagnostic folk-test: it was believed that the grain would "draw out" the venom or rabies, and the animal's willingness to eat the grain indicated the state of the poison.</note>

### FOR RECENT WOUNDS.

The Vervain herb, crushed with butter, is applied to the wound.

### For the bite of a SNAKE.

Small branches of the Vervain herb boiled in wine and crushed: if the wound is closed <note>original: *caeca plaga*, literally a "blind" or hidden wound</note> and accompanied by swelling, applying these first opens it; then they cleanse the sore. Afterwards, they are applied crushed raw with honey and inserted into the ulcer until they lead to health (which happens quickly).

## FOR THOSE SUFFERING FROM THE ROYAL DISEASE, or the jaundiced. <note>original: *morbo regio*, "the royal disease," a traditional name for jaundice, so named because it was supposedly treated with expensive, "regal" remedies or because the patient required a luxurious lifestyle to recover.</note>

One drachm <note>about 3.9 grams</note> of the Vervain herb, three obols <note>a small weight, roughly half a gram</note> of nard <note>an aromatic essential oil from the honeysuckle family</note>, the pressed juice of the raw berries <gloss>of the leaves</gloss>, and a little crushed myrrh, given as a drink in three <term>cyathi</term> <note>a measure of about 45ml each</note> of water, is believed to expel the disease.

<margin>D</margin>

To Paternianus, chapter 222. <note>Referring to *Ad Paternianum*, a late Latin medical text</note>

The Author of the *Pandects*. <note>A reference to the *Pandectae Medicinae*, a common medical encyclopedia</note>

Paulus, the chapter on *Peristereo*. <note>Referring to Paulus Aegineta; *Peristereo* is the Greek name for Vervain, meaning "pigeon plant"</note>

# Wall Germander. A <note>Latin: *Chamædrys*</note>

->Little Germander.<- B <note>German original: *Gamenderlin*</note>

# ON GERMANDER,
## Nineteenth Rhapsody. <note>In this context, a "rhapsody" refers to a compiled collection of writings from various classical authorities on a single subject.</note>
## NAMES

**Greek:** *chamaidrys* <note>χαμαίδρυς</note>, *chamaidryps* <note>χαμαίδρυψ</note>, *linodrys* <note>λινόδρυς</note>.
**Latin:** *Gamandræa*. Lesser *Trixago*. Lesser Oak <note>original: *Quercula minor*, referring to the oak-like shape of the leaves</note>.
**German:** **Little Germander.**

## OPINIONS OF THE AUTHORS on Germander.

### The Description of GERMANDER from DIOSCORIDES, Book 3.

IT GROWS in rough and stony places, and is a short shrub, reaching a height about the span of an open human hand—from the tip of the thumb to the end of the little finger. It has small leaves, similar in shape and divisions to those of an oak, with a bitter taste, and a purplish flower, which is also quite small. The herb should be gathered when it is heavy with its own seed.

### PLINY’S Description of Germander, Book 24, Chapter 15.

*Chamædrys* is an herb which in Latin is called *Trissago*. Some have called it *Chamædropen*, others *Teucrion*. It has leaves the size of Mint, with the color and divisions of an Oak. Others call it *Serrata* [The Serrated One], and they claim the saw was invented from the pattern of this leaf. <margin>Serrated.</margin>

## On the Nomenclature of Trixago by MARCELLO VIRGILIO <note>Marcello Virgilio Adriani (1464–1521) was a Florentine humanist known for his commentary on Dioscorides.</note>

<margin>
Trixago.
Chamædrys.
Chamærops.
</margin>
Trixago is a certain kind of oak of stunted shortness, and from this, it received its name from the Greeks; for *Chamædrys* means nothing other than a humble and ground-dwelling oak. Because of this same shortness, some have given it another name, *Chamæropis*. We believe it should be read this way based on the reliability of the ancient Greeks and Latins, even if some record it as being called *Chamædropa* here. Indeed, all the codices of Pliny before the correction by Barbarus <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a scholar famous for "correcting" the text of Pliny the Elder.</note> stated that Trixago was called *Chamæropen*, not *Chamædropen*. He amended that word based on the reading of this author. Also, the ancient Latin Dioscorides we possess, written in Lombardic letters <note>A script used in Italy from the 7th to 13th centuries.</note>, testifies that Trixago is called *Chamæropa*, not *Chamædropa*. Nor do we have a reason or cause why it should be called one rather than the other; even if some reason must be devised, none will be more likely than that it was once called so because it creeps along the ground. If that is accepted, then it should rather be called *Chamærops*. Being in doubt, we have followed the majority of witnesses and said *Chamæropem*. 

<margin>Teucrion.</margin>
The author himself shows the reason why this would also be called *Teucrion*; and therefore it must be left to us, who have not yet found the origin of the Roman name despite much labor spent searching. For Pliny says nothing else than that the herb *Chamædrys* is called *Trixago* in Latin. Nevertheless, he described it: where this author said "small leaves," Pliny said "the size of Mint"; and where this author spoke of a "shape and notches similar to an oak," Pliny spoke of the "color and division of an oak." He added, moreover, that this herb is called *Serrata* <note>meaning "Saw-edged"</note> by others; and that from it—that is, from those notches which it has around its edge, appearing just like the teeth in a saw today—the iron saw was invented. 

<margin>Theophrastus on Trixago.</margin>
Theophrastus, when he mentioned it in the 9th book of his *History of Plants*, treated its features and parts briefly; but he listed many other medicinal powers than this writer, which should therefore be repeated by us in this place. They are as follows: 

<margin>Medicines of Trixago.</margin>
The leaves of Trixago are beneficial for ruptures and wounds; for this use, they are applied after being crushed in oil. They also benefit spreading ulcers. The seed purges bile. It also helps the eyes; the crushed leaf should be applied to them with oil. Trixago has leaves similar to oak; and its entire growth is a nine-inch span <note>original Latin: *dodrantale*</note>; which was indicated by us in Dioscorides as the measure of an "expanded hand." Theophrastus added, moreover, that this Trixago is fragrant and sweet, an herb easy to find and recognizable everywhere by these signs. 

In its measurement, we and others differ significantly from Barbarus. For he describes it as being four fingers in height; we, as we usually do, always translate <term>spithame</term> <note>a Greek unit of measurement</note> as the extent of a man's entire outstretched hand. For we have observed that this word signifies that. The "four fingers" which he counts in a *spithame* are actually the measure of a palm, which is much smaller than a nine-inch span <note>Latin: *dodrans*</note>; Pliny clearly translates the Greek *spithame* using this word in his seventh book. So also, what that author called a "thin flower," we have simply translated as "small." For here he says <term>mikron</term> <note>Greek: μικρὸν, meaning small</note>. Furthermore, where Dioscorides says <term>agein embrya</term> <note>Greek: ἄγειν ἔμβρυα</note>, which pertains to abortions, that author, believing it pertained to the ease of delivery, said "to provoke birth." <meta>catchword: -pinatus (thought)</meta>

<header>SIMPLE Medicines</header>

<margin>C</margin>

### FROM AVERROES, *The Colliget*, Book 5, Chapter 17.
Wall Germander <note>original: *Chamædreos*</note> is hot and dry in the second degree <note>A classification of potency in Galenic medicine; the second degree indicates a noticeable but not extreme effect.</note>. This is indicated by its bitterness combined with sharpness. It cuts through thick humors <note>The "humors" were the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to govern health.</note> and clears obstructions in the internal organs.

### FROM PLATEARIUS regarding Wall Germander and Ground Pine.
<margin>Error of Platearius regarding Wall Germander and Ground Pine.</margin>
Wall Germander is hot and dry in the fourth degree <note>the most intense level of medicinal action</note>, and Ground Pine <note>original: *Chamæpithyos*</note> is the same. Wall Germander is called "Great Little Oak," while Ground Pine is called "Small Little Oak" <note>original: *quercula maior* and *quercula minor*—referring to the shape of the leaves.</note>. It possesses diuretic and cleansing properties.
Against vomiting caused by indigestion <note>original: *anatrophia*—a Greek term for a stomach disorder where food is not properly absorbed.</note> or from any "cold" cause, let these herbs be boiled for a very long time in salt water—either brine or naturally salty water—and with oil and a bit of vinegar added, let a plaster <note>a poultice</note> be made for the chest. It is a supreme remedy against any vomiting resulting from a cold cause.
<margin>,,</margin> Its powder, given with honey, also kills intestinal worms.
<margin>,,</margin> Against catarrh <note>a buildup of mucus</note>, the warm powders should be placed in a small bag and laid upon the head; it is an excellent remedy.
For dandruff <note>original: *furfures*—literally "scales" or "bran"</note> of the head or beard, let lupine flour be boiled in salt water with vinegar added; after straining the liquid, add the powder of both herbs (or just one), and then wash the head with it.
Against paralysis, apply the herbs boiled in wine to the painful area. Their powder consolidates <note>knits together or heals</note> ulcers and wounds.
To cleanse the womb <note>original: *matricem*</note> and to warm it when it has been chilled by a surplus of phlegm, let those herbs be boiled in water for a long time; let the woman be bathed with the liquid, and let the herbs themselves be applied as a plaster over the private parts.
<margin>D</margin> Let their powder be boiled in oil and a piece of silk <note>original: *bombix*</note> soaked in it be applied; or let a powder be prepared with the juice of Sowbread <note>original: *Mali terræ*—literally "Earth Apple," a common name for Cyclamen</note> and applied.

### FROM HIERONYMUS THE HERBALIST.
The water of Germander <note>original: *Gamãdreæ*</note>, drunk while fasting, purifies the blood and drives away the itch <note>scabies</note>. It also heals *alcola* <note>a medieval term for aphthae or mouth sores</note> and ulcers of the mouth.

### FROM THE HERBAL AGGREGATOR.
They say of this herb that it has such a nature that whoever carries it in their pocket <note>original: *in sinu*—literally "in the fold of one's garment"</note> will be openly hated by everyone.
It also clears the dimness of the eyes when its juice or water is applied to them.

->OPINIONS OF AUTHORS on the Narcissus.<-

->The History of the Narcissus, according to DIOSCORIDES, Book 4.<-
<note>Pedanius Dioscorides was a 1st-century Greek physician whose work "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical authority for 1,500 years.</note>

> The Narcissus has leaves very similar to the Leek <note>original: *Porro*</note>, though they are thin, much smaller, and narrower. The stem is hollow and without leaves, rising to a height of more than a *dodrans* <note>A Roman unit of measurement, approximately 9 inches or 23 centimeters.</note>. The flower is white in the middle, saffron-colored <note>yellow</note> on the inside, and in some varieties, purple. The root is white on the inside, round, and bulbous. The seed is as if contained in a tunic <note>a seed pod</note>, and is black and long. The most highly esteemed variety grows in the mountains and has a sweet scent. In other respects, it resembles the Leek and has a grassy, pungent smell.

<header>...of SIMPLE medicines—</header>

C

### Hermolaus Barbarus’s Judgment on the NARCISSUS.

<margin>Image of the Narcissus</margin>
The Narcissus has a leaf like that of the Asphodel <note>original: *Albuci*</note>, very close to the ground, but broader—thick and fleshy like a Lily, abundant, and narrow, with a leafless, grass-colored stalk. The flower appears at the top after the rising of the star Arcturus <note>late September</note>, and around the equinox, as well as in the spring. It also appears after the Lily and the Violet—specifically the one called the "Flame" Violet <note>original: *Flamẽa*, likely referring to the pansy or *Viola tricolor*</note>. It is enclosed in a membrane as if in a little vessel; it is somewhat large, blackish, and oblong. When it falls off, it sprouts spontaneously, especially if it is fixed into the earth; however, it is also sown by hand. It has a large, round, fleshy root. The stalk and the flower break out together, as in the saffron plant, before the leaf appears; the leaf is not seen until after the flower has faded. The stalk dies away along with its flower. The root is similar to a Bulb, except that it is not scaly.

<margin>The Narcissus often blooms by a miracle of nature. Why the Narcissus is so named. Two kinds of Narcissus according to Pliny. All these points support our opinion.</margin>
By flowering so frequently, the Narcissus demonstrates three different seasons for planting. It is used in flower garlands. It is named from *Narce*, which signifies "torpor" or "numbness" <note>Greek: νάρκη</note>, because its scent weighs down the head—it is not named after the boy in the fables. Pliny established two kinds: one with a white flower and a purple cup <note>likely *Narcissus poeticus*</note>, and another with the same features but with a grass-green cup. He says all of them are late-blooming, for they flower after Arcturus and through the Autumn equinox. He notes that physicians prescribe these two kinds as if there were others they do not accept—which I believe refers to that kind which is born in spring or summer, as we previously mentioned from the opinion of Theophrastus.

<margin>Why the Narcissus is called "black."</margin>
Furthermore, it should be understood that when we read Theophrastus calling the flower "black," he is not referring to the flower itself (which is agreed to be white), but to the seed. This seed is known to be covered by a membrane and is both black and quite long; when it falls to the ground, it propagates itself and sows the Narcissus.

D

<margin>Crotalos, Acacalis, Crotos.</margin>
Eumachus of Cyrene, in his *Book of Roots*, reported that the Narcissus is also called *Crotalon* and *Acacalis*. Regarding the name *Crotos* found in the writings of Hippocrates—which was approved for treating old ulcers and fresh wounds—I do not see what else it could be but the Narcissus. This is unless one takes *Crotos* to mean *Croton*, which is the *Cici* <note>The Castor oil plant, *Ricinus communis*</note> in that context.

<margin>Narcissus is a name for many. The fable of Narcissus.</margin>
Julius Pollux is the authority for the fact that it was Theophrastus’s habit to use the name *Lirium* for the Narcissus; however, Homer used the term *Lirion* to encompass every kind of flower. The people of Thespiae in Boeotia gossip that the Narcissus was born from a youth seized by love for himself and transformed into that flower; they point to the spring *Donaca* as the place where the most foolish boy gazed at himself, unable to distinguish his own reflection from his person. This fable is refuted by the very ancient poet Pamphilus, who sang of Proserpina being abducted by Pluto many years before Narcissus existed, while she was busy plucking Narcissuses.

### The same author again in his COROLLARY ON LILIES.

<margin>Four kinds of Narcissus.</margin>
In Theophrastus, there is a FOURFOLD kind of LILY. The flower of the first kind breaks out in spring, often along with the white Violet, or a little later. This is properly called *Crinon* <note>Greek: κρίνον</note> by him, which is to say, the *Lily*.

<margin>The Lily from across the sea. Cerinthus.</margin>
The second kind he calls *Lirium*, which blooms entirely in the spring, but later, along with the Narcissus. Perhaps this is what Pliny referred to as the "Lily from across the seas." The third kind blooms in summer, and I believe it is specifically called *Cerinthus* <note>Honeywort</note>, although "Cerinthus" signifies other things as well, as will be seen below.

<meta>This page continues the botanical discussion of lilies and Narcissus, specifically focusing on their nomenclature and etymology. It follows a description of the physical characteristics of the Narcissus and now incorporates the scholarly views of Marcello Virgilio Adriani, a noted Renaissance translator of Dioscorides.</meta>

<header>VOLUME One.</header>

<margin>
A
Red Lily.
Crinon.
Cynorhodon.
</margin>
...will be clear. The fourth kind, which the Greeks also call *Lirium* <note>original: *Lirium*, a general Greek term for lilies</note>, blooms in autumn and flashes forth with the first rains. There is also a red Lily, differing (as I believe) from the Purple one, which we saw in Padua in the garden of Felix. The most esteemed are found in Antioch and Laodicea in Syria; next is that of Phaselis, with the one growing in Italy holding the fourth place. Pliny is the authority that this kind is properly called *Crinon* by the Greeks, and its flower *Cynorhodon* <note>original: *Cynorhodon*, literally "dog-rose," though here applied to a lily variety</note>. Hippocrates also accepted this, as he recommends red *Cynorhoda* in wine for women's purgations. Purple Lilies are also produced by art, by soaking the stalks in wine dregs before they are planted in the month of March, and pouring the same dregs around them in the trench; for this purpose, they collect the drying stalks in July, hanging the Lilies in the smoke. Purple ones are sometimes seen with a twin stem, having only a meatier root and a larger bulb; the cup is grass-colored. The Purple ones bloom after the rising of the star Arcturus <note>the bright star in the constellation Boötes, signaling late September</note> and the autumn equinox; one kind of these they call *Narcissus*. This one has leaves at the root and, as we said, grass-colored cups, but is otherwise the same as the white ones. Nothing is more fertile than the white Lily, with one root often nourishing fifty bulbs.

## Judgment of MARCELLO VIRGILIO on the Narcissus.

<margin>
B
Narcissus is related to the Lily.
*Lirion* is specifically the Narcissus.
Aristophanes.
Narcissus is named from *Narce*.
Plutarch.
</margin>
All the ancient writers make the Narcissus a relative of the Lily, treating it immediately after the Lily in a continuous history. Most certainly of all, Theophrastus in the 6th book of his *History of Plants*, while discussing it among other things, says: "Whether it be the Narcissus or the *Lirion*; for some call it this, and others call it that" <note>original Greek: ὅτι δὲ νάρκισσος· ἢ τὸ λείριον, ὅι μὲν γὰρ τοῦτο ὅι δ' ἐκεῖνο καλοῦσιν</note>. This is clear evidence that the Narcissus is a relative, or at least similar to, the Lily. Because of this, it was once able to be called *Lirion*—the word the ancients used for Lilies—and several ancient Greek witnesses have testified that *Lirion* specifically indicates the Narcissus, just as *Crinon* refers only to the Lily. Some have added that even in Homer, all flowers are indicated by the single name of *Lirion*. It is believed that Aristophanes also observed this in his comedies. But as we have noted in this writer and in others, these wandering names were created by similarity and nearly the same nature. This writer clearly shows that the Lily was commonly called *Lirion* by the Greeks when he says: "Some even call the Narcissus *Lirion*, just as they do the Lily." It seems the Latins, by changing only one letter—as babbling children are wont to do, pronouncing *l* for *r*—made their *Lilium* from the Greeks' *Lirion*. This is the same way that the most delightful of Greek comic poets <note>Aristophanes</note> feigned in *The Knights* that Alcibiades spoke with a lisping tongue in the assembly, saying: "Look, Theolus has the head of a flatterer" <note>original Greek: ὁλᾶσ θίωλοσ κεφαλὴν κόλακοσ ἔχει</note>. Yet in what he wanted to be understood, where the letter *l* is heard, the letter *r* should have been understood: "Look, Theoros has the head of a crow" <note>original Greek: ὁρᾶσ θίωροσ κεφαλὴν κόρακοσ ἔχει; the joke relies on the lisp turning 'korax' (crow) into 'kolax' (flatterer)</note>. But to return to our subject, let it be taken as certain that the Narcissus is a relative of the Lily, or entirely similar to it. And since it causes pains and a sluggish heaviness of the head, it was called *Narcissus* by the Greeks from *narce* <note>Greek: νάρκη</note>—the word by which they indicate "torpor" or "numbness"—not from the mythical boy, as the poets imagined. Witnesses for this reasoning behind the name are Pliny, in volume 21, chapter 19, and Plutarch in the first chapter of the third commentary of his *Table Talk*. Plutarch’s words regarding the Narcissus are these: "And they called it the Narcissus as if it were something that dulls the nerves and creates fleshy, sluggish heaviness; wherefore Sophocles also called it the ancient crown of the great gods, that is, of the subterranean ones" <note>original Greek: καὶ τὸν νάρκισσον ὡς ἀμελύνοντα τὰ νεῦρα, καὶ βαρύτητας ἐμποιοῦντα σαρκώδεις, διὸ καὶ σοφοκλῆς αὐτὸν ἀρχαῖον μεγάλων θεῶν τουτέσι τῶν χθονίων σεφάνωμα προσηγόρευκε</note>. This is because the dead, sluggish in death, were deservedly crowned with a sluggish flower. One may also read in Dioscorides that some called the Narcissus *Anydron* <note>meaning "waterless"</note>; we believe this name was given to it because it blooms in mountainous places far from water. To this is also added the name *Autogenes*, a word signifying "born of itself" or "growing by itself," which has its reasoning in what Theophrastus indicated with these words: "This, falling off, produces a spontaneous sprouting" <note>original Greek: ὄυτος δ' ἐκ πίπτων ποιῆ βλάσησιν ἀυτόματον</note>. These things were said concerning the flower and the seed, and they mean: "This, falling of its own accord, germinates and is born." Although the same writer immediately testifies that its seed is collected and sown by human labor, and no less is the root planted, as with other Bulbs. We hear in Dioscorides that it is also called by some the "Vomiting Bulb"; not indeed because it is the same as the Vomiting Bulb described in the second volume, but because it is of a bulbous root and at the same time is an emetic, just as that one is; it has a principal use in ancient medicine. The Narcissus was once sown in gardens for making crowns; now it must be sought in the mountainous places where it grows. It is not difficult to find if it is sought more diligently. For the whole...
