# MEDICINES FROM SIMPLES

<margin>Another illustration of Narcissus.</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
...shape, and the circumference of its cup <note>original: "calathi", referring to the basket-shaped corona of the flower</note>, both of which are smaller than in the Lily; all authors have testified that it resembles the appearance of Lilies. Furthermore, because it is a late-blooming flower (for it blooms after the rising of the star Arcturus <note>late August</note> and toward the Autumn equinox), it cannot remain hidden among the Lilies and other flowers, almost all of which have perished by then. It also possesses other marks in this writer <note>Dioscorides</note> by which it may be identified: leek-like leaves, which Pliny says are at the root, though smaller and narrower; a hollow stem, without leaves, nine inches <note>original: "dodrantali", a measure of three-quarters of a foot</note> in height; and finally a white flower, saffron-colored in the middle—and, as must be the case for another of its kind, purple in some. In this description, unless there is an error in all the Greek manuscripts we have been permitted to see so far, one must reason that there are two types of Narcissus.

<margin>Pliny stumbles on the Narcissus.</margin>
Pliny clearly indicates this in two places. First, in Volume 21, Chapter 5, in his history of Lilies, saying: "They call it Narcissus, another kind of this having a white flower and a purple cup." Shortly after in Chapter 19 of the same book: "The practitioners of medicine recognize two kinds of Narcissus. One with a purple flower, and the other herbaceous <note>grass-like or green</note>." He seems to show no small inconsistency in teaching these varieties. Indeed, in that first description, he said one Narcissus has a white flower and a purple cup; in the latter, he said one has a purple flower and the other is herbaceous.

<margin>Theophrastus.</margin>
Theophrastus, from what I have observed in him so far, although he mentions the Narcissus quite often, used no such division of kinds. He always teaches about it as if there were only one Narcissus, describing now the leaves, now the blooming time, now the stem; from which we believe Pliny called the other kind "herbaceous." Indeed, in his history, among other things, it is heard: "the stem is indeed leafless, but herbaceous" <note>original Greek: "τὸν δὲ καυλὸν ἄφυλλον μὲν ποώδη δὲ"</note>. That is, a stem without leaves, but nevertheless grass-like in color. From this, Pliny could have called that other kind "herbaceous," not because of its flower. However, that does not mean we should not accept that there are two types of Narcissus. For this is handed down by Dioscorides, Pliny, and others. But the differences in their flowers taught by them are not sufficiently certain in either this writer or in Pliny. Other matters, however, as is evident from Theophrastus, possess the same historical truth. For he, in the 6th book of his *History of Plants*, described the Narcissus in these words: "The Narcissus, or Lirium <note>original: "Lirium", for some call it by this name and some by that</note>, has a leaf similar in shape to the Asphodel <note>a hardy perennial of the lily family</note> closest to the ground, yet wider than that of the Asphodel, and as if lily-like. The stem is naked of leaves, yet herbaceous; at the top of which is the flower. The seed is enclosed as if in a small vessel by a certain membrane, large, black, and oblong in shape. This falls and germinates of its own accord. Nevertheless, those who collect it also plant it in the earth. They also plant the root, which is round, fleshy, and large. It is a late-blooming flower. For it blooms after Arcturus and around the equinox."

<margin>Dioscorides says Narcissus has narrow, numerous, and thick leaves.</margin>
The same author, in the same book regarding the science of leaves, says that the Narcissus has narrow, numerous, and thick leaves. Not long after, dealing with the stems of plants, he says: "It is a marvel among all things what happens in the Squill <note>original: "Scylla", the sea onion</note> and the Narcissus. For in others, both those that bear from the start and those that sprout again by themselves, the leaves emerge first in spring, then the stem; but in these—that is, the Squill and the Narcissus—the stem precedes, and in the Narcissus, only the flower's stem." After he had described at length the rising of the Squill's stem and flower, he added: "When this stem has grown old, then after several days the leaves emerge. It happens similarly in the Narcissus, 'except that it has no other stem besides that produced for the flower, as we said, nor any visible fruit, but the flower itself decays along with the stem, and when it has finished flowering, then the leaves arise'" <note>original Greek: "πλὴν οὔτε καυλὸν ἕτερον ἔχει παρὰ τὸν τοῦ ἄνθους ὥσπερ εἴπομεν, οὔτε καρπὸν φανερὸν ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ἄνθος ἅμα τῷ καυλῷ καταφθίνει καὶ, ὅταν ἀνανθῇ τότε τὰ φύλλα ἀνατέλλει"</note>. Furthermore, the same writer testifies a little later that the Squill blooms first, and the Narcissus afterward. And we have collected so many things from him so that a flower of such great name in the garlands of the ancients might be more easily and certainly identified. For what Pliny handed down about it in various places was indeed derived from Theophrastus, but treated with such brevity by him that they are sometimes quite obscure to readers; so that Theophrastus and Dioscorides seem to correspond with one another. For all things concerning the leaves, stems, and seeds are the same in both. Only the color of the flower and the distinction of color is missing in Theophrastus; and readers must observe and distinguish this: especially because he <note>Dioscorides</note> describes it here as saffron-colored and purple in the middle. Pliny calls this the "flower," with a meaning not sufficiently certain as to whether the whole or a part is called the flower; just as we said regarding the flowers of the Black Violet from the teachings of Theophrastus on double flowers.

<margin>The Narcissus as seen by Virgilio in the Apennine mountains.</margin>
In these Apennine mountains of ours, we have seen a frequent flower blooming in the months of August and September, in the shape of a Lily, nine inches in height, with leaves such as are described in this Narcissus; with a single stem, and all other things the same, except for the color, which is neither white nor purple as Pliny teaches, but between white and yellow, with no or very little scent. We have also seen it growing on milder hills, but not so beautiful, and more whitish; and for a long time we believed it to be the Narcissus; nor do we yet depart far from that opinion.

<margin>The name Narcissus is vague, common to many flowers.</margin>
For the mind is inclined to the idea that the name Narcissus could have been vague to the ancients; and as is often the case elsewhere in the study of plants, it is possible that we might establish that there is a yellow-colored Narcissus. Thus we leave it to readers to find this flower, which is white in color with saffron stamens inside, and in some, purple; which is the only distinction in its color handed down by Dioscorides. For us, until now, it has not been possible to see white Lilies...

<meta>This page continues the botanical investigation of the Narcissus, specifically focusing on its identification through ancient Greek and Latin sources, its common German names, and its medicinal applications as recorded by Dioscorides.</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
...shape of the flowers, with filaments or stamens that are purple inside. We also leave it to more experienced minds to consider whether this writer <note>likely referring to Dioscorides or a commentator</note> approved of the Narcissus growing simply in mountainous places to distinguish it from the cultivated and garden variety; or whether something more might be required, such as what Pliny says: that the most highly prized variety grows in the mountains of Lycia <note>A region in modern-day Turkey</note>. We are somewhat more inclined toward this view. For that superlative term <term>beautifully-tressed</term> <note>Greek: *kallikomon*</note> seems to demand, I know not how, a more certain place of origin; and the preceding article can be believed to indicate the same sense. However, let this be a suspicion, not a decree. The same applies to the word <term>to be leek-green</term> <note>Greek: *prasizein*</note>, which follows immediately: whether it signifies to turn green and have a herbaceous color, or rather whether the word was derived from the Leek <note>Latin: *Porrum*</note> and signifies being perceived by the smell of a Leek. We have found this nowhere else among the ancients. All these matters, which must be observed and established more diligently, are left to others.

## OUR JUDGMENT on the Narcissus.

For nearly two years, we have tormented ourselves intensely and have been a nuisance to almost all the learned men of our city, and likewise to those common herbalists, just so that we might inquire after the name of this flower. Truly, we were able to fish out nothing so certain that we could not wonder enough how a plant, otherwise most common and conspicuous in every meadow with the first swallow of spring, could have vanished from all human knowledge. The name for the flower is the <term>February Flower</term> <note>original: "Hornungs Bluom"; Hornung is an archaic German name for February</note>. For that is what they call it in Upper Germany. There were some, therefore, who tried to persuade us that it was the white Violet, because the first flower of spring is the white Violet. Others constantly asserted it was Privet <note>Latin: *Ligustrum*</note>, or certainly something related to it, until we happened upon the Narcissus of Theophrastus and Dioscorides and began to question several herbalists—those who were not wise from books, but were taught by the experience of things. Thus, we noticed that everything matched the Narcissus so well that, unless we are plainly owl-eyed <note>meaning blind in the light of day</note>, we seem to have finally grasped it. Therefore, what we have received from the herbalists, and what we have partly observed ourselves, is this: there are, they say, two kinds of flower, namely Male and Female, purple, yellow, and white. They even bloom twice in a year, once in March, and then in September. It sheds its seed at Pentecost. And indeed, in the beginning, it comes forth with a white and yellow flower, and in winter with a purple flower. They say they have discovered this by a certain miracle of nature. For if anyone tries to dig in March, he scrapes it out easily with one finger; but from that time on, it sinks deeper and deeper into the earth day by day, and this continues until September, at which time it is dug out only with great difficulty. Sometimes it lies hidden in the earth at a depth of one cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>; soon in winter <margin>B</margin> it grows upward again, so that it even leaps above the ground at the first flowering and when Spring has breathed upon it. We too have experienced and observed that this is so: first a tender and bulbous root, and leaves like a Leek or Satyrion <note>a type of orchid</note>; soon the same root hardens, and the leaves become fatter, coming forth from the root alone without a stalk. In September, it is thoroughly hardened and hidden very deeply, with only a delicate and lily-like flower opening on the surface of the earth at the height of a palm’s breadth, after the second mowing of the meadows. Since we saw that the Narcissus of Dioscorides and Theophrastus corresponded to this observation, and finally that the commentaries of learned men agreed with them, we have consistently dared to bestow the name of Narcissus, or <term>February Lily</term>. Thus it is indeed a distinct flower. Furthermore, it proceeds from a single bulbous root, and is called Narcissus by Dioscorides, and <term>Mercury’s Finger</term> <note>original: *Hermodacttylus*</note> by the Arabs and modern writers. However, as to how rightly we have observed these things, and how skillfully those men taught us, we wish the judgment and estimation to belong to others, whom we advise and beseech to also make trial of such a great matter.

## POWERS AND BENEFITS according to Dioscorides.

> The root, when cooked, whether it is eaten or drunk, induces vomiting.
> It is beneficial for those burned by fire when ground with a little honey.
> It glues together cut nerves when applied as a salve.
> It helps dislocated ankles and long-standing joint pains when ground with honey and applied.
> It clears away skin blemishes on the face and white leprosy when used with nettle seed and vinegar.
> With bitter vetch and honey, it cleanses the filth of ulcers.
> It breaks open abscesses that resist ripening.
> It extracts things fixed in the body when applied with darnel flour and honey.

# THE OPINIONS of authors on VIOLETS.

### The Opinion of DIOSCORIDES on purple Violets.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Purple Violet.</margin>
**T**he purple VIOLET—which some call *Dasypodion* <note>meaning "rough-footed" or "hare-footed"</note>, others *Priapeion*, others the Wild Ion, others *Cybelion*—is called the "purple violet" by the Romans. It has a leaf smaller, thinner, and darker than Ivy, though not much different in shape. A small stalk emerges from the root, upon which grows a sweetly scented, purple flower. It grows in shady and rugged places.

---

## Paraphrase of HERMOLAUS BARBARUS on these same purple Violets.
<note>Hermolaus Barbarus (Ermolao Barbaro, 1454–1493) was a Venetian scholar famous for correcting errors in ancient scientific texts.</note>

<margin>The Violet, and why it is called *ion*.</margin>
The Greeks call the flower *Ion*, and the shrub *Violarium Ionian*. Nicander, in his *Georgics*, believes the Violet was called *Ion* because certain Ionian nymphs first gave this flower to Jove <note>Jupiter</note> as a gift. For 
<margin>Phrygana.</margin>
it grows in the manner of a vine from the upper parts—as if you were to say from the stern, not the prow—unlike Rue, Water-mint, or Thyme. For this reason, all call Violets *Phrygana*, which is to say "little twigs" or "dry sticks," except for the Black Violet, which he describes in this chapter. This plant remains green forever, and as some report, if it is cultivated in a certain way, it remains so the whole year. It is sown from cuttings like a vegetable. It blooms in spring, after the White Violet <note>Leucoion/Wallflower</note> and before the Flame-flower. When the Greeks say *Ion*, they almost always mean the Black or Purple variety. This one is low-growing, with a broader leaf that emerges immediately from a thick root without branches; for 
<margin>Strap-footed Violet.</margin>
this reason, we commonly call it the *Loripede* <note>original: *Loripes*, meaning "strap-footed" or "limping," referring to its creeping growth</note> Violet. They distinguish this one from others by name, as it is the only one called *Ia* by the Greeks; 
<margin>Tyrian Violets.</margin>
from which the terms "Ianthine" <note>violet-colored</note> garments and "violaceous" were said. Other kinds of violets we have recorded under the White Violets. I believe the "Sarrane Violets" <note>original: *Violas Sarranas*; "Sarrane" refers to Sarra, the ancient name for Tyre, famous for purple dye</note> mentioned by Columella are the same as the purple ones, named for their color. 
<margin>Vaccinia.</margin>
The grammarian Servius thinks that Purple Violets are called *Vaccinia* and Hyacinths. Dioscorides also writes that the Hyacinth is called *Vaccinium* in Latin. Those who read these things must be advised that purple Violets are held to be of two kinds. 
<margin>Hyacinth.</margin>
Some are among the "Strap-footed" or "Low-sitting" types, which are discussed here; others are among the White Violets <note>Leucoia</note>, and all are fragrant. 
<margin>Low-sitting violets.</margin>
But even among the white ones, they perceive this double distinction. Some are Strap-footed; others are White Violets. By White Violets <note>original: *Leucoia*</note>, I mean those which Mauritania calls *Chieri* <note>Wallflowers</note>; the Strap-footed ones are commonly named "Lame Violets," and in Moorish, *Senephigi*.
<margin>White Violets.</margin>
<margin>Chieri.</margin>
<margin>Lame violets</margin>
<margin>Senephigi.</margin>

## Annotation of VERGILIUS on purple Violets.
<note>Marcello Virgilio Adriani (1464–1521), a Florentine scholar and translator of Dioscorides.</note>

<margin>D</margin>
That dark-purplish hue—or to speak more aptly, a purple color tending toward black—is what caused the Latin poets to call them "rust-colored Hyacinths" and "black Vaccinia." This was the same reason for Theophrastus and other Greek writers to call the Violet we are now treating "black." This distinction of color is so frequent and reciprocal that in many places in Theophrastus's *History of Plants*, nothing is understood more certainly than that whenever he says "black violet" <note>original: μέλαν ϊόν (*melan ion*)</note>, he means the Violet which, with its blackish-purple, blooms first (or among the first) at the base of walls, the edges of gardens, and in hedges, announcing the arrival of spring to mortals. It is well known to the common people and easily found everywhere; it stays green all year and raises its flowers from the earth between the leaves on a thin but rather long little stalk. He rightly compared these leaves to Ivy, 
<margin>Wall Violet.</margin>
since they very closely approach that shape. One reads in Dioscorides that it is called the "Wall Violet" by the Latins. We do not know how ancient that name is, but whatever it may be, it corresponds to its nature: since, as we have said, it grows frequently and beautifully at the base of walls in shady places. For the same reason, it was likewise called the "Wild Violet," because it grows in uncultivated places, and does not have "violet-beds" in gardens like its other namesakes. At one time, it could even be commended by some religious rite or the favor of a deity; thus it was called the *Cybelian* Violet after the most 
<margin>Cybelian Violet.</margin>
ancient goddess Cybele, perhaps as a term of praise rather than a formal name. But we have no certain reasoning or conjecture for that name, just as others are entirely unknown—unless *Priapeios* was named after the ancient deity of the countryside and gardens, Priapus, for a similar reason. Theophrastus described it in the 6th book of his *History of Plants*, saying: <term>it has leaves growing from the root and is evergreen, and as some say, it can produce a flower if it is tended in a certain way</term> <note>original Greek: προσριζόφυλλον καὶ ἀείφυλλον εἶναι, καὶ, ὥς τινες φασί, δυναμένην φέρειν τὸ ἄνθος, ἐὰν τρόπῳ τινὶ θεραπεύηται</note>. That is, its leaves emerge and live only at the head of the root, and it stays green with perpetual foliage. For those two terms signify this. It is easy to see the leafy tuft of this Violet rising from the earth with no stems or branches, which other Violets have; nor does it dry up in the heat of the year or in winter, as others suffer, but after the flowers are lost, it serves for medicine all year with its green leaves. Furthermore, the writer added that some testify this Violet can bloom continuously all year if it is cared for in some way—though he did not report the method, nor in what places men devised this. The writer added in the same book that this violet differs from the rest in its general nature, but especially <term>because it is broad-leaved, and ground-leaved, and fleshy-leaved</term> <note>original Greek: ὅτι πλατύφυλλος, καὶ ἐγγειόφυλλος, καὶ σαρκόφυλλος ἐστίν</note>. That is to say, it has a broader leaf than the other Violets; he understands "other Violets" to be those called White Violets <note>Leucoia</note> by everyone. It is "ground-leaved" <note>original: ἐγγειόφυλλος (*engeiophyllos*)</note> because it does not rise far from the earth, and besides that, it is fleshy and fat. These things may perhaps seem too long-winded to some. But we, consulting the certainty of things, do not wish them to become obscured by brevity. With this plan, we have used this method from the start in designating the color of this Violet: and contrary to the editions of other translators, we call it the Black, not the purple, Viol...

These are counted in the order of those that are branchy; they grow on walls and in gardens, different from the others, with the leaves of the flower arranged differently and many hanging from a single little stalk—these are more properly and truly called "purple." ### ON WHITE VIOLETS, OR WALLFLOWERS. The text of Dioscorides.

<margin>White Violet <note>original: "Λευκόϊον" (Leucoion)</note></margin>
The *Leucoion* is called *Basilion* <note>meaning "Royal"</note> by some Greeks, the "White Violet" by the Romans, *Augustia* by others, and by some the "Autumnal Violet" or *Passarina*. It is a matter of common knowledge, but there is some difference in the flowers. For they are found as either blue, white, purple, or yellow. The yellow ones are of the greatest use in medicine. Their dried flowers, boiled in a decoction, are effective against inflammations of the womb. They also expel the menses. With honey, they heal ulcers of the mouth. With a wax salve, they treat cracks of the seat <note>anal fissures</note>. The seed, taken in the weight of two drachms with wine, or applied with honey, draws out the menses, the afterbirth, and the fetus. The roots applied with vinegar suppress the swelling of the spleen and help those suffering from gout.

### ANOTHER PARAPHRASE BY HERMOLAUS BARBARUS on the White Violets of Dioscorides.

<margin>B</margin>
*Leucoion*, although the name itself signifies a "white Violet," is nevertheless often taken to mean yellow, blue, and purple varieties. Hence, in Columella, one finds "white Leucoia," as if there were also black ones. Hippocrates certainly says, "let the black Leucoia be sought." Paulus says that violet oil <note>original: "ioton"</note>—that is, oil of Violets—is usually made sometimes from purple, sometimes from white, and sometimes from saffron-colored Violets. It should also be known that Dioscorides writes in this place that the Violet, which in Greek is called *Leucoion*, is sometimes named *Ligustria* by the Romans, even if there are manuscripts in which not *Ligustria* but *Augustia* is read. Perhaps Columella in his garden poem understands it as the Violet when he sang:

For the "white Privet" (*Ligustrum*) is taken to be the flower of Cyprus. However, the purple or black variety will be discussed separately later. As for the "Blue Violet," it is not certain what it is, unless one understands it to be the *Cyanus* <note>the Cornflower</note>. The *Cyanus* is a flower shaped like a rose, whose color gave both honor and a name to the color blue <note>cyan</note>. The Amaranth follows the *Cyanus*. As some have thought, the *Cyanus* is a common flower growing in grain fields and also in gardens, used for the garlands of peasants and girls; it has the cup of a rose, but it is rough and somber, and without scent. Truly, its greatest charm is its color, which in the countryside is called *Baptisecula* <note>original: "Baptisecula," likely from "baptis" (dyed/stained) and "secula" (sickle)</note> because it hinders the reapers and mowers, as the sickle becomes blunted when it encounters it.

<meta>This page continues the botanical classification of "Violets," a term used broadly in the Renaissance to include modern violets, wallflowers, and stocks. <margin>C</margin>
...it will be most clearly evident in the following sections. Theodorus <note>Likely Theodorus Gaza (c. 1398–1475), a key translator of Greek botanical texts into Latin.</note> called it the **Flame**, possessing a commendable color but no scent, and growing from seed to be used for garlands. However, this is not 
<margin>Flower of Jove, Flame of Jove, *Diosanthos*.</margin> 
the **Flower of Jove**, or what is the same thing, the **Flame of Jove**, known as the *Diosanthos* <note>original: "Diofanthos," from the Greek *Dios* (of Zeus/Jove) and *anthos* (flower).</note>. I have no doubt of this, because although the Flower of Jove is scentless, used for garlands, and observed to grow from seed, it nevertheless blooms in the summer, not through the winter as the **Flame** flower does. Pliny also says that the Flower of Jove is commended for its color alone, as it lacks scent, just like the one which the 
<margin>Campion <note>original: "Lychnis."</note></margin>
Greeks call *Phlox* <note>Meaning "Flame."</note>. We have said that the **Campion** is also sometimes called the **Flame**, but it is categorized among the roses rather than the Violets. There is another thing among the Greeks called the *Phlogis*; for it signifies both a type of garment—which we call a "flame-colored robe," and its makers "flame-robe weavers" in the plays of Plautus—and also roasted meat, as found in the writings of Strattis. Therefore, the **White** and **Flame Violets** are the most long-lasting. But among the cultivated varieties, the greatest authority is given to the 
<margin>
Tusculan Violet,
Sea Violet,
Basket Violet,
Marigold,
Royal Broom.
</margin>
**Yellow Violets** <note>original: "Luteolis."</note>; this color was sought after for bridal veils in the most ancient rites, and is said to have been reserved entirely for women. For this reason, perhaps, it is not numbered among the "principal" colors—that is, those common to both men and women—since the shared use of colors gave them their high status. The types of Yellow Violets are: the **Tusculan**; and that which is called the **Sea Violet**, with a somewhat broader leaf but less scent (indeed, it is entirely without scent, and has a very small leaf). The **Basket Violet** <note>original: "Calathiana."</note> is a gift of autumn; the rest belong to spring. Closest to it is the **Marigold** <note>original: "Caltha."</note>, which matches it in size and color but surpasses the Sea Violet in the number of its leaves (the Sea Violet having no more than five); however, the Marigold is surpassed in scent. For the Marigold has a heavy odor, no lighter than the one they call **Royal Broom** <note>original: "Scopam regiam."</note>. Though in that plant, it is the leaves that smell, 
<margin>D</margin>
not the flowers, as Pliny says. However, what kind of plant this **Royal Broom** is among the Violets is 
<margin>Turnips, Ironwort.</margin>
not entirely clear. Dioscorides counts Royal Broom among the genus of **Turnips** <note>original: "Naporum."</note>; Pliny, in another place, wishes for the **Ironwort** <note>original: "Sideritin."</note>, which has a very broad leaf, to be called "Royal Broom" by our people. The scent of the Violet is sweeter from a distance; up close, it is dulled. The life of the white variety is longest, lasting three years. From that time on, it degenerates and diminishes, though it continually produces whiter flowers. Their potency is lesser when fresh; 
<margin>Why it is called "Viola."</margin>
therefore, they are used dried after a year. Violets held a place of honor among the ancients after the rose and the lily. The Greeks think the Violet is called *Ion* because when **Io** was turned into a heifer by Jove, the earth brought forth that flower as fodder for the beast. Our people also seem to have called it *Viola*, as if it were a "little heifer" <note>original: "vitulam," a pun on "Viola."</note>, in imitation of the Greek.

### The Best Remarks on the Naming of **VIOLETS**
### from the Commentary of **M. VERGILIUS**. <note>Marcello Virgilio Adriani (1464–1521), a famous Florentine humanist and translator of Dioscorides.</note>

Antiquity granted much to the "whiteness" of this flower, and held it in no small favor for its splendor, 
<margin>Which Violets go by the name of *Leucoion*.</margin>
giving it a single name <note>original: "Leucoion," meaning "White Violet."</note> that indicates three other colors. These are numbered by this writer within the whole genus of Violets, and with one exception, they are seen everywhere every year. For under the name **Leucoion**, all those Violets are indicated in Greek which are the first to put forth their flowers as soon as the air becomes milder and warmer after winter, or later if it remains harsh and cold. Everywhere, however, they announce the arrival of the new year through the spring; and many do not bloom on just one little branch, but on a single stalk. 
<margin>Many-bearing <note>original: "Polyphæræ."</note></margin>
This was the reason why they were called **Many-bearing** among other names. For that is what the word signifies. These bloom everywhere in three colors: white, yellow, and purple. As for the fourth color numbered after these—**blue**—it is seen nowhere in Italy within this genus of Violets, as far as I know. From this, a suspicion has arisen in us that this term might be redundant in the Greek texts, even if it is read in all of them alike. Furthermore, the Latin version of Dioscorides that we possess—of remarkable antiquity and reliability, written in **Lombardic script**—numbers only those three colors known to everyone. This fourth blue color is not found in it. We do not defer to that manuscript so much as to wish one copy to stand for all others, but since the nature of the thing supports our suspicion, we believed it would not be useless to warn readers of this as well, whatever the value of that witness may be. Especially since, as we said a moment ago, nowhere are they show— <note>The text cuts off here with the catchword "oftenden-" (showing/appearing).</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of botanical classification, specifically focusing on how the term "Violet" was used in antiquity to describe a wide variety of flowers, including what we now know as Jasmine and Cornflowers. It references the earlier discussion of Jasmine in Volume I to clarify modern sightings of these plants in Italy and Egypt.</meta>

<header>Volume V, Book One.</header>

<margin>A</margin>
...in this flower, nature provides that color. Otherwise, it will be necessary to remember what was said by us regarding **Jasmine** <note>original: "Iasme."</note> in the first volume, and to bring the lessons taught there at length concerning **Violets** to this place. One might then suppose that this flower grows in a sky-blue color in this or other locations. For the power of nature is wide-reaching, and its majesty is admirable; through it, nature can vary many things everywhere, giving to others what she denied to us and our region. Alternatively, other kinds of flowers may be included under the name of **Violets**, just as we said all **Jasmines** were at that time, provided they are equal and similar to them in size and form. It will also be necessary to understand in the writings of **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician whose *De Materia Medica* was the primary botanical authority for centuries.</note> some other flower of a sky-blue color, such as the **Cornflower** <note>original: "Cyanus," from the Greek *kyanos* (dark blue). Likely *Centaurea cyanus*.</note>, so named by the Greeks from its color—a common flower, known to all among the grain fields, blooming in the months of May and June. <margin>The Alyssum flower.</margin> Our country folk call this flower **Alyssum**, which itself has a triple color: white, purple, but most often sky-blue. However, our mind leans toward that former opinion. We believe that this fourth color was added to this author's text by chance or error. We use this reasoning especially because it is not likely that Dioscorides mixed different genera together; when he was dealing specifically with a certain kind of **Stock** <note>original: "Leuco-ijs," referring to the *Leucoion* or "White Violet," ancestors of modern stocks and wallflowers.</note>, it is unlikely he intended to treat all Violets, which the Greeks call *ia* <note>original: "’ia."</note> and not *leukoia*. For we have observed that the name "Violets" has a wider application and embraces several flowers: <margin>Rusty Violet. *Phlox*.</margin> the **Black** (or if you prefer, **Rusty**) **Violet**, all the **Jasmines**, the **Calathian** <note>Likely the Marsh Gentian, often called *Viola calathiana* in older texts.</note>, and the one the Greeks call **Phlox** <note>Meaning "Flame."</note> (which Pliny calls the **Flame Flower**), and many others which in their shape, size, leaf arrangement, or some other such reason are equal to those properly called Violets. However, this **Stock** <note>original: "leukoion."</note> genus has only these three types, differing only in color, which we described a little while ago from **Theophrastus** <note>Ancient Greek "Father of Botany."</note>; for only these Violets are called *Leucoia*. To this is added that if the **Cornflower** is to be understood in this genus—the word from which we believe that color crept into these Violets—it will seem that Dioscorides haphazardly mixed things that do not bloom at the same time. For the Cornflower blooms only in early summer; it grows by its own accord sometimes on walls and the battlements of walls, and elsewhere among the grain fields. Both can indeed be planted in gardens, but we are treating the simple, natural births and characteristics of nature in this place, not the forced works of art.

### COROLLARIES OF HERMOLAUS BARBARUS <note>Ermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a Venetian scholar famous for his corrections to Pliny’s Natural History.</note>
### & [Marcellus] Virgilius on the Jasmine preparation.

<margin>B</margin>
This ointment is called both *Iasminum* and *Iasme*. This name warns me to understand it as being composed of that Violet which is commonly called **Jasmine** <note>original: "Iesiminum."</note>, which covers garden partitions and reed walls in ornamental gardening. It has a white flower of exceptional sweetness; the leaf is a blackish green, oblong, tapering to a point, with a weak tip, about the size of a rose leaf but narrow. I would call this kind of Violet **Persian** or **Parthian**, and entirely foreign, standing at a great distance from our native White Violet, and (as I think) unknown to the ancients, at least in Italy. More recent writers establish three kinds of Jasmine: white in color, sky-blue, and in Egypt, yellow, such as we now see growing in Venice as well.

### AND MARCELLUS VIRGILIUS <note>Marcello Virgilio Adriani (1464–1521), a Florentine scholar and translator of Dioscorides.</note>.

The flower we all call **Jasmine**, white in color and not unlike Violets in shape, the ancients used to call a **Violet**. It was apparently unknown for a long time in Italy, but now it commends even common gardens with its pleasing scent, being so well known to everyone that it requires no description from us. We believe this writer was dealing with it when the general history of Violets was treated by him in the third volume. For having numbered the white, yellow, or purple Violets, which are common and known to all, he added a fourth kind of a sky-blue color. None such are now recognized in the genus of Violets, and it is necessary that this sky-blue color be referred to the flower of this Jasmine. For later writers, and among them **Serapion** <note>Likely Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century Arab physician whose botanical works were widely translated into Latin.</note>, made three distinctions and types of Jasmine based on color: the White; the Yellow (which he calls **Citrine**); and the Sky-blue (which he calls **Celestial** color). All were once foreign and unknown to Italy, but are now common to everyone. Italy now sees and possesses not only the white but also the **Yellow Jasmines**. Nor should this *Iasme* and Jasmine ointment be understood to come from any other kind of Violet. For that which **Palladius** <note>Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius, a 4th-century AD Roman agricultural writer.</note> teaches as "Violet-colored" (called *iaton* by the Greeks) was prepared from Violets properly so called. We, in the manner of the Greeks, call those **Violets** which are the first to herald the Spring; several bloom on one small branch, with few and tiny leaves, in three colors: white, yellow, and purple, and they are of primary use in medicine. For that which Theophrastus called the **Black**...

### THE FORM OF VIOLETS <note>original: "ἰοτυπία" (iotypia).</note> FROM PLINY, Book 21, Chapter 11.

**C** The first of the flowers announcing spring is the **White Violet**, which in warmer places bursts forth even in winter. Afterwards, there is the one called the **Purple**, and next the **Flame-colored**, which is also called the **Phlox**, though only when it grows wild. And again in the same book, chapter 6: Violets hold the next place of honor <note>After roses and lilies.</note>. Of these there are many kinds: purple, yellow, and white; all are sown from cuttings, like a vegetable. But of those that grow spontaneously in shady and thin soils, the purple ones, with a broader leaf, come out fleshy right from the root, and are distinguished from the others only by their Greek name, being called **Ia** <note>original: "Ia." This is the root of the word "Ianthine."</note>; from these comes the **Ianthine** <note>A violet-purple color highly prized for dyeing garments.</note> garment. But among the cultivated varieties, the greatest authority is given to the yellow. Their kinds are the **Tusculan**, and those called 

<margin>Calathian.</margin>

**Sea-violets**, with a somewhat broader leaf but less scent; indeed, some are entirely without scent and have a tiny leaf. The **Calathian** is a gift of autumn, while the others belong to spring. Next to it is the **Caltha** <note>Likely the Pot Marigold (*Calendula officinalis*).</note>, which is of a similar size and color. It surpasses the Sea-violet in the number of its leaves, as the latter does not exceed five leaves. Yet the *Caltha* is surpassed in scent, for its odor is heavy, being no lighter than the plant they call **Royal Broom**. Its scent is closest to cinnamon, and it grows in thin, dry soil.

### THEOPHRASTUS ON THE VIOLET GENUS, from whom Pliny borrowed his own, Book 6, final chapter of the *History of Plants*.

**D** The first of the flowers, the **White Violet**, shows itself. It bursts forth due to a milder sky immediately, even before winter has ended; where the weather is harsher, it appears later. In spring, sometimes with the White Violet or shortly after, the **Lily** comes out, as does what is called the **Flame Violet**, though only the wild kind. These far outpace all other flowers used by those who make garlands. After these, the **Narcissus** and the **Lily** <note>original: "Lirium."</note> come out. Additionally, the flower of the **Bulb** <note>Likely the Grape Hyacinth.</note> appears; for some even include this in garlands. The **Vine-flower** follows, and also the **Black Violet**. And from the wild ones, the **Aurelia** <note>Literally "Golden-flower."</note> and the **Fremius** genus.

### DESCRIPTION OF VIOLETS from Serapion.

The **Violet** is an herb whose leaves are smaller than those of the **Ivy** <note>original: "Cissos."</note> and darker, and they do not differ much from them in their shape. It has a stem emerging from a single root, and there is a fine hair upon it. At its tips is a flower of good scent and purple color; it grows in shady and rough places. Other species of Violets, as the **Pandectary** <note>Matthaeus Silvaticus, a 14th-century medical lexicographer.</note> says, are species of **Wallflower** <note>original: "Cheiri."</note>.

### EXCELLENCE of all, and Selection.

The greatest authority among the cultivated ones is for the yellow, as Pliny says, but the purple is better, as **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note> contends. Beyond that, the best is whichever is among the first of the season, and which neither the heat of the sun has dried out, nor excessive rain has caused to rot.

### TEMPERAMENT.

They are cold and moist in the first degree. However, those that are dried are less chilling, though still cold and moist. They soothe hot pains, soften, dissolve, and restrain inflammations.

<header>VOLUME One.</header>

# POWERS AND BENEFITS
## Of the Purple Violets from DIOSCORIDES. <note>original: "Dioscoride." Pedanius Dioscorides was a 1st-century Greek physician whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical manual for 1,500 years.</note>
<margin>A</margin>

The leaves, applied on their own or with barley-meal, are most suitable as a liniment for a burning stomach, for inflammations of the eyes, and for a prolapsed anus.

They say that the purple part of the flower helps with quinsy <note>original: "anginis." A severe sore throat or tonsillitis.</note> and the "falling sickness" <note>original: "comicialibus." An old term for epilepsy.</note>, especially in children when drunk in water.

### BENEFITS of the White and Yellow Violets.

The dried flowers of this variety, when heated in decoctions, are effective against inflammations of the womb.

And they provoke menstruation.

With honey, they heal ulcers of the mouth.

With a wax-ointment, they heal fissures of the anus.

The weight of two drachms <note>A drachm was about 3.5 grams.</note> of the seed, drunk in wine or applied with honey, draws out the menses, the afterbirth, and the fetus.

The roots smeared on with vinegar reduce the spleen and help those suffering from gout.

### BENEFITS of the Purple and Flame-colored Violets from MESUE. <note>Masawayh (Mesue the Elder) was a 9th-century Persian physician influential in translating Greek medicine into Arabic.</note>

By purging <note>original: "solutione."</note>, they draw out and restrain yellow bile <term>Cholera: In the four humors theory, this is "yellow bile," associated with heat and bitterness.</term>.

They are beneficial in all inflammations.

They soothe "hot soda" <term>Soda: Derived from the Arabic "suda," this refers to a violent, burning headache.</term> caused by intense heat.

They induce sleep and soothe the chest and throat.

They are beneficial for the uvula and for quinsy.

<margin>B</margin>
They quench thirst and open blockages of the liver.

They dispel jaundice <note>original: "Ictericiam."</note> and inflammatory fevers.

### From SERAPION, Chapter 120. <note>Ibn Sarabi (Serapion the Younger), an Arabic medical author whose work focused on "simples," or single-ingredient medicines.</note>

When a plaster is made from the leaves alone, or with *savich* <note>original: "sauich." An Arabic term for a meal made from parched grain, often barley or wheat.</note>, it cools and assists with inflammation of the stomach opening and hot abscesses of the eyes.

And it is said that the flower itself, by its own property, is drunk with water and helps with epilepsy and the quinsy of children; it is this which the common people call "the Mother of Children."

### From PLATEARIUS. <note>Johannes Platearius, a 12th-century physician from the famous medical school at Salerno.</note>

Sugar of Violets is made in the same way as Sugar of Roses.

<margin>Syrup of Violets.</margin>
But Syrup of Violets is made thus: Let the violets be boiled in water; and from the strained liquid and sugar, let a syrup be made.

Or thus: It is better that the violets be left to soak in water overnight and then the syrup be made. However, if it is made from the juice and sugar, it is even better.

<margin>Violet Oil.</margin>
Violet Oil is made in this way: The violets are boiled in oil and strained; or let the decoction be made in a double vessel <note>Similar to a modern double-boiler or bain-marie.</note>. Or even this way, which is better: Let them be boiled and strained, and then fresh flowers added to the strained liquid; let them be left thus for 15 days in the sun and then strained. If this is done a second and third time, the oil will be of the highest quality. This oil is effective against any overheating of the liver; it is sleep-inducing and narcotic.

Note also that the syrup of Violets must be boiled longer than that of Roses.

### DOSAGE ACCORDING TO MESUE <note>Masawayh (Mesue the Elder) was a 9th-century Persian physician.</note>

A potion made from them is from 4 ounces up to 8. Their juice is from 1 ounce up to 2. Their syrup is from 2 ounces up to 4. And a preserve <note>original: "conditi."</note> made from them is from 1 ounce and 1 drachm <note>A drachm was about 3.5 grams.</note> up to 3.

### FROM JOANNES VIGONIUS <note>Giovanni da Vigo (1450–1525) was an Italian surgeon who served Pope Julius II.</note>

The Violet is the best medicine for erysipelas <note>A bacterial skin infection characterized by a bright red, swollen rash.</note> that has not yet ulcerated, regardless of the method by which it is administered.

### On the planting of VIOLETS, from Columella <note>Roman agricultural writer, 1st century AD.</note> Book 13, and Palladius <note>Roman agricultural writer, 4th century AD.</note> for the Month of February, chapter 21.

Whoever is going to plant Violets should bring manured and turned-over earth to a depth of at least one foot into raised beds; he should have young plants from the current year <note>original: "hornotinas."</note> arranged in small pits a foot deep before the Calends of March <note>March 1st.</note>. Moreover, the seed of the Violet, just like that of vegetables, is sown in plots during two seasons: Spring or Autumn. It is cultivated in the same manner as other vegetables: it should be weeded, packed down, and occasionally even watered.

### On making VIOLET oil and wine, from Palladius for the Month of May.

<margin>D</margin> You should infuse as many ounces of Violets as you have added pounds of oil, and you must keep this in the open air for 20 days. For the wine: you should infuse five pounds of cleaned Violets—so that they have no dew upon them—into 10 sextarii <note>A Roman sextarius was roughly 500ml or one pint.</note> of old wine; after 30 days, temper it with 10 weights of honey.

#### THE TEACHINGS OF AUTHORITIES on the Crow’s Foot.

#### The Opinion of DIOSCORIDES on the
#### Crow’s Foot, Book 2. <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD) was a Greek physician and the most influential pharmacologist of antiquity.</note>

The Crow’s Foot <note>original: "Coronopvs."</note> is a small, elongated herb; it spreads across the ground and has leaves divided by notches.

To the same effect, Pliny writes in Book 22, Chapter 19: The Crow’s Foot is an elongated herb with clefts. It is occasionally planted because its root, when roasted in ashes, is excellently suited for those with digestive disorders <note>original: "coeliacis"; referring to abdominal ailments in ancient medicine.</note>. And again in Book 21, Chapter 16: The stems of some prickly plants creep along the ground, such as the one they call Crow’s Foot.

#### Chapter 20. <note>Referring to the "Herbarium" of Pseudo-Apuleius, a widely used late-antique medicinal manual.</note>

The Cock’s Spur herb prefers to grow in firm soil and along roadsides; its tip is shaped like the foot of a cock.

# PHARMACOLOGY OF SIMPLES

<margin>C</margin>
### OUR JUDGMENT.

<margin>Monkshood <note>original: "Isenhyetlin," a diminutive of the German "Eisenhut" (Iron Hat/Aconite).</note></margin>
The variety of writers regarding this Crow’s Foot <note>original: "Coronopode."</note> is remarkable. To some it is a *Buttercup* <note>original: "Batrachion."</note>, to others a *Spearwort* <note>original: "Flamulam."</note>; some suspect and contend it belongs to a prickly genus, while others say it is entirely without any prickles. Therefore, we believe we shall do something worthwhile if, pausing here for a moment, we include the discussion of Leoniceno <note>Niccolò Leoniceno (1428–1524) was an Italian physician famous for correcting errors in ancient medical texts.</note>. In my opinion, no one has philosophized more prudently about this herb than he. I am also of the opinion that it is no other plant than the one commonly called **Cock’s Foot** <note>original: "Crus Galli."</note> today, which is known even to children, who pick it to cause blisters on one another <note>The plant contains acrid protoanemonin which irritates the skin.</note>. Nor is there only one species. For there is a wild variety which grows in cemeteries, meadows, and around hedges. There is a domestic and garden variety, which is sown, having leafy, yellow, and full flowers, which young women use for making crowns. There is also a variety with blue flowers and color grown in gardens by German matrons, which reflects exactly the foot of a cock or a crow, reaching three cubits <note>About 4.5 feet.</note> when fully grown. In the common tongue they call it **Isenhyetlin** [Monkshood], and I have no other genus to classify it under than that of the Crow’s Foot. No one has yet been able to show me otherwise. However, how correctly we conjecture these things, we leave to the estimation of others; let these words be no divine oracle nor a leaf of the Sibyl <note>A classical reference meaning "gospel truth" or infallible prophecy.</note>.

## NICCOLÒ LEONICENO’S judgment on the Herb Crow's Foot.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Avicenna on the Crow's Foot <note>original: "de Pede Coruino."</note></margin>
<margin>The commentator on Avicenna</margin>
<margin>Johannes Matthaeus de Grado</margin>
Regarding the second herb, called *Pes alacohen* by Avicenna <note>Avicenna (c. 980–1037) was a Persian polymath and influential medical author.</note>, the same commentator writes that it is believed to be the herb called **Crow’s Foot** <note>original: "Pes corui."</note> by physicians. He says in the second chapter of this work, regarding the Crow’s Foot, that the root of this herb, when boiled, helps with chronic diarrhea <note>original: "solutioni antiquæ," literally "old loosening."</note>. However, the root of this herb, which our herbalists call Crow’s Foot, is caustic and causes ulcers, and he argues that the Prince [Avicenna] was not speaking of that one. Here he says further that some have claimed Hippocrates understood *alacohen* to mean fig leaves, which serve no purpose in the present case because they prick and strip the skin due to the hidden milky sap within them. The new commentator on Avicenna follows these points almost word for word, though he has clarified this herb for us no more than he did the previous one. Perhaps it is less shameful for him to have been ignorant of this second one—namely the Crow’s Foot of which Avicenna speaks—when Avicenna himself, though such a great master of medicine, either doubted or did not know what it was. Indeed, in many other herbs he admits his own ignorance, just as in the second book of the *Canon*, he speaks not only ambiguously but even contradictorily about this herb named Crow’s Foot.

These are the words of Avicenna regarding the Crow’s Foot: *“The Crow’s Foot [affects] the members of expulsion; the root of this herb helps with chronic diarrhea. And Paulus <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note> and others said that it helps with Colic, and performs the work of <term>Hermodactyls</term> [Meadow Saffron] without harm.”* But I do not know how the root of Crow’s Foot can benefit chronic diarrhea and perform the work of Hermodactyls, which are quite powerful in purging. Unless, perhaps, Avicenna intends in this place to cure a "loosening" with a "loosening" <note>An early homeopathic concept: treating diarrhea with a laxative.</note>; yet elsewhere he instructs that one "loosening" should not be applied on top of another. However, in the 22nd section of the third book, in the chapter on the relief of <term>gout</term> <note>original: "podagræ."</note> and <term>sciatica</term> <note>original: "ischiadicorum."</note>, Avicenna testifies on the authority of the same Paulus that Crow’s Foot benefits gout rather than colic, writing: *“And certain people said that in the Crow’s Foot there is the action of Hermodactyls, and it does not harm the stomach.”*

Explaining these words, the new commentator on Avicenna writes in this manner: He says some asserted that Crow’s Foot works and purges like Hermodactyls, and does not harm the stomach as they do. And this Crow’s Foot is the herb whose root is used in practice, about which he writes in the second chapter. Paulus and others said that it benefits Colic and performs its work without harm. Then he adds: *“The root of the **CROW’S FOOT**, which we have here, corrodes when applied externally. I have many times applied this to the foot of a person who had a <term>bochium</term> [swelling or growth] on the ankle, and immediately a blister would rise there; when ruptured, the poisonous venom would exit, by which means some were healed. But I have never dared to give this by mouth, although I know some things that cause blisters and ulcers when applied externally are harmful if eaten, such as garlic and onions.”* Thus he says. Although he fears—as indeed he ought to fear—to give the root of Crow’s Foot by mouth, which is a poison as we shall later declare, yet by his last words he seems to hint that if it were given by mouth, it should be given with some reason and not without the authority of the Prince [Avicenna].

However, Johannes Matthaeus de Grado <note>A 15th-century Italian physician.</note>, another new commentator on Avicenna, being more audacious in the explanation of this root, writes these words: *“Understand that when authors use Crow’s Foot, even in this case, they always use its root and not the leaves. So also Master Avicenna in the second book of the Canon approves the benefits of its root.”* These words of the commentator indicate to us that he feared the leaves of this herb, not the root, because Master Avicenna had specifically approved the use of the root and not the leaves. I pity human life, in which I see daily that under Avicenna—not as a prince, but as the younger physicians ap... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "ap-", likely continuing "appear" or "apply" on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page features a scholarly debate on the identification and medicinal safety of the Crow's Foot (Ranunculus), highlighting contradictions in Avicenna's Canon of Medicine. It warns that while the plant can be used topically to blister the skin and draw out "venom," it is potentially poisonous if ingested.</summary>

# Pharmacology of Simples, VOLUME One.

<margin>
Avicenna, the most cruel tyrant of medicine.
Concerning a certain bold physician.
</margin>
...they call him, but they are rather endangered by him as if by a cruel tyrant. For if he should order a poisonous root to be administered internally, certain physicians do not hesitate to apply it to the sick. Conversely, if he should forbid a beneficial root that resists poisons as if it were a deadly medicine, even famous physicians do not dare to give it. One recent commentator on Avicenna does not fear to say that the root of **Crow’s Foot** <note>original: "Pes coruinus." Likely a species of Ranunculus or Buttercup.</note>—which has the power to cause ulcers and should be avoided in medical practice unless applied externally like a poison—should even be taken internally. He relies on the authority of Avicenna in the second book of the *Canon* and the sixteenth chapter of the third book, where Avicenna prefers it over **Hermodactyls** <note>original: "Hermodactylis." A root often identified as Meadow Saffron (Colchicum), used historically for gout.</note>. I truly attest before God that I knew a physician who made pills from this same root, along with other additions, and administered them to those suffering from **gout** <note>original: "podagra."</note>, not without great danger to some who took them; until finally, warned by me of his error, he abstained from such dangerous medicine. Does not the same Avicenna—if there are any so foolish as to believe him in all things—write in the second book of the *Canon* that **Monkshood** <note>original: "Napellū." A highly toxic plant also known as Wolfsbane.</note> is a deadly poison, and then advise it be drunk? For he later adds that it "destroys **albaras** <note>A term in medieval medicine for skin conditions like leprosy or vitiligo.</note> when smeared on or drunk." But the poison which the herbalists of our age call *Napellus* is called **Aconite** <note>original: "Aconitū."</note> by the Greeks and Latins, about which Virgil wrote: *"Cruel step-mothers mix the aconites."* <note>original: "Miscent aconita nouercæ." A quote from Virgil's Georgics, 2.128.</note>

<margin>
Monkshood and Aconite are the same.
Michael Savonarola.
Jacobus de Dondis, the Aggregator.
It is not necessary that the names herbs have now were the same in the previous century.
Crow's Foot is Batrachion, the same as Wild Celery.
The four species of Dioscorides.
</margin>
It now appears that Avicenna imitates the character not just of a tyrant, but even of a step-mother. In contrast, Galen praises Aconite if something must be cleansed from the body, but says one must take care that it is not consumed in drink or food. This same Avicenna writes in the second book of the *Canon* that the root of **Cinquefoil** <note>original: "Pentaphylli." Literally "five-leaved."</note>, which was commended by Dioscorides against deadly poisons, is a destructive medicine. This went so far that **Michael Savonarola** <note>1385–1466, a famous Italian physician and scientist.</note>—a physician famous in his time and ours for his writings and medical publications—did not dare to give it for **quartan fever** <note>A form of malaria where fever occurs every fourth day.</note> for no other reason than that it was condemned by "the Prince" <note>Referring to Avicenna, often called the "Prince of Physicians."</note>. As I was just saying, Avicenna holds such authority among the physicians of our time that he can make a deadly medicine healthy, just as he makes the beneficial Crow's Foot healthy or deadly, like the Cinquefoil root or its juice. For even **Jacobus de Dondis** <note>1298–1359, known as "The Aggregator" for his encyclopedic medical works.</note>, surnamed the Aggregator, lists the juice of this root among deadly poisons based on Avicenna's authority. However, perhaps regarding the root of Crow's Foot, it is not so much Avicenna as the physicians themselves who are to be blamed for not rightly understanding him. For who compels them to think that the herb which the herbalists of our age call Crow's Foot is the same one that the ancient physicians, namely Paulus and Dioscorides, celebrated under the same name? As if it were necessary that the names herbs have now were the same in the previous century. Those commentators on Avicenna whom I noted above ought to have learned that the herb named Crow's Foot by the people of the ancient age is one thing, and the one named by our people is another. If they had known this, they would not have doubted so much regarding Crow's Foot, nor would some of them have ever entertained the idea that the herb called Crow's Foot by our people could be taken internally in pills or any other way without danger. For this is the plant that Dioscorides calls <term>batrachion</term> <note>original: "βατράχιον." Meaning "little frog," likely because it grows in damp places.</note> and **Wild Celery** <note>original: "Apiū syluestre."</note>. Hence the younger physicians called it not only Crow's Foot, but also **Frog Celery** <note>original: "Apiū Raninū."</note>, clearly because of its double resemblance to both the animal and another herb. Dioscorides identified four species of this herb, and one of these he places among the poisons. If the leaves and stem of any of them are applied to the human body, they have the power to cause ulcers and create a scab.

<margin>
The commentators of Avicenna do not grasp Avicenna.
</margin>
Therefore, it should in no way be suspected that those who spoke of Crow's Foot in the medical chapters on the "excoriation of the intestines" (whom Avicenna cites in the sixteenth chapter of the third book) meant this Crow's Foot which the ancients called <term>batrachion</term> (after the frog, whose shape it represents). Nor could Avicenna, in the second book of the *Canon* when he writes that the root of Crow's Foot helps with "ancient dissolution," have meant this one. Therefore, in this regard, perhaps the error is not Avicenna's, but that of those who explain him poorly and do not know what Avicenna understood by "Crow's Foot" in those two places. That is, if he himself even understood what it was. For in the sixteenth chapter of the third book, he even seems to hesitate. In the second book of the *Canon*, however, Avicenna errs entirely by showing that contradiction I touched upon above regarding the root of the same herb: that it both helps with "ancient dissolution" and performs the work of **Hermodactyls** without harm. In these last words, he writes things similar to what he says in the twenty-second chapter of the third book, which I also cited above. But in both places, Paulus and others are poorly cited by Avicenna regarding this medicine that performs the work of Hermodactyls. For **Paulus** <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Byzantine physician.</note> nowhere compares the herb *Cornopoda* (for so the Greeks name the Crow's Foot) to Hermodactyls in helping those with gout; rather, he prefers a composition which is called among the Greeks <term>dia koronopodion</term> <note>original: "διά κορωνοπόδιον." A medicine made "by means of Crow's Foot."</note> over another which is called by the same Greeks <term>dia hermodaktylon</term> <note>original: "διά έρμοδακτύλων." A medicine made "by means of Hermodactyls."</note>. Paulus describes both in his seventh book, in which he treats simple and compound medicines, marking both with their own titles.

Hermodactyls, three units; anise, Ethiopian cumin, ammi <note>Bishop's weed</note>, flower-clusters, thyme, pepper...

# PHARMACOLOGY OF SIMPLES

<margin>C</margin> Of long pepper <note>original: "cris longi," likely a contraction for piperis longi.</note> and ginger, three obols <note>An ancient Greek weight, approximately 0.7 grams.</note> each; of epithyme <note>A parasitic vine, often Dodder.</note>, half an ounce. The dose is four or six obols, given in the morning with preserves or hydromel <note>A mixture of honey and water.</note>.

->The title and description of the second composition, named for Crow’s Foot, is as follows:<-

### The composition through CROW’S FOOT, which serves the same purpose as the other through Hermodactyl, and is useful for the stomach.

Two obols of ginger, three obols of pepper, one obol of agaric <note>A medicinal fungus used as a purgative.</note>, four obols of the inner part of the safflower <note>original: "cnici." Safflower seeds were used as a laxative.</note>, and six obols of the root of **Crow’s Foot** <note>original: "Pes coruinus."</note>. The dose is eight obols. For those whose bowels are not easily moved, twenty-four siliquae <note>Small units of weight based on the carob seed.</note>; it generally causes seven or eight bowel movements.

In the third volume of his medical work, Paul <note>Paul of Aegina (c. 625–690 AD), a Byzantine Greek physician.</note> says, on the authority of Alexander <note>Alexander of Trallies (c. 525–605 AD).</note>, that the second of these two compositions—the one named for **Crow’s Foot**—is better than the first. He claims it produces the same evacuation and eases pain just as well, while also causing no harm to the stomach. Avicenna, in the two places cited previously, misinterpreted the meaning of these words. He writes about **Crow’s Foot** alone, comparing it to **Hermodactyls** <note>original: "Hermodactylis." A root traditionally used for gout, often identified as Meadow Saffron.</note> as if the root of **Crow’s Foot** that Paul mentions were equal to the root of **Hermodactyls** in moving the bowels, rather than having an astringent <note>Binding or contracting</note> quality. This is how Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD).</note> feels about it, testifying that it benefits those with chronic diarrhea <margin>Celiac disease.</margin> <note>original: "cœliacis." In ancient medicine, this referred generally to chronic abdominal or bowel distress.</note>. Even Avicenna himself, in the first book of his *Canon*, says the same root is useful for long-standing looseness of the bowels; and in the sixteenth chapter of the third book, he testifies that some have named it among medicines for intestinal ulcers. This is because the "celiac" condition is a disease similar to lientery <note>A form of diarrhea where food passes through undigested.</note>, which also arises from ulcers of the intestines. Therefore, Avicenna does not write incorrectly about all these aspects of the **Crow’s Foot** root. However, he is wrong to say that it performs the same action as **Hermodactyls**.

If anyone wonders how the entire composition named for **Crow’s Foot** can cause the same evacuation as the one named for **Hermodactyls**—since **Crow’s Foot** (or its root) has an astringent power while **Hermodactyls** are more purgative—let him know this: the said **Crow’s Foot** composition does not derive its purgative power from the **Crow’s Foot** itself, but from the agaric and the safflower (which more recent physicians call *Carthamus*). It purges just as much as the other composition named for **Hermodactyls** because its dose is double the dose of the other; and for those with stubborn bowels, the proportion is much greater than double, as can be seen from Paul’s opinion which we wrote earlier. Nor should anyone wonder that a purgative composition takes its name from a medicine that binds the bowels. In pains of the feet <note>gout</note> and sciatica <note>original: "Ischiadicis."</note>, we seek no less to restrain the flow of humors to the aching parts than we seek the evacuation of those humors which have already flowed there.

<margin>D</margin> Hence, another composition for gout is found in Paul's works, named for **Coral**, which nevertheless includes rhubarb and aristolochia <note>Birthwort.</note>, which are evacuating medicines. Avicenna also mentions these same two compositions, which we noted above according to Paul, in the twenty-second *Fen* of his third book, in the chapter on the relief of gout and sciatica. In certain medicines, however—but especially in the weights of the medicines—he differs from Paul, as can be seen by those who wish to compare what Avicenna writes with what Paul had previously noted.

At this point, someone might step forward and object to me with the same point I previously raised against Avicenna and his commentators: that it is not clear from their explanations what the "Dyer’s Herb" (or "Yellow Herb") is, nor what the **Crow’s Foot** is that Paul understood (however poorly he was cited by Avicenna). For it is clear from what we said before that there is a herb called **Crow’s Foot** by the ancients, from which the whole composition took its name; however, it has not yet been declared what it is or what it looks like. Since we have already taught what the "Dyer’s Herb" mentioned by Avicenna is and by what name it was distinguished among the ancients—just as we did for the herb our herbalists call **Crow’s Foot**—it remains for us to teach what **Crow’s Foot** was to the ancients, to Dioscorides, to Paul, and to Avicenna. This is especially necessary since Avicenna himself wrote about the plant of which **Crow’s Foot** is a part, so that those who wish to make the whole composition do not hesitate over the **Crow’s Foot** (as some of Avicenna’s commentators have done) or, like others, accept a <margin>Dioscorides on Coronopus.</margin> deadly root in place of a healthy one.

**Coronopus**—that is, **Crow’s Foot**—says Dioscorides, is a small herb, oblong, spread upon the ground, with divided leaves. This is also boiled as a vegetable. Some call it *amoneos*, others *astrium*; the Africans call it *atirfitte*, the Romans *catirice*; some call it *stillagine*, and some call it **Sanguinaria** <note>Likely *Plantago coronopus*, the Buckshorn Plantain, prized for its ability to stop bleeding.</note>. Its root, taken in food, helps those with bowel distress. It grows in uncultivated places, in thickets, and by the roadsides. Leaving aside the foreign names for this herb (about which we cannot judge whether they are written correctly or incorrectly), let us inspect the Roman names more diligently. Thus, if any of them are corrupted, we may correct them and arrive at the knowledge of the herb we seek. <margin>Coronopus is the Cock’s Foot.</margin> *Caciatrice* <note>Referring to the 'catirice' mentioned above.</note> certainly seems to be a corrupted word. It is neither Greek nor Latin; therefore, I think it should be read as *gallitricem*—or, what corresponds more closely to the Greek name, *Galli crus* <note>Cock's leg or Cock's spur.</note>. By a similar reasoning, it was called *Galli crus* among the Romans. There is indeed a herb in the author of *On Simple Medicine* (whom some think was <margin>Apuleius.</margin> Apuleius <note>Pseudo-Apuleius, the author of a famous 4th-century herbal.</note>) called *Galli crus*, and also named **Sanguinaria**.

<summary>This page analyzes pharmacological recipes for gout, explaining that while "Crow's Foot" (Coronopus) is an astringent herb, it was used in purgative formulas to prevent the flow of harmful humors to the joints. The author clarifies historical botanical terminology, identifying Crow's Foot with Sanguinaria and correcting Avicenna's taxonomic errors.</summary>

Volume One

<margin>
**Crow’s Foot** <note>original: "Coronopus"</note>
**Bloody-herb** <note>original: "Sanguinaria"</note>
**Little Goat** <note>original: "Capriola"</note>
**Prickly Grass** <note>original: "Gramen aculeatum"</note>
</margin>
This name has also been corrupted or shortened in the works of Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note>, for "sanguinari" is read instead of **Bloody-herb** <note>original: "sanguinaria"</note> in many manuscripts. Regarding this herb, the same author—whoever he may be—in his work on simple medicines, reports the same things about **Crow’s Foot** as Dioscorides: namely, that it grows in rough places and around roadsides. He adds the reason why it is called both **Cock’s Foot** <note>original: "Galli crus"</note> and also **Bloody-herb**: specifically because, when placed in the nostrils, it causes blood to flow, and it has (as he says) a "cock's foot" at its tip. Indeed, if I were to reveal how well-known this herb is to the common people, and its common name at the same time, I fear I would bring great shame upon Avicenna <note>The famous Persian polymath (c. 980–1037 AD) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard text.</note> and his commentators, who hesitated over a matter well-known even to children. However, to hide these things is not so much to spare the ancients as it is to neglect life itself, which, as we have said before, is endangered under the authority of Avicenna and his commentators. This is undoubtedly that herb which we commonly call partly **Bloody-herb** from the effect already mentioned, and partly **Little Goat** <note>original: "Capriola," likely Bermuda grass or a similar creeping plant.</note>. Pliny identifies one species of Grass and calls it **Prickly Grass**, because it has many prickles at its tip which, as Pliny himself says, people insert into the nostrils and pull out for the sake of drawing blood. Although Pliny writes these words in Book 25 regarding the second species of Grass, as we said, he nevertheless listed it in Book 21 among the prickly herbs under the Greek name **Crow’s Foot** <note>original: "Coronopodis"</note>. He was unaware, I believe, that it was the same herb that the Greeks call *Coronopoda* and the Romans call **Prickly Grass**. For as we have recently demonstrated regarding darnel, cockle, aegilops, oats, cleavers, and burdock, and most recently in the cases of loosestrife and weld, Pliny was ignorant of the Greek nomenclature for many herbs he knew by Latin names. We have also demonstrated this lack of knowledge by Pliny regarding woad, bindweed, butcher's broom, and Celtic nard in our other small book published on the errors of Pliny and others.

### HERMOLAUS BARBARUS’S
->Corollary on Crow’s Foot.<-

<margin>
**Silago**
**Stillago**

Greek Name for **Crow’s Foot**
</margin>
**Crow’s Foot** <note>original: "Coronopus"</note>—that is, "Raven's Foot"—is placed by Theophrastus <note>The "Father of Botany" and successor to Aristotle.</note> among the prickly and wild-growing plants. Occasionally it is also sown for medicinal use. It is called *Silago* or *Stillago* by our people, and also *Coronopodion* by the Greeks, as in Galen. There are Arabs who call this "Corvine" <note>original: "Coruinum," meaning pertaining to a crow or raven.</note>. I do not forbid anyone from using whatever words they please, provided the matter is understood. However, they must be warned that the herb now called **Crow’s Foot** by the apothecary shops and herbalists does not seem to be *Coronopoda* so much as a type of **Buttercup** <note>original: "Ranunculi," literally "little frog."</note> which is nicknamed **Many-flowered** <note>original: "Polyanthemon"</note>. This is because the herb **Crow’s Foot** is described as prickly and oblong, and beneficial for the bowels. The [modern] "Crow's foot," however, is seen to resemble that bird and the **Buttercup**; it has many divisions in its leaves, and by its touch alone, blisters are raised on bodies like burns; it has a golden and abundant flower. By these signs, they conclude it is the **Buttercup** called "Many-flowered."

### MARCELLO VIRGILIO’S Annotation on Crow’s Foot.

<margin>
Praise of Niccolò Leoniceno.
**Cock’s Foot**.
Theophrastus.
</margin>
Niccolò Leoniceno <note>An Italian physician and humanist (1428–1524) known for correcting botanical errors in Pliny.</note>, a man in our age worthy of much respect from those eager for good literature, wrote many things about this **Crow’s Foot** long ago in that short commentary he published on several errors of Pliny. Among other things, he attempted to show that what Pliny calls by the Roman name for *Coronopodis*, **Caciatrix** <note>A likely corruption in Pliny's text; Leoniceno argued it was a misreading of "Cock's Foot."</note>, was called **Cock’s Foot** <note>original: "Galli crus"</note> by Apuleius; and that from "Cock's Foot," the word *Caciatricem* was created in this writer by unskilled Greek scribes. If I dared to confirm this, I would believe myself to be prophesying rather than judging. For no traces of that word remain here, nor does any conjecture offer itself by which what is unknown and hidden might be brought to light. It is rather to be accepted that, since the Greeks named it from the foot of a crow, it is likely the Latins gave it a name from the **Cock's Foot**, other signs being congruent, due to the similarity; just as by some it is called not "Raven's Foot" but "Crow's Foot." Furthermore, he says the same plant is called **Prickly Grass** by Pliny in Book 24. No one would doubt this if Pliny had either called it "prickly" here or added something to indicate prickles. For this reason, not without cause, someone might hesitate regarding Pliny, hearing **Crow’s Foot** numbered by him among the prickly plants in Book 21 and again in the second [section]. We do not accuse Pliny, but we marvel at the variety of the account, that this mark could be missing in Dioscorides. Theophrastus in Book 8 wrote of it that the stalks grow on the ground, which Dioscorides says here—that it is spread across the earth. He counts it among the prickly and wild-growing plants. This herb is common and grows almost everywhere.

Frog-herb <note>original: "Batrachion"</note>, also known as Buttercup <note>original: "Ranunculus"</note> or Scrophula-herb <note>original: "Strumea"</note>: so named because it heals scrophula <note>A swelling of the lymph glands, usually in the neck</note>. For "Strumus" is a type of Nightshade <note>original: "Solanum"</note>. Buttercup is also called Bee-balm <note>original: "Apiastrum"</note>, which is to say, Wild Parsley, and it is poisonous in Sardinia. This is a clear error of the most learned man Nigidius <note>Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero</note>, who uses the name "Bee-balm" for "Melissa-leaf" <note>original: "Mellissophyllo"</note>; although both Varro and Dioscorides follow him in this. It delights in shady places. The first type has a leaden color, with leaves approaching the width of Mallow. The second type has stems that are tall, according to Pliny, though Dioscorides says they are smaller than the first; unless this was the fault of scribes writing *shorter-stemmed* <note>original Greek: "mikrokauloteron"</note> instead of *longer-stemmed* <note>original Greek: "makrokauloteron"</note>.

<margin>
Many-flowered <note>original: "Polyanthemos"</note>.
</margin>
A completely different genus from these seems to be the Frog-herb nicknamed "Many-flowered" <note>original: "Polyanthemos"</note>, which, by its caustic power, breaks open scars and restores them to their natural color, and blends away skin spots <note>original: "vitiligines"</note>. Pliny does not otherwise indicate what sort of plant it is. Unless one were to group and place this among the four species—specifically, the one which both Pliny and Dioscorides describe as having very many divisions in its leaves, commonly called **Crow’s Foot** <note>original: "Pes coruinus"</note>, which is entirely different from the **Crow’s Foot** <note>original: "Coronopus"</note> mentioned above.

<margin>
**D**
Sardinian herb.
,,
,,
Sardonic laugh.
See Erasmus’s *Adages*.
<note>Erasmus's *Adagia* (Chiliades) was a famous Renaissance collection of Greek and Latin proverbs.</note>
</margin>
Regarding the poisonous plant, Sallust <note>A Roman historian</note> says: In Sardinia there grows a certain herb called the Sardinian herb, similar to Bee-balm. This herb contracts the faces and mouths of men with pain, and kills them while they appear, for a time, to be laughing. On that island, as Pausanias and Solinus hold, it grows quite abundantly in damp places, yet it does not poison the water. Strabo says that the Spaniards prepare a type of poison from this very herb which, when drunk under the pressure of extreme necessity, releases one from human affairs without pain. From this plant comes what is commonly called the "Sardonic laugh" <note>original Greek: "sardánion gélōs"</note>, which Dioscorides also mentions in his work *On Poisons*. Homer called it a "Sardonic laugh" in that verse: *he smiled in his soul a very Sardonic smile* <note>original Greek: "meídēse dè thymō sardánion mála toîon" from the Odyssey</note>. Plato also mentions it in the *Republic*. Timaeus gave one origin for this proverb, Clitarchus another, and the poets Sophocles and Simonides yet another: we have deferred these details to our annotations on Pliny.
