#### DIOSCORIDES On Nettles. <note>Dioscorides was a Greek physician of the 1st century AD whose botanical writings served as the standard medical reference for over 1,500 years.</note>

**T**HERE ARE TWO types of NETTLES: namely, the wilder kind, which is rougher, with wider and darker leaves, and a seed like linseed, but smaller. The second is not as rough, with a tiny seed.

->Summary by HERMOLAUS<-
->BARBARUS concern-<-
->ing all Nettles.<-
<note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493) was an influential Italian scholar who translated and annotated classical texts by Pliny and Dioscorides.</note>

<sig>D</sig> The Nettle is the best known among all types of prickly plants. From its cups <note>original: "acetabulis," referring to the flower-bearing structures</note> in bloom, it pours forth a purple down. It often grows taller than two cubits <note>approximately three feet</note>. Among the wild types, the female is the milder, which is called
<margin>Dog Nettle</margin> <note>original Latin: "Vrtica Cania"</note>
Dog Nettle; the more stinging kind, with a biting stem and fringed leaves, is called
<margin>Herculean Nettle.</margin> <note>original Latin: "Herculeana"</note>
Herculean. The seed is abundant in all, and black. It is a marvel that, without the barbs of thorns, the down itself is harmful, and even by a light touch, itching and blisters similar to a burn arise. The remedy of oil is well known. But this biting quality does not arise immediately with the plant itself, nor until it is strengthened by the growth of the leaves. Growing indeed in the Spring, it is used for food by many—even religiously so—to drive away the diseases of the entire spirit. The root of the wild varieties also makes all meat tenderer when cooked along with it. The mildest of these, which has leaves that do not bite,
<margin>Idle Nettle.</margin> <note>original Latin: "Vrtica iners"</note>
is called *Lamium*, or *Anonium*, and by some the Idle or Dead Nettle. This has a white mark in the middle of the leaf, which is useful for "sacred fires" <note>original: "sacris ignibus"; a historical term usually referring to Erysipelas or other inflammatory skin conditions</note>. Some of our people have distinguished the types by seasons, calling one the Autumnal kind, and the rest by the same logic...

VOLUME One.

<margin>Praise of Nettles</margin>
<margin>Nettle: Nida, Cnida, Clida.</margin>
Pliny mentions the Sea Nettle <note>original: "Marinam cognomine Plinius"</note> for bladder ailments. Phanias the naturalist <note>original: "Phanias physicus"</note> records the praises of the Nettle, claiming it is most useful in food when cooked or aged. If livestock refuse to mate, he shows that the Nettle should be rubbed on their genitals. In Egypt, oil is made from the Nettle. The seed should be gathered during harvest. The Alexandrian kind is most highly praised for all things. Hippocrates seems to have called the Nettle *Nida*, while others call it *Cnida*. There are places where you might read *Clida* in a corrupted form, as I believe, unless it is another genus. He says sixty grains of *Clida* should be injected as a clyster <term>clyster: a liquid preparation injected into the body, usually an enema</term> into wombs troubled by bile.

### Also by VIRGIL regarding the same.

<margin>Use of Nettles</margin>
Nothing grows in the census of vegetables more hated than the Nettle, burning with a fiery itch: and its name is derived from this <note>The Latin "Urtica" is etymologically linked to "urere," to burn</note>. Nevertheless, the ancients used to eat it. That it was used as food is attested by ancient Latin poets, for whom it was pleasant to refresh themselves with Basil <note>original: "Ocimo"</note> and Nettle. This herb is so well known everywhere and to everyone that there is no need to give warning about it. Except that it was called *Cnide* by the Greeks, from their word *knidein* <note>original Greek: "κνίδειν"</note>: which means to be stung with pain or to be vexed.

<margin>Acalyphae.
<image-desc>a small hand symbol pointing left</image-desc></margin>
Aristotle also called the Nettles in the sea *Acalyphas*, having the same power of burning when touched. It heals many diseases in the human body and abounds in many remedies. For that reason, it must be cared for by doctors and gardeners no less for medicine than for food.

### On GALIOPSIS, a herb similar to Nettles, according to DIOSCORIDES.

<margin>Lip-nettle.</margin>
Galiopsis is called the Lip-nettle <note>original: "Vrtica labeo"</note> by the Latins. The shrub has the stem and leaves of a Nettle, but smoother, which give off a heavy odor when crushed. It has a delicate purple flower. It grows around hedges, buildings, and pathways everywhere.

### Division of Nettles according to PLINY.

<margin>Sex of Nettles.</margin>
There are several differences among Nettles. The wild kind, which they call female, is milder. And among the wild ones, the one called *Cania* is sharper, with a biting stem and fringed leaves. However, the one that also gives off an odor is called *Herculanea*. All have an abundance of black seeds. It is a marvel that, without any prickly thorns, the down itself is harmful, and from such a light touch, an itch and blisters immediately arise, similar to a burn. The remedy of oil is well known. But the sharpness is not born immediately with the herb itself, nor until it is strengthened by its leaves <note>original: "folibus," likely a typo for "foliis" (leaves)</note>. Indeed, beginning to grow in the Spring, it is a food that is not unpleasant and even sacred <note>original: "religioso"</note> to many, for warding off the diseases of the whole year. The root of the wild kinds also makes all meat tenderer when cooked together. However, the kind that is harmless and lacks a bite is called *Lamium* <note>commonly known as the Dead-nettle</note>.

### TEMPERAMENT.

Nettles are hot and dry in the third degree, according to Serapion <note>Serapion the Younger was a 12th-century Arab physician whose work on medicinal "simples" was a standard reference in Europe</note>.

### POWERS AND BENEFITS from Dioscorides.

The leaves of both types, when applied with salt, heal dog bites.
They heal gangrene, carcinomas, foul ulcers, and those called *cacoëthe* <term>cacoëthe: malignant or "ill-natured" ulcers that are particularly difficult to treat</term>.
Likewise, they heal dislocations, inflammatory swellings, tumors, inflammations of the parotid glands <note>glands near the ears</note>, and suppurations.

Medicines of SIMPLES <note>original: "SIMPLICIVM Pharmas"</note>

<margin>C</margin> They are applied with a wax-salve for those with spleen disorders <term>lienosis: chronic swelling or disease of the spleen</term>. 
They are effective for nosebleeds <note>original: "profluuia narium"</note> when ground with juice and placed in the nostrils. 
They provoke menstruation when the same [leaves] are ground fresh with myrrh and applied. 
They force prolapsed wombs to retract upon contact. 
The seed, when drunk in raisin wine <term>passo: a sweet wine made from dried grapes</term>, stimulates sexual desire <note>original: "Venerem stimulat"</note> and opens the womb. 
When licked with honey, it benefits orthopnea <term>orthopnææ: a condition where one can only breathe comfortably when upright</term>, as well as inflammations of the side and lungs. 
It purges the chest. 
It is mixed with corrosive <note>original: "erodentibus"</note> medicines. 
The leaves, when cooked with shellfish, soften the bowels, stimulate urine, and dispel gas. 
Boiled with barley water <term>ptisana: a medicinal decoction of pearl barley</term>, they draw out ailments of the chest. 
They call forth women’s periods when drunk with a small amount of myrrh. 
The juice, used as a gargle, suppresses the uvula <term>uuam: literally "the grape," referring to the uvula at the back of the throat</term> when it is swollen with inflammation.

->From SERAPIO, Chapter 150.<-

Nettle oil is more laxative than safflower oil. 
It encourages sexual intercourse <note>original: "Mouet coitum"</note> when eaten with onions and egg yolks. 
And it is among its properties to expel raw phlegm. 
When the seed of the Nettle is husked, ground, and mixed with honey, it <margin>D</margin> purges the bowels strongly. 
And caution must be taken that it does not touch the tongue or the top of the throat <note>original: "caput meri," likely referring to the epiglottis or esophagus</note>, lest it burn them. 
And its dose is from twenty grains up to thirty.

->From AEMILIUS MACER.<-

The Greek calls it *Acalephen* <note>original: "Acalephen," derived from the Greek "akalēphē"</note>, we call it the Nettle.
A power not moderately fiery is said to be in it,
From which it seems to have taken its name quite rightly,
Because the Nettle <note>original: "Vrtica"</note> burns the fingers of the one holding it.
This herb is accustomed to help the Jaundiced <term>ictericos: those suffering from jaundice or yellowing of the skin</term> when taken with wine.
Its seed with honey cures those with colic.
It also cures an old cough if it is drunk frequently.
It drives out cold from the lung and swelling from the belly.
A powder joined with honey benefits all these things,
Or the green juice drunk more often with wine.
A poultice <term>cataplasma: a soft, moist mass of herbs applied to the skin</term> made from its leaves with salt,
Benefits ulcers and cleanses foul wounds,
And this poultice is effective against dog bites.
This cures cancers and parotid swellings <term>parotidas: swellings of the glands near the ear</term> and dislocations,
And by this, the flesh that has separated from the bone is restored.
And this is accustomed to dry out aching shoulders.
The root ground with sharp wine checks a swelling
Of the spleen; in this way, it also aids gout <term>podagræ: a form of inflammatory arthritis, often in the big toe</term>,
And thus it assists all diseases of the joints.
Added on top of all these things, it benefits, or joined to itself
If you cook this in oil and bathe the limbs with this ointment.

Placed in the nostrils, the juice or a leaf draws out blood <note>original: "cruorem elicit"</note>, for such is its innate power of heat.
But if you wish to restrain flowing blood, smear the forehead with Nettle juice; it holds it back.

Its seed, collected at harvest time and dried,
Will be useful for many causes.
For all these, the powder joined with honey is beneficial.

*Botanical Illustration of White Horehound:*

The illustration presents a detailed study of the White Horehound, a perennial herb of the mint family. The plant is characterized by its sturdy, upright stem and pairs of rounded, wrinkled <term>rugose: having a crinkled or wrinkled texture</term> leaves with notched edges. Clustered tightly at the points where the leaves meet the stem are the flowers, arranged in dense, hairy circles <term>verticillasters: a ring of flowers that appears to be a whorl but is actually composed of two dense clusters</term>. The artist has included a side shoot to show the plant's bushy growth habit and a thorough rendering of the root system at the bottom, showing the thick, woody base from which the stems arise. 

White Horehound has been valued since antiquity for its medicinal properties, particularly as a remedy for coughs and respiratory ailments, often prepared as a syrup or candy.

# SIMPLE MEDICINES <note>original: "Simplicium Pharma"; "Simples" were medicinal preparations consisting of only one primary ingredient, usually a plant.</note>

### CHAPTER XXV: A COMPILATION ON HOREHOUND.

-> ¶ Names. <-

**Greek:** *prasion*, *eupatorion*, *phyllopharis*, *tripedilion*, *kamelopodion* <note>meaning "camel's foot"</note>, *haima taurou* <note>meaning "bull's blood"</note>, *aphrosthe*, *gonos horou* <note>meaning "seed of Horus"</note>.
**Latin:** Marrubium, Prasium, Eupatorium, Bull’s blood, Ulcer-herb.
**German:** Horehound. God’s-forgotten. <note>original: "Andorn. Gottes vergess."</note>

-> THE OPINIONS OF AUTHORS <-
-> regarding Horehound. <-

#### A description of HOREHOUND according to DIOSCORIDES, Book 3. <note>Pedanius Dioscorides was a 1st-century Greek physician whose work "De Materia Medica" was the standard pharmacological text for 1,500 years.</note>

<margin>C</margin> It is a shrubby plant, branched from one part, hairy, and whitish, with four-angled stems. The leaves are similar to a human thumb, slightly less than round, hairy, wrinkled, and bitter in taste. It has seeds at intervals along the stems. The flowers are rough and arranged in the shape of whorls <term>verticils: a circular arrangement of flowers around a stem</term>. It grows around the courtyards of houses and among ruins.

#### The description of Horehound from THEOPHRASTUS, Book 6, Chapter 2. <note>Theophrastus, a student of Aristotle, is often called the "Father of Botany."</note>

<margin>D</margin> There are two kinds of Horehound. One consists of a grassy leaf that is more saw-toothed, distinguished by deeper and therefore more visible notches; perfume-makers were accustomed to using this for certain things. The other is rounder and very grayish-white, like <margin>* that is, sage.</margin> *sage*, having more obscure notches and being less saw-toothed.

#### PLINY on Horehound, Book 20, Chapter 22. <note>Pliny the Elder was a Roman naturalist who compiled vast amounts of ancient knowledge into his "Natural History."</note>

Castor records two kinds of Horehound: the Black, and the White, which he approves of more.

#### THE ERROR OF PLINY regarding Horehound, observed by Niccolò Leoniceno in his book on the errors of Doctors. <note>Leoniceno was a 15th-century Italian physician and humanist famous for identifying botanical and linguistic errors in Pliny's ancient texts.</note>

<margin>Many herbs are similar to Horehound.</margin> Dioscorides, Galen, and Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century medical encyclopedist.</note> write that many herbs and shrubs have leaves similar to Horehound <note>original: "Prasio"</note>. Pliny, however, records that all of these have leaves similar not to *Prasium* [Horehound], but to *Prasum*, which is to say, the Leek. Thus, in Book 22, he said that *Horminum* <note>Clary sage</note> has a seed similar to Cumin, but otherwise resembles the Leek. So too with *Balloten* <note>Black Horehound</note>, which is called Black Horehound by another name because of the similarity of its leaves. Pliny, in Book 27, wrote that the Greeks call it by another name, "Black Leek," and that it consists of leaves larger than those of the Leek. He also noted in Book 29 that *Stachys* <note>Woundwort</note> bears a resemblance to the Leek, but with longer and more numerous leaves.

#### THE REFUTATION OF LEONICENO’S CALUMNY by Pandolfo Collenuccio. <note>Collenuccio was a lawyer and diplomat who defended Pliny against Leoniceno's criticisms in the "Plinian Wars" of the Renaissance.</note>

Leoniceno was the first to teach that *Prasium* is the Greek name for what we call Horehound, while *Prasum* is what we call the Leek. He himself learned (as I believe) the "poetic medicine" of a certain good man, in which it is written: "The leaves of Horehound are *Prasia*, and *Prasa* are Leeks."

Since Pliny did not know how to distinguish these, he said that *Horminum*, *Balloten*, and *Stachys* consisted of Leek leaves, not Horehound as he ought to have. Then those three witnesses, who are one, because above do—

<meta>This page continues the scholarly defense of Pliny the Elder and the classification of Horehound-like plants. It addresses a famous Renaissance debate regarding whether ancient authors misidentified certain herbs, specifically focusing on the shapes of leaves and the classification of "Horminum" and "Balote."</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
...we cite Dioscorides, Galen, and Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note> as supporting this opinion. The Emperor Hadrian forbade trusting witnesses who bring forward one and the same story (as if by a pre-arranged pact). However, I myself will not allow Pliny to have erred, as he clearly showed in his 20th book that *Marrubium* <note>White Horehound</note> is called *Prassium* in Greek, and in his 7th and 20th books that a *Leek* is called *Prasum*. Nor would I believe Dioscorides erred, but rather this "scourge of Pliny" <note>original: "Pliniomastigen"; likely referring to Niccolò Leoniceno, a Renaissance scholar famous for pointing out Pliny's errors</note> himself: who thought Dioscorides understood Horehound in a certain way only because he himself did not know what those herbs were. It is better to attribute this to the man's ignorance, or to a flaw in the manuscript, rather than to Dioscorides. For our friend Leoniceno should have acted differently: when he seemed ready to correct Pliny, he should not have denied that Pliny described the plant, but rather taught us what and of what sort that plant is now. One should not say what each thing is *not* (as is usually said of God), but say what it *is*. One should build up, not tear down; one should not overturn Pliny’s view on an unclear matter based solely on Dioscorides' opinion. For Dioscorides can just as easily be overcome by Pliny’s authority, or by reason, or by the evidence of the thing itself. As we have said, nothing is less fitting for a philosopher than to say something without reason. In designating herbs, it is not the authority of the writer, nor the judgment of Leoniceno, but the power, the form, and the thing itself that must be considered, and whatever medicinal substance is being discussed must be openly displayed. If it remains unknown (for no mortal knows everything), let the writer's authority remain intact among us, and let us confess our own ignorance of human matters rather than impudently judging that another has erred. Thus we shall also deal with these matters as much as possible, beginning first with *Horminum*.

### ON CLARY SAGE <note>original: "DE HORMINO"; likely Salvia horminum</note>.

<margin>Horminum, Geminalis.</margin>
<margin>Galenus.</margin>
Theophrastus in his *History of Plants*, Book 8, and Pliny in his *Natural History*, Book 18, clearly indicate that *Horminum*, which is also called *Geminalis* in Latin, is a type of grain and is counted among the cereals. For Pliny, following Theophrastus, says that grains are divided by the time they are sown; he makes some "Winter" grains, such as wheat, emmer, and barley, and "Summer" grains, such as panic grass, millet, and *Horminum*. Galen also, in the first book of *On Aliments*, seems to have placed *Horminum* among the grains when he affirms that it can be reduced to a fine flour. However, both Pliny and Theophrastus (discussing the differences between grains and legumes in the same passage) write that all grain-like plants consist of a reed-like leaf <term>reed-like: long, narrow, and grass-like</term>. Pliny said that *Horminum* consists of leek-like leaves. Which, then, has a leaf more similar to a reed? A leek, or Horehound? Now, if we must fight with reason (where the thing itself is not shown), *Horminum* is among the grains, grains have reed-like leaves, and a leek has a leaf more similar to a reed. Therefore, he who said *Horminum* has leaves similar to a leek certainly spoke more truly than if he had said it was like Horehound, which has no kinship at all with a reed. Pliny (who is sharp and diligent in handing down the descriptions of herbs) used a similar comparison for rice.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Rice. Rizum.</margin>
For *Rice* <note>original: "Oriza"</note> is itself a type of grain, which we commonly call *Rizum*, known to everyone. Describing this in his 18th book, Pliny said it has leaves similar to a leek. For no other reason did he write that *Horminum* also consists of leek-like leaves. For there is no more suitable comparison for a leek-like leaf than a reed-like one (by which these authors classify grains). Add to this that Pliny and Theophrastus number *Horminum* among the summer grains like panic grass and millet; but if the leaves of millet and panic are to be described, they would be painted by the example of no plant's leaves more than those of the leek. Thus, the leaves of *Horminum*, being counted with panic and millet, ought to be shaped like leek leaves, not Horehound (than which nothing is more unfit for the forms of grain-like plants). I have written these things regarding *Horminum* following reason and the evidence of the thing itself; if Nicolaus <note>Leoniceno</note> had inspected these things deeply, he would not have accused Pliny of ignorance regarding a very well-known grain, nor of the Greek name *Prasios*.

### ON BLACK HOREHOUND <note>original: "DE BALOTE"</note>.

<margin>Balote.</margin>
In describing *Balote*, why should we believe Pliny erred because of the similarity between the words *Prasios* and *Prasum*? Who but the most ignorant would believe he was ignorant of what true *Balote* was (since it grows everywhere in great abundance)? In Book 20, he says the Greeks call *Marrubium* "Prasion"; and following the opinion of his teacher Castor, he writes that there is also a "black" kind of Horehound—so we know he could call it "Black Horehound," just as he called it "Black Leek" when dealing with *Balote*. Pliny says the Greeks call *Balote* "Black Leek" <note>original: "Porrum nigrum"</note>, with leaves larger than a leek. He adds: it is hairy, foul-smelling, and effective for dog bites. In no kind of Horehound do the leaves "clothe" <note>original: "uestientibus"; likely meaning sheathing the stem</note> the stem; but in leeks, garlic, and reeds, they do. He said they are larger than a leek. Pliny was not ignorant that leek leaves are large; therefore, he added "larger." It is certain that in no kind of Horehound is there a foul smell (unless it is rubbed by hand). If those kinds are sown, they do not give off a foul smell, but an acrid and not unpleasant scent between *Abrotanum* <note>Southernwood</note> and *Absinthium* <note>Wormwood</note>. In the case of the "Black Leek," you might rightly call it foul-smelling, as it gives off a stinking, heavy, and head-harming odor; and for that reason, it is not eaten in medicines, but applied externally. The opposite happens in the kinds of Horehound. But are not the things committed to faithful eyes usually more moving? The meadows are full of *Balote*, especially at the foot of mountains, with the same signs by which it is described: with large, black, spotted leaves like a leek. That is why I think it is called *Balote*.

<margin>Ulcer-herb.</margin>
Some of the Latins call it *Ulceraria* <note>Ulcer-herb</note>, and the country folk call it "Dog Leek."

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of Pliny the Elder’s botanical classifications against the criticisms of Renaissance scholars like Niccolò Leoniceno. <header>PHARMACY of SIMPLES</header> <note>original: "SIMPLICIUM Pharma"; "Simples" refers to medicinal plants used on their own rather than in complex mixtures.</note>

<margin>Ision’s blood. Dog-leek.</margin> <note>original: "Isionis sanguis. Cynosprason"</note>
...from that which I think was said, because it is opposed to the diseases of dogs <note>original: "canis morbibus"; likely referring to rabies or skin conditions</note>, it does not so much resemble the herb as it reflects the name of its power. However, what Dioscorides and those who follow him believed, let Nicolaus <note>Niccolò Leoniceno, a 15th-century physician known for critiquing Pliny</note> see to it. Let us listen to Pliny, weighing these matters with Roman judgment, and to the thing itself: even though Dioscorides, when he enumerates many names for *Ballote* <note>Black Horehound</note>, among which are both Black Horehound and Great Horehound, and also "Ision’s blood." He asserts, however, that others call *Ballote* by the name "Dog-leek" <note>original: "Cynosprason"</note>: which signifies nothing other than a "Canine Leek," and we have already said that the name itself passed down from rustic simplicity.

### ON STACHYS.

<margin>Vine-leek. Vine-like Leek. Little-leek.</margin> <note>original: "Ampeloprafon. Vitigneũ Porrum Porrastellum."</note>
I confess that I am ignorant of what *Stachys* <note>possibly Hedge Woundwort or a similar Lamiaceae</note> finally is: I think Leoniceno is involved in an equal, or certainly greater, ignorance, since he is ignorant of *Stachys* itself, and believes that Pliny erred in a single instance (as if it were of great importance), yet he does not consider Pliny's words or his intent. Pliny had written in his 20th volume that Horehound is called *Prasion* by the Greeks, and that a black kind of Horehound is found: and he said that it was too well-known to need pointing out. But in the 4th and 20th books, when he had said that *Ampeloprasum* <note>Vine-leek</note>—that is, the vine-like leek, which we commonly call *Porrastellum* <note>Little-leek</note>—consists of leek-leaves, he immediately adds and subjoins: "That which is called *Stachys* also has a resemblance to the Leek, but with longer and more numerous leaves." Pliny says *Stachys*, like the Vine-leek, has a resemblance to the Leek, with longer leaves. If the Greeks had said *Stachys* was similar to *Prasion* (that is, Horehound)—since Pliny reports that he held Horehound to be most thoroughly examined, and that it consists of small, rounded leaves—then it would have been credible at some point that Pliny had erred: if he had not compared *Stachys* to the Leek as he did the Vine-leek, or had simply said it was similar to the Leek. But truly, when he numbers *Stachys* among the leek-like herbs, and gives it longer leaves than the Leek, who can now doubt that Pliny did not err in the resemblance of the herb, which he had found to be true? For the leaves are long for the Leek, but not for Horehound, which (as he himself says) is unknown to no one. Added to this is the fact that whoever translated Galen’s eighth book *On Simple Medicines* into Latin interpreted *Stachys* as being similar to the Leek. This is a great argument for the truth: that Pliny and the one who interpreted Galen (whoever he may have been) agreed on the same opinion regarding *Stachys*.

#### The Judgment of ERMOLAO BARBARO on HOREHOUNDS.

<margin>White Horehound. Black Horehound.</margin>
There are two kinds of Horehound: one with a herbaceous leaf, serrated with deeper notches, sought after by ointment-makers for certain things, as Theophrastus says. This I would call "White." The other has a rounder leaf, exceedingly rough <note>original: "squalido"; in botanical Latin, this often means rough, scurfy, or dull-colored</note> like Sage, and more obscurely serrated: which I indeed interpret as either *Ballote* itself, of which we have spoken, or something very similar to it. For the medicinal uses also agree in Pliny.

#### The Judgment of MARCELLO VIRGILIO on Horehounds.

<margin>Sphacelus, a kind of Sage.</margin>
Theophrastus, in the 6th book of his *History of Plants*, made two kinds of Horehound. One which had a more herbaceous leaf, more divided by notches: which those who handle drugs and remedies for diseases use in some cases. The other which was of a rounder and rougher leaf: such as is seen in the other kind of Sage, which they name *Sphacelus*, and in that it has thinner notches. And it seems this division was made by him only in this kind of Horehound. But that which Pliny, on the authority of Castor, handed down as "black" and "white," clearly encompasses the *Ballote* described a little while ago, and this herb. Unless perhaps, what Pliny distinguished here by color alone, Theophrastus indicated by the notches of the leaves, and besides the notches, by the herbaceous color and roughness: so that from these, the black color and the white might be understood. Indeed, "blackness" in the leaves of plants is to be understood as a fuller and darker green, and in "roughness," a cinerous <note>ash-colored</note> and whitish color is often seen in plants. Our mind inclines toward this part: that not different things, but the same thing was spoken of differently by Theophrastus and Pliny regarding both types of

<margin>The honor of Horehound among the ancients.</margin>
Horehound, we believe. This plant was held in great honor of names among the ancients, just as it also had much use in medicine, especially in relaxing the spleen and liver, and in curing all the diseases and vices <note>ailments</note> which are enumerated in this chapter by Dioscorides.

## ON THE HERB BALLOTE, or Black Horehound, [from] DIOSCORIDES Book 3.

They call *Ballote* by another name, Black Horehound, or Great Horehound; some call it *Nophthan*, others *Notianoscemin*, others *Nosprasson*, others *Nothera*, others *Nochlin* or *Nostelim*, others *Nophrim*, others *Gnoturim*; the Romans [call it] *Ulcera* <note>The text ends mid-sentence; "Vlcera" likely refers to "Vlcera canina" or a similar Latin name related to its use for sores.</note>

<meta>This page continues the philological and botanical critique of Pliny the Elder, specifically focusing on the herb Ballote (Black Horehound). It features commentaries from Renaissance scholars Ermolao Barbaro and Marcello Virgilio Adriani, who identify a linguistic error in Pliny’s work where he confused the Greek words for "leek" and "horehound."</meta>

<header>...of Doctors, VOLUME One.</header>

<margin>A</margin>
...or Black Horehound <note>original: "Marrubium nigrum"</note>, others call it Horse-Horehound <note>original: "Cantherinum"</note>, the Egyptians call it *Aspho*, and the Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests/astrologers often cited in early botanical texts for their mystical plant names.</note> call it "Ision’s blood." It produces square, black, slightly hairy stems, many from a single root. The leaves are larger than those of common Horehound, rough, spaced apart, somewhat round, foul-smelling, and very similar to Lemon Balm <note>original: "Apiastrum"</note>; for this reason, some have called it Lemon Balm.

### The Corollary of BARBARO on Ballote.

<margin>Barbaro agrees with Leoniceno.</margin>
<margin>Leek.</margin>
<margin>Horehound.</margin>
*Ballote* is a shrubby herb. I do not see how I can defend Pliny, who says, "The Greeks call it Black Leek <note>original: "Porrum nigrum"</note>." And further down he says, "*Ballote* has leaves like a Leek, but larger and blacker." But the Greeks, without any controversy, name Black Horehound <note>original: "Marrubium nigrum"</note> as *Ballote*. Its leaves are not like a leek at all, but like Horehound and Balm <note>original: "Citraginis"</note>. It is certain he was deceived by the similarity of the names, reading *Prason melan* <note>Greek: "black leek"</note> instead of *Prasion* <note>Greek: "horehound"</note>. For *Prason* is a Leek, while *Prasion* is Horehound. Pliny commits this same error regarding the herb *Stachys*.

### The Judgment of M. VERGILIUS on the same.

<margin>Vergilius on Pliny.</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Ballote, Horehound.</margin>
<margin>Ulcer-herb.</margin>
<margin>Horse-herb.</margin>
Others have long ago detected Pliny’s shameful slip in Book 27, Chapter 8 regarding *Ballote*, where he calls it "Black Leek." This error has been tossed about against that writer for a long time; it is a fault that cannot be excused in a man of his stature, being such an obvious mistake and an easy target for criticism. We leave aside what has already been brought to judgment, thinking it too harsh to recall it for a new censure. We warn those eager for the liberal arts, and especially Greek literature, that no amount of diligence is ever enough in their profession: for in the change, addition, or subtraction of a single letter, there is such danger that someone might teach "Leek" to others instead of "Horehound." Now, *Ballote* is known to everyone; it is called Horehound <note>original: "Marrubium"</note> because of the similarity of the leaves, and "Black" because of the difference in color. Indeed, the stem is white in Horehound, but black in *Ballote*, while all other features are similar and equal, as is easy to know from the history of both. Some have called this "The Other Horehound"—that is, the second kind—by a clear indication: since the former is primary and this one is secondary, not by the order of nature, but by human honor and naming. It also has another name, "Ulcer-herb" <note>original: "Ulceraria"</note>, for a certain reason based on its use and powers; just as it could be called "Horse-Horehound" <note>original: "Cantherinum"</note> by the Romans because gelded horses <note>original: "cantherii"</note> would feed on it.

### THE TEMPERAMENT of Horehound from Johannes Serapion, chapter 198, on *Farasio*.

Its primary virtue is hot in the second degree, dry in the third, in the middle of it toward the end. Its second virtue is that it cleanses and dissolves. The third is that it opens blockages of the liver and spleen, and cleanses the lungs and chest. And it also cleanses and dissolves when applied externally.

### A Dish made from Horehound, from PLATINA’S Book 3, *On Right Pleasure*.

Horehound <note>original: "Marrubium"</note> is what the Greeks so name because of its bitterness, and they count it among the foremost herbs. Its crushed seeds and leaves are useful against serpents, and they soothe pains of the chest and side, or a cough. From both types of Horehound, finely chopped and worked into flour, little morsels <note>original: "offellae"</note> are made; when these are fried in oil in a pan, we eat them at the start of a meal for our health. They are believed to drive away intestinal worms, and for this reason, they are usually served to children.

<header>PHARMACEUTICS OF SIMPLE MEDICINES</header>

## WINE OF HOREHOUND from Columella, Book 12, Chapter 32.

<margin>C</margin> Many believe that Wine of Horehound <note>original: "Vinum Marrubii"</note> is very useful for all ailments of the intestines, and especially for a cough. When you perform the vintage, gather the tender stalks of Horehound, especially from uncultivated and thin soils, and dry them in the sun. Then make small bundles, tie them with palm or rush cord, and place them into a wine jar <note>original: "seria," a large earthenware vessel</note> so that the cord hangs out. Add eight pounds of Horehound to two hundred sextarii <note>A Roman unit of volume, roughly equivalent to a pint.</note> of sweet must <note>Unfermented grape juice.</note>, so that it may ferment together with the must. Afterward, remove the Horehound, and carefully seal the purified wine.

### A description of the same wine by DIOSCORIDES, Book Five.

Pound the leaves of mature Horehound and place eight sextarii into a *metreta* <note>A Greek liquid measure, roughly 9 gallons.</note> of must, and perform the rest of the process in the same way. This wine is suitable for ailments of the chest and for all conditions for which Horehound is used.

### A genuine description of HOREHOUND, from the expert herbalist HIERONYMUS.

<margin>
Why Horehound is so named.
Male and female Horehound.
</margin>
Horehound is called <term>Andorn</term> by the Germans, because it is a familiar and present help for a disease of that same name <note>likely referring to "Andorn" as a folk name for respiratory congestion</note> to which children are quite prone. It is held to be of two types: Male and Female. The Male is blackish, similar to the Great Nettle, except that it appears darker in its greenness and does not sting at all. The Female has round, pale leaves, and a round stem a cubit high.

<margin>
What is understood by the sexes in the name of Horehound.
</margin>
<margin>D</margin> It is the observation of Doctors that when the name Horehound is used without an attached sex, they frequently understand it to mean the female. Sometimes they administer the male variety to men and the female to women.

### On the preparation of Horehound from SERAPION.

When Horehound is dry, it is decocted in water with its seed; but when it is fresh, it is crushed and its juice is squeezed out. And that juice, which is taken from its leaves after it has been dried in the sun, is dissolved in honey and administered to sharpen the eyesight. It is also made into a sternutatory <note>A substance used to induce sneezing.</note> for those with jaundice, to cleanse the color of the skin. It is also mixed with medicines for long-standing ear pain.

### Its POWERS AND BENEFITS from DIOSCORIDES.

Its dried leaves, decocted in water with the seed, or the juice of the fresh plant, is given with honey to those suffering from shortness of breath, those coughing, and those reduced by consumption <note>original: "tabitudinem," a wasting disease like tuberculosis</note>.
Along with dried Iris, it expels thick phlegm from the chest.
It is given to women who have not been cleansed after childbirth, so that it may draw out the menses and the afterbirth.
Likewise, it is used in difficult labor, and for those who have swallowed poison or have been bitten by serpents.
It harms the bladder and the kidneys.
The leaves are applied with honey to cleanse foul ulcers.
They stop <term>Pterygia</term> <note>A wing-like growth on the eye.</note> and <term>Nomas</term> <note>Spreading or gangrenous sores.</note>.

### From APULEIUS, for a severe cough.
Boil the herb Horehound in water and give it to those who cough severely to drink; it will heal wonderfully.

### For STOMACH pain.
Drinking the juice of the Horehound herb will take away stomach pain; if the patient has a fever, drinking it in water raises their strength sufficiently.

### For INTESTINAL WORMS.
Equal weights of the herbs Horehound, Wormwood, and Lupines, boiled in honey-water with wine and placed twice or three times on the navel, kills intestinal worms <note>original: "lumbricos"</note>.

Burn the Horehound herb and rub in its ash: it will heal <note>original: "condylomata"; refers to swellings or growths in the anal or genital region</note>.

Horehound herb crushed with lard <note>original: "axungia"; rendered animal fat used as a base for salves</note> and applied heals wonderfully.

If someone, exhausted from work, falls into weakness and has pain in the tendons, anoint them with the juice of the Horehound herb mixed with rose oil: they will be healed without delay.

### FROM PLATEARIUS.
The leaves of Horehound <note>original: "Prassij"; the Greek-derived name for Marrubium</note> are especially suitable for medicinal use, as are the barks of the root; secondarily, the herb itself and the seeds, collected and hung up, can be kept for a year with great effectiveness. For they have the power of dissolving and consuming through their qualities. Because of their bitterness, they are diuretic, and they dissolve, attract, and open <note>referring to the "opening" of blockages in the bodily humors or vessels</note>.
Against intestinal worms, its powder is given with honey.
Against ear-worms, the juice is poured into the ears.
Against hardness of the spleen, the bark of the root is soaked with the herb for five days in wine and oil; afterward, a decoction is made, and wax and oil are added to the strained liquid to make an ointment.
Against strangury and dysuria <note>difficulty or pain in urination</note>, the wine from its decoction is given; or a plaster is made from it and placed over the pubic region <note>original: "pectinem"</note>.

<header>THE MEDICINES OF SIMPLE PLANTS</header>

<margin>C</margin>
[...] with branches, five or six from the root, leafy, and astringent to the taste. It grows in grain fields and cultivated places. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist</note> says much the same in Book 27, Chapter 9.

Now, whether of these descriptions corresponds more truly, and which hits the mark more closely—the school of the "barbarians" <note>A common Renaissance term for Medieval or Arabic authors whose Latin was considered unrefined</note> or the private judgments of the modern scholars today—we wish to leave to your judgment, reader. For our part, although our mind inclines toward the opinion of the younger scholars, yet since they have very few followers who first persuaded themselves they had discovered this error, we cannot rashly condemn the faith of the ancients, received for so many centuries, because of one or two arguments. But more on these matters will be discussed in the section on Ivies.

### CONSTITUTION <note>original: "Temperamentum"; referring to the plant's qualities in Galenic medicine</note>

It is said to be of a cold and dry complexion. It possesses the power of cleansing, drying, promoting the growth of flesh, and healing wounds.

### BENEFITS of the plant called Ground Ivy <note>original: "Chamæcissos"</note>

Those suffering from sciatica <note>original: "ischiadici"</note> find it most suitable to drink the leaves, in a dose of three obols <note>A small unit of weight, roughly half a gram</note>, in three cups of water, for thirty or forty days. Drunk in the same manner for six or seven days, they purge the "Royal Disease" <note>original: "regium morbum"; a historical name for jaundice</note>.

<margin>D</margin>
### BENEFITS OF ELATINE <note>A low-growing plant, historically associated with types of ivy or fluellen</note>

It helps with eye discharges and inflammations when the leaves are ground with pearl barley <term>polenta</term> and applied as a poultice.

The same plant, when cooked and used as a broth, stops dysentery.

### Benefits of the common Ground Ivy according to GIOVANNI DA VIGO <note>A famous Italian surgeon (c. 1450–1525) who served Pope Julius II</note>

The blood of a male goat that has been fed on this plant for a long time powerfully cures those suffering from stones <term>calculosis</term>.

And when crushed with lard and hellebore, it drives away every kind of scalp mange <note>original: "tineam capitis"; a fungal infection of the scalp</note>.

### From JEROME the herbalist <note>Likely Hieronymus Bock, also known as Tragus, a contemporary German physician and botanist</note>

The water or decoction of Ground Ivy, in a weight of two ounces, benefits women suffering from swelling of the limbs or the belly.

It will provide the same benefit if applied as a compress <term>epithimetur</term>, and that twice a day.

### ON EYEBRIGHT,
#### Rhapsody XXVII.
##### NOMENCLATURE,

->Greek: *Ophthalmika* <note>original: ὀφθαλμικά; meaning "pertaining to the eyes"</note>.<-
->Latin: *Eufragia*.<-
->German: **Augentroft** <note>literally "Eye-comfort"</note>.<-

<margin>
Eyebright was unknown to the ancients.
</margin>
Hermolaus Barbarus <note>A 15th-century Italian scholar known for his corrections to Pliny’s natural history</note> mentions Eyebright in his discussion on the *Saxifage* of Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and father of pharmacognosy</note> in this way: It is similar to the pimpernel, only with a smaller leaf, more serrated, and somewhat sticky. Our herbalists call it *Eufragia*. It is less shrubby, with a yellowish flower, and is of particular excellence for all defects of the eyes. They believe it was unknown to the ancients, just like the plant called *Cartofilago* by the wound-healers <note>folk surgeons or healers who treated injuries</note>. We think it should be called *Ceratophylax* <note>meaning "guardian of the horn"</note> because it defends the *ceratoid* part of the eyes—that is, the Cornea—and restores it to health when it has been afflicted. It has leaves like *Seriphium* <note>possibly Sea-Wormwood</note>, or rather like Rosemary, or even Flax, with dry flower heads and yellowish tendrils. I read nothing more about it among the more modern authors.

# ON FLAX.
## Rhapsody XXVIII.

### NOMENCLATURE
->Greek: *Linon* <note>original: λίνον</note>, *Linokalamos* <note>original: λινοκάλαμος; literally "flax-reed"</note>, *Linon agrion* <note>original: λίνον ἄγριον; "wild flax"</note>.<-
->Latin: *Linum*.<-
->German: **Flax-seed. Flax.** <note>original: Linsomen. Flachs.</note><-

The name FLAX is derived from the Greek, as [Hermolaus] Barbarus <note>A 15th-century Italian scholar who updated classical botanical knowledge</note> says. Its seed is called *Linospermon* <note>Greek for flax-seed</note>. Once the oil has been pressed from the seeds, the dregs and residues are also stored away; these are used for fattening various kinds of draft animals, especially oxen that are intended to be notable for their girth alone.

<margin>Types of Flax.</margin>
The types of flax include *Cholorcium*, which the Greeks nonetheless call *Sardonicum* <note>Sardinian flax</note>. There is also Egyptian flax, from which "woody garments" <note>original: Xylinę ueſtes</note> are made, which they also call *Gossampine* <note>a term often used in antiquity for cotton or very fine linen</note>. Legal experts call this "woody wool" <note>original: Laneam ligneam; likely referring to the fiber's plant origin compared to sheep's wool</note>.

### A Praise of Flax from the preface of PLINY’S nineteenth book.

<margin>D</margin>
To begin with the acknowledged benefits of flax—which have filled not only all lands but even the seas—it is sown as a crop, yet it cannot truly be called either a grain or a garden plant. But in what part of life does it not appear? Or what miracle is greater than that there exists an herb which brings Egypt so close to Italy? Indeed, [the prefect] Galerius reached Alexandria from the Strait of Sicily on the seventh day, and Babillius in six; both sets out in summer. Just last summer, Valerius Marianus, a senator of praetorian rank, reached Alexandria from Puteoli in nine days with a very gentle breeze. It is a miracle that an herb can bring the Pillars of Hercules at Gades <note>modern-day Cádiz, Spain</note> to Ostia <note>the port of Rome</note> in seven days, hither Spain in four, the province of Narbonne in three, and Africa in two—which even happened to Gaius Flaccus, the envoy of the proconsul Vibius Crispus, with the mildest of winds.

It is a daring life, full of crimes, to sow a plant merely so that it may catch the winds and storms; as if it were not enough to be carried by the waves alone! Furthermore, sails are no longer large enough for our ships, and although single trees <note>masts</note> may suffice for the breadth of the yardarms, nevertheless, other sails are added above them...

The Wonder of Flax.

...and to be spread out, some at the prows and others at the sterns, and that death is provoked in so many ways. Finally, that from so small a seed is born that which carries the whole world to and fro; from so slender a stalk, not raised high from the earth; nor is it woven by its own strength, but having been steeped, beaten, and forced into the softness of wool—by an injury to nature and the highest audacity. And where no curse is sufficient to reach against the inventor <note>Pliny is referring to the inventor of sails/navigation, often identified in myth as Daedalus or similar figures</note> (spoken of by us in his proper place), for whom it was not enough for man to die on land, unless he also perished even unburied at sea. 

But we, in the previous book, warned that rains and winds were to be guarded against for the sake of the crops and fruits; and behold! it is sown by the hand of man, and harvested by the ingenuity of that same man, so that he might wish for winds upon the sea. Furthermore, so that we may know that punishments have been favored, nothing grows more easily: yet so that we may feel that it is done against the will of nature, it burns the field and makes the soil itself worse.

## Concerning the sowing of FLAX, and its varieties, and how it is prepared; and concerning Napkins, and incombustible Flax; and when Awnings were first used in Theaters.

<margin>
B
The clothes of the Germans were once made of flax. Weaving among the Germans.
</margin>
<margin>
What were once considered the best linens.
</margin>
It is sown mostly in sandy places, with a single furrow, and nothing else grows more quickly. Sown in the spring, it is pulled in the summer; and in this too it does injury to the earth. Yet someone might forgive Egypt for producing it, so that she might bring in the wares of Arabia and India: but is it thus that the Gauls are assessed for this revenue? And that mountains are set against the sea is not enough, nor that from the side of the Ocean the very "void" <note>original: "inane"; referring to the vast, unknown Atlantic</note> (as they call it) stands in the way. The Cadurci, Caleti, Ruteni, Bituriges, and those considered the furthest of men, the Morini—indeed, all of Gaul weaves sails. Already indeed even the enemies across the Rhine do so, and their women know no other more beautiful garment. 

In which reminder it occurs, what Marcus Varro relates, that in the family of the Serrani it is a family custom that women do not use linen clothing. In Germany, however, they perform this work dug in and underground. Similarly in Italy, for another reason. For between the rivers Po and Ticino lie the <term>Abiterna</term> <note>A regional variety of linen named for the town of Acerra</note> linens. In Europe, the prize for flax is fruitful. For in the vicinity of Hallio they take up <term>Retovina</term>, and on the Aemilian Way the <term>Faventine</term> are prized for their whiteness. The Faventine are always preferred over the raw linens of Hallio; in the Retovine, there is the highest thinness and density. Their whiteness is equal to the Faventine, but there is no downiness. This finds favor with some, and offense with others. The strength of the thread is almost more even than spider webs, and it has a ringing sound when one chooses to test it with a tooth; therefore the price is double that of others. 

And Nearer Spain has a particular brilliance of flax, thanks to the nature of the stream in which it is polished, which flows by Tarraco <note>Modern-day Tarragona</note>. And its thinness is wonderful, <term>carbasus</term> <note>fine linen or lawn fabric, often used for sails or luxury garments</note> having first been discovered there; for lately from the same Spain, Zoëlic flax has come into Italy, most useful for hunting-nets. That is a city of Callaecia near the Ocean. There is also its own glory for Cumaean flax in Campania, for the capture of fish and birds. The same material is used for nets. 

<margin>
Snares made of flax for fish and wild beasts.
</margin>
For we do not stretch out fewer snares for all animals with flax than we do for ourselves. But Cumaean nets cut down boars, and these, or the "casses" <note>small-mesh hunting nets</note>, overcome the edge of sharp iron. And we have already seen them of such thinness that they could pass through a man's ring along with their draw-ropes, with one man carrying a multitude of them to surround the glades. # Simple Remedies

**C** ...threads consisting of one hundred and fifty; just as was recently the case with Julius Lupus, who died while serving as the prefect <note>governor</note> of Egypt. Those who are ignorant of the past may marvel at this, yet in the temple of Minerva on the island of Rhodes, the breastplate of a former Egyptian king, whom they call Amasis, is displayed; it is shown that each individual strand consists of three hundred and sixty-five threads. Mucianus, who was three times consul, recently reported at Rome that he had tested this himself, and that only small remnants of it now survive due to the damage caused by those who try to verify it. 

<margin>Egyptian Flax.</margin>
Italy still holds the Pelignian flax in honor, but it is only used by fullers. No flax is whiter or more similar to wool; likewise, for mattresses, the Cadurci <note>a people of Gaul, in modern-day Cahors, France</note> obtain the highest glory. This invention for stuffing bedding also came from the Gauls; indeed, the custom in Italy still survives in the name *stramentum* <note>original: "stramenti"; literally "straw" or "bedding"</note>. Egyptian flax has the least strength but brings the most profit. There are four varieties there: Tanitic, Pelusiac, Butic, and Tentyritic, named after the regions in which they grow. The upper part of Egypt, verging toward Arabia, produces a shrub which some call *Gossypion* <note>original: "Gossipiō"; this is the cotton plant</note>, and many call *Xylon* <note>original: "Xylon"; from the Greek for 'wood'</note>: and therefore the linens made from it are called *Xylina* <note>cotton cloth</note>. It is a small plant and bears a fruit similar to a bearded nut, from whose inner down a wool is spun. No other fabrics are preferable to these in whiteness or softness. Garments made from it are most pleasing to the priests of Egypt. They call a fourth kind Orchomenian; it is made from a marsh reed, or rather from its tuft. 

**D** In Asia, they make flax from broom <note>a flowering shrub</note>, which is excellent for nets and lasts a long time in fishing after the shrub has been soaked for ten days. The Ethiopians and Indians make it from apples <note>likely referring to the kapok or silk-cotton tree</note>, and the Arabs from gourds grown on trees, as we have said.

<margin>Book 19, chapter 1. The ripeness of Flax.</margin>
Among us, its maturity is understood by two signs: the swelling of the seed or a yellowing color. Then, having been pulled up and tied in hand-sized bundles, it is dried hanging in the sun with the roots turned upward for one day; then for five more days, with the tops of the bundles turned toward each other so that the seed falls into the middle.

<margin>Preparation of Flax.</margin>
This plant has medicinal power, and was once used in a certain rustic and very sweet food in Transpadane Italy <note>the region of Italy north of the Po River</note>, though for a long time now it has been used only for religious sacrifices. Then, after the wheat harvest, the stalks themselves are submerged in water that has been warmed by the sun, held down by some weight. For no substance has greater lightness. A sign that they are properly soaked is when the outer skin becomes loose. They are then turned over again and dried in the sun as before.

<margin>Tow.</margin>
Soon, once dried, they are beaten on a stone with a tow-mallet. That which was closest to the bark is called *Stuppa* <note>Tow</note>; it is flax of inferior quality, mostly fit for the wicks of lamps. Even this, however, is combed with iron hooks until all the outer skin is stripped away.

<margin>Spinning flax is honorable even for men.</margin>
The inner fiber <note>original: "medullae"; literally "marrow" or "pith"</note> has a more numerous distinction of quality, noted for its whiteness and softness. To spin flax is considered honorable even for men. The husks that are beaten off are used for heating ovens and furnaces. The art of combing and sorting it is such that from fifty pounds of bundles, fifteen pounds of carded flax should be produced. Then it is polished again in the thread, being struck frequently against flint in water; and once woven, it is beaten again with clubs, for it is always improved by such "injury."

<margin>Living Flax.</margin>
Something has now been discovered that is not consumed by fire. They call it "living flax" <note>original: "Linum vivum"; this is asbestos, which the ancients believed was a rare plant fiber</note>; I have seen napkins made of it glowing at banquets, and when they were thrown into the fire, the stains were burned away, leaving them more brilliant than they could ever be made by water. The funeral tunics of kings are made from it to separate the ashes of the body from the rest of the pyre. It grows in the deserts...

Volume One

A B

...and scorched by the sun of India, where no rain falls, among dreadful serpents, it becomes accustomed to living through fire. It is rare to find and difficult to weave because of the short length of the fibers. Its color is otherwise reddish, but it shines brilliantly in the fire. When it is found, it equals the price of the finest pearls. <margin>Asbestos Linen</margin> It is called *Asbestinon* <note>original: "Asbeſtinum"; from the Greek word for "unquenchable" or "inextinguishable"</note> by the Greeks, according to the evidence of its nature. The author Anaxilaus states that a tree wrapped in this linen can be cut down with "deaf" blows—strikes that cannot be heard. Therefore, this linen holds the highest rank in the whole world. <margin>Byssus.</margin> Next to this is Byssus <note>original: "Byſſino"; a exceptionally fine and costly golden-hued fiber</note>, which is the greatest luxury for women; it is grown near Elis in Achaia <note>a region in the northern Peloponnese, Greece</note>. Its stalks were once exchanged for four denarii each, just like gold. The lint recovered from linen ship sails, especially those from the sea, is of great use in medicine, and the ash of *Spodium* <note>original: "Spodij"; a term for metallic ashes or slag used in ancient pharmacy</note> has similar power. There is also a certain kind among poppies from which linens derive a remarkable whiteness. 

Attempts were also made to dye linen, so that it might take on the "madness" of colored garments; this first occurred in the fleets of Alexander the Great while he was navigating the Indus River. When his generals and prefects varied the insignias of their ships in a contest, the shores were stunned as the wind filled the multi-colored sails. Cleopatra came to the Battle of Actium with Mark Antony with a purple sail, and fled with the same. This was the mark of the imperial ship. Later, linen was used only to provide shade in theaters; Quintus Catulus was the first of all to invent this when he dedicated the Capitol. <margin>Linen Sails/Awnings.</margin> Next, Lentulus Spinther is said to have been the first to draw canvas sails <note>original: "Carbaſma"; fine linen or cotton awnings</note> over a theater during the Apollinarian Games. Soon after, Caesar the Dictator covered the entire Roman Forum with woven fabric, as well as the Sacred Way from his own house all the way up the slope to the Capitol—a sight said to be more marvelous than the gladiatorial show itself. Later, even without games, Marcellus (the son of Augustus's sister Octavia), during his time as aedile and while his uncle was in his eleventh consulship, shaded the Forum with sails on the first of August, so that those involved in lawsuits might stand there more healthfully. How much things had changed from the customs of Cato the Censor, who had proposed that the Forum should be paved with sharp shells! Recently, awnings colored like the sky and studded with stars have been used; red ones are even stretched over the ropes on the ground in the amphitheaters of the Prince Nero, and in the courtyards of houses, to protect against moss and the sun. Otherwise, a persistent preference for white linen remained. 

Linen also held honor in the Trojan War. For why should it not be present in battles as well as in shipwrecks? Homer is a witness that at least a few fought in linen breastplates. From this, the more learned scholars have interpreted that the rigging of ships mentioned by the same poet was made of linen; for when he said *sparta* <note>original: "ſparta"; usually referring to Spanish broom or esparto grass used for ropes</note>, he meant things made of flax.

### ON THE SOWING OF FLAX
->From the 11th book of Palladius.<-

In the month of October, we shall sow the flax seed, if it pleases; though because of its "malice," it ought not to be sown, for it exhausts the richness of the earth. But if you wish, it should be sown in the richest and moderately moist soil, at a rate of eight *modii* <note>a Roman dry measure, roughly two gallons</note> per *jugerum* <note>about 0.6 acres</note>. Some sow it thickly in thin soil; in this way, they ensure that a fine, delicate flax is produced.

### ITS TEMPERAMENT.

The seed has the same powers as Fenugreek. It is hot, roughly in the first degree. In terms of moisture and dryness, it is situated roughly in the middle.

Pharmacology of SIMPLES <note>In historical medicine, "simples" were individual plant, animal, or mineral ingredients used on their own rather than in complex mixtures.</note>

<margin>C</margin>
# ITS POWERS AND BENEFITS
# according to DIOSCORIDES, book 2.

It disperses and softens all inflammation, both internal and external, when boiled with honey, oil, and a little water, or when combined with cooked honey.
It removes blemishes of the skin on the face and pimples when used raw.
Applied as an ointment with natron <note>original: "nitro"; a naturally occurring mineral salt used for cleansing</note> and ash from a fig tree, it disperses swellings of the parotid glands <note>the salivary glands located near the ears</note> and other hardened growths.
Boiled with wine, it cleanses spreading ulcers and honeycomb-like sores <note>original: "fauos"; likely referring to *favus*, a type of fungal infection of the scalp</note>.
It removes rough nails when mixed in equal parts with watercress and honey.
It draws out ailments of the chest if it is substituted for honey in the form of an electuary <note>original: "eclegmatis"; a thick medicinal paste meant to be licked or dissolved in the mouth</note>.
It soothes a cough and stimulates sexual desire <note>original: "Venerem"; literally "Venus," often used to refer to libido or fertility</note> if linseed flour and honey are mixed with pepper and consumed in a larger quantity as a cake.
A decoction of this is injected for erosions <note>painful lesions or ulcers</note> of the intestines and the womb.
It draws out waste from the bowels.
It is extremely useful for inflammations of the womb when used in sitz baths <note>original: "deſeſſionibus"; therapeutic baths where the patient sits in shallow water</note>.

->From the Miscellanies of SERAPION, chapter 21.<-

From Mesue <note>A celebrated Persian physician of the 8th or 9th century</note>: The property of linseed is this: when a plaster is made from it mixed with wax and honey, it benefits white spots on the fingernails.
From Albugerig <note>Likely a Latinized reference to an Arabic medical author, possibly Al-Bujairami or similar</note>: It benefits ulcers of the bladder and kidneys, and matures abscesses <note>brings them to a "head" to be drained</note> when made into a plaster.
When it is drunk roasted, it helps a hot and moist cough.
From Mesarugie <note>Another Latinized Arabic source, often associated with Masarjawaih</note>: It quickly expels the fetus and excess fluid.
<margin>D</margin> And a decoction of linseed is mixed with oil to be used as an enema for ulcers of the intestines, and it benefits them magnificently.
From Rhazes <note>original: "Rafi"; the famous 9th-century Persian physician Abu Bakr al-Razi</note>: It benefits pains and sharp stings in the intestines.
From Paulus <note>Paulus Aegineta, a 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note>: When flax is burned, its fine smoke benefits nasal congestion <note>original: "corrizæ"; a head cold or catarrh</note> and "suffocation of the womb" <note>an ancient medical term for a variety of conditions believed to be caused by the movement of the uterus</note>.

### HARMFUL EFFECTS of Flax, from Galen book 1
### on foods, chapter 27.

However, it is bad for the stomach and is difficult to digest. Furthermore, when parched, it strongly binds the bowels. It also "burns" <note>depletes the nutrients of</note> the field in which it is sown and makes the soil itself worse.

The base of the plant shows a thick, tapering root with smaller lateral roots.]

# Explanation of Hound's-tongue, by M. Vergilius. <note>Marcellus Virgilius Adriani (1464–1521) was an Italian humanist and translator of Dioscorides.</note>

<margin>Why Hound's-tongue is so called.</margin>
All of Etruria <note>modern-day Tuscany</note> knows this herb as "Dog’s Tongue" <note>original: "Canis lingua"</note>; for it is used for ulcers and minor wounds. He <note>Pliny</note> describes it as being without a stem, and slightly smaller than the other plants known to this writer. It grows mostly among vines and remains green throughout the whole winter. We have often seen it in a leafy tuft, with a root the thickness of a human thumb, of a whitish color, and a textured roughness running over it. We believe this texture was the reason for its name and its comparison to a dog's tongue. For a dog, like many other animals, has a tongue that is somewhat rough, like a rasp. <note>original: "scobinae," a file or rasping tool.</note>

## PANDECTARIUS on Hound's-tongue. <note>Matthaeus Silvaticus, author of the *Pandectae Medicinae*, a 14th-century medical encyclopedia.</note>

Dog’s tongue is similar to Plantain <note>original: "Arnoglosso"</note>, except that it has visible ribs in its leaves, yet they are smooth, and there is a visible fuzz <note>original: "borra"</note> upon them.

## OUR JUDGMENT.

We have identified two species of Hound's-tongue. One, with the leaf of a Plantain, is the true and genuine one described by Dioscorides. The other, which the apothecary shops today show as being similar in almost every way to Wild Bugloss (having thinner, leathery leaves), is one we have great doubts about. Michael Herr <note>original: "Michael Herus," a contemporary German physician and translator.</note>, a physician and our friend, raised this concern to us; he firmly asserts that the doctors of Montpellier <note>original: "montis Pessulani," home to a famous medical university.</note> classify this second type as a Bugloss. I am inclined to believe this because I do not see it corresponding to Dioscorides’ description. Indeed, it is so similar to Bugloss that it appears to be a variety of it. As for the other species mentioned by Pliny, which bears small burrs, I have not yet discovered it.
<margin>Michael Herr</margin>

## TEMPERAMENT. <note>In Galenic medicine, "temperament" describes the qualities of a plant—hot, cold, moist, or dry—which were used to balance the humors of the body.</note>

It is of a cold and dry temperament.

## POWERS AND BENEFITS
### from DIOSCORIDES, Book 2.

Its leaves, chopped and cooked with old pig fat <note>lard</note>, heal the bites of rabid dogs, hair loss <note>original: "ἀλωπεκίας" (alopekias); literally "fox-mange," referring to what we now call alopecia</note>, and burns. 
The same leaves, boiled and drunk with wine, soften the belly <note>act as a laxative</note>.

## FROM GIOVANNI DA VIGO. <note>Giovanni da Vigo (c. 1450–1525) was a famous surgeon and physician to Pope Julius II.</note>

<margin>B</margin>
The juice of Hound's-tongue, mixed with the juice of Plantain, pomegranate wine, and a little Lycium <note>a medicinal extract from thorny shrubs</note>, and thickened slightly over a fire, is effective for ulcers of the mouth, nose, gums, and genitals.
It is also effective when mixed with honey of roses and turpentine for ulcers caused by "cold humors."
<margin>An Experiment</margin>
Therefore, as experience has shown us, it works most powerfully against the old ulcers of the **French disease** <note>original: "morbi gallici," a common Renaissance term for syphilis</note>. It easily softens, purges, and cleanses them of all thick and deep-rooted blockages <note>original: "trumbositate," referring to hard, clotted, or congested tissue</note> as if by a strong binding. This is especially true if the aforementioned juice is thickened over a fire with a little syrup of roses, or oxymel of squill <note>a mixture of honey, vinegar, and sea-onions</note>, if you wish for a stronger effect.
Likewise, the leaves of this herb, when placed upon "cold ulcers" or scrofula <note>original: "scrophulis," a form of tuberculosis causing swollen lymph nodes in the neck</note>, heal them by their natural property.

## From the noble HIERONYMUS the herbalist. <note>Likely Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), a pioneer of modern botany.</note>

A potion of Hound's-tongue water heals hemorrhoids if they are internal; or washing them with Hound's-tongue water if they protrude externally.
Nothing cleanses all wounds and ulcers quite as well.

Ground-laurel <note>original: "Chamædaphne"</note> consists of a single small branch, about a cubit <note>An ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm.</note> high, with a thin leaf resembling the Laurel: the seed is reddish and attached to the leaves.

## JUDGMENTS OF THE MODERNS <note>original: "NEOTHERICORVM," referring to contemporary Renaissance scholars.</note> regarding the Periwinkle.

### The Judgment of HERMOLAUS BARBARUS <note>An Italian humanist and scholar (1454–1493) known for his corrections to Pliny's natural history.</note> on Ground-laurel and Periwinkle.

<margin>Ground-laurel appears to be different from the Periwinkle.</margin>
Ground-laurel has a thin leaf. Some consider the same plant to be the Periwinkle. It is a topiary herb <note>A plant used for ornamental hedging or decorative gardening.</note>, evergreen, surrounded by leaves at the joints like a cord, and was used by the ancients to make up for a scarcity of flowers; its young shoots are even eaten like asparagus. Furthermore, it seems to me that the Periwinkle is different from the Ground-laurel; for the Periwinkle does not lift itself up, but creeps, stretching itself out like a cord, as I said before, with a purplish-blue flower. Ground-laurel rises to a cubit’s height, as Dioscorides and Pliny confirm. However, Ground-laurel can also be called Periwinkle—a point Pliny agrees with—but let it be recorded that they are not entirely the same genus. Otherwise, their medicinal uses would not vary somewhat. Periwinkle is said to be beneficial for dropsy, the ears, and the bowels; Ground-laurel for headaches, promoting urine and menstruation, stomach burns, and griping pains.

### The Judgment of MARCELLUS VIRGILIUS <note>Marcello Adriani (1464–1521), a Florentine scholar and translator of Dioscorides.</note> on the same.

Ground-laurel is a low and terrestrial Laurel, admitted to the name and honor of the Laurel by the Greeks solely due to the similarity of its leaves. It is a topiary herb, if we believe Pliny, and was called *Vincaperuinca* by the Latin herbalists of his age. If this is the plant that Tuscany <note>original: "Ethruria"</note> now calls the *Vinca* herb—with which, among our people, deceased virgins are carried out for burial crowned in wreaths, and with which certain families among us, by their ancestral right, receive the Archbishop entering the city for the first time, meeting him at the gate crowned with it, crowding around him and accompanying him through the city—it is very easy to recognize. It grows everywhere in gardens, with very slender vines, creeping along the ground rather than rising from it with stalks, as Dioscorides says...

<header>PHARMACOLOGY of Simples</header>

<margin>C</margin> ...rising up: and with leaves more like those of the Olive tree than the Laurel. Indeed, this differs greatly from Dioscorides' account of Ground-laurel <note>original: "Chamædaphne"</note>, due to the characteristics we listed just before, and many other marks which will be very easy for those willing to observe them. Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> mentions Ground-laurel at the end of his third volume on the *History of Plants*, but so briefly that nothing else can be understood from him except that Ground-laurel bears fruit attached to the leaves: which is very far removed from the Periwinkle <note>original: "Vinca"</note> of our age. Furthermore, it is not used as food in any way now, which the ancient Greek physicians testify was once the case with Ground-laurel. For instance, Paul of Aegina <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note>, treating it in his sixth book, says, "the pulp is eaten" <note>original: "χυλὸν ἐσθίεται"</note>. Moreover, in the first book, in the chapter where he teaches about the "asparagus" <note>In ancient botany, "asparagus" referred to the tender, edible young shoots of various plants, not just the vegetable we know today</note> of all garden herbs, after having discussed many at length, he added: "similarly also the asparagus-shoot of the Ground-laurel" <note>original: "παραπλησίως δὲ καὶ ὁ τῆς χαμαιδάφνης ἀσπάραγος"</note>, that is, it also provides nourishment. By these clues and authors, we are persuaded that the *Vinca* herb of Tuscany is not the Ground-laurel. Nevertheless, what Pliny describes as *Vincaperuinca* in Volume 21, chapter 11, corresponds well enough to the *Vinca* of our nation. Indeed, he says *Vincaperuinca* is always green in the manner of a line, surrounded by leaves at the joints, a garden plant, and sometimes makes up for a lack of flowers. All these things belong to our Ground-laurel <note>The author is reconciling Pliny's "Vincaperuinca" with the local plant they call Ground-laurel</note>, with its Laurel-like leaf, cubit-long <note>about 18 inches</note> rods, round and reddish fruit attached to the leaves, whose asparagus-shoots could be used for food.

### A Rebuking of Pliny, Theodorus Gaza, Hermolaus Barbarus, and Marcello Virgilio, by Nicolaus Leonicenus, in his book "On the Errors of Physicians."

<margin>Which is the true Periwinkle in Dioscorides?</margin> This same Theodorus <note>Theodorus Gaza, a 15th-century translator of Aristotle and Theophrastus</note> interprets the Ground-laurel in Theophrastus as the Periwinkle <note>original: "Vincaperuinca"</note>, although Ground-laurel is actually another plant, whose description is very different from the Periwinkle in Dioscorides. To those who contemplate the nature and appearance of the Periwinkle more accurately, it will seem to be that plant which is designated by Dioscorides and Pliny alike by the names *Clematitis*, *Daphnoides*, and *Polygonoides*.

And again elsewhere: Regarding Ground-laurel in Book 15. You think the old reading and punctuation are correct if one writes: "There is also a wild shrub Ground-laurel, and an Alexandrian one," so that two types are understood. One is Ground-laurel, which the Latins call *Laureola* <note>Spurge-laurel</note>, as you say; although that which is called *Laureola* in Latin today is not Ground-laurel, but rather *Daphnoides*, described immediately afterward by Pliny. The other is the Alexandrian Laurel, according to Pliny, Galen, and Dioscorides. You indeed excuse Pliny in this way, so that he does not seem to have designated Ground-laurel differently in different places: since in this place—specifically in Book 15—he only depicted the Alexandrian Laurel, just as in Book 24 he depicted Ground-laurel. But two doubts remain in Pliny that can by no means be hidden. Why, when Pliny described the other kinds of Laurel in that same place in Book 15, did he leave Ground-laurel alone undescribed? Why, when the other kind is not called simply "Alexandrian," but "Alexandrian Laurel" by Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and Galen—indeed, by all Greek authors—did Pliny, omitting the proper name, give only a nickname taken from the place or <margin>D</margin> person? Or when he later added, "others call it *Daphne*," he placed the proper name last, against its nature: since the true name of this shrub is neither *Daphne* alone, nor *Alexandrina*, but the whole name, as we said, is *Daphne alexandrina* <note>Alexandrian Laurel</note>.

And again: Pliny in Book 15 describes Ground-laurel thus: "There is also the wild shrub Ground-laurel, and the Alexandrian, which some call *Idaea*, some *Hypoglottis*, others *Daphne*, others *Carpophyllon*, and others *Hypelate*. It spreads branches from the root nine inches <note>original: "dodrantales"</note> long, used for garden and garland work, with a leaf sharper than myrtle, softer and whiter, with a larger red seed among the leaves; it is most abundant on Mount Ida and around Heraclea of Pontus, and only in mountainous places." Pliny later describes the same Ground-laurel in Book 24 thus: "Ground-laurel consists of a single small branch, about a cubit long, with a thin leaf, in the likeness of a Laurel," and so forth. Who does not see that Pliny provides different descriptions for the same plant? For the first description is of the Alexandrian Laurel, but not of the Ground-laurel handed down by Dioscorides in Book 4. That Ground-laurel is indeed different from Alexandrian Laurel is shown not only by Dioscorides, but equally by Galen and Paulus in their books on simple medicines.

## A Defense by Pandolpho Collenuccio for the Moderns and Pliny, against
### N I C O L A V S L E O N I C E N V S.

The more Nicolaus strives to heap criticisms upon Pliny, the more he stains himself with marks of ignorance: so much so that he considers neither Pliny's words, nor his order of writing, nor the differences of the matters. Therefore, it is now better to laugh at his manifest follies than to refute them. Leonicenus says that Pliny provides different descriptions for the same plant, that is, for the Ground-laurel. But let us consider from this very Ground-laurel how different he himself is from what we thought. Pliny, in Book 15, in describing the kinds of Laurel tree, says: "There is also the wild shrub Ground-laurel": and he makes no further mention of Ground-laurel, nor does he depict it (as Nicolaus previously thought) from the name...
