<meta>Continuing from page 180, the author continues to resolve the botanical confusion surrounding the various species of Ground-laurel (Chamædaphne) and their classification by ancient authorities like Pliny and Dioscorides, while defending Pliny against the criticisms of Nicolaus Leonicenus.</meta>

<page-num>181</page-num>
<header>...of the Physicians, VOLUME First.</header>

<margin>A</margin>
...doubtless you are uncertain whether it might be an herb, which he named a shrub. Here, therefore, the [meaning] of the words must be noted. Then Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist and author of *Natural History*</note> proceeds by enumerating the kinds of Laurel and says: "And the Alexandrian, which some call the Idaean, others Hippoglottin <note>original: "Hippoglottin," literally "horse-tongue"</note>, and others Daphne." Indeed, he describes this Alexandrian Daphne. This is the very one which Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> and others also describe. But in book 20, chapter 12, when he had described the kinds of shrubs and sub-shrubs, he says: "To these we shall subjoin those which the Greeks, by a commonality of names, have made ambiguous as to whether they were trees." Then, in the very next chapter, he continuously speaks of Wall-germander <note>original: "Chamædry"</note>, Ground-laurel <note>original: "Chamædaphne"</note>, Spurge-olive <note>original: "Chamælea"</note>, Ground-fig <note>original: "Chamæfice"</note>, Ground-ivy <note>original: "Chamæcisso"</note>, and others of this sort. And in that place, he describes the Ground-laurel, which he had only touched upon in book 15. These matters, therefore, stand thus: Pliny enumerates seven kinds of Laurel in book 15; then three species of Laurel-shrub: Ground-laurel, Alexandrian, and Daphnoid. He describes the Alexandrian and the Daphnoid; but Ground-laurel—because he was going to include it among those which a "commonality of names" (as he says) had made doubtful as to whether they were trees or herbs—he described beautifully in book 20, in which he spoke of similar herbs in their proper order.

<margin>The logic and utility of punctuation.</margin>
You see how, because of a punctuation mark (as is also said in jokes), Leonicenus <note>Nicolaus Leonicenus (1428–1524), a Renaissance scholar famous for pointing out "errors" in Pliny’s work</note> was caught out. If, between those two names, Ground-laurel and Alexandrian, in that 15th book, he had interposed some delay and a point (which even the rules of grammar required by the intervention of the conjunction "and"), he would not have fallen into these snares. A wonder comes over one considering the nature of this good man and friend, Leonicenus; if you saw him walking, you would say he was slow and lingering rather than swift or fast. Yet, in <margin>B</margin> accusing Pliny, he runs so headlong that in reading him and reviewing the points of accusation, he hates all delay and slowness; he does not hold his breath, nor his spirit; he punctuates nothing, and stops at no point. In this matter also, that man of most sagacious wit, Politianus <note>Angelo Poliziano, a prominent Italian humanist scholar</note>, in that letter which he wrote to this same Leonicenus concerning Ivy-herb <note>original: "Cisso & Cistho"</note>, notes excellently that in book 20, chapter 10, because Nicolaus did not punctuate between *Hypocisthis* and "which we shall speak of among the herbs," he seemed to have little wisdom, and to have understood poorly about the Rock-rose <note>original: "Cistho"</note> in that place; thus, as we have said, he is often convicted because of a punctuation mark.

<margin>Two plants are called Ground-laurel.</margin>
But lest the name "Ground-laurel" should ever cause doubt for readers, it is necessary to know that there are two plants which are equally called Ground-laurel <note>original: "Chamædaphne"</note>. Specifically, this one of which we are treating, which is commonly called Spurge-laurel <note>original: "Laureola"</note>; and that which is called Periwinkle <note>original: "Vincaperuinca"</note>, sought after for wedding crowns; with leaves far smaller than the Laurel; creeping on the ground in the manner of wild thyme; with a blue flower, scentless, round, and distinguished by five small but continuous petals.

### Benefits of Periwinkle from P L I N Y, book 21, chapter 27.

Periwinkle, or Ground-laurel, when dried and crushed, is given to those with dropsy <note>term: "hydropicis" — people suffering from edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</note> in water, in the measure of a spoonful, and it returns the water most quickly. The same, boiled in ash and sprinkled with wine, dries up tumors. It heals the ears with its juice. It is said to be of great benefit when applied to the bowels.

### ON THE THROUGH-LEAF, Chapter XXXI.
<note>original Latin: "Rhapsodia XXXI." In this context, Rhapsodia refers to a section or collection of observations.</note>

While we were stuck in the very middle of this work, and now these, then other herbs were brought to us, utterly without any selection or order (for neither could the designers, painters, and sculptors of our work follow an alphabetical sequence, nor did our plan allow for it), a certain **Through-leaf** <note>original: *Perfoliata*</note> was also offered to us among the others. For that is what the apothecary shops <note>original: *officinæ*</note> call it. Regarding this plant, although we have troubled ourselves greatly and for a long time, we could "fish out" nothing certain—neither from the medical doctors, nor from the shops, nor even from the old women and herbalists—except that it was called *Perfoliata*, or in our own language, **Through-leaf** <note>original German: *Durchwaschß*</note>. Therefore, following the pharmacists, we too have labeled it as *Perfoliata*, though it is a false one. For Lucas the pharmacist showed us another *Perfoliata* that was far different from this one; it had small stalks actually penetrating the little leaves, not very dissimilar to the genus of spurges, or a larger *Esula* <note>a medicinal plant in the spurge family</note>, reaching about nine inches <note>original Latin: *dodrantali*</note> in height. That plant so appropriately matched the German name that I believe those herbalists are plainly mistaken who [gave] us this one which we have provided...

### The history of the same plant, EMPETRON, from PLINY, book 27, chapter 9.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Calcifraga <note>Lime-breaker</note>.</margin>
*Empetron* <note>original Greek: ἔμπετρον (*empetron*), "on the rock"</note>, which our people call *Calcifraga* <note>meaning "lime-breaker," as in calcium or bladder stones</note>, grows in maritime mountains, usually on rock. The closer it is to the sea, the less salty it is. Furthermore, he mentions *Saxifragia* <note>Stone-breaker</note> in book 22, chapter 21, in the division on Maidenhair fern.

### Examination of the History of Dioscorides by HERMOLAUS BARBARUS, chapter 2. *Sarxiphagon*.

*Saxifragum* and *Saxifraga* are the Latin names. Likewise it is called *Calcifraga*, if indeed this is the same plant which both Pliny and Dioscorides call *Empetron* in another place, and which Paulus calls *Sarxiphages* <note>original Greek: σαρξίφαγος (*sarxiphagos*), meaning "flesh-eater," likely referring to its ability to dissolve flesh or stones</note>. Pliny says *Empetrum* grows mostly on rock. Its powers are in the fresh plant; it loses them with age. They affirm that stones which are "boiling up" <note>likely referring to the agitation of bladder stones</note> are broken by it. There is also considered to be another kind of *Saxifraga*, which we shall explain under Maidenhair fern. The Greek manuscripts are corroded and burnt in this section, and it is impossible to discern in any way what the leaf of this herb is like; and in the text of the words itself, a small blank space remains.
<margin>Picture of the true Saxifrage.</margin>
Furthermore, I have seen an ancient illustration of this herb in a manuscript of Dioscorides, with no more leaves than minute <term>Cirri</term> <note>tendrils or curls</note>, placed at intervals along the branches, and not crowded; at the top of the small forks are tufts, appearing more like dried bits than little flowers: with a somewhat reddish root, not without fibers. In Rome, such a plant is shown only in maritime and mountainous places, not with a reddish root, but a white one, and with small white flowers as well. More recent authors agree very little concerning this herb. Some say it has the shape of wheat leaves, others say it is similar to the sea *Batis* <note>Samphire</note>, others to what is commonly called *Tormentilla*.
<margin>D</margin>
<margin>
Tormentilla.
Clove-flower.
Pampinula.
Pimpinella.
Bipennula.
Sanguisorba.
</margin>
However, it is (as they will have it) *Tormentilla*, similar to the <term>Cinquefoil</term> <note>five-leaved</note> herb, except that it has nearly seven leaves, not five. A fourth kind is the herb which bears the flower called *Caryophyllon* <note>Clove-pink or Carnation</note>, of which we have spoken elsewhere. A fifth is that same *Saxifraga*, or very close to it, which is called *Pampinula*, *Pimpinella*, *Bipennula*, and *Sanguisorba* <note>Burnet</note> in the countryside; for when applied to wounds, it extracts iron and arrowheads easily and without the sensation of pain. It has a small, round leaf, serrated at the edges, which is also commonly chewed, prepared with oil, salt, and vinegar; with many dense shoots from the same root, which are reddish along with the root, so they say. In certain places, a "little worm" is dug up [from the roots], which, when prepared, makes an incomparable Purple dye, especially for dyeing silks, surpassing all other colors in a certain splendor and cheerfulness <note>This "worm" refers to the Polish Cochineal, an insect found on the roots of certain plants like Knawel, used for red/purple dye</note>.

### THE SAME AUTHOR in the Chapter on EMPETRON.

<margin>Prasoides <note>Leek-like</note>.</margin>
This *Empetron* is named *Phaconides* <note>Lentil-like</note> by Dioscorides, and *Prasoides* <note>original Greek: πρασοειδής (*prasoeidēs*), meaning "leek-colored"</note> by Galen and Paulus. It grows mostly on rock. Its powers are in the fresh plant; it loses them with age. They affirm that stones which are "boiling up" are broken by it. This we also said of *Saxifraga* according to the opinion of Pliny, as one who indicated that it does not differ from it: since he himself assigns to this *Empetrum* all the medicines which Dioscorides enumerates separately in each mention.
<margin>Pliny's lapse.</margin>
Therefore, one must either believe this, or confess that Pliny erred. Paulus [Aegineta], certainly following Dioscorides, has two mentions as if of two different kinds. Galen has only one.

It highlights the plant's reputation for dissolving bladder stones and mentions its use in extracting arrowheads and producing purple dye from root-dwelling insects.</summary>

First Volume.

Aetius also affirms that *Empetron* <note>Greek: ἔμπετρον, meaning "in the rock"</note> was commonly called by that name.
<margin>A</margin>

### The JUDGMENT of MARCELLO VIRGILIO on both 
### Saxifragia and Empetron.

<margin>Epipetron,</margin>
The name *Empetron* sufficiently indicates that it is born in rocks. Some of the older writers also called it *Epipetron* <note>Greek: ἐπίπετρον, "upon the rock"</note> with the same meaning. Pliny says that *Saxifraga* <note>Stone-breaker</note> is called so by the Latins, not only because it resembles the shape and appearance of a lentil (for which reason it is called *Phacoides* <note>Greek: φακοειδής, "lentil-like"</note>), but also because it is similar to Horehound (called *Prassoides* <note>Greek: πρασοειδής, "leek-like" or "horehound-like"</note>). He mixes this plant with the one that Dioscorides described specifically and separately as *Saxifraga* in this very volume. Because of this, we are forced to suspect again—as we said regarding *Saxifraga* earlier in this volume—that no other plant should be accepted under that name by this writer. Or, if it is—though it is unlikely—due to variations in history and medicine, the same plant was treated twice: once shortly before under the Latin title *Saxifraga*, and again now under *Empetron*, which is an entirely Greek word. Indeed, Paul of Aegina <note>A 7th-century Byzantine physician</note>, who seems to have transcribed all of Dioscorides with great brevity in the sixth book of his medical work, clearly mentions *Empetron* but never *Saxifraga*. He would not have omitted it if *Saxifraga* were then read in Dioscorides, or if he himself had accepted it as a different plant. We would also believe *Saxifraga* and *Empetron* to be the same, were their history and medicinal uses not entirely different. For this reason, we leave this to more experienced men, who may find a more certain conclusion as to what should be accepted and established regarding *Saxifraga*.

### The Reproof of Pliny in distinguishing Saxifragia 
### and Empetron, by NICCOLO LEONICENO.

<margin>B</margin>
Pliny writes in Book 27, in the same manner as Dioscorides, where *Empetrum* grows and what powers it has in drawing out bile and phlegm <note>original: pituita</note>. However, he joins other faculties to it—that it moves urine and breaks stones—which are reported by no other author regarding this *Empetrum*. On the contrary, Galen testifies in his sixth book that *Empetrum*, which is also called *Prassoides*, is useful only for purgations. But Pliny, deceived by the ambiguity of the name, ascribed to this *Empetrum* (which has purgative power) the effects he had read about in the other *Empetrum*—which is also called *Sarxiphages* <note>Greek: σαρξίφαγος, "flesh-eater"</note>—as reported by Greek authors, and especially Dioscorides.

### PIETRO COLLENUCCIO’S
### Defense of Pliny.

<margin>Empetrum,</margin>
Pliny reports that *Empetrum* is called *Calcifragum* <note>Lime-breaker</note> by our people, and that it breaks stones. It does not follow that it fails to break stones simply because none of those whom Niccolò [Leoniceno] read wrote of it. Pliny, a great and abundantly praised author, says this plant has that power; his opinion is found to be true both by experiment and by common belief. For *Empetrum* (which our Leoniceno was ignorant of) is that herb which is now considered most pleasing for salads <note>original: acedarijs, referring to foods prepared with vinegar</note>. All of Venice, by adding or changing a single letter, calls the herb *Sampetra* <note>Rock Samphire, *Crithmum maritimum*</note>. <margin>Sampetra, Basichia, Baticula, Rumpisaxum,</margin> Many call it *Basichia*; others *Baticula*. The people of Picenum <note>A region in eastern Italy</note> call it *Rumpisaxum* <note>Rock-breaker</note> from the faculty of the herb itself. Its leaves almost approach those of Rue, but are thicker and sharper. In its flower and seed, it resembles the appearance of both Anise and Fennel in its umbels <note>original: muscarijs, cluster-heads</note>. It has a pleasant smell and a taste between sour and salty that provokes an appetite for food. It grows (as Pliny also taught) in maritime mountains, almost always on rocks; this can be seen along that entire tract of land stretching between Fano <note>original: phanum Fortunae</note> and the Gargano promontory, and on the crags of Istria and the cliffs of Liburnia, from whence a great deal is brought to the Venetians. It is also kept as a cultivated plant in the gardens of monasteries, though not with easy cultivation.

<margin>Batis marina,</margin>
We are also led by certain reasons to think it is the same plant Pliny called *Marina Batis* <note>Sea Samphire</note> in another place—another kind of *Empetron* which our people call *Saxifragum*. This was not hidden from Pliny, who placed it in Book 22 among the kinds of Maidenhair fern, with branches of a greenish-black color and leaves like a fern, marvelously expelling and breaking stones—hence the name. We do not see it growing in shady rocks (as the Greeks perhaps thought) or in the spray of walls. Pliny was therefore not deceived by the similarity of names when he presented both kinds of *Empetrum* under the different names *Calcifragum* and *Saxifragum*; rather, it was our Niccolò who neither weighed Pliny's words nor recognized the herbs themselves, as would befit an accuser.

<summary>This page presents a scholarly debate over the identification of the plant Empetron (Rock Samphire), with Marcello Virgilio and Niccolò Leoniceno questioning Pliny the Elder's accuracy, while Pietro Collenuccio defends Pliny by identifying the plant with the common "Sampetra" used in Venetian cuisine.</summary>

# PHARMACY of SIMPLES
<header>PHARMACY of SIMPLES</header>
<sig>C</sig>

### Opinions of the MODERNS.
#### Description by SIMON OF GENOA.

<margin>Other types of Saxifrage.</margin> Regarding the herb Saxifrage, some take it to be the herb whose leaves are similar to the leaves of Burnet <note>original: "Pimpinellæ"</note>, though larger, and it has small branches spread out over the ground. However, another kind was shown in the areas of Rome, similar in every way to Sea Samphire <note>original: "Cretano marino"</note>, except that it is thinner and leaner; this is because it grows on sunny mountains and emerges from the cracks of rocks; and for this reason, the inhabitants call it
<margin>Stone-splitter.</margin> Stone-splitter <note>original: "Petra findula"</note>, because in its growth it seems to split the stones, approaching Samphire in smell and taste. According to the Botanist, that first one is the primary kind.
<margin>Burnet is called Saxifrage by some.</margin> For he says of Burnet that many have called it Saxifrage, and that it is similar to it, just as "Saxifrage of Tyre" <note>original: "Saxifragia tyraria"</note> was called by the ancients.

#### THE LEXICOGRAPHERS.
Saxifrage is an herb similar to Burnet, not differing except in the hairiness which Burnet possesses.

#### HIERONYMUS the Herbalist.

<margin>Four species of Saxifrage.</margin> Saxifrage is of many kinds. Namely: the Greater, with white flowers, a somewhat reddish stem, and a slender root to which nodules like Lentils or Peas adhere—which they say is its seed. The Lesser is known to everyone, creeping on the ground atop rocks, commonly called **Stone-herb** <note>original: "Steynkraut"</note>, because it is especially a remedy for sciatica <note>Pain affecting the back, hip, and outer side of the leg</note>. The third is the White kind, which is "Sun-millet" <note>original: "Miliū solis" or Gromwell</note>, in German, **Sea-millet** <note>original: "Meerhyrß"</note>.
<sig>D</sig> <margin>Asfarengi.</margin> mentioned in Dioscorides book 3. The fourth they have named *Alkakengi*, an Arabic word; in German, **Winter-cherry / Bladder-cherry / Jew’s-cherry** <note>original: "Schlutten / Bobozellen / Judenkyrssen"</note>. More on this will be found in the section on Nightshade <note>original: "Solano"</note>.

### TEMPERAMENT of SAXIFRAGE 
### according to Platearius. 28.

It is hot and dry in the third degree; it has diuretic, expulsive, and thinning properties. It erodes and crushes stones <note>referring to kidney or bladder stones</note>.

#### Powers and benefits of Saxifrage from DIOSCORIDES.

Boiled in wine and drunk immediately, it helps those suffering from fevers.
It is beneficial for strangury <note>A condition where urine is passed painfully drop by drop</note>.
It settles hiccups.
It breaks bladder stones and promotes urination.

#### The benefits of that which is called Empetron <note>Greek: ἔμπετρον, "in the rock"</note>, from the same DIOSCORIDES.

It draws out bile, phlegm, and water, if drunk in some broth or honey-water.

#### FROM PLATEARIUS.

Against stones in the kidneys and in the bladder, and against the Iliac passion <note>Severe abdominal pain or intestinal obstruction</note>, strangury, and dysuria <note>Painful or difficult urination</note>, the wine of its decoction is effective, or its powder in the weight of two drachms taken in a soft-boiled egg; a compress <note>original: "fomentū"</note> also made from it contributes much to the aforementioned conditions.

<header>First VOLUME of the Herbs.</header>

## Preservation of Saxifrage from PLATINA’S *On Rightful Pleasure*, Book 9.

<margin>A</margin>
Apuleius <note>Pseudo-Apuleius, the supposed author of a popular late-antique herbal</note> asserts that it is called Saxifrage <note>literally "Stone-breaker"</note> because it breaks and shatters small stones in the bladder. Its root is very similar to Stone Parsley <term>Petroselinum: a rock-growing parsley used as a diuretic</term>; which, when removed, washed, and cut into pieces, then eaten with salt, oil, and vinegar, shatters the stone (as we have said) on account of its heat and dryness. It cleanses the kidneys and bladder. It cooks slowly because of its dryness, which is contrary to the process of digestion; conversely, moisture and heat assist digestion.

### On BURNET <note>original: "Pimpinella"</note>, *thryllion* <note>Greek: θρύλλιον</note>.

<margin>Macer, Book 5 of the Letters.</margin>
We testified a little while ago, following Hermolao Barbaro <note>a Venetian scholar known for correcting Latin translations of Greek science</note>, that Burnet, or *Pampinula*, is the fifth species of Saxifrage. I believe this plant was also neglected by the ancients, or rather unknown to them. Theodorus Gaza <note>a Greek scholar who translated Aristotle and Theophrastus into Latin</note> translated this from Book 7, Chapter 10 of Theophrastus's *Inquiry into Plants* with these words: "The spiny ones are therefore Dog’s Eye, Fox Tail, and Plantain, which is called Lamb’s Tongue by some and Quail-grass by others. Similar to this in some way is that which is called *Bibinella*." However, I do not yet sufficiently grasp which plant he intends to be understood, or whether he intends it to be said of our common Burnet. It is known to be of a hot and dry
<margin>Temperament.</margin>
temperament, just like Saxifrage, and to be effective for the same purposes in all respects.

### Certain EMPIRICAL observations concerning BURNET.

These are the things we have received privately from the practitioners of experience <term>Empirics: physicians who relied on observation rather than ancient theory</term> regarding it.
<margin>B</margin>
That a decoction of it relieves a continuous fever, and also one that recurs every fourth day <term>quartan fever, often associated with malaria</term>.
The juice, when drunk, relieves a tertian fever <term>a fever recurring every three days</term>, provided it is taken before the onset of the fit.

### Use it thus against CONSUMPTION.

Take 2 ounces of Burnet, very finely powdered, a sufficient amount of fresh Burnet water and sugar, and let an Electuary <term>a medicinal paste or syrup</term> be made from it: take 2 drams of this daily.

## Preservation of Burnet from PLATINA’S Book 9,
## *On Rightful Pleasure*.

The power of Burnet—which is also called *Bibinella* in Greek <note>original: "Bibinella græce"</note>—is hot and dry: for this reason, it is digested slowly, yet it brings pleasure to those eating it. Collected and washed, it should be placed in a dish with its own stem if it is tender, and seasoned with salt, oil, and vinegar. If it is too hard, only the leaves are taken. This food opens the fibers of the liver, provokes urine, and [breaks] stones, just like Saxifrage: however, it does not shatter them quite as much.

Everyone interprets *Hepataria*, or *Hepatica*, as the *Lichen* found in Dioscorides <note>a 1st-century Greek physician</note>, Book 2, Chapter "Lichen" <note>original: λειχήν</note>. Lichen, or *Lechen*, is a moss, such as this one, and likewise another herb growing in rocky places; the name was devised for both because they are preferred above all other remedies against "lichens" <note>In antiquity, 'lichen' referred to both the plant and a type of skin eruption or spreading rash it was thought to cure</note>. ## LIVERWORT.
<margin>A</margin>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a liverwort (Marchantia), showing a flat, spreading, lobed thallus with a textured surface, characteristic of its growth on damp rocks or soil.</image-desc>

<gloss>Common Liverwort <note>original: *Marchantia polymorpha*, L C.B. 262. This is the thallose liverwort, which looks more like a mossy carpet than a flowering plant.</note></gloss>

**Liverwort.** <note>original: *Leberkraut*</note>

It is so named because it is seen to resemble the fibers of the liver. There is a different plant by the same name among us, growing everywhere on the shore, and sold in the vegetable market during the time of fasts; it has a leaf almost like ivy, a purple flower, and the appearance of a tiny lily. The herb winds itself around whatever it approaches. It loosens the bowels when cooked or raw, taken in the manner of garden vegetables.

### SERAPION, *Book of Simples*, Chapter 113.
<margin>B</margin>
->Concerning Liverwort.<- <note>original: *de Hepatica*</note>

*Hazez alfacher* <note>An Arabic term for Liverwort</note>, that is, Liverwort <note>original: *Hepatica*</note>, G. <note>Likely referring to the Greek name or a specific authority</note>. It grows on damp stones, and dew falls upon it, and it is similar to water-lentil <note>duckweed</note>.

### PLATEARIUS, Chapter 5.
<note>Matthaeus Platearius was a 12th-century physician from the medical school of Salerno, known for his work on "Simples" or single-ingredient medicines.</note>

Liverwort <note>original: *Hepatica*</note> is an herb growing in watery and especially in stony places, having tiny leaves clinging to the earth and stones. However, the larger its leaves are, the better it is; and it is called *Hepatica* because it is especially helpful to the liver <note>original: *hepatis iuuatiua*</note>.

### HIERONYMUS the Herbalist,
<note>Refers to Hieronymus Brunschwig, a 15th-century German surgeon and botanist whose "Herbarius" was a foundational text in early printing.</note>
->Concerning Liverwort.<-

Liverwort is held to have a triple variety. The first is that which clings to old and ruined fountains in the open air and to rocky stones, with leaves pinnate <note>feather-shaped</note> in turn, adhering to one another, not very unlike that which is commonly called Lungwort <note>original: *Pulmonaria*</note>. The second is what they now call Wood-mother <note>original: *Matrisyluam*</note> or Star-herb <note>original: *Stellarem hærbam*</note> everywhere, in German: **Woodruff** <note>original: *Waltmeyster*</note>; although they also commonly call Field-leaf <note>original: *Campifolium*</note> the "Mother of the Woods." The third is Golden Trefoil, [which] the Germans...

192. Simple Medicines

<margin>C</margin> Behold, **Golden Clover** <note>original German: *Guldener Klee*</note>, which grows in forests and rugged places.

## OUR JUDGMENT

I have found only this much regarding Liverwort among the accepted authors that I can remember. The first two [varieties] were missing while we were painting these illustrations <note>original Greek: *eikonas*</note>. We have provided the third. We shall provide the earlier ones in later volumes, if life remains my companion <note>a humble way of saying "if I live long enough to finish this work."</note>. Truly, the first and third varieties do not differ in their descriptions, and they harmonize beautifully with the descriptions of Hermolaus Barbarus and Hieronymus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus was a Venetian scholar who corrected translations of Dioscorides; Hieronymus likely refers to the herbalist Hieronymus Bock.</note>.

## TEMPERAMENT
## from SERAPION
<note>Serapion the Younger was an influential 12th or 13th-century Arabic medical writer whose "Book of Simple Medicaments" was a standard university text.</note>

Its first quality is to dry, and it does so excessively.
The second is to cleanse.
The third is to prevent skin eruptions <note>original: *impetiginem*</note> and any hot swellings <note>term: *apostemata* — inflammatory swellings or abscesses.</note>.

## POWERS AND BENEFITS

A plaster made from it restrains menstruation and settles hot swellings and skin eruptions. It is also very beneficial for swellings of the tongue and all "flows of humors" <note>discharges or weeping wounds</note> because of its drying and astringent <note>original: *stipticitatem*</note> nature.

## From PLATEARIUS
<note>Matthaeus Platearius was a physician from the famous medical school of Salerno; his work focused on the practical application of herbs.</note>

It is effective against blockages <note>original: *opilationem*</note> of the liver and spleen caused by "hot matter," and against heat of the liver.
<margin>D</margin> A syrup made from a decoction of this plant with rhubarb heals jaundice <note>original: *Ictericiam*</note>. And take note that Liverwort should be included in all syrups intended for blockages and overheating of the liver. For hot swellings, it is applied crushed at the very beginning of the ailment. It works by repelling the matter that is flowing into the site.

## From GIOVANNI DA VIGO
<note>Giovanni da Vigo (1450–1525) was the personal surgeon to Pope Julius II and a major authority on wound surgery.</note>

Liverwort is cold and dry in the first degree. Its leaves, crushed and mixed with barley flour in pomegranate wine, along with a little white sandalwood, rose oil, and unripe olive oil <note>original: *omphacino*</note>, disperse and dissolve hot swellings of the liver by repelling them.
A decoction of it made with garden and wild endive, a little Maidenhair fern <note>original: *Capillorum Veneris*</note>, and a little chicory, prepared with water and sugar and a small amount of pomegranate wine, is an excellent remedy for those suffering from a "hot imbalance" <note>term: *dyscrasia* — a medical theory where illness is caused by an imbalance of bodily fluids or "humors."</note> of the liver. It is called "Liverwort" <note>original: *Hepatica*</note> specifically because it so greatly helps with ailments of the liver <note>original: *hepatis*</note>.

## ¶ On Toadflax, Chapter 35 <note>The original uses the term "Rhapsody," a term sometimes used in this period to denote a section or collected discourse.</note>

### ¶ NOMENCLATURE
**Greek:** *peristereon* <note>literally "dove-plant"</note>, *pseudolinon* <note>literally "false flax"</note>.
**Latin:** *Linaria*, *Pseudolinum*, Bastard spurge <note>original: *Esula adulterina*</note>, Urinary herb <note>original: *Herba urinalis*</note>.
**German:** **Toadflax** <note>original: *Lynkraut*</note>, **Urine-herb** <note>original: *Harnkraut*</note>, **Flax-herb** <note>original: *Flachskraut*</note>.

<margin>Dr. Johann Lotzer</margin>
Dr. Johann Lotzer, a physician, in his collections of simple medicines, translated the herb Toadflax as *peristereon* in Greek and *Crista galli* <note>literally "Cock's Comb"</note> in Latin. However, certain species of Verbena also carry that name. I read nothing more among the more reliable authors, except that Pandectarius <note>Mattheus Silvaticus, a 14th-century medical lexicographer</note> and Simon of Genoa <note>Simon Januensis, author of a famous medical dictionary</note> identify this as "false flax" and a type of "bastard spurge," placing it as a middle species between the two. This is because Spurge <note>original: *Esula*</note> produces a milky sap, whereas Toadflax is without milk.

-> Its TEMPERAMENT <-

We have found its temperament to be cold and humid in the second degree. It possesses the power of dissipating, cutting <note>term: *incidendi* — the pharmaceutical property of breaking up or "cutting" through thick, sticky humors</note>, thinning, and expelling.

-> From the HERBALISTS: Its Powers and Benefits are stated as follows. <-

The juice of this plant, as well as the juice of Pimpernel, cools *erysipelas* <note>a painful, red bacterial skin infection</note>.
There is also nothing that heals "cancer" and "carcinomas" <note>term: *carcinomata* — in this period, likely referring to any malignant-looking ulcer or hard swelling</note> quite so well.
<margin>B</margin>
The herb itself, when placed inside one's shoes, is said to suppress and soothe the pains of a suffering body.
Toadflax water, drunk with the inner bark of Dwarf Elder <note>original: *Ebuli*</note> in the quantity of a hazelnut, expels water through the urine in a wonderful manner for those suffering from dropsy <note>edema or swelling caused by fluid retention</note>.
The same water is healthful for reddened eyes when applied moderately, both in the evening and while fasting. This has been frequently confirmed by a great many people.

-> PHARMACOLOGY of SIMPLE MEDICINES <-
# ON SPURGE, Section 39 <note>original: *Rhapsodia*, used here to denote a specific chapter or discourse</note>

### ¶ NOMENCLATURE ¶

**Greek:** *pityousa* <note>original: πιτύουσα</note>.
**Latin:** *Esula*.
**German:** **Wolf's milk** <note>original: *Wolffsmilch*</note>.

<margin>C</margin>
I do not agree with Simon of Genoa <note>a 13th-century physician and medical lexicographer</note>, who denies that this plant should be listed among the seven species of Spurge <note>original: *Tithymalorum*</note>. I believe it to be either the Cypress-leaved Spurge <note>original: *Cyparissiam Tithymalum*</note>, or certainly that *Pityusa* mentioned in Dioscorides' fourth book. This is not merely a suspicion; rather, in a very ancient book by a certain Bolognese physician regarding the simple medicines of Dioscorides, we find it written as follows regarding how it corresponds to our pharmacies: "The Spurge shrub <note>original: *Frutex Tithymalus*</note> is known as Sea Lettuce, or Goat’s Lettuce, and also the Milking-herb. There are many kinds of it: the fruit of one is called the 'vomic nut' <note>term: *vomicam Nucem* — not the modern Strychnine tree, but a purging nut from the spurge family</note> in the pharmacies; another they call the Lesser Spurge <note>original: *Esulam minorem*</note>. They call the *Pityusa* 'Maurisebra,' and the pharmacies also call it the Greater Spurge <note>original: *Esulam maiorem*</note>, which grows everywhere."
     Four differences are observed in it: some are tender, some have a thicker root, some are larger, and some are quite small. However, what is held to be the true Spurge today presents a likeness to the Toadflax herb <note>original: *Linariae herbae*</note>.

### Its Selection according to MESUE <note>Mesue the Younger, an influential but likely pseudonymous Arabic pharmacological authority</note>.

<margin>D</margin>
It is a great evil, as it cuts through the internal organs <note>original: *abscindens viscera*</note>; however, the small variety is what should be chosen. The better part of the plant is the bark of its root, and its milky sap is sharper and stronger. The better root is one that possesses five good properties: its bark is thinner and lighter, it breaks easily, it has a reddish tint (much like *Cassia*), and it is over six months old. If it is fresh—only a month old—it is bad. The black variety is deadly. Likewise, those grown in the locations of hot springs are bad. The best time for collecting the root is the beginning of spring, and for its milk, the end of spring.

### Temperament and Properties.

It is of a hot and dry <term>temperament</term> <note>original: *complexio* — the balance of bodily humors</note> in the beginning of the third degree. Its milky sap is hotter. It is composed of a "fiery" substance that is sharp and thin, and an "earthy" substance that is <term>astringent</term> <note>original: *stiptica* — having a contracting or drying effect</note>. It has the power of cutting <note>term: *incisiuum* — the ability to break up thick humors</note>, thinning, and drying out "submerged" materials <note>likely referring to deep-seated fluids or phlegm</note>; it is also liquefying, opening, and capable of breaking open the mouths of veins.

### CORRECTION of the Harms of Spurge.

IT HARMS THE HEART, liver, and stomach; it breaks veins and flays the bowels; it leaves behind inflammations that cause one to fall into fevers. The first harm feared from it is amended by mixing it with medicines that support the heart, body, and liver. The second and third harms are corrected by improving its quality with binding <note>original: *conglutinando*</note> medicines...

<summary>This page discusses the identification, selection, and properties of Spurge (Esula), debating its classification among the Tithymalus species and quoting Mesue on its dangerous potency. It highlights the herb's "fiery" nature and the necessity of mixing it with other substances to prevent internal damage.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of Esula (Spurge) from the previous page, shifting focus from its botanical identification to its pharmaceutical preparation, dosage, and specific medicinal effects as cited by various medieval and classical authorities.</meta>

...with binding, assisting, and consolidating substances, such as tragacanth <note>original: *dragagantum*; a natural gum used as a stabilizer</note>, various gums, bdellium <note>a semi-transparent oleo-gum resin</note>, psyllium mucilage, purslane juice, and similar things. The fourth type of harm it causes is neutralized by mixing it with certain cooling and "extinguishing" substances. Among those who do this, my preference is for it to be steeped in dandelion juice <note>original: *Altaraxacon*</note>, or in endive juice with a little vinegar, or in the juice of purslane or nightshade <note>original: *Solatri*</note> and vinegar. If it is the vinegar from a decoction or infusion of quinces, it will be even better. Myrobalans <note>plum-like medicinal fruits from India</note> also fix its known beneficial qualities, as do wormwood and aloe. <margin>A</margin> And "The Jew" <note>likely referring to the medieval physician Isaac Israeli</note> said: "Let it be steeped in sweet milk or vinegar; let the milk be renewed in it many times, then let it be dried. For in this way it is restrained from its own malice." And Rufus <note>Rufus of Ephesus, a 1st-century Greek physician</note> said: "If the purging caused by it is excessive or occurs with great difficulty, let the purged person sit in cold water." To me, this also seems an unsuitable statement. For the surrounding cold traps and assists the power of the medicine, strengthening it. Furthermore, it aids the medicine toward the paths of expulsion and repels the matter, as we have made known to you. One must therefore provide aid at that time as we have stated in the *Canon* <note>referring to Avicenna’s *Canon of Medicine*</note>.

### The composition of Alsebram pills, beneficial for dropsy.
Take four parts of prepared spurge, four parts of yellow myrobalans, five parts of aloe; mix them with the juice of fennel or endive. The dose of these is from one and a half drachms up to three. And some people make wafers <note>original: *oblatas*</note> from its milk and flour, and purge with them. And some make a preparation with vinegar, sugar, and its milk. <margin>B</margin> And some make a good purgative with the flesh of quinces and mastic <note>a resin from the terebinth tree</note>.

## POWERS AND BENEFITS.

Through purging, it powerfully draws out phlegm, "yellow water" <note>serous fluid associated with edema</note>, and melancholic humors, as well as matter from the joints, and it assists with their pains. It is one of the great medicines for dropsy <note>term: *hydropoſim* — an old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</note>. Nevertheless, it harms the liver and dries out the body of the person using it. It consumes the sperm, and its milky sap does this even more vehemently. It also causes one to fall into fevers.

## ITS DOSAGE.

Of its root bark: from 2 to 7 carats <note>term: *Caractis* — a small unit of weight used by apothecaries</note>. And of its milk: from one carat up to three.

## USE AND ADMINISTRATION

### Regarding Spurge, from Platearius.
<note>Johannes Platearius was a 12th-century physician from the famous school of Salerno.</note>
Spurge is hot and dry in the third degree. It is a shrub whose root alone is suitable for medicinal use. If its root bark is collected in the spring, it is preserved with great efficacy for two years. However, it is better if it is renewed every year. It possesses the power to purge phlegmatic humors primarily. Therefore, it is effective against ailments arising from phlegm.

Note that it purges jaundice by its sharpness. After Scammony <note>original: *Scamonea*; a potent purgative resin</note>, Spurge is more useful and can be given more safely. For it is not so greatly loathsome that the stomach would, as it were, be offended by it; but if it is, let a warm tile be placed over it.

# SIMPLE Medicines <note>original: *SIMPLICIVM Pharma*</note>

<margin>C</margin> Against a daily fever caused by natural phlegm, joint pain, gout in the feet, gout in the hands, paralysis, the intestinal disease <note>referring to ileus or severe bowel obstruction</note>, and white phlegm <term>leucophlegmatia; a form of dropsy or edema characterized by pale, swollen skin caused by an excess of phlegm</term>, this powder of Petruncellus <note>likely a specific pharmaceutical recipe named after a practitioner</note> should be given. Take 5 scruples <note>a scruple is a small unit of weight, about 1.3 grams</note> of Spurge <note>original: *Esulæ*</note>, and a small amount of cinnamon, fennel seed, anise, and mastic <note>a resin from the mastic tree used to settle the stomach</note>. For those suffering from white phlegm but otherwise healthy, it is effective as a preventative when given with warm wine, warm water, or with a soft-boiled egg in broth, or with a thin soup. The "Blessed Spurge" <note>original: *Benedicta Esulata*; likely a specific refined preparation</note> is effective against the aforementioned conditions, and especially against colic: let it be administered as an enema <note>original: *clystere*</note> with salt water, oil, and honey; this is excellent.

Specifically against white phlegm, the use should be as follows: let fennel juice boil a little, then let it settle; take the clear liquid floating on top, add the powder of Spurge and sugar, and let it be given. Or let a syrup be made; it is very beneficial.

For refined patients <note>original: *Delicatis*; referring to those with sensitive constitutions or a distaste for harsh medicines</note> who loathe medicines, let its powder be placed to cook with meats. Or they may eat the bark <note>the root-bark of the spurge</note> itself and those meats, and drink the broth.

It is effective against the aforementioned ailments if a spiced medicinal wine <note>original: *claretum*</note> is made from its powder, in wine and honey, and other spices. For it is not very unpleasant to take.

The "Theodoric anacardine" <note>a complex medicinal confection containing cashew nuts, named after a famous physician</note> or the "holy electuary" <note>original: *hieralogodion*; a "sacred" purgative medicine</note> are appropriately strengthened by the addition of the aforementioned Spurge.

->FROM GIOVANNI DA VIGO <note>original: *IOANNE VIGONIO*; a famous 16th-century Italian surgeon</note><-

<margin>D</margin> The power of Spurge is to purge black bile <note>original: *Melancholiam*</note> and phlegm. And its milky sap <note>original: *lac*</note> most powerfully removes warts and skin growths <note>original: *porros*; literally "leeks," a term for certain types of warts</note>, drying out their roots.

[of Physicians], VOLUME One. CONCERNING ALL MALLOWS. Rhapsody 35.

<margin>A</margin>
### ¶ Naming of the Garden Mallow.

Greek: *Malache* <note>original: μαλάχη</note>, *Kepete* <note>original: κηπευτή</note>, *Anthema* <note>original: ἄνθεμα</note>.
Latin: Garden Mallow, Goat’s Spleen, Mouse Urine.
Common names: **Mallows** <note>original German: *Pappelen*</note>.

---

## OPINIONS OF AUTHORS concerning Mallows.

### The History of the Garden Mallow from PLINY, Book 20, Chapter 21.

The Mallow is held in great esteem, both the cultivated and the wild varieties. There are two kinds, distinguished by the size of their leaves. The Greeks call the larger cultivated kind *Malope*. The other they call *Malache* <note>from the Greek word *malakos*, meaning soft</note>, because they believe it emollient to the bowels; it is of the wild variety, has a large leaf and a white root, and is called *Althea* <note>Marshmallow</note>. Because of its excellent effects, it is called *Aristalthea* <note>Best Althea</note> by some. They make any soil in which they are planted richer.

### THEOPHRASTUS ON THE MALLOW, which is called Hibiscus, Book 9, Chapter 19.

<margin>B</margin>
They tell of a certain thorn which, when cast into water, causes it to congeal. And they say the root of the Hibiscus can thicken a liquid if you cast it in after it has been ground and place the liquid under the open sky. It is agreed that the Hibiscus has the leaf of a Mallow, though larger and hairier; it has a soft stem, a honey-colored flower, and fruit like a Mallow, being very similar in its stalks. Its use is for ruptures and coughs, taken with sweet wine, and for ulcers when applied in oil.

### APULEIUS on the same plant, Chapter 38.

By the Greeks it is called *Althea*, others call it *Ororiza*, others *Aeleomolochen*, others *Molochen agria* <note>wild mallow</note>, or *Cretican*, others *Anadendramalachen*, others *Sycophyllon* <note>fig-leaf</note>. The Italians call it Hibiscus. It grows in damp places and fields.

### THE SAME AUTHOR on the Wandering Mallow.

The Greeks call it *Malachin agrian*, others *Aeleomolochen*, others *Acopon*, others *Malachin*, others *Helionstrophon* <note>sun-turner</note>, others *Osyriacam*, others the Rural Mallow, and others the Wandering Mallow. It grows everywhere in cultivated places.

### ANOTHER HISTORY OF ALTHEA from Dioscorides, Book 3.

*Althea* <note>Marshmallow</note>, which some call *Althiocon* and others Hibiscus, is of the genus of wild Mallows. It has round leaves like Cyclamen that grow with a downy covering; it has a rose-colored flower, a stem two cubits high <note>about 3 feet</note>, and a tough root that is white inside. It is named *Althea* because it is useful among the first of plants and is powerful in many remedies <note>derived from the Greek *altho*, meaning to heal</note>.

### Concerning that which is called ALCEA, which I believe to be that which is today called Saint Simeon’s herb, commonly **Sigmundts wurtz**. From the same DIOSCORIDES, Book 3.

*Alcea* <note>likely the Vervain Mallow</note> is assigned to the genus of wild Mallows. It has divided leaves, very similar to Vervain; it has three or four stems covered in a hemp-like bark, a small rose-like flower, and five or six white, broad roots, which are at most a cubit long.

<margin>C</margin>
### Opinions of MODERN AUTHORS concerning the aforementioned species of Mallows, and the explanations of the authors. And first, HERMOLAUS BARBARUS in his *Corollarium*.

The Mallow, he says, through the work of cultivation, grows into a tree within six or seven months; its wood is used for spears and walking-staffs in Arabia, and also in Mauritania <note>modern-day Morocco and Algeria</note> at the city of Lixus near the estuary, toward the Gardens of the Hesperides and near the shrine of Hercules. There are two primary genera of them, distinguished by the width of the leaf. The Greeks call the larger cultivated kind *Malache* <note>original: "Malachen"</note>. They believe the other is called *Malache* among the wild varieties from its ability to soften the bowels <note>referring to its laxative properties</note>; it has a large leaf and white roots, and is named *Althea* <note>Marshmallow</note>. There is also one that grows with a single stalk, named *Monocaulos* <note>original: "Monocaulos," meaning single-stemmed</note> from that fact. Every soil in which Mallows are grown becomes richer. Concerning the *Althea*—which is likewise called *Dendromalache* <note>Tree-mallow</note>, or *Anadendromalache* <note>Climbing-tree-mallow</note>, and *Ibiscus*—it is discussed in the third volume. There is also the *Alcea* <note>Hollyhock or Vervain mallow</note>, which is of this general kind and should be noted separately.
<margin>Single-stemmed Mallow.</margin>

#### THE SAME AUTHOR again on the ALTHEA.

<margin>D</margin>
Physicians, by using the name *Althea*, understand it to mean the Wild Mallow, as Theophrastus says. Because of its excellent effects, it is called *Aristalthea* <note>original: "Aristalthea," meaning "Best Althea"</note> by some, and *Anadendromalache* by Galen. Likewise, it is called *Ebiscus* or *Ibiscus*. Although Pliny separated the *Althea* from the *Ibiscus* in medical use. He says the *Ibiscus* differs from the parsnip only in its thinness; it is rejected as food and is useful only for medicine; the Greeks, he says, call it the "wild mallow" <note>original: "μαλάχην ἀγρίαν"</note>, and some call it *Pistolochia*. The leaf of the Althea is described by Theophrastus as being like a Mallow, but larger and hairier; the stems are soft, the flower is yellow <note>original: "luteus"</note>, the root is white and fibrous, the seed is like a Mallow's, and the taste of the stems is also like the Mallow.

### MARCELLUS VERGILIUS’S explanation of the Althea.

To the Greeks, *Althea* is nothing other than if you were to call it a "medicinal plant" simply because of its healing power; for them, *althos* <note>original: "ἄλθος"</note> signifies a medicine, drug, or remedy, and the verb *althainein* <note>original: "ἀλθαίνειν"</note> means to heal. Similarly, in his *Theriaca* <note>a poem on venomous bites</note>, Nicander often calls something *althentha* <note>original: "ἀλθήντα," meaning healing or cured</note>. Palladius testifies in the month of October that this plant is called *Ibiscus*, using these words: "Althea, that is, the leaves of the Ibiscus," etc. And he uses it, to use his own words, so that a strong wine might be made from a weak one. Theophrastus, in the 9th book of his *History of Plants*, confirms that it is a Wild Mallow with these words: "And that which some call Althea, others call the Wild Mallow." Galen called it *Anadendromalache*, as if it were a tree-like or arborescent Mallow. Pliny, in various places in volumes 19, 20, and 21, describes several types of Mallows, but he does not provide a sufficiently certain history of them. We, following the Greeks and especially this writer <note>Theophrastus</note>, have established two principal genera of Mallows, one treated in the second volume and the other in this third volume. We are not unaware that these themselves are divided again by some, and in both genera, the cultivated and the wild-growing are counted. In that former category is the garden mallow, which is used as a vegetable for food, and that which grows in uncultivated places, as we then said at greater length in our commentaries on the Mallow. In this latter category is the wild mallow, which becomes taller than those two in every respect and rises higher from the ground; when planted in gardens, it grows like a tree and produces much larger flowers, no less in circumference than Roses. Nevertheless, those which become better through human skill and labor should not be considered of a different genus for that reason. Theophrastus described this *Althea* in the same book. However, he gave it a yellow flower—something which I have not yet seen in any Mallow flower, nor heard of from others. Nor do we know how that color can correspond to nature or to other writers concerning the Mallow. Nature shows every year in every Mallow a flower shining between red and purple. Here he also says it is *Rhodoides* <note>original: "Rhodoides," meaning rose-like</note>, which means like a Rose; this ought to refer no more to the shape than to the color. Thus, we leave this serious dispute to be settled by those more skilled between Theophrastus and other writers.
<margin>Two types of Mallows.</margin>

# Explanation of the Alcea by HERMOLAUS <margin>A</margin>
# BARBARUS.

The Alcea <note>likely the Hollyhock or Vervain Mallow</note> has leafy stems. It grows in rich, not dry, soil; some also call it *Peristeron* <note>Greek for "pigeon-plant"</note> because of the similarity of its leaves [to a pigeon's foot], as I conjecture. The Greeks also call the Alcea "Lion’s Tail" <margin>Lion’s tail.</margin> <note>original: "Leonis cauda"</note>—a part of the animal where its strength resides—according to the testimony of Homer, Catullus, and Pliny. The difference between the plant and the animal's tail, as some prefer to note, is that the herb's name is spelled without a diphthong in the second-to-last syllable. It is also called *Cercis* <note>original: "Cercis," meaning a weaver's shuttle or a tail</note>. However, there is also another plant called *Cercis* from which weavers' shuttles <margin>Cercis.</margin> are made, which is where it gets its name.

## On the same plant again, MARCELLUS
## VERGILIUS.

The history and medicinal use of this Alcea is brief among the ancient Greek physicians. Pliny treats it no differently than Dioscorides does in Book 27, Chapter 4. We likewise have nothing further to add to their accounts. We only wish to mention that in the oldest Latin manuscripts, this plant was joined to the one preceding it, and both were discussed in a single chapter. Their similar nature seems to have prompted this arrangement.

### Concerning its TEMPERAMENT.

The wild variety possesses a moderate power to disperse and soften <note>referring to its ability to break up blockages and soothe inflammation in the body’s humors</note>. The garden variety, however, contains a somewhat greater amount of watery moisture, and to that extent, its medicinal power is weaker. The "barbarians" <note>a term Renaissance scholars often used for medieval Arabic or non-Classical authors</note> declare it to be cold in the first degree and moist in the second.

## ON THE BENEFITS OF MALLOWS
## and the common Mallow, from Dioscorides, Book 2.

The cultivated variety is far better for eating than the wild one. It is disagreeable to the stomach. It aids the bowels, but the stems do so much more.
<margin>B</margin>
It is useful for the intestines and the bladder.
Raw leaves chewed with a small amount of salt heal *aegilops* <note>an ulcer or fistula in the corner of the eye</note> when combined with honey. However, once the wound begins to scar, the leaves should then be used without salt.
Applied as a poultice, it is effective against the stings of bees and wasps.
Those who rub themselves with the leaves crushed in oil will not be stung.
It heals weeping ulcers on the head and dandruff when applied with urine <note>a common antiseptic and cleansing agent in ancient pharmacology</note>.
For "Sacred Fire" <note>likely erysipelas, a skin infection, or shingles</note> and burns, the boiled and crushed leaves are most usefully applied with oil.
A decoction of the plant softens the womb when used as a sitting-bath.
It is helpful for erosions <note>painful irritations or sores</note> of the bladder, intestines, womb, and rectum when infused as an enema.
The broth of the plant boiled with its root acts as an aid against all poisons, provided it is vomited back up immediately after drinking.
It is a remedy against the bites of venomous spiders <note>original: "phalangiorum," referring to the Phalangium spider</note>.
Drunk in wine, it stimulates milk and semen; with the addition of wild Lotus seed, it eases the torments of the bladder.

## from DIOSCORIDE Book 3.

Boiled in wine or honey-water, it is effective as a drink against wounds,

<header>Simple MEDICINES</header>

<margin>C</margin> [The root] treats parotid swellings <note>inflammation of the glands near the ears</note>, abscesses, breast inflammations, abrasions of the seat, bloating, and stiffness of the nerves. Indeed, it disperses and ripens [infections], causes them to burst, and leads them to the formation of a scar.

When cooked, as has been said, with the addition of pig or goose fat, or turpentine, so that it becomes a supple emollient <note>original: "malagmatis," a softening ointment</note>, it treats inflammations of the womb and blockages when applied as a pessary.

A decoction <note>a concentrated liquor made by boiling</note> performs the same function.
It draws out burdens of the womb and the remains from childbirth.
The juice of the decocted plant drunk with wine aids in difficulty of urination, the pains of those with bladder stones, dysentery, sciatica, tremors, and ruptures <note>likely hernias</note>.
It soothes the pain of teeth when boiled with vinegar and used as a mouthwash.
The green seed, or the dry seed when crushed, improves skin spots <note>original: "vitiligines," white patches on the skin</note> when rubbed on in the sun.
Those rubbed with the same seed and oil are not struck by venomous creatures.
It is effective against dysentery, the spitting of blood, and discharge of the bowels.
Boiled in vinegar-water <note>original: "posca," a common drink of water and soured wine</note> or wine, it is drunk against all the stinging strikes of wasps, bees, and similar insects.
The leaves with a small amount of oil are smeared upon bites and burns.
It is established that water, with the crushed root added, thickens when left under the open sky.

### The BENEFITS of Alcea according to DIOSCORIDES.

<margin>D</margin> The roots drunk with wine or water heal those with dysentery and ruptures.
The Empirics <note>physicians who relied on observation and experience rather than theory</note> use it in an eye-salve; they say that even if it is merely hung from the chest, it benefits those with dimming vision.

## The BENEFITS of All Mallows according to
## PLINY, Book 20, Chapter 21.

This plant has a more effective power against all stinging strikes, especially those of scorpions, wasps, and similar creatures, as well as the shrew-mouse. Furthermore, those rubbed beforehand with it crushed in oil, or those who simply have the plants with them, are not struck. A leaf placed upon scorpions brings on a state of numbness. They are effective against poisons. Applied raw, they draw out all stingers, or when drunk with dill. Indeed, boiled with their own root, they restrain the poisons of the sea hare <note>a type of toxic marine mollusk used in ancient poisons</note>, even, as some say, if the poison is vomited up. <margin>,,</margin> Other wonderful things are passed down concerning them. But most notably, if one daily <margin>,,</margin> swallows half a cup of juice from any of them, one will be free from all diseases. They heal running sores on the head; and when rotted in urine, they heal lichens <note>skin diseases characterized by papules</note> and, with honey, ulcers of the mouth. The decocted root heals dandruff and looseness of the teeth. Regarding the variety that has a single stem, prick the aching tooth with the root until the pain stops. The same root cleanses scrofulous swellings <note>original: "strumas," swellings of the lymph nodes</note>, parotid swellings, and superficial tumors <note>original: "panos"</note>, with the addition of human saliva, without leaving a wound. The seed drunk in black wine frees one from phlegm and nausea. The root assists with ailments of the breasts when bound in black wool. Cooked in milk and taken as a broth, it cures a cough within five days. Sextus Niger says they are useless for the stomach. Olympias of Thebes <note>an ancient Greek writer on medicine and midwifery</note> claims they cause abortions when taken with goose fat. Some say women are purged <note>referring to menstruation</note> by taking a handful of the leaves in oil and wine. <header>First VOLUME of Medicines.</header>

<margin>A</margin>...that the afterbirth <note>original: "uulua," here referring to the placenta</note> may follow. They also give the juice to be drunk by those in labor on an empty stomach, a hemina <note>about half a pint</note> decocted in wine. Furthermore, they tie the crushed seed to the arm of those who cannot contain their genitals <note>likely referring to incontinence or lack of sexual restraint</note>. Indeed, these plants are so born for Venus <note>the goddess of love, implying aphrodisiac qualities</note> that Xenocrates reports that the seed of the single-stalked Mallow, when sprinkled upon the genitals of women, increases desire to an infinite degree. Likewise, three roots tied nearby are most usefully applied for tenesmus <note>the constant urge to evacuate the bowels</note> and those with dysentery. Likewise for ailments of the seat <note>the rectum</note> or if they are bathed. The warm juice is also given to the melancholic in three small cups <note>original: "cyathis"</note>, and to the insane in four. A hemina of the decocted juice is given to those with the falling sickness <note>original: "comitialibus," epilepsy</note>. This is also applied warm for those suffering from bladder stones, flatulence, griping pains, or opisthotonos <note>a condition where the body arches backward due to muscle spasms</note>. For "sacred fires" <note>original: "sacris ignibus," likely erysipelas or shingles</note> and burns, the leaves decocted in oil are applied; and for the onset of wounds, the raw leaves are applied with bread. The juice of the decocted plant benefits the nerves, the bladder, and the gnawings of the intestines. It softens the womb both as food and as an infusion in oil; the juice of the decoction makes the passages of the pores smooth. The root of the Althea <note>Marshmallow</note> is more effective in all the aforementioned cases, especially for convulsions and ruptures. Boiled in water, it binds the bowels. The leaves decocted in white wine and applied as a poultice remove scrofula <note>original: "strumas," swelling of the lymph nodes</note>, parotid swellings <note>inflammation near the ears</note>, inflammations of the breasts, and glandular swellings <note>original: "panos"</note>. These same leaves, when dried and boiled in milk, very quickly cure any pernicious <margin>B</margin> cough. Hippocrates gave the juice of the decocted root to be drunk by the wounded and those thirsty from loss of blood. And he applied it to wounds with honey and resin; likewise he applied it to convulsions, dislocations, swellings, and to muscles, nerves, and joints. He also gave it in wine to be drunk by those with asthma and dysentery. It is a wonder that water, with this root added, thickens and becomes milky when left under the open sky. However, it is more effective the fresher it is.

### FROM JOHN OF VIGO <note>Giovanni da Vigo, a famous 16th-century surgeon</note>.

Mallow boiled in chicken or pullet broth, with barley flour, until it reaches a solid thickness; then pounded with two egg yolks and a sufficient quantity of oil of Violas and a little saffron, mixing all together, heals choleric <note>inflammatory or "hot"</note> and very warm abscesses best, both in resolving them and in ripening them, if nature wishes to attempt maturation.

### FROM PLATEARIUS <note>A 12th-century physician from the School of Salerno</note>.

Against hot abscesses in the beginning, let the leaves of Mallow be crushed and placed upon them. To ripen them, let them be crushed with fresh pig fat <note>original: "assungia"</note> and placed over a warm ruler <note>likely a flat medical instrument or compress</note>. This is also effective against hardness of the spleen and liver.

A fomentation <note>a warm, medicinal soak</note> from the decocted water is effective around the feet.

To provoke sleep in acute fevers, Mallow cooked and eaten loosens the belly.

It is effective in fevers because of constipation of the belly.

From its water, let a suitable softening clyster <note>an enema</note> be made.

A certain experiment to provoke the menses: take its root, about the thickness and length of a finger, or even longer; let it be scraped a little, and let the powder of scammony <note>original: "scamo," a potent purgative resin</note> be sprinkled over it, and then apply it <note>as a pessary</note>; however, smear it first with honey, if you wish.

Marshmallow <note>original: "Maluauiscus"</note> softens and ripens more, whether the leaves alone or, more so, the crushed root.

<header>SIMPLE Medicines</header>

<margin>C</margin>
When mixed with lard <note>original: "assungia"</note>, slightly warmed and applied, it matures abscesses <note>original: "apostemata," inflammatory swellings or boils</note>, relaxes hardness, and softens the skin. The herb also, when cooked with its root until the water is nearly consumed, will produce a certain viscosity; this, when applied, matures abscesses and relaxes and resoftens what is hard.
From the water, with wax and oil added, an excellent ointment is made for the aforementioned conditions.
The water from a decoction of the seeds of this herb is effective against a dry cough.
It benefits those with consumption <note>original: "ethicis," referring to hectic fever or wasting diseases like tuberculosis</note>.
Furthermore, the seeds, when bundled <note>original: "facellata"</note> and cooked in oil, dissolve and soften the hardness of the spleen.

### On the sowing of Mallow, from PALLADIUS, book 10, concerning the month of October.

In this month, Mallow should be sown, so that its height will be restrained by the arrival of winter. It delights in a rich soil and enjoys moisture. Its plants are transplanted with manure once they have begun to have four or five leaves. The plant takes hold better when it is tender; for if it is larger when transplanted, it will wither. Its flavor is better if they are not transplanted; but so they do not quickly rise into a stalk, clods of earth or small stones are placed in the middle of them. It 
<margin>D</margin>
must be planted sparsely. It delights in frequent hoeing. Thus they must be cleared of weeds, so that the roots do not feel any disturbance. If you tie a knot in the root of the plants to be transplanted, they will grow low to the ground <note>original: "sessiles"</note>.

### The PREPARATION of Mallow, from PLATINA, book 8, on Honorable Pleasure.

<margin>Two kinds of Mallow.</margin>
Those who are ignorant of the nature of Mallow will perhaps wonder that I have placed this herb among edible things. But let them cease to wonder and observe with what great praises it is to be extolled. There are two kinds of Mallow, the Garden variety and the Wild, and both are to be praised. That which is called Althea <note>Marshmallow</note> is named so because it rises high <note>original: "quod alte surgat"</note>. They are distinguished by the size of the leaf. The Garden variety is smaller; the Greeks called this *malachē* <note>original: "μαλαχὴν"</note> from its ability to "soften the belly." Every soil in which Mallow is sown becomes rich. This herb is effective against all stinging bites, especially those of scorpions, wasps, bees, and the shrew-mouse <note>original: "muris arachnei," often used for a venomous spider or shrew</note>. Moreover, when crushed with oil and spread upon the skin, it defends a person from the injury of such little beasts. Raw, applied to a wound, it extracts all stingers.
They say a person will lack all diseases if every day they swallow some of the juice of Mallow. This juice is also effective (though somewhat unpleasant for the stomach) against "black bile," especially that which already leads to insanity. The stalk of tender Mallow is boiled with the top removed, and placed in a dish in the manner of asparagus; it is eaten with salt, oil, and vinegar. The flowers are also prepared in the same way. Nor is this type of preparation considered unhealthy, since it cures those with bladder stones, flatulence, griping pains <note>original: "torminibus," or colic</note>, and "sacred fires" <note>original: "sacris ignibus," likely referring to erysipelas or shingles</note>.

# ON CORIANDER
## Discourse 34.
### NOMENCLATURE

**Greek**, *korion, korianon* <note>original: "κόριον, κορίανον"</note>.
**Latin**, *Corium. Corianum. Coriandrum*.
**German**, **Coriander**.

#### On the reasoning for the name of Coriander, by MARCELLO VIRGILIO <note>Marcello Virgilio Adriani (1464–1521) was a Florentine scholar and translator of Dioscorides.</note>.

Some have believed that among the Greeks, bedbugs <note>original: "cimices"</note> gave the name to Coriander, because its leaves and stems smell like them. And since the Greeks call that insect *koris* <note>original: "corin"</note>, they named the plant *korion* because it smells of them. There are others, however—since the Greeks call coriander *korianon* <note>original: "korian"</note> more frequently than *korion* <note>original: "corio"</note>—who wish to say it was named not from bedbugs, but as if it were *koriamblon*, that is, "dulling the pupils of the eyes." For the Greeks likewise call the pupil of the eye *korē* <note>original: "κόρην"</note> and "to dull" *amblynein* <note>original: "ἀμβλύνειν"</note>. How true this might be, the more learned will understand. For [Dioscorides] determines nothing regarding Coriander that specifically pertains to the eyes. Of all its names, the former [*korion*] is more frequent in this and other medical writers. That the latter [*korianon*] was in more common conversational use is indicated by Aristophanes in his play *The Knights*. By whatever name it is called, the plant is known to everyone, and its seed especially; therefore, it need not be discussed further by us. It is enumerated by this same writer in the 6th volume...

<header>Pharmacology of SIMPLES</header>

<margin>C</margin> It is notable among poisons: and is detected especially by its odor, which in its whole body feels similar to living Coriander. Nicander also mentions this in his *Alexipharmaca* <note>A Greek poem on treatments for poisoning</note>, where his commentator says that wild Coriander possesses a poisonous quality; he describes it as having broader and longer leaves, many offshoots, a numerous root, and many flowers. I do not know if this is true: as Pliny testifies in the 20th book, chapter 20, that Coriander is not found among wild plants. We shall have to discuss this again in the sixth book.

### IMAGE <note>original: "Εἰκὼν" (Eikōn)</note> of CORIANDER.

The herb has a rather short root, very fibrous, with many stems and branches, and bare seeds that are firm and long-lasting. It ripens toward the rising of the Dog Star <note>The mid-summer period known as the 'dog days'.</note>.

### On the sowing of Coriander by COLUMELLA, 
### book 12, chapter 3.

Mustard and Coriander, and no less Rocket <note>Eruca</note> and Basil <note>original: "Ozymũ"</note>, once they are sown, remain unmoved in their place; nor is their cultivation anything other than being manured and weeded. They can, however, be sown not only in Autumn, but also in Spring.

### Much the same from PALLADIUS for the month of March.

From this month until the whole of October, Coriander is sown. It loves rich earth, but it also grows in thin soil. Seed is thought to be better the older it is. It delights in moisture. Once well sown, it grows with its scent everywhere. Seed is thought to be better the older it is. <note>The repetition of this sentence appears in the original text.</note>

### On the CONSTITUTION <note>original: "TEMPERAMENTO"</note> of Coriander.

It has a cooling power, as Dioscorides says. To Galen and others, it appears to consist of contrary qualities.

<margin>D</margin>
### Its POWERS and benefits from Dioscorides.

> Applied with bread or polenta, it heals "sacred fires" <note>original: "ignibus sacris" - likely referring to Erysipelas, a bacterial skin infection</note> and creeping ulcers.
>
> It heals night-sores <note>original: "Epinyctidas" - sores that erupt or are most painful at night</note> with honey or raisins, as well as inflammations of the testicles and carbuncles.
>
> With crushed beans, it disperses scrofula <note>original: "strumas" - swelling of the lymph nodes</note> and small tumors.
>
> It expels intestinal worms if the seed is drunk with raisin wine.
>
> It increases the production of semen.
>
> Taken too abundantly, however, it disturbs the mind not without danger. For this reason, continuous and excessive use should be avoided.
>
> The juice applied with white lead <note>original: "cerusa"</note> or litharge <note>original: "spumae argenti" - lead monoxide</note>, as well as vinegar and rose oil, cures burning inflammations of the surface of the skin.

### From PLINY, book 20, chapter 20.

It is effective against one kind of serpent, which he calls the *amphisbaena* <note>A mythical or real snake-like creature capable of moving forward or backward</note>, if it is drunk and applied topically.

It also heals other wounds, night-sores, and pustules when crushed.

Likewise all tumors and collections of fluid with honey or raisins. For "panos" <note>Swelling of the glands</note>, however, it is crushed with vinegar.

The seed drunk with water binds a loose belly <note>diarrhea</note>.

Some order three grains of the seed to be swallowed for tertian fevers <note>A fever that recurs every third day, typically malaria</note> before the onset, or for more to be applied to the forehead.

There are those who believe it is effective to place it under pillows <note>original: "ceruicalibus"</note> before sunrise.

The green herb has great power for cooling burning heats.

<header>Volume One of the MEDICAL WRITINGS.</header>
<sig>s 3</sig>

<margin>A</margin>
It also heals spreading ulcers when applied with honey or raisins. Likewise, it treats the testicles, burns, carbuncles, and ear ailments when mixed with human breast milk, as well as <term>epiphora</term> <note>excessive watering of the eyes</note> and fluxes of the belly and intestines. 
The seed is drunk in water with Rue to treat <term>cholera</term> <note>in this period, refers to acute digestive upset or the purging of bile</note>. 
Taken as a seed with pomegranate juice and oil, it expels intestinal parasites. 
Xenocrates relates a wonder, if it be true: that the menstrual flow is delayed by one day if a woman drinks one grain of the seed; by two days if she drinks two; and for as many days as the number of grains she has taken. Marcus Varro believes that meat can be kept from spoiling in the summer if it is preserved with crushed coriander and vinegar.

## FROM MACER <note>Macer Floridus, a medieval source for herbal lore written in verse</note>.

To drive roundworms and tapeworms from the belly,
It is usually drunk crushed with wine; 
Or inhaled as smoke when mixed with vinegar.

## FROM GIOVANNI DA VIGO <note>A famous 16th-century Italian surgeon</note>.

Some say that Coriander is cold and dry; others, however, say it is hot. It is known to be hot by its effect, because it resolves <term>flatulence</term> <note>original: "ventoſitatem"</note> and <term>scrofula</term> <note>swelling of the lymph nodes, often associated with tuberculosis</note>. On the other hand, they show it to be cold and dry because, when taken after food, it checks the vapors of the meal and prevents them from rising to the head. Therefore, its decoction—made with bean flour, rose oil, and myrtle oil, heated to form a solid plaster—most powerfully resolves hot <term>abscesses</term> <note>original: "apoſtemata"</note> of the testicles by mitigating the pain. 
And its juice, mixed with the juice of Lettuce and Plantain, egg white, and <term>omphacine</term> <note>oil made from unripe olives or grapes</note> rose oil—all beaten together—greatly assists in cases of hot abscesses and <term>erysipelas</term> <note>a bacterial skin infection characterized by large, red, inflamed patches</note>.

## FROM APULEIUS, chapter 108 <note>Referring to the Herbarium of Pseudo-Apuleius</note>.

<margin>B</margin>
So that a woman may give birth quickly, let 11 or 13 grains of coriander seed be tied in a clean linen cloth fresh from the loom; a boy or a virgin girl should hold this against her left thigh near the groin. As soon as the birth has been completed, the remedy must be quickly removed from the boy <note>the person holding it</note> lest the intestines follow out <note>a folkloric warning against uterine prolapse</note>.

### On the HARMFUL EFFECTS of Coriander, from
#### Dioscorides, book six.

Coriander cannot be hidden because of its odor. Swallowed, it roughens the voice and induces a madness similar to drunkenness, accompanied by shameful talkativeness. The odor of Coriander is even felt in the whole body of the person who has swallowed it.

### On its CORRECTION <note>methods to neutralize its harmful effects</note>.

The remedy is, once you have drawn it out of the stomach using Iris oil (in the manner demonstrated elsewhere), to drink pure wine with wormwood; nor is it useful to drink it by itself. To counter Coriander, it is also useful to drink the shells of eggs, crushed and diluted with brine. Indeed, the brine itself may be drunk on its own, as well as the salty broth of chicken or goose, or raisin wine with lupines.

### ON BASIL <note>original: "Ozymo"</note> Rhapsody XXXV.
#### NOMENCLATURES
**Greek**, *okymon* <note>original: ὤκυμον</note>.
**Latin**, *Ozymum*. *Basilicum*.

#### THE OPINIONS OF AUTHORS on Basil.
<margin>On the reasoning behind the name Ozymum: Battista Pio <note>a 15th-century Italian humanist scholar</note> in his commentaries on the "Gardens" of Columella <note>a Roman authority on agriculture</note>.</margin>
One should not read the name as *OCIMA*, but rather *Ozyma*, referring to a fragrant herb suitable for seasonings, which is derived from <term>*ōzein*</term> <note>original: ὤζειν; meaning "to emit a scent" or "to be fragrant"</note>. Basil grows very quickly when sown in gardens; nothing is more prolific than it. They <note>ancient authorities such as Pliny the Elder</note> even instruct that it should be sown with curses and insults, so that it might come forth more abundantly.
