...of the First VOLUME. 207

<margin>A</margin>
...Pliny in his twenty-first book. Likewise Columella in his twelfth book. Around the Ides of May <note>the 15th of May</note>, Basil is sown; when the seed is buried, it is carefully packed down with a small rammer or a roller. For if you leave the earth loose, the plant is often ruined. Persius also writes of this:

> When the slovenly slave-boy sings of Basil. <note>original Latin: "Cum bene discincto cantaverit Ozyma vernæ." From Persius' Satires, suggesting the plant was common or associated with simple garden tasks.</note>

<margin>
Sweet Basil.
Fodder-Basil.
</margin>
Now the error of those must be corrected who think that *Ozymum* <note>Sweet Basil</note> is the same as *Ocimum* <note>a type of fodder crop</note>. It does not matter that Pliny says that "Ocima" come forth quickly. For not everything that happens prosperously or quickly should be called "Ocima." We call *Ozymum* in our common tongue "Basil" <note>original: "Basilicum"</note>; but *Ocimum* is numbered among the fodder plants, being as distant from Sweet Basil as the Hypanis river is from the Eridanus <note>a metaphorical way of saying they are worlds apart</note>. Pliny mentions *Ozymum* in his 21st book among the garden plants, but *Ocimum* in his eighteenth book.

### THE CONTROVERSY CONCERNING BASIL <note>original: "OCIMO"</note> from PLINY'S 20th book, chapter 12.

Chrysippus <note>a Greek Stoic philosopher who also wrote on medicine</note> harshly rebuked Basil, saying it was useless for the stomach, for urine, and for the clarity of the eyes; furthermore, he claimed it caused madness, lethargy <note>original: "lethargos"; a state of deep sleep or coma</note>, and defects of the liver, and that for this reason goats avoided it. He judged that humans should also flee from it. Some add that if it is bruised and covered with a stone, it generates a scorpion. If chewed and placed in the sun, it brings forth worms. Others say that if someone who has eaten Basil is struck by a scorpion, they cannot be healed. Indeed, some report that a handful of Basil bruised with ten sea-crabs or river-crabs will attract all the scorpions from the surrounding area. Diodorus, in his books on empirical medicine, even says that eating Basil produces lice.

<margin>B</margin>
The following age vigorously defended the plant. For they say that goats do eat it, and that no less than Mint and Rue, it heals the stings of land scorpions and the venom of sea-creatures when taken with wine and a little added vinegar. It has also been found by use that for those who are fainting, its scent in vinegar is life-saving. Likewise, it is good for those suffering from lethargy, inflammations, and for cooling the body. It is applied to headaches with rose oil, myrtle oil, or vinegar. It is also applied with wine for watery eyes <note>original: "epiphoris"</note>. It is also useful for the stomach. Taken with vinegar, it dissolves flatulence and belching. Applied externally, it stops the bowels; it also provokes urine, and thus benefits the "royal disease" <note>jaundice</note> and the dropsical <note>those with edema or swelling</note>. Cholera and "distillations" <note>catarrh or runny discharges</note> of the stomach are inhibited by it. Therefore, Philistion even gave it for celiac disease, and Plistonicus gave it boiled for dysentery and colic. Some give it in wine for tenesmus <note>a distressing urge to evacuate the bowels</note> and for those spitting blood. It also dries up the production of milk. It is most useful for the ears of infants, especially when mixed with goose fat. The seed, crushed and drawn into the nostrils, provokes sneezing, and applied to the head, it clears distillations. In food with vinegar, it purges the womb. It removes warts when mixed with shoemaker's ink <note>original: "sutorio atramento"; a substance containing iron sulfate</note>. It stimulates lust; for this reason, it is given to horses and donkeys at the time of breeding.

### CONCERNING THE OTHER BASIL, WHICH IS a type of fodder, from the same PLINY, book 18, chapter 16.

Among the ancients, there was a type of fodder which Cato calls *Ocimum*, which they used to stop the bowels of oxen. It was made from fodder, specifically from a green crop that failed before it froze. Sura Manilius interprets this differently, and records that ten bushels of beans, two of vetch, and as many of bitter vetch were usually mixed and sown on an acre in autumn. It is even better if "Greek oats" are mixed in, whose seed does not fall out. This was called *Ocymum* and was usually sown for the sake of oxen; Varro says it was named for its speed <note>original: "celeritate"</note> of growth, from the Greek word *okys* <note>original: ὠκύς; meaning "swift"</note>.

### THE SAME AUTHOR CONCERNING BASIL <note>original: "OCYMO"</note>, book 19, chapter 7.

Nothing is more prolific than Basil. Since it must be sown with curses and reproaches...

### On its planting, COLUMELLA in his garden.

> Then also, when the fallow land is split and watered,
> Sow the Basil, and press it down with heavy rollers,
> Lest the heat of the loosened dust burn the seedlings,
> Or the tiny flea creeping in bite with its tooth,
> Nor the greedy ant be able to pillage the seeds.
> <note>These lines are from Columella’s "De Re Rustica," Book 10, a poetic guide to gardening. He emphasizes the need to pack the soil tightly to protect the seeds.</note>

# Concerning Basil <note>original Latin: "Ozymo"</note>, certain things most worthy of knowing, from the Corollary of HERMOLAUS BARBARUS.

<margin>Basil.</margin>
Basil <note>original: "Ocimum"</note> bursts from the earth very quickly and flowers bit by bit, unlike other vegetables: specifically, first from the lower part, and finally from the upper. Because of this, it also flowers for a longer time, in the same way as the Bean and the Heliotrope <note>a plant that turns toward the sun</note>. A single thick and quite woody root descends deep into the earth. The others from the sides are slender and long. The seed is covered by a husk. Water is given to Basil at noon, whereas other plants are watered in the morning. It is also said to come forth more maturely if sprinkled with boiling water. It turns white under the Dog Star <note>the hottest period of summer, "canis" or Sirius</note>. There seems to be a difference between *Ocymum* <note>Sweet Basil</note> and *Ocimum* <note>a type of fodder</note>, for the latter was the name given to a certain kind of animal feed and mash. This comes from the word *ocys*, which means "quick," as Varro prefers; or from the fact that it moves the bowels of oxen, and is therefore given to them so they may be purged. For Cato, too, *Ocimum* was a fodder plant, but it actually bound the bowels of his oxen. This was made from the green crop cut before it froze. Although Cato instructs that it should be plucked by hand and not cut with a small sickle, so that the crop might grow back. Sura Manilius interprets this differently, and reports that ten pecks of beans, two of vetch, and the same amount of bitter vetch should be sown per acre: he adds it is better to mix in Greek oats, whose seeds do not fall out, and that these were usually sown in autumn for the sake of the oxen. Among the ancients, this mixture was called *Ocimum*. Regarding Basil, there are some who write that goats reject it and that it causes madness. If crushed and covered with a stone, it is said that a scorpion is born <note>an example of the "spontaneous generation" theory common in Renaissance science</note>. If a handful of it is crushed with ten crabs—either from the sea or the river—all nearby scorpions will gather to it.

<margin>D</margin> [It is said that] in food it produces lice. Others insist that goats do eat it. There is also a Wild Basil, which is different from *Acinos* <note>Mother of Thyme</note>. Although Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician</note> thinks that *Acinos*, just like *Ocimoides*, is called "Wild Basil" <note>original: "Ocimastrum"</note> by the Romans. We must be warned of this: Dioscorides wrote nothing about "Wild Basil," and Pliny wrote nothing about "*Ocimoides*." Martial is said to have written a wonderful thing about Basil: how it produces sometimes purple, sometimes white, and sometimes rose-colored flowers; and if it is sown frequently from that same seed, it is accustomed to turn now into Wild Thyme, now into Water Mint. The more recent Greeks, who wrote on agriculture, call Basil *Basilikon* <note>Royal</note> and *Misodulon* <note>Slave-hater</note>. They proclaim that there is a discord between it and women, such that if it is placed under a pot without a woman knowing it, she will not be able to touch the food until the plant is removed. Perhaps the poet Persius alluded to this in that verse:

<margin>Wild Basil.</margin>

> As long as it does not taste worse than the Panutian nut-shell,
> When she has charmed the Basil away from the slovenly slave.
> <note>original Latin: "Cum bene discincto cantauerit Ocima uernæ." This is a difficult passage from Persius’s Satires; the author here interprets "cantauerit" as "to charm away" or "exclude."</note>

This stands for "sung out," that is, excluded by singing. For both Varro and Plautus, as Nonius says, use "to sing out" <note>original: "Excantare"</note> to mean "to exclude." We read in comedies of a certain little prostitute in Corinth called "Basil": just as another was called *Abrotonum* <note>Southernwood</note>, which was also the name of the mother of Themistocles. Although there are those who write that she was called Euterpe, and another was named Thryallis, another Water Mint <note>Sisymbrium</note>, another Meconis <note>Poppy-like</note>, another Creeping Thyme <note>Herpyllis</note>, and another Myrrine <note>Myrtle</note>.

# Explanation of Basil <note>original: "Ozymi"</note> by MARCELLO VIRGILIO.

To Basil, as well as to many others in the discipline of the countryside and gardens, there is the same fortune and logic as that of human virtue. For it improves through ill-treatment and injury. And just as virtue, buried by some misfortune, or neglected or poorly treated by Princes, loses nothing of its worth, but (as with iron and other metals) shines more and more with long friction and usually emerges more beautiful; so also, by a similar logic, Asparagus comes forth more joyfully when trodden upon. The Crocus <note>Saffron</note> rejoices to be walked on and worn down by the foot, and comes forth more joyfully by being "perished." Celery will never become curly in gardens unless the gardener, when its growth has begun, restrains it by rolling a cylinder over it. While Rue is being planted, those present pursue it with curses: for antiquity believed that this vegetable would not grow with greater goodness in any other way. Basil is of this kind: and it too rejoices, when the seed is buried in the earth, to be diligently stamped down with a small rammer or a roller. For if the gardener leaves the earth loose, the whole thing is very easily corrupted and dies. And—what someone would scarcely believe—when sprinkled with boiling water, it even comes forth more quickly.

->The Pronouncements of the Foreigners regarding Basil <note>original Latin: "Pronunciata Barbarorum de Ozymo." In this context, "Barbarorum" refers to non-Classical authors, particularly the medieval Arabic and Persian physicians whose works were translated into Latin.</note>.<-

### The Judgment of SIMON OF GENOA <note>Simon Genuensis (13th century) was a physician and lexicographer famous for his medical dictionary "Synonyma Medicinae."</note>.

Basil <note>original: "Ozymum"</note>, which is also called *Basilicum*, has many species. For there is the common type, which is found everywhere, with broad leaves. There is also the Clove-scented type <note>original: "Gariofilatum"</note>, with narrower leaves, smelling of small cloves; and the lemon-scented type <note>original: "citratum"</note>, with even broader leaves, having the scent of a citron: which in Arabic is called *Turungen* <note>original: "Turungen," referring to the citron fruit or its scent</note>. Some call it "River-Basil" <note>original: "Fluviate"</note>.

### THE PANDECT-WRITERS <note>Referring to the authors of the "Pandectae Medicinae," a standard medical encyclopedia of the Middle Ages.</note>.

<margin>Curly Basil,
Large Basil.</margin>
One kind of Basil is Clove-scented, one is common, and one is broad-leaved. More than the others, there is one called "Citron-Basil." Clove-scented Basil is that which is praised by authors: the Citron and common types are disparaged. Clove-scented Basil is suitable for medicine, both the herb and the seed: however, when it is simply prescribed in a medicine, the seed ought to be understood, and especially in electuaries <note>medicinal pastes made with honey or syrup</note>: but in ointments and plasters, the herb is understood.

### THE HISTORY OF BASIL FROM
->Serapion, chapter 156.<-

<sig>C</sig>
<margin>Curly Basil</margin>
According to Isaac ben Amram <note>Isaac Ebenamram was a 9th-century Jewish physician in Kairouan</note>, Clove-scented Basil has small leaves, the color of which is between green and greyish-blue: and the scent of this herb is similar to the scent of Cloves: and its stem is four-angled, the color of which is like the color of its leaves: and its seed is very small, black, and is gathered in the month of June.

<margin>Chapter 157.</margin>
The Basil that is not Clove-scented is a small shrub, and has black-colored leaves, similar to the leaves of *Herendarog* <note>likely a Latinization of an Arabic plant name, possibly referring to a species of Nightshade or similar herb</note>, but larger and broader.

Domestic Basil has broad leaves, green four-angled branches: and the color of its flower is white: and its seed is like the seed of [other] Basil, and it is hot and dry in the second degree <note>in Galenic medicine, "degrees" measured the intensity of a plant's qualities on a scale of 1 to 4</note>. It opens blockages of the brain, and provides relief in cases of catarrh <note>excessive buildup of mucus</note>.

### Concerning its TEMPERAMENT.

According to Hippocrates in his book *On the Regimen of Living*, and in book 1 *On the Passions* which happen to the human body externally, it dries, heats, and binds: it is reckoned among those things which strengthen the heart.

### The TEMPERAMENT and its complexion according to
### AVICENNA in his book *On the Powers of the Heart*.

Basil <note>original: "Basilicon"</note> is hot and dry in the first degree. It possesses an aromatic quality and astringency <note>original: "stipticitatem"</note>, along with a subtle nature. Besides these things, there is also a superfluous moisture within it. It gladdens the heart by its very nature: which is aided by its aromatic quality, joined with its astringency and refinement. Ultimately, however, its use for gladdening is not praiseworthy. For the nutritive substance within it is contrary to its medicinal substance. Indeed, the medicinal substance performs the actions mentioned above: but the nutritional part generates turbid and melancholic blood: and that superfluity which is in it furthermore causes bloating in the veins.

### Its powers and benefits according to DIOSCORIDE.

When eaten in excessive amounts, it dulls the sharpness of the eyes.

# MEDICINES of the SIMPLES <note>original Latin: "SIMPLICIVM Pharma." In Renaissance medicine, "Simples" were medicinal plants or substances used on their own rather than in complex mixtures.</note>

<margin>C</margin>
It softens the bowels.
It moves the <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritum," referring to the "vital spirits" or breath believed to circulate through the body to sustain life</note>.
It drives out urine.
It calls forth milk <note>it is a galactagogue, a substance used to increase breast milk production</note>.
However, it is digested with difficulty.
Applied as an ointment with <term>barley meal</term> <note>original: "polline polentæ"</note>, vinegar, and rose oil, it is a help for inflammations of the lungs.
It is beneficial by itself for the stings of the sea-dragon and the scorpion, and with Chian wine for pains of the eyes.
The juice wipes away the dimness of vision.
It dries out <term>distillations</term> <note>original: "destillationes," referring to catarrh, rheum, or fluid discharges from the head</note>.
The seed, when drunk, is suitable for those suffering from madness, for difficulty in urination, and for those who are bloated.
Drawn into the nostrils, it repeatedly provokes sneezing.
The herb itself does the same.
But it is necessary to squeeze the eyes shut when the urge to sneeze strikes.
There are those who believe it should be rejected from food, since when chewed and placed in the sun, it generates little worms.
The Africans <note>original: "Aphri"</note> however add that if those who have eaten Basil <note>original: "Ozymon"</note> are struck by a scorpion, they are tormented by no pain.

### FROM SERAPION <note>Serapion the Younger was a highly influential 13th-century Arabic medical author whose compendium was a standard European textbook.</note>

Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus (c. 850–950), a famous Jewish physician and philosopher whose works were fundamental to medieval medicine</note> said: It benefits a cold stomach and causes coarse food to be digested. And it benefits the liver and the heart.
<margin>D</margin>
Al-Masawaih <note>original: "Alenmesuai," referring to Mesue the Younger, an influential Arabic medical authority</note> said: It opens obstructions of the brain and benefits <term>cardiac distress</term> <note>original: "cardiacæ," which in this era referred to heart palpitations or distress arising from the stomach</note> which arises from phlegm and melancholy.
Sindaxar <note>an Indian physician frequently cited in Arabic medical texts</note> said: It increases the <term>choler</term> <note>original: "choleras," referring to the yellow bile humor</note> and benefits hemorrhoids.
Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alcalamẽ," likely referring to the philosopher and physician Al-Kindi</note> said: It is more temperate than Marjoram, nor is there so much dryness in it.

### FROM PLATEARIUS <note>Matthaeus Platearius was a 12th-century physician from the School of Salerno, known for his work on medicinal plants, "Circa Instans."</note>

It is effective against a flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note> caused by coldness, when taken with a small amount of powdered <term>Acacia</term> <note>a medicinal gum derived from the acacia tree</note>, boiled in rain water, and drunk.
A decoction of the herb itself in water cleanses the <term>matrix</term> <note>original: "matricem," the womb</note> and provokes the menses, especially if a <term>fomentation</term> <note>a warm, moist medicinal application</note> is made from it around the private parts.
Boiled in wine and oil, it does the same.
<margin>Constantine says almost the same things <note>referring to Constantine the African, the monk who translated many Arabic medical texts into Latin</note>.</margin>
Used as a poultice, it is effective against <term>tenesmus</term> <note>original: "tenasmonem," the painful and constant urge to evacuate the bowels</note>.

# May Lily. <note>original German: "Meyenblümlin"</note>

## ON THE LILY OF THE VALLEY, OR THE WILD LILY. Rhapsody XXXVI. <note>The term "Rhapsody" is used here by Brunfels to denote a specific chapter or section of his botanical collection.</note>

### NOMENCLATURE.

In Latin: Lily of the Valleys <note>original: "Lilium Convallium"</note>.
In German: **May-flowers.** <note>original: "Meyblümen"</note>

I read the name "Lily of the Valley" only among the Barbarians <note>In the Renaissance, "Barbarians" usually referred to medieval authors who did not write in the pure classical style of the Greeks or Romans</note>; it is nowhere in the works of Dioscorides <note>The primary ancient Greek authority on medicinal plants</note>, as far as I have observed. For this reason, we have delayed here a while on these common Herbals, until we might learn something more worthy of trust and more certain, either from our own reading or from learned herbalists. For we preferred to frankly admit what we do not know, rather than by a rash daring to innovate anything, or to label it with a private name, for which we did not first have either certain reasons or at least probable conjectures. 

However, to say what I think, it appears to me that there are many species of one kind: the Narcissus, the Flowers of March <note>referring to early spring flowers like violets</note>, those resembling the white Privet <note>original: "alba illa Ligustra"</note>, and the Lily of the Valley—all of the lily kind <note>original: "liliacei generis"</note>. Some are wild, some also domestic, some fragrant, others devoid of scent. One may conjecture this, partly from

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Lily of the Valley (Convallaria majalis) from page 211. <page-num>212</page-num>
<header>Medicines of the SIMPLES <note>A "simple" is a medicinal herb used on its own, rather than as part of a complex mixture.</note></header>

<margin>C</margin>...from the division of Lilies by Theophrastus <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Botany"</note>, a little from the annotations of Marcello Virgilio <note>an Italian humanist scholar known for his 1518 translation of Dioscorides</note>, and from the commentaries of the "barbarians" <note>A term used by Renaissance humanists for medieval scholars who did not write in classical Latin</note>. The physicians whom we have consulted on this matter we found to be more silent than fish. It is a wonder that they promise themselves so much "purple" <note>original: "purpuram," referring to the status and robes of high-ranking academic doctors</note>, and conduct their experiments through deaths, yet remain ignorant of these smallest and most common things of nature.

### On the TEMPERAMENT of the LILY of the Valley.

All affirm it to be of a cold and moist complexion <note>The "complexion" or temperament refers to the balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile</note>, cooling and comforting, much like Violets, Lilies, and Roses.

### ITS POWERS AND BENEFITS.

It strengthens the heart, brain, liver, and the other "spiritual members," as they call them <note>In traditional medicine, the "spiritual members" were the vital organs responsible for the "spirits" or life force</note>. For this reason, it is administered to those with heart trouble, those seized by vertigo, epileptics, those suffering from apoplexy <note>likely referring to strokes</note>, the frenzied, and those frequently prone to fainting.

Likewise for those who suffer from tremors of the heart and stinging pains in the chest <note>original: "praecordiorum," the area around the heart or diaphragm</note>, which also causes the limbs to tremble.

It has also been discovered to close off the passages at the onset of leprosy, so that the evil does not spread further or send its roots deeper.

It suppresses scabies and skin rashes <note>original: "impetiginem"</note> when applied; this should be done several times using the distilled water of the plant.

<margin>D</margin>This same water dulls the stings of venomous and stinging animals—such as wasps, spiders, bees, and others of that kind—so that they do not swell up, if the area is repeatedly smeared with it.

It hastens childbirth and menstruation, but quite gently, and thus without distress.

Eye doctors also use it for inflammations and cloudiness of the eyes.

### WINE OF LILY OF THE VALLEY
#### prepared thus:

Take one measure of the best and most full-bodied old wine, and one pound of Lily of the Valley flowers. When you have placed these in a glass vessel, cook it in the sun for 20 days. Once it has sat in the sun, extract the liquid through an alembic <note>an early chemical distillation apparatus</note>, once and then again. To the extracted liquor, add a small amount of lavender water and some ground pepper. Nothing is more precious than this wine.

It strengthens the brain, prevents apoplexy, settles colic pain, and assists the strength of the heart in a marvelous way.

## Rhapsody XXXVII. <note>In this context, a "rhapsody" refers to a collection of diverse writings or opinions gathered from various classical and medieval authorities on a single subject.</note>

### [NOMENCLATURE of the Greater kind,

## OTHO’S JUDGMENT on Figwort.

<margin>Simon of Genoa.</margin> <note>original: "Simon Ianuenfis." A 13th-century physician and lexicographer known for his medical dictionary.</note>
As for the plant Figwort, which is found in the works of Dioscorides <note>The primary Greek authority on herbal medicine.</note>, while I would not dare to pronounce its identity rashly, its root clearly indicates that it should be classified among the "testicular" and "glandular" plants. However, no description of the "testicular" plants in Dioscorides has yet satisfied me. For this reason, we have delayed following the "Barbarians" <note>A term often used by Renaissance humanists to refer to medieval Arab or Latin scholars who strayed from original Greek texts.</note> for a while, until we might become more certain of its proper name, or until someone else depicts it for us with more certain evidence from the same author. I have observed, however, that there are three types: namely, the Greater, the Lesser, and the Middle. Regarding the Greater kind, Simon of Genoa says this: "Figwort is the name given to a certain herb, or..."

The author, Otho Brunfels, expresses scholarly caution about how these plants align with the ancient botanical descriptions of Dioscorides.</summary>
<keywords>Figwort, Lesser Celandine, Scrophularia, Ficaria, Otho Brunfels, Simon of Genoa, Doctrine of Signatures, botanical nomenclature, Renaissance medicine</keywords>

<header>Pharmacology of SIMPLES</header> <note>original: "S I M P L I C I V M Pharma"; "Simples" are medicines made from a single natural ingredient, usually a plant.</note>

<margin>C</margin>
It is named so because it has certain swellings, like scrofula <note>original: "schrophulas"; referring to the "King's Evil" or tuberculosis of the lymph nodes, which causes neck swellings similar in appearance to the plant's roots.</note>, around its root; or because it is effective at destroying scrofulous sores. It has leaves similar to the Nettle <note>original: "Vrticę"</note>, but larger and somewhat blackish. The whole plant is similar, with one straight stalk, two
<margin>Thousand-ail-herb. Castrangula. Figwort. Dead Nettle.</margin> <note>original: "Millemorbia Caftrangula. Ficaria. Vrtica mortua."</note>
cubits long <note>roughly 3 feet</note>, and blackish seeds at the top. This "Thousand-ail-herb" <note>original: "Millemorbia"</note> is called *Castrangula* by some. It is also called Figwort <note>original: "Ficaria"</note>, and as some would have it, Dead Nettle <note>original: "Vrtica mortua"</note>, because it has leaves like a Nettle but they do not sting.

### PANDECTARIUS on the Lesser Figwort.
<note>Pandectarius refers to Matthaeus Silvaticus, a 14th-century physician known for his encyclopedia of medicinal plants.</note>

<margin>Regarding this, see below under Lesser Celandine, to which it seems related.</margin>
Priest's Testicle <note>original: "Testiculus sacerdotis"</note>, or *Zemac* <note>An Arabic name for the plant</note>, is a herb spread out upon the ground. Its leaves are thick and round. Its flower is saffron-colored. The root is full of small, white tubers resembling testicles. It disappears after the month of May and is seen no more.

### On the Middle Figwort, by HIERONYMUS the herbalist.
<note>Likely referring to Hieronymus Bock (1498–1554), a pioneering German botanist.</note>

Middle Figwort <note>original: "Schrophularia media"</note> grows with thick, round leaves of a sea-green <note>original: "glaucis"</note> color, succulent, with a stalk of one and a half palms' length, and a twisted, knotty root. It is commonly called **Boy’s-herb** <note>original: "Knabenkraut"</note>, **Wound-herb** <note>original: "Wundkraut"</note>, or **Fool's-heal** <note>original: "Gauchheyl"</note> by the Germans—though there is another herb of that same name—or **St. John’s herb** <note>original: "s. Johans kraut"</note>, because it fades away and appears around the Feast of St. John, and then hides itself back in the earth. I would readily believe that empirical healer in this regard. Nevertheless, it does not escape me that others classify this among the Comfreys <note>original: "Consolidas"</note>, and still others among the Purslanes <note>original: "Portulacas"</note>, among whom is our Theobald
<margin>Theobald Fettich.</margin>
Fettich <note>A 16th-century physician and translator of botanical texts.</note>.

### T E M P E R A M E N T.

It has the power of dissolving <note>original: "resoluendi"; referring to the ability to break down tumors or "humors".</note>.
<margin>D</margin>
The Lesser variety is hot and dry, as Vigonius <note>Giovanni de Vigo, an influential Italian surgeon.</note> says.

### B E N E F I T S.

Both the Greater and the Lesser varieties drive away hemorrhoids, whether applied as an ointment or taken as a drink.
The Greater also dispels redness of the face, specifically that which has a certain appearance of leprosy.
The powder of the Greater root, rubbed into honey or mixed with fine wheat flour and a very good old wine, if swallowed and you then lie down in bed, will first draw out sweats, and thereafter [heal] the scrofulous swellings that appear in the neck or in the internal parts of the anus.

### REMEDIES of the Middle Figwort.

The Middle is a wound-healing <note>original: "vulneraria"</note> herb; for it most effectively glues together and heals recent wounds.
Furthermore, its juice stops bleeding.
And if thrown into a pot in which meats are boiling and frying, it causes the cut pieces of meat to grow together <note>A common historical claim illustrating the plant's powerful "astringent" or binding properties.</note>.
Certainly, empirical practitioners use it to constrict the female genitalia, so as to restore virginity to those who have lost it.

## OTHO BRUNFELS.

WE HAD DECIDED right from the very beginning of our work that whatever plants of this kind were unknown to us, and about whose names we were in doubt, we would append to the end of the book. We intended to take up for description only those which were clearly the most common, and therefore also in use in the <term>pharmacies</term> <note>original: "officinis"; the apothecary shops where medicinal "simples" were prepared.</note>. However, it has turned out quite otherwise, and the risks of the undertaking itself have taught us that sometimes one must serve the scene and **"serve the time"** <note>original Greek: "καὶ καιρῷ λατρεύειν" (kai kairō latreuein); a proverb meaning to adapt to circumstances or seize the moment.</note>, as the saying goes. For since the illustrators and wood-carvers were delaying us considerably, we were forced to seize upon whatever was most nearly at hand, lest the presses should meanwhile stand idle. We have therefore presented these plants alone, of which only the German names are known to us, and nothing else. For we were unable to search out the Latin names from either physicians or herbalists—far from being able to identify this plant from Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical authority for 1,500 years.</note> or any of the ancients. We have included them more so that they might fill the space and provide an opportunity for the more learned to deliberate upon them, than...

# ON MAIDENHAIR FERN
## NOMENCLATURE

**Greek**, <term>Adianton</term> <note>original: "ἀδίαντον"; literally "unwetted," because the leaves repel water.</note>. <term>Polytrichon</term> <note>original: "πολύτριχον"; "many-haired."</note>. <term>Trichomanes</term> <note>original: "τριχομανές"; "hair-thin."</note>.
**Latin**, <term>Capillus Veneris</term> <note>"Hair of Venus."</note>. <term>Coriandrum putei</term> <note>"Coriander of the well," referring to its tendency to grow on the damp stones of wells.</note>. <term>Capillus porcinus</term> <note>"Pig's hair."</note>.
**German**, **Maurruten. Steynruten.** <note>Wall-rue and Stone-rue.</note>

---

<margin>B</margin>

## THE TEACHINGS OF THE
### ANCIENT AUTHORS regarding Maidenhair Fern.

## THE DESCRIPTION OF MAIDENHAIR
### fern, from Dioscorides, Book 2.

<term>Adianton</term> bears tiny leaves, similar to Coriander, but serrated. The little stalks upon which they grow shine with a black color, are very thin, and reach a span in height. It has leaves like a fern, but extremely slender, and its root is of no use. It brings forth neither a [main] stalk, nor fruit, nor flower.

## THEOPHRASTUS’S History of Adiantum, Book 7, Chapter 13.

The leaf of the <term>Adiantum</term>—that is, the Maidenhair—never grows wet in water, nor does any moisture stick to it; from this fact the plant received its name <note>The Greek "a-diantos" means "not wetted."</note>. There are two kinds: the White and the Black. Both are useful for preventing hair loss when crushed in oil. They grow mostly in damp places.

## PLINY’S DESCRIPTION OF
### Maidenhair, Book 22, Chapter 21.

There is another miracle regarding the <term>Adiantum</term>. It stays green in summer and does not wither in winter. It rejects water when sprinkled, and when submerged, it remains like a dry thing—such a great separation of moisture is observed. Thus it is named by the Greeks, and is otherwise used as a <term>topiary</term> <note>original: "frutici topiario"; a plant used for ornamental gardening or decorative hedging.</note> plant. Some call it <term>Callitrichon</term> <note>"Beautiful hair."</note>, others <term>Polytrichon</term>; both names come from its effect. For it dyes the hair, and for this purpose it is boiled in wine with celery seed, with a generous amount of oil added, to make the hair curly and thick. Furthermore, it prevents hair from falling out. There are two kinds of it: the whiter, and the blacker which is shorter. The larger one is called <term>Polytrichon</term>, the other <term>Trichomanes</term>. The branches of both shine with a black color, with leaves like a Fern...

[...of the leaves] of which the lower parts are rough and dark, all of them densely packed together from opposite stalks. There is no root; it prefers shady rocks, the damp surfaces of walls, and especially the mouths of caves near springs and dripping stones. This is remarkable, as the plant does not seem to absorb the moisture. It wonderfully expels and breaks up stones <note>Calculi or kidney/bladder stones.</note> from the body, especially the black variety. For this reason, I believe it was called "Saxifrage" (Stone-breaker) by our people, rather than simply because it grows among rocks.

### MARCELLO VIRGILIO’S <note>Marcello Virgilio Adriani (1464–1521) was a Florentine humanist scholar famous for his commentary on the ancient physician Dioscorides.</note>
### Annotation on Maidenhair, and some thoughts 
### on the origin of its name.

Maidenhair fern crowns the inner walls of wells and the edges of springs; as if thirsty, it leans toward the waters it yet hates and rejects. It is like a person who diligently and continuously seeks wealth, yet wretchedly abstains from it once found. Pliny boasts of this as a "miracle" in the plant, as if many other things were not seen everywhere which, through a natural dissociation of bodies, cannot be mixed together no matter what force is applied. From this comes the reason for its name, which Nicander passed down in two small verses in his *Theriaca* <note>An ancient Greek poem about venomous stings and their cures.</note>. It is of this sort: <note>original: "ἀχραὲσ ἐπ' ἀδίαντον ὃν οὐκ ὄμβροιο ῥανέντοσ, λειπαλεῖν πίπτουσα νοτίσ πετάλοισιν ἐφίζει."</note> "Pure Maidenhair, upon which even when the rain descends, the smallest droplet falling from the sky does not settle on the leaves." Theophrastus taught the same in Book 8 of his *History of Plants*: <note>original: "τό τε ἐπὶ τοῦ ἀδιάντου συμβαῖνον, οὐδὲ γὰρ ὑγραίνεται τὸ φύλλον βρεχόμενον, οὐδ' ἐπίδηλόν ἐστὶ, διὰ τό πὼ ὅτιαν μὴ ἐπιμένειν ὅθεν καὶ ἡ προσηγορία."</note> "And this is what happens with Maidenhair: its leaf does not become wet when sprinkled with water, nor does any trace of moisture remain on it. Whence also its name was given." Pliny also writes in Volume 22, Chapter 21: "Another miracle of Maidenhair: it is green in summer, does not wither in winter, rejects water when sprinkled, and when immersed, it remains like something dry; such a dissociation is observed. Hence its name from the Greeks." Among all the Greeks and Latins, there is the same reasoning and opinion regarding the origin of the name. The word itself even indicates it. For <term>Adiantum</term> is nothing other than "that which is not moistened" <note>original: "οὐ διαίνται" (ou diainetai).</note>. Pliny also testified that it is called <term>Polytrichon</term> and <term>Callitrichon</term>, but for different 

<margin>Polytrichon.
Callitrichon.</margin>

reasons. It is called <term>Polytrichon</term> <note>"Many-haired."</note> because it fills in falling hair. It is called <term>Callitrichon</term> <note>"Beautiful-haired."</note> because it dyes the hair and makes it more beautiful; for it has both effects. Theophrastus says nothing more than <note>original: "ᾧ χρήσιμα εἶναι ἀμφότερα πρός ἔκφυσιν κεφαλῆσ τριχῶν ἐν ἐλαίῳ τριβόμενα"</note> "both kinds are useful for the growth of hair on the head when rubbed in with oil." Following these names is <term>Trichomanes</term>, which belongs specifically to the second kind, which we must discuss soon. There follows also a name read equally in all Greek texts, <term>Ebenotrichon</term> <note>"Ebony-hair."</note>. From this, we believe the name used in common speech, **Venus’s Hair** <note>Capillus Veneris.</note>, was formed in Latin. I have not yet found this in the more ancient authors—by which I mean Theophrastus, Pliny, and their contemporaries. Therefore, a suspicion has arisen that "Venus’s Hair" was made from a corruption of that word *Ebenotrichon*. For the Greeks pronounce the syllable "be" as "ve" <note>This refers to the phonetic shift in later Greek where the 'beta' (b) sound became a 'v' sound.</note>. It was an easy slip from hearing *Euenotrichon* to *Veneris trichas*, that is, "Venus’s hair." However, we wish this to be a suspicion, not a decree. Otherwise, the name was made from ebony, which is black in color, and transferred to the black stalks of Maidenhair and Trichomanes. 

<margin>Ebenotri-
chon.</margin>

For *Ebenotrichon* signifies nothing other than "Ebony-hair"—that is, black, and of the color that ebony is. The other names for Maidenhair read in Dioscorides have sufficiently certain causes and origins, and so we leave them. But we must not leave what Theophrastus reported in the same book: <note>original: "γίνονται' αὐτοῦ δύο, τὸ μὲν λευκόν, τὸ δὲ μέλαν... χωρία δὲ φιλεῖ σκιερά."</note> "There are two kinds of it: one white, the other black. Both are useful for growing hair on the head when rubbed in with oil. They grow mostly in watery places, and as many believe, the one called *Trichomanes* works for the dripping of the bladder <note>Strangury, or painful, drop-by-drop urination.</note>. It has a stem similar to the black Maidenhair, with small, very dense leaves growing opposite one another. It has no root and loves shady places." This is the summary of what Theophrastus says for Maidenhair and Trichomanes. These things were rendered by Pliny in almost the same words in the place we mentioned, though they are far different from what Dioscorides teaches. Dioscorides describes Maidenhair with the leaf of Coriander; he does not count any "white" kind among them, but describes both this and *Trichomanes* as having black stalks. But even Theophrastus did not report in what part that kind might be white. Nevertheless, as one may observe from what Theophrastus indicates, the name for the entire genus is Adiantum. It is immediately divided into white and black. They called the white one that which, compared to the other, has whiter leaves. For as far as the stalks are concerned, the whole genus—

--- Page 228 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical discussion of Adiantum (Maidenhair fern), specifically comparing the "black" and "white" varieties. It transitions from classical descriptions (Dioscorides, Pliny) to the opinions of medieval and "modern" (Renaissance-era) authorities like Mesue and Simon of Genoa.</meta>

...the black variety] has black [stems]; however, in the white variety, as the little stalks grow, they become progressively less black, ending in a deep green color at the top. But the more certain distinction is in the leaves: in the black variety, they are smaller, winged <note>pinnate</note>, and arranged in the manner of a Fern; in the white variety, they are like those of Coriander, sprouting at irregular intervals and divided by notches at the tips. Likewise, the white is longer than the black. Following this reasoning, Pliny says, "There are two kinds of it: the whiter, and the blacker and shorter." Some call the shorter one *Polytrichon* <note>Meaning "many-haired."</note>, while others call it *Trichomanes*. This comprises the entire history given by that writer, who first identifies the white kind by the name *Adiantum*, and then the black as *Trichomanes*. 

It is not difficult to find both. However, because the former grows more frequently and possesses the same medicinal powers as the latter, it is better known and in more common use; for this reason, people now generally call it "Venus’s Hair." Anyone who acts as an eyewitness and trusts their own senses will very easily understand everything in Dioscorides. For they will not be able to doubt what are called "leaves like Coriander" in *Adiantum*, and how they are "split at the tip" <note>original: "ἐπ’ ἄκρου ἐσχισμένον"</note>, which other translators have described as "saw-toothed" or "divided at the peaks." Yet, the notches of the leaves are unequal and cut differently than the teeth in a saw; they are not only at the peaks but are divided all around the edges. 

We believe that the statement read in descriptions of *Adiantum*—that it "abounds with leaves similar to a Fern"—was transferred from the description of another genus into the history of this one, and therefore a mark of error has been added to that passage. For this *Adiantum* has nothing similar to a Fern leaf, even if you compare the whole leaves or their individual segments to one another. For that reason, I had intended to leave those two or three words out as useless; however, I have preserved them since they are found in all Greek and Latin manuscripts—especially since Pliny says, "The branches of both shine with a black color and have the leaves of a Fern." Nevertheless, as we pointed out just a moment ago, the leaves of the same plant cannot be compared to both Coriander and a Fern at the same time. 

We suspected, and still suspect, that the first part of this chapter is not complete, and that some words have perished which would have made the history of the whole *Adiantum* more certain. Those fragments which are now read with such uncertainty are the remnants of that original text; being mutilated, they confuse the understanding and force readers to waver in their minds between *Adiantum* and *Trichomanes*. But the history of both is as we said just a little while ago. Ancient medicine always used the name *Adiantum* for this entire genus; it is a word for the whole kind, and the medicinal powers of every *Adiantum* are the same for all purposes. When Paul of Aegina <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note> treated *Adiantum*, he handed down nothing concerning *Trichomanes*, having stated beforehand that it had been covered under *Adiantum*.

<margin>B</margin>
# OPINIONS OF THE MODERN AUTHORS,
# regarding Venus’s Hair.

## MESUE <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (c. 777–857), a Persian or Arab physician whose works were standard in medieval Europe.</note> on Venus’s Hair.

Venus’s Hair is called by some "Hair of the Springs." It is also called "Woodland Man’s Hair." Others call it "Coriander of the Well." It is an herb whose leaves are similar to the leaves of Coriander, green and thin. Its stalk is about medium length, and they are like hog bristles; they are a color between red and black, but declining more toward black, especially near their roots. The further they grow out, the more they lean toward black. They are without flowers, and their place of origin is in springs and in wells.

<margin>Fine Greek [glosses].</margin>
### THE PANDECTS. <note>Referring to the *Pandectae Medicinae*, a medieval medical encyclopedia by Matthaeus Silvaticus.</note>

Stephanus on Venus’s Hair: By the ancients, it was called *Adianthon* or *Polytrichon*, as is clear through Dioscorides and Alexander. Thus all of those—namely Venus’s Hair, *Adianthon*, and *Polytrichon*—are accepted as the same thing. Because all these names that end in *-trichon* sound like "hair": from this, *thrix* in Greek is "hair," and *thrica* is "of hair." Hence *Gallithricum* <note>Commonly identified as Clary Sage.</note>, *Polythrichon*, and *Adianthon* are all the same in their effect.

### SIMON OF GENOA. <note>A 13th-century physician and medical lexicographer.</note>

Modern authors distinguish different herbs by these names: one as Venus’s Hair, another as *Adianthon*, and another as *Adiantum*, although the first three species are very close in their medicinal virtue.

### OUR JUDGMENT.

You see, Reader, that the description of the ancients does not agree with that which the apothecary shops show today...

->PHARMACEUTICAL SIMPLES<-

<margin>C</margin>...Venus’s hair, and therefore the modern writers also say contradictory things: so that we know nothing less today than the true *Adiantum* <note>original: "Adianthon," the Greek name for Maidenhair fern</note>. From this it appears that this "Venus’s Hair" is rather a species of Saxifrage <term>Saxifragia: from the Latin "saxum" (stone) and "frangere" (to break), referring to plants believed to break up kidney stones</term>, as Pliny also suggests, which we gather today from walls and ruins, rather than the true Venus’s hair. Nevertheless, since no other variety was available at hand, we have illustrated the common one until we can demonstrate another.

### SELECTION AND PROOF
### of the better kind, from Mesue.

The better ones are those that have green leaves and are more robust in all parts of the plant. However, those that are thin, common, and leaning toward a yellowish color lack spirit <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to the plant's medicinal potency or "vital force."</note>.

### ITS TEMPERAMENT ACCORDING TO
### Averroes and Galen.

<margin>Galen, Book 6 of *Simple Medicines*, chapter 7.</margin>*Custaralber* <note>original: "Custaralber," a Latinization of the Arabic "Kuzbarat al-bi'r," meaning "Coriander of the Well"</note>, which is Venus’s hair, is said by Galen to be temperate in its primary qualities <note>In Galenic medicine, "temperate" means it is not excessively hot, cold, moist, or dry</note>, although it has many secondary and tertiary actions. Some of these are strengthening and "repelling" <note>reductive of inflammation</note>; some are "dissolving" <note>breaking down morbid humors</note>; some cause hair to grow; some dissolve scrofula <note>swelling of the lymph nodes, often in the neck</note>; and some break up stones.

### ITS POWERS and benefits from DIOSCORIDES.

A decoction of the herb, when drunk, is beneficial for difficulty breathing, for those who are short of breath <note>original: "suspiriosis," referring to asthma or gasping</note>, for the spleen, for those suffering from jaundice <note>original: "felle suffusis," literally "overflowing with bile"</note>, and for difficult urination.
It breaks up stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>.
It stops the bowels <note>treats diarrhea</note>.
<margin>D</margin>It is an aid against the bites of serpents.
It is drunk in wine against stomach fluxes.
It promotes the afterbirth and menstrual flow.
It inhibits the spitting up of blood.
It is applied raw as an ointment against snake bites.
It makes hair grow thick in cases of alopecia.
It disperses scrofulous tumors, scales on the face <note>rashes or dandruff</note>, and running sores of the head when treated with lye <note>a solution of wood ashes used as a cleansing agent</note>.
It holds hair that is falling out when used with ladanum <note>a sticky resin from rockrose</note>, myrtle oil, and lily oil <note>original: "fusino"</note>, or hyssop and wine.
A decoction of it infused with lye and wine performs the same.
It makes quails and roosters more aggressive when added to their feed.
It is sown for the benefit of cattle.
It grows in caves, shady and marshy places, around the spray of walls, and in the hollows of springs.

The drink made from their decoction, when a laxative effect is desired, is approximately one pound.

Venus’s Hair is of a cold and dry tempered nature. # Henbane.

## ¶ Concerning Henbane, Chapter XXXIX. <note>original: "Rhapsodia," used here to denote a specific section or collected account</note>

### ¶ N O M E N C L A T V R E

**Greek:** <term>Hog-bean</term> <note>original: "ὑοσκύαμος" (Hyoskyamos)</note>, <term>Bean of Zeus</term> <note>original: "Διοσκύαμος" (Dioskyamos)</note>, <term>Python-plant</term> <note>original: "πυθώνιον" (Pythonion), likely referring to the plant's association with the prophetic trances of the Pythia at Delphi</note>, <term>Sleep-inducer</term> <note>original: "ὑπνοτικός" (Hypnotikos)</note>.
**Latin:** <term>Henbane</term> <note>original: "Hyoscyamus"</note>, <term>Herb of Apollo</term> <note>original: "Herba Apollinaris"</note>, <term>Hog-bean</term> <note>original: "Faba suilla"</note>.

--- Page 232 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Henbane (Hyoscyamus) from page 224, specifically focusing on its etymology, the botanical descriptions provided by Dioscorides, the methods for collecting its juice, and its specific medical applications for pain and swelling.</meta>

...of Simples, VOLUME One.
<u>u</u>

<margin>
A
</margin>
The Greeks seem to have called it <term>Hyoscyamon</term> <note>original: "Hyoscyamon"</note>, which means <term>Hog-bean</term> <note>original: "Faba suilla"</note>, for the reason that, as Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 2nd-century Roman author and teacher of rhetoric</note> says, boars are weakened and seized with convulsions by eating this herb. But they know the remedy: they immediately go to the water and hunt for crabs, and thus are straightway restored to health.

<gloss>There are</gloss> varieties of Henbane according to **DIOSCORIDES** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> in his fourth book.

It is a shrubby plant sending forth thick stalks and broad, oblong, divided, black, and hairy leaves. The flowers come out from the side of the stalk in order, like the <term>blossoms of pomegranates</term> <note>original: "punicorum Cytini"</note>, with little cups full of seeds, like those of the Poppy. There are three different kinds. One has a black seed, with flowers that are almost purple and resemble bindweed, with very hard and thorny leaves like the <term>Cytisus</term>. The second has a yellowish seed, like <term>Hedge-mustard</term> <note>original: "Irionis"</note>. Its flowers are yellow, and its leaves and pods are simpler. Both of these produce madness and a deep stupor. Therefore, they are condemned for common use. The third kind, because it is the mildest, has been accepted by physicians; it is fatty, downy, soft, with white flowers and seeds, growing in coastal areas and amidst ruins. When this is lacking, the reddish variety ought to be used. The black variety is rejected as the worst.

->On its COLLECTION and USE.<-

<margin>
B
</margin>
The juice is collected from the tender seeds, leaves, and small stalks. For this purpose, everything is pounded together, and the expressed juice is dried in the sun. However, it lasts for only one year, for it putrefies very easily. The juice is also collected specifically from the seeds when they are already dry; hot water is poured over them while they are being pounded, and then everything is crushed and pressed. Moreover, this expressed juice is more harmless than the former one, and more effective at driving away pain by inducing sleep. The leaves themselves are also pounded, and after sprinkling in flour made from <term>spring wheat</term> <note>original: "trimeſtri tritico," literally "three-month wheat"</note>, they are formed into <term>lozenges</term> <note>original: "pastillos"</note>, and once formed, they are preserved.

->On its TEMPERAMENT.<-

Both the flower and the seed of the white variety are of the third order of <term>cooling</term> substances, and of the second order of <term>drying</term> ones. <note>In Galenic medicine, "degrees" or "orders" measured the potency of a drug's effect on the four bodily humors.</note>

->POWERS AND BENEFITS<-

That juice is useful for driving away pain by inducing sleep.
It is also useful against sharp and hot <term>rheums</term> <note>inflammations or discharges</note> in the eyes, earaches, and ailments of the female parts.
With flour or barley-meal, it is used against <term>gout</term> <note>original: "podagras"</note>.
Applied in the manner of a plaster, it soothes eye pains.
The seed also serves the same purposes.
It is usefully mixed with other things that are prepared as poultices to drive away pain by sleep.
Moreover, the fresh leaves, applied as a plaster, kill all pains more effectively than all other remedies.
With its root, teeth are usefully rinsed when in pain, after it has been boiled and held in the mouth.
It wonderfully mitigates earache.
It easily dispels and calms all tumors of the feet, groins, testicles, the pubic region, and the thighs.

## The HARMFUL EFFECTS of the same herb, from Dioscorides,
## Book Six.

<margin>C</margin>
If the <term>Apollinaris herb</term> <note>Another name for Henbane, often associated with the god Apollo due to its use in oracles</note> is consumed in food or taken in drink, it causes a madness similar to drunkenness.

They report, furthermore, that if someone has an ulcer in the large intestine, which he calls the <term>Colon</term>, and should infuse the herb into it by means of a <term>clyster</term> <note>An enema; a liquid injected into the rectum for medicinal purposes</note>, the same insanity occurs.

## R E M E D I E S.

Those suffering from the effects of this herb are helped by <term>aqua mulsa</term> <note>Honey-water</note> and milk, especially donkey milk; but if that is not available, goat or cow milk. Pine nuts or cucumber seeds taken with <term>passum</term> <note>A sweet wine made from dried raisins</note> are also beneficial.

Furthermore, salty wine is given with fresh pig fat and raisin wine.

Likewise, nettle seed, chicory, mustard, watercress, radishes, onions, and garlic—each taken with wine—are useful.

Rest must also be ordered for these patients, so that they may digest the wine they have drunk through sleep.

## FROM PLATEARIUS.

<note>Matthaeus Platearius was a 12th-century physician from the famous medical school at Salerno.</note>

Observe that when Henbane is found in a prescription intended to be taken by mouth, the seed must be used; if it is for external use, the herb itself. However, the seeds possess greater efficacy.

To induce sleep in an acute illness, use it in this way: make a <term>fomentation</term> <note>A warm, medicinal soak or compress</note> from the water in which that herb was boiled, applied around the feet, forehead, and temples; but perform a washing first. Afterward, make this plaster: mix its finely ground seeds with egg white, <term>woman's milk</term> <note>A common ingredient in historical medicine for its perceived soothing properties</note>, and prepare it with a little vinegar, and apply it to the forehead and temples.

<margin>D</margin>
To check <gloss>excessive</gloss> tears, the same plaster works when mixed with a little <term>olibanum</term> <note>Frankincense</note>.

Against <term>hot abscesses</term> <note>original: "calida apostemata," referring to inflamed, red, or feverish swellings</note>, at the beginning, make a plaster from the crushed herb itself and place it over the area, or use its seed and oil of roses.

Against <term>dysuria</term> <note>Painful or difficult urination</note>, make a plaster from its seed, egg white, and a little vinegar; place it over the <term>pecten</term> <note>The pubic region</note> and the kidneys.

For sudden pain arising from "hot matter," this is a quick remedy: the herb itself, slightly crushed and applied, takes away the pain.

<margin>Proven Remedy</margin>
For toothache, the seed is placed upon hot coals so that the patient may receive the smoke through the mouth, specifically through a reed; afterward, the teeth are washed with water.

The seed itself may be preserved for up to ten years.

## A U T H O R S.

->Dioscorides, books four and six.<-

### Pennyroyal.

### On PENNYROYAL, Rhapsody 41.
<note>The term "rhapsody" here refers to a gathered collection of writings or a specific chapter in this botanical compendium.</note>

### ¶ NOMENCLATURE

Greek: *glēchōn*, *glisophris*, *blēchron*.
Latin: *Pulegium*.
German: **Poleyen.**

Pennyroyal was once a common food used by the ancients for the sake of health; for this reason, it was preserved in salt, in the manner of other <term>pickled preserves</term> <note>original: "salgamorum"</note>, as <term>Columella</term> <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a Roman writer on agriculture from the 1st century AD</note> notes in the final part of his work. It is a well-known herb everywhere.

### The Corollary of HERMOLAUS BARBARUS on Pennyroyal.
<note>Hermolaus Barbarus was a 15th-century Italian scholar famous for his "Corollaries," or additions, to the works of Pliny the Elder and Dioscorides.</note>

Pennyroyal sprouts and reflourishes in the <term>larders</term> <note>original: "carnarijs," literally meat-storage areas or meat-hooks</note> on the very day of the winter solstice. This happens even if the small branches have been separated from the parent plant, much like the <term>Squill</term> <note>A bulbous plant known for its hardiness</note>. It also grows without being sown. However, once it has been sown, it lasts for a long time. There is a great kinship between <term>Catmint</term> <note>original: "Nepeta"</note>, Mint, and Pennyroyal. The "female" variety is more effective and has a purple flower; the "male" variety has a white flower. When burned fresh, both kill fleas: this is why it is called <term>Pulegium</term> <note>The name is derived from the Latin "pulex," meaning flea</note>. It is also considered...

# PHARMACOLOGY of Simples
<note>original: "SIMPLICIVM Pharma" — "Simples" are medicinal plants used on their own rather than in complex mixtures.</note>

<margin>C</margin>Wild Pennyroyal is similar to Oregano, but with smaller leaves than the cultivated variety; some call it **Dittany**, though this name arose by chance from those who call Cretan Dittany "Wild Pennyroyal." The Greeks call Pennyroyal *glēchōn*, and in the Attic dialect *blēchōn*, though they also say *blēchron*, as Dioscorides mentions. I see in Galen's writings that Hippocrates used the word *blēchron* to refer to a certain type of legume. Pennyroyal, as I have said, can be called a "winter solstice herb," just as others are called "summer solstice herbs." Pliny says that **Condurdon** is a summer solstice herb with a red flower which, when hung around the neck, shrinks <term>scrofula</term> <note>original: "strumas" — swellings of the lymph nodes, often associated with tuberculosis</note>. Plautus also writes in his play *Pseudolus*:
"I was like a summer herb for a little while,
Suddenly I sprouted, and just as suddenly I withered."

## The Temperament of PENNYROYAL.

It heats, thins, and powerfully <term>concocts</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, "concoction" is the process where the body's heat "ripens" or breaks down harmful humors.</note>. Because of this, it makes it easy to spit up moist, thick, and sticky humors from the chest and lungs.

### Its POWERS and benefits according to DIOSCORIDE, book three.

It brings down the menses, the afterbirth, and expelled fetuses.
When drunk with honey and aloes, it clears out ailments of the lungs.
It provides relief to those suffering from convulsions.
Mixed with <term>posca</term> <note>A common Roman drink made of vinegar, water, and sometimes herbs.</note>, it soothes nausea and stomach cramps.
It drives out "black bile" through the bowels.
It is most useful when drunk in wine against the bites of serpents.
When held to the nostrils with vinegar, it revives those who have fainted.
The ash of the dried plant strengthens the gums.
Applied as a poultice with pearl barley, it calms all inflammations.
<margin>D</margin>Applied by itself, it assists those with gout, provided it is left on until the area turns red.
Mixed with a wax salve, it clears up pimples.
It is a useful application for those with spleen issues when mixed with salt.
A decoction of it soothes itching when used as a wash.
It corrects a displaced womb.
It is suitably added to warm baths for cases of swelling or hardening of the womb.

### From PLINY, book 20, chapter 12.

There is a great kinship between Pennyroyal and Mint for reviving those who have fainted; for this purpose, sprigs of both are placed into glass bottles of vinegar.
For this reason, a crown made of Pennyroyal is declared more worthy for dizziness in our chambers than one made of Roses.
For it is also said to relieve headaches when applied.
Furthermore, it is handed down that its scent protects the head against the injuries of cold or heat, and against thirst; they say that those who keep two sprigs of Pennyroyal behind their ears while in the sun do not suffer from the heat.
It is also applied for pains with pearl barley and vinegar.
<margin>On the female Pennyroyal.</margin>The female plant is more effective. This one has a purple flower; the male has a white one.
When drunk in cold water with salt and pearl barley, it stops nausea.
It acts the same way for pains of the chest and belly.
Moreover, taken in water, it stops gnawing pains of the stomach, and with vinegar and pearl barley, it stops vomiting.
Boiled with honey and <term>nitre</term> <note>A naturally occurring mineral salt, likely potassium nitrate or sodium carbonate.</note>, it heals intestinal ailments.
It provokes urine when taken in wine—especially if it is <term>Aminaean wine</term> <note>A highly prized vintage in Ancient Rome, known for its strength and quality.</note>—and expels stones and all internal pains.

...of the [Medical] VOLUME One.
<note>original: "corum T O M V S Primus"</note>

<margin>A</margin>
When taken with honey and vinegar, it settles the menses and the afterbirth. It corrects a displaced or turned womb. It expels a dead fetus.
For those who have lost their speech, the seed is held to the nose to be smelled.
For those with the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>, a measure of one <term>cyathus</term> <note>about 1.5 ounces</note> is given in vinegar.
If unhealthy water must be drunk, the herb is crushed and sprinkled into it.
It reduces the saltiness of the body if administered with wine.
For nerve conditions and in cases of <term>opisthotonos</term> <note>a severe muscle spasm where the body bows backward</note>, it is rubbed on with salt, vinegar, and honey.
A decoction is drunk for the bites of serpents; for scorpion stings, it is crushed with wine—especially the variety that grows in dry places.
It is considered effective for mouth ulcers and for a cough.
The scent of the fresh flower, when burned, kills fleas.
Xenocrates records among his remedies that a sprig of Pennyroyal wrapped in wool should be given to be smelled before the onset of tertian fevers, or placed under the bedcovers so the patient is positioned over it.

### Remedies for Wild Pennyroyal from the same PLINY.

The wild variety has the same power but is more effective. It is similar to Oregano, though with smaller leaves than the cultivated kind; some call it **Dittany**. When tasted by sheep and goats, it provokes a bleating. Because of this, some Greeks, changing the letters, called it *Blechon* <note>original: "Blechon" — a play on the Greek word blēchē, meaning the bleating of sheep</note>. Its nature is so burning that it blisters the skin where it is applied. For coughs and chills, it is best to rub it on before bathing and before the shivering fit of a fever begins. It is wonderfully helpful for convulsions, griping pains in the bowels, and gout. For liver patients,

<margin>B</margin>
it is given to drink with honey and salt. It makes lung ailments more bearable <note>original: "execrabilia facit" — literally 'detestable', implying the herb helps the body reject or expel the corruption in the lungs</note>. It is useful for the spleen when taken with salt, and for the bladder, shortness of breath, and bloating when the juice is boiled down in equal parts. It also corrects the womb. It is especially effective against every kind of bite. The root is used against spreading ulcers. Fresh, it is most powerful; however, when dried, it brings a healthy appearance to scars. Similarly, Pennyroyal is closely related to Catnip <note>original: "Nepetae"</note>.

### FROM PLATEARIUS.

Pennyroyal is hot and dry in the third degree. It is collected at the time of flowering and may be kept for two years. The leaves and flowers are used in medicines, while the stems are discarded.
It is effective against "cold rheum" <note>an excess of cold phlegm or mucus</note> when a poultice for the head is made from Pennyroyal.
A gargle made from a vinegar decoction of Pennyroyal and dried figs dries out the moisture of the <term>uvula</term> and the gums.
A wine made from a decoction of the herb and dried figs is effective against a cold cough caused by sticky or watery humors.
This wine also works for pain of the stomach and intestines caused by a "cold" cause. A plaster of the herb boiled in wine works in a similar way.
A <term>fomentation</term> <note>a warm, medicated soak or compress</note> made from its decoction-water dries the moisture of the matrix <note>the womb</note> and wonderfully tightens the womb. The women of Salerno <note>The "Mulieres Salernitanae" were famous female medical practitioners and midwives from the medical school at Salerno</note> use this fomentation.

# ON CATAPUCIA,
## Section XLI.
<note>original: "Rhapfodia XLI." — here used to denote a specific entry or chapter in the compilation.</note>

### NAMES
**Greek**, *lathyris* <note>original: "λαθυρίς"</note>.
**Latin**, *Catapucia*. *Lathyris*. *Granum regis* <note>King’s grain</note>. *Sponsa solis* <note>Bride of the sun</note>.
**German**, **Sprinckkörner** <note>Jumping seeds, referring to the way the pods burst</note>. **Scheyſſkörner** <note>Shitting seeds, referring to its potent laxative effect</note>.

---

->PANDOLFO COLLENUCCIO on<-
->Catapucia.<-

<margin>C</margin>
Catapucia is a herb that common people nowadays call sometimes *Cazzapuzola*, and sometimes *Guardalhorto* <note>literally "Garden-watcher"</note>. However, its proper name is *Lathyris*, about which Dioscorides wrote in his fourth volume and Pliny in his twenty-seventh, describing both its powers and its form.

---

->The Description of Catapucia from Dioscorides,<-
->book four.<-

<margin>D</margin>
**L**athyris, which some call *Tithymalus* <note>Spurge</note> and classify among the varieties of spurge, produces a hollow stem a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> in height and as thick as a finger. At the top, "wings" and oblong leaves grow on the stem, very similar to almond leaves but wider and smoother. Those which appear on the topmost branches are seen to be smaller, shaped like *Aristolochia* <note>Birthwort</note> or long ivy. At the summit, it bears fruit on the highest shoots, notable for its three-part seed pod; it is round like a caper, containing seeds separated by membranes. These seeds are larger than bitter vetch, round, and when stripped of their husks, they are white and sweet to the taste. The root has no use. The whole shrub is full of milky sap, just like the *Tithymalus*. Six or seven seeds taken as a pill <note>original: "catapotio"</note>, or with figs or dates, purge the bowels. However, cold water must be sipped afterward. They draw out bile, phlegm, and fluids. The juice, collected in the same manner as spurge juice, provides the same effect. The leaves are boiled in chicken broth or with vegetables for the same purposes.

# ON CINQUEFOIL
## Section XLII.

### NAMES.

<margin>A</margin>
**Greek**, *pentaphyllon* <note>original: "πεντάφυλλον" — literally "five leaves"</note>.

**Latin**, *Quinquefolium*. *Pentaphyllon*. *Mercurij Herba* <note>Herb of Mercury</note>. *Pentadactylus* <note>Five-fingered</note>.

**German**, **Fünffingerkraut** <note>Five-finger herb</note>.

<margin>B</margin>
### THE OPINIONS OF THE AUTHORS,
### regarding Cinquefoil.

#### THE ACCOUNT OF DIOSCORIDES,
#### regarding Cinquefoil.

It bears thin, forked branches a palm <note>about 3–4 inches</note> in height, upon which the seed is found. The leaves are like those of Mint, five to each stalk—rarely more—and saw-toothed around the edges. The flower is a pale yellow, sometimes rivaling the color of gold. It grows in moist places and by irrigation channels. It has a reddish, oblong root, thicker than that of Black Hellebore <note>original: "Veratro nigro"</note>.

#### THEOPHRASTUS’S 
#### account of Cinquefoil, from book nine, chapter fourteen.

<margin>
See above on folio 86, how all these details correspond to Tormentil <note>A related plant in the rose family, often used for its astringent properties</note>.
</margin>
The root of Cinquefoil, or *Quinquepeta*—for it is also called by this name—is red when it is dug up, but as it dries, it turns black and becomes squared in shape. It has a leaf like that of a Grapevine, but very small and similar in color to the vine; it grows and withers away along with the Vine. There are always five leaves, which is the source of its name. It sends out very thin stalks and is made up of frequent joints.

S I M P L E Medicines

<margin>C</margin>
## PLINY ON CINQUEFOIL
## Book 25, Chapter 9.

Cinquefoil <note>original: "Quinquefolium"</note> is known to everyone, especially since it is also recommended for the production of strawberries. The Greeks call it *Pentapetes*, *Chamaezeleon*, or *Pentaphyllon* <note>original: "πεντάφυλλον" — meaning "five leaves"</note>. When it is dug up, it has a red root; as this dries, it turns black and becomes angular. It takes its name from the number of its leaves, and the plant itself begins and ends its growing season along with the grapevine.

### THE ACCOUNT OF APULEIUS regarding the same.

The Greeks call it *Pentaphyllon*, others *Pentapetes*, and the Italians *Quinquefolium*. It grows in meadows that are cultivated and clean; it has a harsh taste and a soft, milky sap. The leaves resemble Mint, most often five to a stalk. It has a pale flower and a long, somewhat reddish root.

### OUR JUDGMENT.

You see that Theophrastus, Pliny, and Apuleius conflict with one another, and consequently, the apothecary shops <note>original: "officinas"</note> today disagree with each of them, making it inevitable that some have fallen into error here. Who they might be can easily be judged from the controversy between Nicolaus Leonicenus and Pandolfo Collenuccio, which we have set out below. You may judge for yourself to whom the prize <note>original: "palma" — literally the palm of victory</note> is owed.

### THE JUDGMENT OF NICOLAUS LEONICENUS,
### regarding that passage of Pliny where he describes Cinquefoil.

<margin>D</margin>
By a similar error, Pliny took Cinquefoil and the herb that bears strawberries to be the same thing, and he decided that the characteristics and powers of the strawberry plant should be attributed to Cinquefoil, in addition to the name of Cinquefoil. Thus, in Book 25, he reported concerning Cinquefoil: "Cinquefoil is known to everyone, since it is also recommended for the production of strawberries." Nevertheless, I would think that in such a well-known matter, the error belongs to the manuscript <note>original: "codicis"</note> rather than Pliny, and that "Trefoil" <note>original: "Trifolium" — three-leaved plant</note> ought to be read instead of "Cinquefoil." For the herb that is recommended for producing strawberries, and which is known to everyone, does not consist of five leaves, but of three. This is true unless Pliny later added other Greek names and introduced other signs that belong to no other herb than Cinquefoil.

### THE DEFENSE OF PLINY BY P. COLLENUCCIO.

<margin>
Crowfoot is Cinquefoil to Leonicenus.
</margin>
No one will deny that we defended Pliny excellently regarding the Heliotrope, where we attributed the fault of a single word that disturbed everything to the manuscript—as was proper—and not to Pliny. Indeed, Nicolaus [Leonicenus] was prepared to excuse Pliny using the same argument regarding Cinquefoil, as he says himself, had he not been such an overly delicate critic; because everything did not correspond to the number [of leaves] in the opinion he had formed about Cinquefoil, he did not consider himself satisfied. But in this case, he himself seems to be the first to err in excusing Pliny, just as he always does in accusing him. I shall make this clear regarding this Cinquefoil of which we treat. Leonicenus believed Pliny erred most in saying that the Cinquefoil herb also bears strawberries. "For the herb that bears strawberries," he says, "consists not of five, but of three leaves." But it is necessary to know above all else that Leonicenus is entangled in a triple error. First, because he thinks that Cinquefoil is that plant which is seen everywhere in gardens, at the edges of fields, and along paths and ways, which is commonly called both Cinquefoil and Crowfoot <note>original: "Pes Coruinus" — likely a species of Ranunculus</note>. It is well known to many that he affirmed this to be the Cinquefoil of which the ancient physicians spoke, when by chance the conversation turned to our defense and his accusation. He even pulled a small branch from the earth (for the matter took place in a garden), showed it, and said that it was the Cinquefoil in which Pliny had so evidently erred. Secondly, because through lack of experience he believed no herb bears strawberries except that which has three leaves, which was better accustomed to be called Trefoil, and which the learned and common people alike know and call the Strawberry plant <note>original: "Fragaria"</note>. Thirdly, because he seems to have poorly understood what a leaf is, or in what way it ought to be understood in the description of this most healthy herb. Add, if you please, a fourth [error]...
