<meta>This page continues the scholarly investigation into the plant Cinquefoil, specifically addressing the botanical disagreements between the ancient authorities Pliny, Dioscorides, and Theophrastus, and the Renaissance critic Nicolaus Leonicenus.</meta>

[...of Doctors], VOLUME One.

<margin>A</margin>
...and he himself <note>referring to Nicolaus Leonicenus</note> picks at even the smallest details in Pliny) because Leonicenus unskilfully calls these fruits "fragra" rather than "fraga" <note>original: "fraga" — strawberries; Leonicenus apparently used a non-standard spelling</note>, whether they belong to the Five-leafed or Three-leafed plant (as Virgil always does, and our own Maro in his *Palaemon*). Once we have examined what Theophrastus, then Dioscorides, and finally Pliny said about the Five-leafed plant, we shall show both that Pliny is a true authority and that Leonicenus is a slanderer.

The root of Cinquefoil, or Five-feathers <note>original: "Quinquepennæ"</note> (Theophrastus says in Book 9), is red when it is dug up; but as it dries, it turns black and becomes square-shaped. It has a leaf like a Grapevine, but very small, and it is similar in color to the vine; it grows and withers away along with the Grapevine. All the leaves are in fives, which is the source of its name. But in his fourth book, Dioscorides enumerates many names for *Pentaphyllon* <note>Greek: πεντάφυλλον — "five-leaf"</note>, among which are *Pentadactylon* <note>Greek: πενταδάκτυλον — "five-fingered"</note>, *Pseudofelinon* <note>Greek: ψευδοσέλινον — "false celery"</note>, and *Quinquefolium* <note>Latin: "five-leaf"</note>. He says it bears thin branches a span long, upon which is the fruit; it has leaves similar to Mint, five on each little stalk, though rarely more, divided into a circular curve. It has a flower that is whitish with a pale tint (for so I see *ochroleucon* <note>Greek: ὠχρόλευκον — yellowish-white</note> can be translated), and a reddish, oblong root, thicker than Black Hellebore, which is very much in use.

Pliny, however, in his twenty-fifth book, says: "Cinquefoil is unknown to no one, as it is even recommended for the production of strawberries <note>original: "fraga"</note>. The Greeks call it *Pentapeton*, or *Chamæselinon* <note>Greek: χαμαισέλινον — "ground celery"</note>, or *Pentaphyllon*. When it is dug up, it has a red root. This turns black as it dries and becomes angular. It takes its name from the number of its leaves. The plant itself begins and ends its season with the Grapevine." These, then, are the accounts held regarding *Pentaphyllon*, that is, Cinquefoil. No author older than these, as far as I know, describes it. For Galen only reveals its powers, not its physical form.

First, it is sufficiently clear from these accounts that the common Cinquefoil described by Leonicenus is not the one we are discussing. For his plant has neither a white flower, nor fruit on the stalks, nor a red root, nor a thick one; nor does it turn black or square when drying; nor does it follow the emergence and passing of the grapevine, but remains green perpetually. If anyone denies these things, he is proven wrong simply by looking at the plant itself. But I also think it is clearly established—both by Pliny’s authority and Dioscorides’ description—that our *Pentaphyllon* also bears fruit. Pliny writes that it is "recommended for producing strawberries," and Dioscorides reports that it has "thin branches a span long, upon which the fruit is found." Furthermore, one can see from everyone's descriptions that the leaf is not what Leonicenus thought. For Theophrastus recorded that it has a leaf similar to a Grapevine, with all leaves in fives; while Dioscorides said it has leaves divided into curves or sickle-shapes, five on each stalk. Moreover, among the names, he calls it *Pentadactylon* ("Five-fingered"), by which name the *Cici* (or Wild Sesame) is also known, whose leaf is clearly very similar to the Grapevine. He also calls it *Pseudofelinon*, which can be called "False Celery."

<margin>B</margin>
Pliny calls it *Chamæselinon*, as if "Low Celery," and both use the same reasoning: because Celery <note>original: "Apium" — likely wild celery or smallage</note> seems to have something in common with the Grapevine, and its leaves are curved in this same way. From the number of these leaves, the plant was called Cinquefoil and Five-feathers: because it sends out five such whole leaves from the root. It is not distinguished by five little leaflets (as in the plant we previously said is called Crow’s Foot) nor like the common Cinquefoil of Leonicenus, but is shaped with five more extended angles (if I may put it that way), after the likeness of the Grapevine and Celery, roughly in this manner. This is that *Pentaphyllon* which, according to Dioscorides, produces fruit, which are called strawberries <note>original: "fraga"</note> by Pliny. Its extraordinary powers are handed down by Dioscorides and Pliny; it is added to the compositions of Theriac <note>term: Theriaca — a famous ancient "universal" herbal antidote against poison</note>; it is used for cleansing houses; and Dioscorides said its root is very much in use. If our friend Leonicenus had inspected it with sharper eyes, he would not have presented a most useful herb (the common one) in place of this most useful and celebrated one which has no use in medicine, nor would he have barked so out of season against Pliny.

Indeed, that plant which has three distinct leaves, and which we see everywhere in the mountains of Italy and sown in monastery gardens bearing many strawberries, has its own name. It is called *Fragaria* <note>Strawberry plant</note> by the herbalists, and its fruit is called *Fraga* by Pliny. Nor would it seem likely to anyone that Pliny wanted to describe Cinquefoil here with so many names and so many signs if he had meant the Strawberry plant, which is common, and which he had already called "fraga" in previous sections. And therefore, he did not simply say that Cinquefoil bears strawberries, but described it with the addition of a conjunction: he said it is "recommended *even* for producing strawberries." He would not have added that intensive conjunction <note>original: "copulam... augentem" — referring to the Latin "etiam" (even/also)</note> unless he recognized that there was another plant that bore strawberries, namely the one he had indicated in earlier volumes. To this, it seems necessary to add (so that it is less surprising that Cinquefoil can also bear strawberries) that our Strawberry plant is so similar in proportion to this *Pentaphyllon* we are discussing, that it seems to be of the same genus. For while studying these things, we have observed that it too has a reddish root, often thicker than a finger, which turns black as it ages...

# PHARMACY of SIMPLES.

C ...rarely sends out more than five small branches from the root, and rarely more, in which those first little leaflets are divided.

We say, therefore, that there are two herbs. One which bears strawberries, or at least fruits similar to strawberries, which is called *Pentaphyllon* <note>Greek: "five-leaf"</note> and *Quinquefolium* <note>Latin: "five-leaf"</note> by Dioscorides and Pliny, and which is exceptional for medical uses. The other is the common one, which bears strawberries and is designated by no other name than the fruit itself; Pliny mentions this in the fifteenth chapter of the first volume and the twentieth. But if you ask me whether I think this is still the Cinquefoil today, or what I believe its name to be? I will tell you what I found while investigating, and—as one who never decides anything finally, yet conceals nothing that might move and excite the minds of scholars toward the inquiry of truth—I will share it. There is in Venice, in that street they call the Apothecaries’ Row <note>original: "uico Specierium"</note>, the shop of a certain notable pharmacist, which has the "Head of the Ethiopian" as its sign. In it is a Book of Herbs, painted with such skill and diligence that you would believe the herbs were born on those pages, not merely depicted. In it, we saw painted with the very same signs we have described here an herb with five leaves, which themselves had longer angles and curves, just as we have drawn. But also the fruits, which you would call Strawberries, and both the Latin name *Sanicula* <note>Sanicle, a healing herb</note> and the German name *Sanickel* were written next to the herb itself. Cited therein as writing about this Sanicle are Galen (in the *Diadimidis*), and that Peter of Spain who later held the highest Papacy and was named John the Twenty-first; he wrote the book on medicine titled *The Treasure of the Poor* <note>original: "Pauperum thesaurus"</note>; then a certain Bishop of Cervia, Maffeo of Lodi, and Gilbert the Englishman, all surgeons. Whether this Sanicle is the same as the Cinquefoil, I have no reason to affirm, nor do I see why I should deny it. These are the things I had to say about Cinquefoil, Strawberries, and Sanicle, through which I think it should be admitted that Pliny did not err, but taught the name and power of a most delightful herb.

### The Judgment of HERMOLAUS BARBARUS on the Five-leafed Plants.

<margin>
On this above,
on leaf 85.
</margin>

D *Pentaphyllon* and *Pentapteron* <note>Greek: "five-winged"</note> in Theophrastus; Gaza <note>Theodorus Gaza, a 15th-century translator</note> translates these as Five-leaved and Five-feathered. Aetius records that this is called *Hermubotanem*, that is, the herb of Mercury; the Egyptians also call it *Dissyphi*. The Dacians call it *Drocila*. The Italians call it *Psyllitum*, *Solota*, and *Thebeotin*, though I think these names are corrupted. For I also find it called *Therumbros* and *Theodorefron*. The root, when fresh, is reddish; it turns black when it dries and is four-angled. The leaf is like a small Grapevine; it grows and withers away along with the vine. The stems are thin with frequent joints. The name comes from the number of leaves. Certain Greeks call it *Chamaezeleon*, as if it were a shrub of the earth. Pliny believes that Cinquefoil is commended for producing terrestrial strawberries. I do not understand how that can be true. For the herb that produces strawberries is Three-leafed, not Five-leafed; it has a white flower, not a yellow one, and it is still frequent along the roads in the Rhaetian and Vindelician Alps <note>mountainous regions in modern-day Austria and Germany</note>. Hippocrates seems to have known two Cinquefoils: the White, which is both grass-like and taller from the ground, and the Black, which is lower. There is also what is commonly called *Tormentilla* <note>Tormentil</note>, which is very similar to Cinquefoil, except that it has seven leaves, not five. We can call it *Heptaphyllon*, that is, Seven-leafed. From its root, the apothecary shops (gods help us!) substitute lozenges of theriac <note>a famous ancient medicinal paste used as an antidote</note> instead of viper's flesh, because, as they think, it is never seen in the manner of a viper.

### Annotation of M. VERGILIUS on the reason for the name PENTAPHYLLON.

<margin>
Five-petals.
Five-cut.
Five-fingered.
False celery.
</margin>

All rural folk know Cinquefoil, and it is held in some honor everywhere by this name alone. Theophrastus, in Book 9 of his *History of Plants*, said that in his time it was called not only *Pentaphyllon*, but also *Pentapetes* <note>Greek: "five-petaled" or "five-spread"</note>, a name given by some from the feathers of birds, as Gaza believed; but as we think, it is because it spreads and extends itself into five leaves. That same shape of the leaves also caused it to be called *Pentatomon*, that is, divided into five parts. Likewise *Pentadactylon*, because just as there are five fingers on a human hand, so in that plant there are just as many divisions of the leaves. It was also called *Pseudofelinon* because it imitates Celery <note>original: "Apium" — a term for celery or parsley</note>, and is somewhat similar to it in the sections of the leaves. Other names given to it by various nations had some similar reason, such as *Callipetalon* <note>beautiful leaf</note> and *Xylopetalon* <note>woody leaf</note>, named for the appearance and hardness of the leaves. It is likely that in those foreign <note>original: "barbaris" — meaning non-Greek/Latin</note> names there lies some reason, currently unknown to us, based on its shape or powers. Treating its root and leaf in Book 9 of the *History of Plants*, Theophrastus added that the root of Cinquefoil turns black once dug up and dried. This was not mentioned by Dioscorides because he believed it would be enough to say what it was like when it was dug; for after that time, he left it to the physicians to keep it stored in a designated place. He also added that the leaf of Cinquefoil is like a Grapevine—not in size (for it is small) but in color and shape—and as if it followed the nature of the vine, growing and withering with it. The stems are spread thin across the ground, having frequent *knemas* <note>Greek: "shins" or segments between joints</note>; he uses this term for the intervals between two joints because they resemble the shape of a human leg. It should also be seen how this author says Cinquefoil has a leaf like Mint, while that author says it is like a Grapevine. It seems to us that the leaves of those plants can be poorly compared to each other; just as the color of the flower is said to be both "whitish" and "golden yellow." Yet this is not so difficult as the other, for we sometimes see both those colors in the paleness of a human face.

..., Volume One.

### ON THE TEMPERAMENT OF CINQUEFOIL.
<sig>A</sig>
The root of **Cinquefoil** <note>original: "Pentaphylli", meaning five-leaf</note>, as Galen says in the 8th book of *On Simple Medicines*, dries in the third degree. Yet it is not at all pungent, and for that reason it is considered very useful. It is, indeed, composed of thin parts.

### ITS POWERS AND BENEFITS
->according to Dioscorides.<-

The juice of the root, boiled down to a third of its volume, relieves toothaches if held in the mouth.
It stops rotting ulcers of the mouth if used as a wash.
It smoothes the roughness of the windpipe <note>original: "Arteriæ"</note> when used as a gargle.
It is helpful against flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note> and dysentery.
Likewise, it is drunk for the pains of the joints and the hips <note>sciatica</note>.
Cooked in vinegar and applied as a poultice, it checks spreading ulcers; it disperses <term>strumas</term> <note>swollen lymph nodes, often associated with scrofula</note>, tumors, hard lumps, abscesses, and swellings.
It heals <term>sacred fires</term> <note>original: "Ignes sacros," typically referring to erysipelas or shingles</note>, hangnails, <term>condylomata</term> <note>wart-like growths</note>, and the itch.
The juice of the tender root is beneficial against defects of the liver and lungs.
Likewise, it is used against poisons.
Furthermore, the leaves are drunk with <term>hydromel</term> <note>honey-water</note>, or diluted wine and a little pepper, against the cycles of fevers: specifically, four sprigs for a <term>quartan fever</term>, three for a <term>tertian fever</term>, and one for a daily fever.
Also, thirty leaves, drunk for thirty days, are beneficial for those with the <term>comitial disease</term> <note>epilepsy</note>.
The juice of the leaves, drunk in the amount of three <term>cyathi</term> <note>small cups</note> for several days, very quickly cures the <term>royal disease</term> <note>jaundice</note>. <sig>B</sig>
Applied with honey and salt, they are a remedy for both wounds and <term>fistulas</term> <note>abnormal passages in the flesh</note>.
They provide aid to those with intestinal hernias.
Cinquefoil <note>original: "Quinquefolium"</note> stops the flow of blood whether drunk or applied.
It is gathered for purifications, rites of chastity, and eruptions of blood.

### FROM JOHN OF VIGO.
Cinquefoil has a powerfully drying virtue; however, it does not seem to participate in any manifest heat.

# Celandine. <note>original German: "Schölkraut"</note>

## ON CELANDINE, Chapter 42.

¶ **Names**
In Greek: <note>original: "χελιδόνιον"</note> Chelidonion; <note>original: "παιονιά κραταιά"</note> Strong Peony; <note>original: "γλαύκιō"</note> Glaukion; <note>original: "πάνδιον ῥίζα"</note> Pandion’s Root.
In Latin: <note>original: "Chelidoniū, siue Chelidonia"</note> Chelidonium or Chelidonia; that is, the Great Swallow-wort <note>original: "Hirundinaria maior"</note>.
In German: **Celandine. Celandine-root. The great Swallow-herb.** <note>original: "Schölkraut. Schölwurz. Schwalwẽkraut dz groß."</note>

## THE OPINIONS OF THE AUTHORS on Celandine.

### The History of Celandine according to DIOSCORIDES, Book 2.
Celandine is of two kinds: the Greater and the Lesser. The Greater has a stem a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note> long or taller, which is branched. It has many leaves similar to the Crowfoot <note>original: "Ranunculi"</note>, yet they are softer and of a bluish-gray color. The flower is like that of the White Violet, emerging next to each leaf. Within it is a juice the color of saffron <note>original: "succus croci"</note>, which is biting, sharp, and somewhat bitter, hav...

<header>[Of Medicines], VOLUME One.</header>

...foul smelling. <margin>A</margin> The root is single at the top, but frays into many saffron-colored hairy fibers. The seed pod is like that of the horned Poppy, thin and long. In which seeds larger than those of the Poppy are enclosed.

### On the LESSER [Celandine].

The Lesser is a small herb, consisting of runners, without a main stem, with leaves like Ivy, but much rounder and smaller, tender and slightly succulent. It has several roots, very small, like grains of wheat, gathered in heaps, of which three or four extend lengthwise. It grows near water.

->Theophrastus on Swallow-wort, Book 7, chapter 12.<-

Swallow-wort, which brings forth its flower at the arrival of the swallow, appears to have a cause for this that is partly natural and partly coincidental.

->The History of Celandine from Pliny, Book 25, chapter 8.<-

Animals also discovered herbs, especially Celandine. For with this, swallows restore sight to the eyes of their chicks in the nest—even, as some claim, if the eyes have been plucked out. There are two kinds. The Greater has a shrubby stem, with a leaf larger than the wild Parsnip, reaching a height of two cubits <note>roughly 3 feet</note>; the color is whitish, and the flower is yellow. The Lesser has rounder leaves like Ivy, less white. The juice is a stinging saffron color, and the seed is like a Poppy. It flowers at the arrival of the swallows; they wither at their departure.

### On the Temperament of Celandine.

It has a cleansing power and is sufficiently warming, and the juice is acidic. <note>In Galenic medicine, "temperament" describes the qualities of a plant, such as hot, cold, moist, or dry.</note>

### Its Powers and Benefits from DIOSCORIDES.

<margin>B</margin> The juice, boiled with honey in a bronze vessel over hot coals, brings clarity to the eyes. The juice is pressed from the leaves, stem, and root at the beginning of summer, and dried in the shade to be formed into lozenges <term>pastillos</term>.
The root, drunk with anise and white wine, cures the "royal disease" <note>Jaundice, so named because it was thought to be cured by the touch of kings or due to the golden color of the skin</note> and spreading ulcers. Applied with wine or chewed, it soothes toothache.

### From GIOVANNI DA VIGO.
<note>Giovanni da Vigo (1450–1525) was a prominent Italian surgeon and physician to Pope Julius II.</note>

Celandine is hot and dry in the third degree, and is very helpful for the eyes. Therefore, its power is most usefully added to eye-washes <term>collyrijs</term> that sharpen the sight. Its juice, when placed within the teeth, causes them to fall out after a period of time. Its root is less drying, possessing the power to draw out and dissolve. Therefore, for toothache caused by a cold humor, the aforementioned root, slightly crushed, sprinkled with vinegar, and held against the teeth, heals most effectively.

### From PLATEARIUS.
<note>Matthaeus Platearius was a 12th-century physician from the famous medical school at Salerno.</note>

Celandine is hot and dry in the fourth degree.
When it is used in a prescription <note>original: "receptione"</note>, the root should be used, not the herb.
The root can be kept for three years with great efficacy. Based on its qualities and substance, it has the power of dissolving, consuming, and drawing out.
To purge the head and a womb filled with cold humors, let the well-crushed roots be boiled in wine; the patient should take the steam through the mouth, and then use the remainder as a gargle.
Against the "colic passion" <note>severe abdominal pain</note>, let the crushed herb, boiled in wine, be applied externally, or a sponge soaked in the wine from the decoction, or let the powder of its root be applied frequently.
To provoke menstruation and to cleanse the womb, a warm compress <term>fomentū</term> should be made frequently from the water of the decoction.
For a canker <note>original: "cancrum", referring to a spreading ulcer or sore</note> of the mouth, bone, or nerves, let the powder of its root be prepared with powder of roses and vinegar, and boiled to a medium thickness like mustard; let the cankerous parts be anointed, for it helps much.
Against a fistula <note>a narrow, pipe-like ulcer</note>, let its powder be prepared with lye <note>original: "capitello", a strong alkaline solution</note> and placed into the opening of the fistula.

### On the PIMPERNEL, Chapter 43. <note>original: "Rhapsodia XLIII"</note>

#### [ NAMES ]

Greek: *anagallis* <note>original: ἀναγαλλίς</note>, *aeritis* <note>original: ἀερίτις</note>, *aegitis* <note>original: αἰγῖτις</note>, *sauritis* <note>original: σαυρῖτις</note>.

Just as the name "Consolida" <note>a term for various "wound-worts" or healing plants like Comfrey</note> is common to so many herbs (indeed, we have specifically touched upon five of its species), so also under the name of Pimpernel, for some it refers to "Mouse-ear" <note>original: "Auricula muris"</note> or *Pilosella*; for others, it refers to that which is called "Hen’s-bite" <note>original: "Morsus gallinae"</note> or commonly *Ippia* <note>referring to Chickweed</note>. Some designate other species as well, which I shall pass over. Regarding the genuine Pimpernel, however, the situation is as follows.

->Description <note>original: Εἰκὼν (Eikon) meaning image or depiction</note> of the Pimpernel from Dioscorides, Book 2.<-

There are two kinds of Pimpernel, which differ only in their flower. For that which has a blue flower is called the female; the male is that which has a crimson flower <note>original: "phoeniceo" - a reddish-purple or scarlet</note>. They are small shrubs lying on the ground: with leaves on a square stem, tiny, somewhat round, approaching the leaves of *Helxine* <note>referring to Pellitory-of-the-wall</note>: with round seed.

### Female Pimpernel. <note>original: "Gauchheyl weyblin"</note>

<margin>Pliny, Book 26, chapter 7.</margin>
Pliny and Serapion <note>an influential 9th-century Arabic medical writer</note> say almost nothing different. We have added the Corollary of Hermolaus Barbarus <note>a 15th-century Venetian scholar famous for correcting errors in classical texts</note> below, since it serves to clear up a previous error.

->Barbarus’s Corollary on the Pimpernel.<-

Pimpernels grow with a delicate shrubby stem, no higher than a palm’s width, in gardens and watery places. The former <note>referring to the female variety</note> blooms with a blue flower. It is a wonder that cattle avoid the female plant; or if they are deceived by its similarity—for they differ only in the flower—and have tasted it, they immediately seek a remedy in the plant called *asyla* <note>original: "asyla," possibly a reference to a plant used against stings or as a refuge</note> (or as other manuscripts have written, *casyla*, called "beast’s eye" <note>original: "ferus oculus"</note> by our people). It is commanded to those about to dig it up that, before sunrise and before they say anything else, they should greet it three times, and then, having taken it up, they should press out the juice; in this way, its powers are most potent. Dioscorides says that the Pimpernel is also called *Sauritis* <note>original: σαυρῖτις, "Lizard-wort"</note>. There are manuscripts in which one reads *Gauritis* instead of *Sauritis*. Hippocrates, by naming the *Anagallis*, seems to have understood it as useful for bites and for drying out ulcers. Aetius <note>a 6th-century Greek medical writer</note> recommends the herb *Nycterida* <note>original: "Nycterida," "Bat-herb"</note> for white spots in the eyes <note>term: albugines; a condition where the cornea becomes opaque</note>; I believe this should be taken to mean the Pimpernel, since it is also called *Nycteritis* <note>original: "Nycteritis"</note> by Dioscorides. Those who commonly call the plant *Passerina* <note>term: Passerina; "Sparrow-wort"</note>, which bears a white flower, are mistaken in thinking it is the Pimpernel. Just as those who have depicted *Myosotis* <note>term: Myosotis; "Mouse-ear"</note> (that is, Mouse-ear) as the Pimpernel...

Paul of Aegina <note>a 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note> remembers that the scarlet pimpernel <note>original: "Anagallidem phoeniciam"</note> was also called "Coral" because of its color. ->*On the Temperament of the Pimpernel.*<-

Both varieties have the power to soothe and to cleanse; they are also somewhat warming and drawing.

## Its POWERS and BENEFITS
### according to DIOSCORIDES. <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a 1st-century Greek physician and author of the foundational herbal *De Materia Medica*</note>

It wards off inflammation.
It extracts thorns or splinters driven into the body.
It checks spreading sores <term>nomas: corrosive or gangrenous ulcers that "feed" on the flesh</term>.
Its juice, used as a gargle, purges the head.
And poured into the nostrils, it eases toothache, provided it is injected into the nostril on the opposite side [of the pain].
With Attic honey <note>honey from Mount Hymettus near Athens, prized in antiquity for its purity</note>, it clears up spots on the eye <term>argema: a small white ulcer on the cornea</term>.
It aids dulled or weakened vision.
Drunk with wine, it is useful against viper bites and ailments of the liver and kidneys.
They report that the variety which bears a blue flower pushes back a prolapsed anus <note>original: "prociduam sedem"</note>. However, the scarlet variety, applied as an ointment, draws it out.

PHARMACY of SIMPLES

<margin>C</margin>

## Concerning NIGELLA. Rhapsody 44. <note>The author uses "Rhapsody" to denote a specific chapter or section of this botanical compilation.</note>

### ❧ NOMENCLATURE

Greek: Black-flower <note>original: "μελάνθιον" (melanthion)</note>, Wild poppy <note>original: "μήκων ἀγρίον" (mēkōn agrion)</note>, Black poppy <note>original: "μήκων μέλαν" (mēkōn melan)</note>.
Latin: Nigella, Gith <note>Gith is an archaic name for Nigella sativa, or Black Cumin</note>.
German: *Ratten* <note>In older German, "Rade" or "Ratten" often referred to both Nigella and the common corn-cockle, which were frequently confused due to their similar black seeds.</note>

->Opinions of the authors regarding NIGELLA.<-

### The History of Nigella from DIOSCORIDES, Book Three. <note>Pedanius Dioscorides was a 1st-century Greek physician whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical manual for 1,500 years.</note>

**I**t is a small shrub, often exceeding two palms <note>about 6–8 inches</note> in height. Its leaves are small, like those of Groundsel <note>original: "Senetionis"</note>, but much thinner. It has a slender head at the top, oblong like a poppy, with membranes running throughout the inside. Enclosed within these is the seed: black, pungent, and fragrant, which is sprinkled upon breads.

->PLINY'S History of Nigella, Book 19, Chapter 8.<-
->Book 20, Chapter 17.<-

Gith is grown for bakeries, while Anise and Dill are grown for kitchens and physicians. Among the Greeks, some call Gith *Melanthion*, others *Melanspermon* <note>meaning "black seed"</note>. The best is that which has the most pungent odor and is the darkest black.

### Description of Nigella by Hermolaus Barbarus. <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493) was a Venetian scholar famous for his "Corrections to Pliny," aiming to reconcile classical botany with actual plants.</note>

<margin>D</margin>
**M**elanthion, which is also called *Melanspermon*, is occasionally called *Melanthe* by Hippocrates. Theophrastus <note>the "father of botany"</note> (as Theodorus believes) calls it *Anthemon* or *Anthemion*, interpreting it as Nigella. However, *Anthemon* is an entirely different species from *Melanthion*, or Gith, or as Palladius calls it, *Giddi*. For *Melanthemon* is actually Chamomile, and *Melanion* is the Black Violet. The best Gith is of the most pungent scent and the deepest black. Its smoke kills gnats and flies. It is a wonder to note that its juice is poisonous to one who takes it too liberally, yet the seed itself most pleasantly seasons the bottom crust of bread with a grain-like flavor. There appears to be another entirely different kind of Gith which is seen growing everywhere in grain fields; this can be called "False Melanthion" or *Githago* <note>Corn-cockle</note>, having long leaves almost like a leek, a purple flower, and a seed and entire shrub larger than the true *Melanthium*, and lacking any scent. But the true Gith, which Dioscorides mentions here, has leaves like Fennel or Groundsel, and a blue flower. The scent of the seed is pleasant, and it does not grow everywhere. Hippocrates recommends the variety from Cyprus. There is another herb, *Melandryum*, growing in grain fields and meadows with a white flower and a sweet scent; they recommend its little stalk be ground for the liver and taken with old wine.

### The Annotation of Marcellus Vergilius on the same Nigella. <note>Marcellus Vergilius (Marcello Virgilio Adriani, 1464–1521) was a Florentine scholar and translator of Dioscorides.</note>

**I**n the months of May and June, throughout the countryside, one sees Nigella growing in the meadows, hedges, and along all boundaries; nothing is more frequent than that shrub, and nothing more common. Once, the seed of Nigella was used to recommend bread with its pleasing flavor. Indeed, it was crushed and sprinkled on the bread before baking, just as Poppy seed is; not unlike how we now mix Anise into sweets. What one might rightly marvel at in Nigella is the craftsmanship of wise Nature in shaping its little vessels <term>vascula: the seed pods or capsules</term> in which the seed is conceived, ripened, and preserved—black in color and the size of millet seed. These vessels are far smaller than those of the poppy, nor are they as long in their proportions. Furthermore, they do not have a "star" <note>the radial stigma</note> at the top as Poppies do, but rather a wider navel; nor do they have membranes running inside in the same way to separate the seed chambers. For in the Poppy, there are channels falling between them like supports or mounds; in Nigella, there are walls passing through the middle, like partitions by which those little seed chambers are divided. There is also this difference: that there are single vessels on each Poppy stalk, but in Nigella they are more numerous; thus, what is lacking in the number of seeds in each individual vessel is made up for by the number of vessels. It was only this shape of the vessel that led some to call the wild and black Poppy "Nigella." The Greeks named it *Melanthion* from the color of the seed, and following their example, the Latins named it Nigella <note>from "niger," meaning black</note>.

## On the Temperament of Nigella.

It heats, as Galen says in the seventh book of *Simples*, and it dries according to the third order <term>third order: a high level of intensity in the humoral system, where the effect is strong but not yet destructive to tissue</term>, and it is seen to consist of "thin parts" <note>meaning it has a subtle, penetrating substance rather than a dense one</note>.

### Its Powers and Benefits from Dioscorides.

It aids against headaches when smeared upon the forehead.
It clears away recent cataracts <note>original: "suffusiones"</note> of the eyes, when ground with oil of Iris <note>original: "Irino"</note> and poured into the nostrils.
It removes leprosy, freckles, hardened spots, and old tumors when applied with vinegar.
It drives out corns <note>original: "clauos"</note> that have been scraped around the edges when applied with old wine.
It is beneficial for toothaches when boiled with vinegar and pine-resin <note>original: "teda"</note>.
It expels roundworms from the belly when the navel is rubbed with it mixed in water.
It helps those suffering from catarrh <note>original: "Destillatione," referring to a runny nose or respiratory congestion</note> when ground in a linen cloth and smelled.
It provokes urine and menstruation when taken for many days.
It also draws out milk.
It relieves difficulty in breathing when drunk with wine.
It provides aid against the bites of spiders <note>original: "Phalangiorũ," likely referring to venomous spiders</note> when a drachm’s weight <note>about 3.5 grams</note> is swallowed with water.
By its smoke, serpents are driven away.
They report that if drunk too liberally, it kills.

---

### FROM PLINY.

It heals the wounds of serpents and scorpions.
I find it is applied with vinegar and honey, and that serpents are driven away by its smoke.
One drachm is drunk against spiders.
It clears away catarrh in a marvelous way when crushed in a small linen cloth and smelled.
The root provides the same benefit when held in the hand.
<margin>B</margin>
It aids headaches when applied with vinegar and poured into the nostrils.
With oil of Iris, it helps eye discharges <note>original: "epiphoras"</note> and tumors.
For toothaches, it is boiled with vinegar.
For difficulties in breathing, it is drunk with added wine.
It is applied to hard spots, old tumors, and abscesses <note>original: "suppurationes"</note>.
It increases the milk of women when taken for several consecutive days.
Its juice is collected, just like that of Henbane <note>original: "Hyoscyami"</note>.
Similarly, in larger amounts it is a poison, which is surprising since the seed most pleasantly seasons even bread.
It also purifies the eyes and provokes urine and menstruation.
Indeed, I find that even by just tying 30 grains in a linen cloth, the afterbirth <note>original: "secundas"</note> is drawn out.
They also say it heals corns on the feet when ground in urine.
The smoke kills gnats and likewise flies.

MEDICINES from SIMPLES. <note>original: "SIMPLICIVM Pharma."</note>

# ON THE FIRST SPECIES OF FEVERFEW, known as Parthenion. Chapter 45. <note>original: "Rhapsodia XLV."</note>

### NOMENCLATURE

| | |
|---|---|
| Greek, | *Parthenion*. <note>original: "παρθένιον"</note> |
| Latin, | Feverfew. <note>original: "Matricaria." The name comes from "matrix," meaning the womb, as it was used for uterine health.</note> Fever-driver. <note>original: "Febrifuga."</note> |
| German, | **Mettram.** |

<margin>C</margin>
The recent name "Matricaria" has cast clouds and darkness upon us, so much so that we cannot certainly designate which plant this was in the works of Dioscorides <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note>. We have nothing certain except what we have observed from the commentaries of the "New Scholars," namely from the *Pandectary* <note>A medical encyclopedia by Matthaeus Sylvaticus</note> and Hermolaus Barbarus <note>A 15th-century Italian scholar</note>. Both of them distinguish three kinds of it. The first, the *Pandectary* calls *Artemisia* <note>Mugwort</note>. The second, Tansy or *Athanasia*. The third, common Feverfew. We have placed the judgment of Barbarus under the plant *Helxine*, which stands as follows.

*Helxine* <note>A name applied to several climbing or sticking plants</note> is twofold according to Dioscorides and authors in general. One is *Parthenion*, the other is called *Cissanthemos* from its ivy-like leaves. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist</note> likewise makes it twofold, but differently. One is the subject here, called *Parthenion* and *Perdicion* (or *Perdiciades*) because partridges <note>Latin: "perdices"</note> chiefly feed on it. Its leaves, however, he does not attribute to *Mercurialis* as Dioscorides does, but says they have a mixed likeness of Plantain and Horehound. He says its dense little stalks dye wool, and the seeds, in bur-like heads, stick to clothes; from which they also want it to be called *Helxine* <note>From the Greek word for "to drag" or "pull," referring to how it clings</note>. The Aeolian people and the Egyptians eat this. It has thick and very many roots, as Pliny says. The other kind, the same author says, is the "truer" *Helxine*, which has a leafy root from which a thistle-like growth full of seeds, like an apple, swells out. It is called *Acanus* by Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher often called the father of botany</note>; when its top is cut, a tear-like sap of pleasant taste breaks out, called "Acanthic Mastic," and for that reason, it is used for adulteration, as we have said. It sprouts and blooms in summer with leaf and stem, having thorny down. This is what Pliny says. We believe this is called not *Helxine*, but *Ixine*—as was said regarding the White Chameleon plant—even though the former *Helxine* is called *Perdicion* and *Parthenion*. 

However, following Pliny, I understand another plant to be *Perdicion*, which <margin>D</margin> our people call the "Pitcher-herb" <note>original: "Vrceolaris," likely Pellitory-of-the-wall, used to clean glass vessels</note>, and others *Astericum*. It has leaves like Basil, only darker, growing on roof tiles and walls. Because of this, it is commonly called *Parietaria* <note>Wall-herb</note>, *Muralium*, *Muralis*, and *Vineago*. It is also called *Parthenion* because it was shown by Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom and war</note> in a dream to Pericles, the leader of the Athenians, for use against falls and precipices when a little slave dear to him had fallen from a height (he was called *Splachnoptes* <note>The "organ-roaster," a slave who worked at the sacrificial altars</note>). Turtle-doves, pigeons, and chickens are said to cast off their annual sluggishness by feeding on *Helxine*, according to Pliny. 

Therefore, I find three kinds of *Parthenium*. One with the leaf of Coriander, which is called *Amaracus* by Galen and *Parthenium* by Dioscorides; it is commonly called *Matricaria* <note>Feverfew</note>. A second with the leaf of *Mercurialis* according to Dioscorides in this place (or Plantain and Horehound according to Pliny), which is called *Helxine*, and is the subject being discussed here. A third with the leaf of Basil, which is called *Parietaria* and *Muralis*. It is strange that Dioscorides gives no instructions about this one, as far as I know—unless one says he included this also under *Helxine* since it is slightly hairy and sticks to clothes, and does not differ much from the leaves of the *Mercurialis* plant, except that on *Mercurialis* the leaves are slightly serrated, while on *Parietaria* they are not. There are those who also call *Mercurialis* itself *Parthenion* and *Helxine*, as Dioscorides left written in the entry for *Myosotis*. It was also called *Alsine*, although it is read corruptly as *Asine* in Theophrastus, where Theodorus interprets it as "Bird-herb" <note>original: "Volucrum"</note>, because it strangles trees in the manner of clinging Ivy.

### The text of DIOSCORIDES on Parthenion, Book 3.

Some call *Parthenion* "Amaracon," others "Anthemis," others "Leucanthemon" <note>White-flower</note>, others "Chamaemelon" <note>Ground-apple or Chamomile</note>, others "Chrysocalin," others "Melabathron," and some "field flower." The Romans call it "Sun-cycle" <note>original: "Solis feculum"</note>, some "Thousand-leaf" <note>Yarrow/Millefolium</note>, the Etruscans "Cauta," the Africans "Thamath." It has leaves like Coriander, thin, with a flower that is white around the edge and honey-colored in the center, with a heavy smell and a bitter taste. Dried and drunk with honey-vinegar or salt, it draws out bile and phlegm, just like *Epithymum* <note>Dodder-of-Thyme</note>. It is beneficial for those who are short of breath and for those suffering from melancholy. The herb without the flower is drunk with great benefit by those with bladder stones and those panting for breath.

It details the plant's medicinal use for respiratory issues and melancholy, while recounting the legend of Pericles' slave being healed by a plant revealed by Minerva.</summary>

Volume One. <note>original: "TOMVS Primus"</note>

<margin>A</margin>
The decoction is effective as a sitz bath for hardness and inflammation of the womb <note>original: "uuluarum"</note>. It is applied to St. Anthony’s fire <note>original: "sacro igni," a skin infection now known as erysipelas</note> and to abscesses when mixed with the flower.

## THE COROLLARY OF HERMOLAUS BAR-
## barus, regarding the same Parthenion, which similarly
## supports our identification of Feverfew.

<margin>Otherwise called *Pelecynum*</margin>
The flower of Parthenion has the scent of an apple <note>original: "Mali"</note>. It grows in hedges: many think it is called Feverfew <note>original: "Matricariam"</note>. There are those who call it *Cotula* <note>Mayweed</note>. For Dioscorides himself testifies that it is called *Cauta* by the Etruscans, from which the name *Cautula* is derived, and then *Cotula*. But Pliny <note>A 1st-century Roman naturalist</note> also calls this plant *Leucanthen* and *Tamnacum*—unless it be a scribal error <note>original: "librariorum menda"</note> of those writing *Tamnacum* for *Amaracum* <note>Marjoram</note>. For it is also called *Amaracus* by Dioscorides, and likewise by Galen and Paulus. Among us, Celsus <note>A 1st-century Roman medical writer</note> calls it *Pallecium* and *Muralium*, as Pliny understands it. I myself contend that Celsus spoke of a different Parthenion when he used the name *Muralium*; one which does not grow in hedges, but on walls and partitions. Because of this, it is commonly named *Parietaria* <note>Pellitory-of-the-wall</note>, as we taught in the section on *Helxine*. There is also a *Parthenis* used for *Artemisia* <note>Mugwort</note>; though there are some who read *Artemin* and not *Parthenin*, immediately correcting the error of the physicians who wished for the Parthenion we are currently discussing to be Mugwort. Regarding Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine"</note>, Galen doubts which herb he meant by the name *Parthenion Microphyllon* (that is, small-leaved): Galen writes that it should be understood as the same as Dioscorides' *Helxine*, or even *Mercurialis*. But what if Hippocrates understood it as the second kind of Mugwort, which is said to have minute leaves? Or even as the Feverfew treated here, which is described as having the leaves of Coriander?

## M. VERGILIVS on the difference of Parthenion from
## Perdicion, and the common Chamomile.

This Parthenion is different from the one which Celsus, in his third book, records as also being called *Perdicion*, which both suppresses and cools. That plant is called *Helxine muralis* and *Perdicion*: this one, known by many names found among the *Anthemis* <note>Chamomile-like plants</note> species, must be believed to be similar and related to it. That former plant was reported by Nicander in his *Theriaca* to heal poisons: this one is fit for healing breathing difficulties <note>original: "suspirijs," often meaning asthma</note>, black bile <note>original: "atræ bili," one of the four humors</note>, and those suffering from stones, as well as for inflamed and hardened parts of the female anatomy. This one is similar to Chamomile <note>original: "Chamæmalo"</note>, with a flower that is white around the edge and yellow in the middle. The former plant is described with the leaves of the Mercury herb: and, not to be too long-winded, they are different from each other in all their characteristics; they deceive readers only by having the same name. However, Parthenion deceives not by name, but by its physical appearance, being so similar to Chamomile that it is often plucked in its place by the unskilled. It has a flower similar to that one in almost
<margin>B</margin>
every respect. It differs in size, which is larger in every part in the Parthenion. It also differs in shape: for while the colors in the flowers of both are equal, the flower of Chamomile swells in the middle and is raised high, whereas its petals hang down toward the ground; in Parthenion, the petals stand level with the center around the circumference. For us, based on what we have long observed, our mind inclines toward it being related to Chamomile: and as happens in most other cases, it is distinguished from others by some private mark, which in this Parthenion is a rank, pungent smell <note>original: "uirosus odor"</note>. Just as in *Bupthalmum* <note>Ox-eye</note>, which will be discussed soon, size alone is what distinguishes that plant from this Parthenion.

<margin>The opinion of a certain learned man.</margin>
But even this opinion of Barbarus has its opponents, and there are those who think it false to assume a connection based on the similarity of the flower between Feverfew and Chamomile. For Serapion, they say, accepts the former as a species of Chamomile, that is, *Anthemis*. And whatever is brought forward in the chapter on Chamomile from Dioscorides, those things were said by Dioscorides regarding *Anthemis*: although the description of both herbs indicates they are entirely of one species and quality. For the name *Chamæmilon* (that is, "earth-apple") indicates that they breathe the scent of an apple, having flowers that are white on the edge and golden within. Therefore, whether we take Feverfew for the second species (that is, for Parthenion, as Hermolaus believed), or any other herb similar to Chamomile, it is certainly necessary that they have nearly similar effects.

## THE DEBATE OF NICOLAVS LEO-
## nicenus and P. Collinutius regarding the Parthenions.

Leoniceno, in his book *On the Errors of Physicians*, writes that Pliny in his 21st book says that Parthenion is called *Perdicium* and *Muralium* by Celsus. Then he adds that the same names are given to Parthenion, which...

<meta>This page continues the botanical debate regarding the various plants known as Parthenium (Maiden-herb or Feverfew). <header>MEDICINES of Simples <note>original: "SIMPLICIVM Pharma"</note></header>

<margin>
C
Chamomile
Mayweed.

Pellitory.

Pellitory-of-the-wall.
Pellitory-of-the-wall.
Pellitory-of-the-wall
cools.
</margin>
...is the name given to it. The powers which Dioscorides attributes to the second *Parthenion* <note>Feverfew</note> are because *Chamæmilon* <note>Chamomile</note> is called by another name, since it differs very little in leaf and flower from the herb Chamomile. However, some of the more recent physicians call this *Parthenion*—a herb similar to Chamomile—by the name *Cotula* <note>Mayweed</note>. But this plant is not called *Perdicium* or *Muralium* by Celsus; rather, that name belongs to the other plant which is called *Helxine* <note>likely Pellitory or Bindweed</note>, and at the same time is named *Perdicium* and *Parthenium*. By the Latins, it is called *Parietaria* <note>Pellitory-of-the-wall</note> and *Muralium* because it grows everywhere on partitions <note>original: "parietibus"</note> or walls. In our own age, the common people—dropping a single letter—call it *Paritaria* instead of *Parietaria*. Celsus mentions this same herb, whether it be called *Muralium* or *Parietaria*, in his third book *On Medicine* among those things which have the power to suppress as well as to cool. Indeed, nearly all medical authorities attribute this faculty to the *Parthenion* which is called *Perdicum* and *Parietaria*, but not to the other one which is also called Chamomile. For these are the words of Dioscorides concerning the same: "The leaves have the power of binding and cooling." Neither Paulus nor Galen have handed down anything different concerning it. Pliny likewise, in his 22nd book, confirms that the same plant is named both *Parthenium* and *Perdicum*.

->P A N D O L F O  C O L L E N V C C I O<-
<note>Pandulphus Collenutius (1444–1504) was an Italian humanist and lawyer interested in botany.</note>

<margin>
Three kinds
of Parthenion.
</margin>
In explaining what he thinks are Pliny’s errors regarding *Parthenion*, Leonicenus <note>Niccolò Leoniceno, a famous Renaissance physician</note> has fallen into great errors himself, as can be recognized from the descriptions and differences of the herbs themselves. We shall understand that Pliny understood and distinguished these, while Leonicenus confused them through ignorance of the plants. We shall deal with them as follows: Pliny writes in his 21st and 22nd volumes of three herbs called by the name *Parthenion* (for we are not speaking now of the fourth, which is *Mercurialis*), and to all of these he assigned the specific powers they possess. According to the opinion of those whom he enumerates in such great number, the first—which is called *Parthenium*, *Leucanthis*, and *Thamnacus* by the Greeks, and *Pelecynum* and *Muralium* by our people and Celsus—grows in garden hedges, has a white flower, the scent of an apple, and a bitter taste. The second is that which is called *Helxine*, *Siderites*, and *Perdicium* (named after a bird <note>the Partridge, *Perdix*</note>); it has leaves of a mixed similarity to Plantain and Horehound, dense stalks that are slightly reddish, and seeds in burr-like heads that cling to clothes, which is why they want it called *Helxine* <note>from the Greek word for "to drag" or "cling"</note>. The third is likewise called *Perdicum* and *Aftericium*, but by our people it is called the "Jar-herb" <note>original: "herba Vrceolarum"</note>; it has a leaf similar to Basil <note>original: "Ocymo"</note> but darker, growing on tiled roofs and ruined walls. If Leonicenus had known these distinctions of *Parthenion*, and had at the same time more diligently inspected Celsus, and Pliny who writes these things clearly, and his own Dioscorides, he would not have so rashly protested. So that students may fully understand, I shall reveal what they are and propose them for debate, making room for those who might bring forth truer findings.

<margin>
Leucanthis.
Thamnacus.
Muralium.

Pelecynum.

Genfeminum.

Amaracum.
</margin>
The first indeed received the name *Leucanthis* from the whiteness of its flower, and *Thamnacus* from the density of the shrub and its tuft. The same was called *Muralium* by Celsus (perhaps in those books which it is certain he wrote on agriculture), either from the sweetness of its scent or because the flower was most suitable for ointments. It was as if it were called *Myralium* <note>relating to 'myrrh' or 'ointment'</note>, with the Greek "y" turned into our "u," a practice which the ancients used very frequently (as in *Murrha*, *Murena*, and *Mure*) and which Cicero writes is familiar to the Latins. *Pelecynum* <note>meaning 'alluring'</note> seems to have been named for the same reason: that the shrub itself, by the sweetness of its scent, entices <note>original: "pelliciat"</note> one to it. Or perhaps because, like the herb *Pelecynum* which grows in grain fields, it needs support and creeps up garden hedges; something we see happening in our own age through human industry. We commonly call this *Genfeminum* <note>possibly Jasmine</note>, with a white flower, the scent of an apple, and a bitter taste. This is that *Parthenium* which some have perhaps more correctly called *Amaracum* <note>Marjoram</note>, which, breathing with flowers and sweet shade, embraced the resting Ascanius <note>a reference to Virgil’s Aeneid, where Venus hides the boy Ascanius in a grove of Marjoram</note>. From this came that celebrated ointment once prepared on the island of Cos, which was called *Amaracinum* or *Samfuchinum*. From this, perhaps, the common people twisted the name into *Genfeminum*, so that I think those in Dioscorides who called *Parthenium* "Amaracum" understood no other kind of shrub or herb. Otherwise, if that plant which he records the Etruscans call *Cauta* <note>Mayweed</note> is Dioscorides’ *Parthenium*, how could the distinguished poet <note>Virgil</note> have written that the shade of such a short herb embraced the boy with sweetness? For everyone clearly understands that *Cauta* itself is neither suitable for shade due to its shortness, nor for the pleasure of scent or ointment due to the heavy smell of its flowers. Indeed, someone might think it better that, on the authority of the same Dioscorides, some called that plant which is named *Cauta* both *Chamæmilon* and *Anthemis*, since it is placed among the species of Chamomile, of which he produced three types.

<margin>
Two Cotas.
</margin>
For there are two herbs which are even now commonly called *Cauta* or *Cota*. One, which is nicknamed "The Healthy One" <note>original: "sana"</note> and is incorrectly called *Millefolium* <note>Yarrow</note> by some, we believe is the plant called *Leucanthemon* by Pliny in his 21st volume; it is similar in scent to Southernwood <note>original: "Abrotono"</note>, has a white flower, is leafy, and is useful for those suffering from shortness of breath. The other is more similar to Chamomile and bears the nickname "The Stinking One" <note>original: "putidæ"</note> from the foulness of its odor. This could also be Dioscorides’ *Parthenium Millefolium*, if he had not attributed the leaves of Coriander to it. But the second *Parthenium* is seen in many fields, growing among the stubble, with the same signs by which it is painted by Pliny; its leaves are almost those of *Mercurialis*, and its rough, black seed is sought after by partridges. Because the seeds of this plant cling to the clothes of those walking by, some of the Greeks wished it to be called *Helxine*, while the Romans called it the "Burr-herb" <note>original: "herba Laparia"</note>. Likewise, the common people at this time call it *Grapella* <note>Cleavers</note>.

<summary>This page features a scholarly debate led by Pandolfo Collenuccio, attempting to clarify the confusing nomenclature of ancient botany. He distinguishes between different varieties of Feverfew, Chamomile, and Pellitory based on their physical traits, scents, and classical literary references.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and botanical investigation into the plant known as Parthenium, focusing on its various names—such as Pellitory-of-the-wall and Feverfew—and reconciling the descriptions provided by Pliny, Dioscorides, and Celsus against the critiques of Renaissance scholars like Leonicenus.</meta>

<header>Of Physicians, VOLUME One.</header>
<sig>Y</sig>

<margin>A</margin>
...as if you might call it *Rapella* <note>Little-snatcher</note> from the act of "snatching" <note>original: rapiendo</note>. The third type is indeed that which is called *Astericum* <note>Star-wort</note>, because it has leaves encircling the little stems in the shape of a star; and because it can cling to clothing with a certain snatching downy fuzz, it is seen to be called *Helxine* <note>Sticky-herb</note> by Dioscorides. Because it is found by experience to be effective for scouring small pitchers and glass vessels, it is called *Urceolaris* <note>Pitcher-herb</note> by Pliny, and commonly by us it is also called *Vitriolum* <note>Glass-cleaner; not to be confused with the chemical sulfate</note>. Because it grows on walls and partitions, it is called *Muralis* <note>Wall-herb</note> by Celsus in the second book of *On Medicine*, and is rightly called *Parietaria* <note>Pellitory-of-the-wall</note> by the physicians of our time. It was sacred to Minerva, and therefore called *Parthenium* <note>Maiden-herb</note> because the goddess revealed it in a dream.

Do you see how Pliny was deceived in nothing—if those who read him understand—and how he is vindicated from error? Do you now see the manifest calumny of this "bindweed" <note>original: conuoluuli</note> of ours: how it twists itself like a vine-shoot with its own Dioscorides? He calls his own plant *Parthenium* and *Chamæmelum* <note>Chamomile</note>, and asserts that it is called *Solsequium* <note>Sun-follower or Marigold</note> and *Millefolium* <note>Thousand-leaf or Yarrow</note> by the Romans. Indeed, nothing more absurd can be said than these names, even among those who have only a modest touch of botanical knowledge; for they are not ignorant that those names belong to herbs entirely different from *Parthenium*. And Leonicenus, in the first genus of *Parthenium*, writes *Perdicium* <note>Partridge-herb</note> instead of *Pelecynum* <note>Hatchet-vetch</note>, which the ancient and printed codices have. In the third, he puts *Muralium* instead of *Muralis*. And what Celsus writes concerning *Muralis* in the second book of *On Medicine*, he here shamelessly affirms that Celsus wrote about *Muralium* in the third book. Then, for *Leucanthe* <note>White-flower</note>, a herb with a white flower (from which it gets its name), he conjectures about some *Cota* or *Cauta*—translating Dioscorides, I believe—and he claims it does not have a white flower, but a yellow one crowned with small white leaves; and that it has the scent not of an apple, but of *Abrotanum* <note>Southernwood</note>, as Pliny says, or else an unpleasant and grim scent (if he understands it to be the one nicknamed "Stinking"). And now, what he first objected to in Pliny could be retorted somewhat more vehemently against Nicolaus himself: who, having been deceived not only by the similarity of men and things, but also by his reputation for Greek learning, <margin>B</margin> poured out many things intemperately. Thus far Collinutius.

There are those who call it *Febrifuga* <note>Fever-flee or Feverfew</note>, and by another name, the Greater Centaury: whether this is so, we propose only as a dispute, so that we may provide an opportunity for the more learned to inquire further into this herb.

## ITS POWERS AND BENEFITS

The herb *Matricaria* <note>Motherwort or Feverfew</note> has the powers of Wormwood and Centaury, and whether eaten or applied as a poultice to the belly, it disperses griping pains of the abdomen. If boiled in wine and eaten before the onset of a chill, it drives away fever. It provokes menstruation, expels worms, and promotes urine.

# On Tansy, the Second Species of Feverfew and Partheniums, Chapter XLVI <note>original: *Rhapsodia*; used here to denote a specific section or chapter of the treatise.</note>

All later physicians call the common herb Tansy <note>original: *Tanacetum*</note> by names such as Wild Celery, Middle Feverfew, Domestic Wormwood, and St. Mary’s Herb; in German, it is called **Tansy, Worm-herb, or Peasant’s Parsley.** <note>original: *Reyn farn, Wurmkraut, Baurenepff*</note>. I am led to believe by Marcello Virgilio <note>A famous 15th-century translator of Dioscorides</note> that this is not the same plant that others identify as *Ambrosia* or *Athanasia* based on Dioscorides; here is his note regarding *Ambrosia*:

<margin><unclear>It seems [...]</unclear></margin>
The name *Ambrosia* was once not just a fluctuating and vague name among certain herbs; rather, among poets and other writers, anything that pleased by the sweetness of its scent or flavor was called by this same name by the ancients. It was so named as if it granted immortality to those who used it. The name is frequent and well-known everywhere, yet the thing itself is unknown and not easily found among herbs. Different authors describe it differently, and almost all confuse it with Wormwood <note>original: *Artemisia*</note>. Nevertheless, the herbalists of our age dare to point it out as a plant three spans high <note>about 27 inches</note>, or sometimes taller as it says here, branched, with seeds in clusters all along the stalk, but with leaves far larger than those of Rue. And as it says here, the clusters never flower, being downy and woolly, with no scent of wine or anything else. Thus it happens that regarding this plant, which we believe is foreign to Italy, we dare not establish anything for certain. Pliny, in his 27th volume, chapter 4, inserted a whole chapter of this writer into his commentaries; yet not much earlier in Book 25, chapter 7, while dealing with Wormwood, he said: "There are those in the Mediterranean who use the same name *Artemisia* for a plant with a single stalk, very small leaves, and a not unpleasant scent, which some call *Botrys* and others *Ambrosia*." From this, it is clearly perceived, as we said a moment ago, that the name *Ambrosia* is vague and applied to many things: plants, foods, and drinks—to the point that the Athenians used this name for all kinds of fruits, oil, wine, and other liquids that they offered to the Gods on the altar. Our mind inclines toward the view that this is a plant foreign to our world and peculiar to Cappadocia <note>A region in modern-day Turkey</note>. For the herb shown by our herbalists under this name is common, grows everywhere, and is very easy to find, especially by the clusters of heads which are full of down, and which we have never seen flower.

<margin>B</margin>
## The *Pandectary* <note>Referring to the *Pandectarum Medicinae* by Matthaeus Silvaticus, a 14th-century medical encyclopedia</note> on TANSY.

The *Pandectary* says this about Tansy: "Another type of Wormwood is called *Tagetes*, which is tender, having tiny seeds and a single stalk full of leaves. It grows in Mediterranean and higher elevations. The flower is honey-colored and delicate, and more pleasant compared to other Wormwood. This is called *Tagetes* or *Tanacetum* by the Greeks, and in the Latin language we call it *Thamasia* or *Athanasia*."
<margin>Poor Latin. <note>The author is criticizing the linguistic quality of the source text.</note></margin>

## Its POWERS and Benefits from the same *Pandectary*.

The Wormwood which is called *Tagetes* <note>Tansy</note> helps with bladder pain and difficulty urinating <term>strangury<gloss>a condition where urine is passed painfully or drop by drop</gloss></term> when two drachms of the juice are given in wine.

For those suffering from fever, two measures <note>original: *cyathis*; a small cup or ladle</note> are given in hot water.

Roasted with lard and vinegar, it treats hip pain <note>sciatica</note> if bound to the area until the third day.

To make an infant more cheerful, use Tansy as a fumigant <note>herbal smoke</note>, and it will turn away all attacks of evil things.

Crushed with oil, it wonderfully heals nerve pain and swelling of the feet.

It provides the same benefit for foot pain if taken as a drink.

## From HIERONYMUS the Herbalist <note>Hieronymus Bock, also known as Tragus (1498–1554), a pioneer of modern botany</note>.

Tansy extinguishes heat <note>inflammation</note> if applied as a compress.
The seed, when drunk or eaten, kills worms.
It also expels both urine and kidney stones.

# ON SIMPLE MEDICINES <note>original: *Simplicium Pharma*; "Simples" were medicinal herbs used on their own rather than in complex mixtures.</note>

<margin>C</margin>
## ON CHAMOMILE, THE THIRD 
## species of Feverfew, Chapter XLVII <note>original: *Rhapsodia*; used here to denote a specific section or chapter of the treatise.</note>

### ON ITS NOMENCLATURE
<margin>Anthemis, Chamomile <note>original: *ἀνθεμίς χαμαίμελον*</note></margin>
Some call this plant *Anthemis*, others *Leucanthemon* <note>meaning "white-flower"</note>, and others *Heranthemon* because it blooms in the spring <note>original: *uere*</note>. Some call it *Chamæmelon* <note>meaning "ground-apple"</note> because it has the scent of an apple; some call it *Melanthemon* <note>meaning "honey-flower"</note>, others *Chrysocoma* <note>meaning "golden-hair"</note>, and others *Callia*. The Romans call it *Mallium*, and the Africans call it *Aftertiphen*. There are three types, differing only by their flowers. Its branches do not exceed a palm’s length <note>about 3–4 inches</note>; they are shrubby, with many "wings" <note>referring to the leaf structures along the stem</note>, and are hollow. It has slender small branches, round heads, and flowers that are golden in the center, while the outer circular petals are white, honey-colored, or purple, with leaves the size of Rue. It grows in rough places and along paths. It is harvested in the spring.

### ITS POWERS AND BENEFITS.
The roots, flowers, and the herb itself have the power to heat and to thin <note>in the sense of thinning bodily humors</note>. Taken as a drink or used in a sitz bath, they provoke menstruation, assist in childbirth, and promote the flow of urine and the passing of stones. They are drunk to treat bloating and the torments of the intestines <note>colic or "iliac passion"</note>. They purge an overflow of bile and heal defects of the liver. A decoction made from them is used to bathe the bladder. Among all these types, the most effective for treating stones is the one with the purple flower, which is somewhat larger in size. This type is properly called *Heranthemon*.

<margin>D</margin>
The variety named *Leucanthemo*, as well as the one called *Chrysanthemo*, are more powerful diuretics. When applied as a poultice, they heal *aegylops* <note>a lachrymal fistula or sore at the inner corner of the eye</note>. When chewed, they heal eruptions of ulcers in the mouth. Some use them in enemas mixed with oil. They are ground into a meal to drive away the cycles of fevers. The flowers and leaves ought to be stored, and when crushed separately, formed into pastilles <note>medicinal lozenges</note>. The root should also be dried. When the need arises, two parts of the herb should be given for every one part of the flower or root; or conversely, two parts of the flower to one part herb, doubling the weight on alternating days. It should be drunk in wine diluted with honey-water <note>original: *mulso*</note>.

---

## THE COROLLARY OF HERMOLAUS BARBARUS <note>A 15th-century Italian scholar known for correcting translations of ancient botanical texts.</note> on Chamomile.

<margin>
Pliny, book 22, ch. 21.
Theophrastus, book 7, ch. 13.
</margin>
The *Anthemis*, which is also called *Leucanthemis*, is the same as the plant commonly called *Chamæmilon*; it was celebrated with great praise by Asclepiades <note>A Greek physician who practiced in Rome</note>. Theophrastus calls it *Anthemon* and *Anthemion*, while Dioscorides calls it *Anthemis*, and Hippocrates (I believe) calls it *Euanthemon*. He establishes two types: one which only has leaves from the root, and another which has them on the stalk. Both begin to lose their blossoms from the tips downward, whereas other plants begin from the bottom. The flower is white, with a grass-colored center in a circle. The seed is the same color as the flower. These fall away just as in thorny plants, leaving behind an empty receptacle. It seems that Theodore <note>Theodore Gaza, a translator of Theophrastus</note> understood *Anthemon* to be *Melanthium* <note>Nigella or Black Cumin</note>, as he interpreted it as such. The flowers of *Anthemis* are set aside for use in garlands, but only if gathered in the spring. There is also a popular name for a dance mentioned in Athenaeus called the *Anthema*, accompanied by this playful verse:

> Where is the Rose, where is the Violet, where is the flowering Parsley? <note>original: *Apium*; can refer to celery or parsley.</note>
> Where is this Rose? Where is this Violet? Where is this flowering Parsley?

<margin>A</margin>
## From Marcello Virgilio’s commentary on Chamomile. <note>Marcello Virgilio Adriani (1464–1521) was an Italian humanist and scholar known for his translations of Dioscorides.</note>

In this *Anthemis* <note>the Greek name for Chamomile</note> there is no name among so many appellations that does not have a certain significance joined to the nature of the plant. We omit those which he himself has already declared: *Eranthemum* <note>original: *Eranthemō*</note>, because it blooms in the spring <note>original: *uere*</note>, and *Chamæmalum* <note>meaning "ground-apple"</note>, because it is said to have the scent of an apple. The others were also coined from the color or scent of the flower by the consensus of various nations. Depending on whether they preferred the inner or outer color of the flower, they identified it as *Leucanthemon* from the white color, or *Chrysanthemon* or *Chrysocome* from the yellow color of gold. For it is read both ways in this author. Similarly, it is called *Melanthemon* from the apple-scent which it possesses, for that word signifies the "apple-flower" <note>original: *Mali florem*</note>. To these I am pleased to add that in the eighth book of *The History of Plants* by Theophrastus, it is more often called *Anthemon* in the neuter gender. And what are commonly read in Greek texts as "nine-inch-long branches" <note>original: *dodrantales ramuli*</note> are described in the most ancient manuscripts of both nations as a herb of "two nine-inch-lengths" in height. Not much later, where one commonly reads "long, slender branches and small leaves" <note>original: *κλωνάρια μακρὰ λεπτά φυλλάρια*</note>, it ought to be read not as "branches," but as "leaflets." For the branches had already been discussed previously; therefore, it was time to discuss the leaves of the herb. The oldest Greek manuscripts and the ancient interpretation of Dioscorides indicate this; by their help, we have forced those things which other interpreters had mixed up to return to their proper places, and we have said: "with small, thin, and numerous leaflets," etc. The other facts regarding Chamomile are sufficiently known in themselves, and therefore need not be treated by us at greater length.

### POWERS and Benefits of it from Aemilius Macer. <note>Aemilius Macer was a Roman poet whose name was attached to a famous medieval herbal poem, *De viribus herbarum*.</note>

> *The author Asclepius commends the Anthemis with more praise*
> *Than we, who call it Chamimola or Chamomile;*
> *This is a highly fragrant and short herb.*
> *It is so similar to a herb which the common people rightly*
> *Call Amarisca <note>Stinking Mayweed</note>, which stinks and is bitter,*
> *That when compared, they are scarcely distinguished by scent.*
> *Authors say there are three species of it,*
> *Which they teach can be distinguished by the color of the flowers alone.*
> *All of them have a golden center in the flower:*
> *But that flower is surrounded by various petals,*
> *Which are of a white, or black, or purple color.*
> *It is properly called Anthemion, the petals of which*
> *Are purple in color; this variety is larger and stronger.*
> *But Leucanthemion is recognized by its white petals.*
> *Chrysanthemon by its honey-colored ones. The nature of all of them*
> *Is granted to be dry and hot in the first degree.*
> *Any of these, drunk with wine, provokes urine,*
> *Breaks stones in the bladder, and purges the menses,*
> *If the womb is bathed in water in which the herb was boiled,*
> *Or if it is drunk more frequently with wine.*
> *Thus it soothes cramps, and bloating of the stomach*
> *Is driven away by such a drink; it removes scales from the face,*
> *If you apply it alone when crushed, or joined with honey.*
> *A decoction of it taken is beneficial for those with jaundice <term>Ictericis: people suffering from yellowing of the skin and eyes</term>,*
> *And it is wonderfully beneficial for liver complaints when drunk.*
> *Drunk with wine, it is reported to expel a miscarriage <note>Historically used to mean clearing the womb or inducing labor</note>.*
> *If you bathe a person with fever in oil in which this was boiled,*
> *You will drive away the chill, and also often banish the fever.*
> *Swollen flanks <term>hypocondria: the upper abdominal region</term> are purged by such an ointment.*

<header>OF SIMPLE MEDICINES</header>

<margin>C</margin>
Taken at the weight of a drachm with wine,
Anthemis <note>the Greek name for Chamomile</note> prevents the poisonous bites of snakes from causing harm.
Pliny affirms that if this is taken for forty days,
twice each day at the weight of a drachm,
with two measures of refined white wine,
along with urine, it gradually cleanses the entire spleen.
It cures *aegilops* <note>a sore or fistula in the inner corner of the eye</note> if one chews it
and applies it as a poultice; in this way, it also cleanses foul ulcers.
The head often tends to throb with the heat of a fever,
or when humors have collected within it,
producing ulcers (which the Greeks call <term>Exanthemata</term> <note>original: *Exanthemata*; refers to skin eruptions or rashes</note>).
Fresh green Chamomile, boiled in oil, drives these away.
But if the green herb is unavailable, let it be steeped in vinegar,
and wash the head with it; no ointment provides better relief.

->FROM GIOVANNI DI VIGO.<-
<note>Giovanni di Vigo (1450–1525) was an Italian surgeon and the personal physician to Pope Julius II.</note>

*Chamomile* is hot and dry in the first degree.
Its virtue is to dissolve [swellings] without drawing humors to the site, while providing a certain softening and strengthening of the area.

<margin>
D
The Blessed Oil.
</margin>
Therefore, its oil is named "Blessed," because it dissolves [congestion] without attraction. A decoction of it—made with the tips of wormwood, and the roots of Licorice, Fennel, Parsley, and Asparagus, along with the "four greater cold seeds" <note>a traditional blend of cucumber, melon, gourd, and watermelon seeds</note>, with Jujubes and Sebesten <note>a type of plum used in pharmacy</note>, in pomegranate wine and Endive water, sweetened with sugar—if taken on an empty stomach in the amount of half a cup, most powerfully provokes urine, expels stones, mitigates pain of the spleen, liver, and flanks, and even heals jaundice.

->FROM AVERROES.<-
<note>Averroes (1126–1198) was an influential Al-Andalusian philosopher and physician.</note>

*Chamomile* has a property above all others for mitigating pain in the belly.

->The Preparation of Chamomile Oil FROM PALLADIUS.<-
<note>Rutilius Taurus Aemilianus Palladius was a 4th-century Roman writer on agriculture.</note>

For every pound of oil, infuse one ounce weight of the golden flowering chamomile herb (after discarding the white petals that surround the flower), and let it stand in the sun for forty days.

### ANNOTATION OF A CERTAIN
### LEARNED man on Stinking Mayweed.

A herb grows commonly among the grain that is so similar to Chamomile that it frequently deceives even expert herbalists; in its leaves and flowers, it seems to differ in no way at all, yet its odor is much fouler. The Germans call this herb **Dog’s Herb**, or **Dog’s Flower.** Its scent is harmful to the head, and if used frequently, it is believed to induce a <term>Frenzy</term> <note>original: *Phrenesim*; a state of delirium or mental agitation</note>. Perhaps Dioscorides thought this was <term>Parthenion</term> <note>a Greek name for feverfews or mayweeds</note>, as he says that plant has a rank smell. It grows among the grain and beside paths, almost always mixed with Chamomile. Furthermore, Dioscorides asserts that *Parthenion*, when drunk with honey like <term>epithyme</term> <note>a parasitic plant often used as a purgative</note>, draws out phlegm and bile through the bowels; he indicates that it treats Melancholy and those suffering from shortness of breath, meaning it has a stronger purging power than Chamomile. I would easily judge this to be true both from the smell and the taste of that
<margin>
Dog’s Herb <note>original: *Cynobothane*</note>.
Dog’s Flower <note>original: *Cynanthemis*</note>.
</margin>
herb, which the Germans call *Cynobothanen* or *Cynanthemin* <note>Greek-derived terms meaning Dog's Herb and Dog's Flower</note>—which is, as I said before, the **Dog’s Flower**. However, as I do not see it in common use, I have not dared to define anything strictly. As
<margin>D</margin> far as concerns the three species of <term>Anthemis</term> <note>Chamomile</note> described by Dioscorides—of which one has white flowers, another purple, and the third honey-colored—I think this was said of those herbs which we commonly call "grain-field plants," among which are those that have purple flowers. Some think this is **Fennel-flower** <note>original: *Melanthion*; likely *Nigella sativa*</note>, because it has black seeds; but Fennel-flower is seen to be more fragrant. Truly, the passage is somewhat obscure, and so we leave the conjecture to others.
