<sig>A B</sig>

### CONCERNING THE FIFTH SPECIES OF FEVERFEW,
### that is, the Ox-eye, or Cow-eye, or Non-stinking Mayweed. Chapter 49.
<note>original: *Rhapsodia XLIX*. In this context, a "rhapsody" refers to a collected section or chapter of compiled knowledge.</note>

->DIOSCORIDES, Book 2, on the Ox-eye.<-
<note>Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD) was a Greek physician and the primary authority on herbal medicine for 1,500 years.</note>

Some call the Ox-eye <note>original: *Buphthalmon*</note> *Cachlam*, others *Balsamenam*; the Magi call it *Haemoran*, others "Seed of Mercury," others "Seed of Aphthitis," or *Mnesitheu*. The Romans call it *Cappacorania*, and the Africans *Narat*. It sends up thin, soft little stalks and has leaves like Fennel. It produces a yellow flower larger than the Chamomile <note>original: *Anthemide*</note>, resembling the shape of an eye, from which it takes its name. It grows around towns and in flat fields. The flowers, when ground with a wax-salve, disperse tumors and hard swellings. They say that if a decoction is drunk by those suffering from the "royal disease" <note>original: *regio morbo*; an old term for jaundice, so named because it was supposedly treatable with expensive, "regal" remedies or because the patient's skin turned the color of gold</note> after they emerge from the bath, it restores their natural color over time.

---

->HERMOLAUS BARBARUS, Commentary on the Ox-eye.<-
<note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493) was an Italian scholar known for correcting errors in ancient botanical texts.</note>

The Ox-eye <note>original: *Buphthalmos* or *Buphthalmon*</note>, or as Hippocrates called it, *Euanthemon* <note>meaning "well-flowered"</note>, is a shrubby plant with stalks that can be eaten when boiled. Its flowers are perceived to be much larger and sharper than those of the Chamomile. It differs from the marsh-shrub *Butomus* found in great quantities at Lake Orchomenus, which has a very smooth stalk with a peculiar gloss, angular leaves like a reed, and a black fruit the size of an apple, appearing in two sexes. The male is fertile, while the female is useful for weaving. The tender part near the root is eaten and is a pleasant food for children. Truly, I believe the Ox-eye to be the same as the plant called the "Gold-flower" <note>original: *Chrysanthemo*</note>, concerning which Dioscorides repeats these same details in his fourth book. This is what the poet Alcman does when he names it *Calchan* or *Cachlan* (that is, the Ox-eye), describing it as a golden necklace made from these flowers: "a golden necklace of slender petals of the ox-eye" <note>original Greek: χρύσειον ὀρμὸν ἑκὸν ῥαδινὰν πετάλοισι κάχλαν</note>. Nicolaus Damascenus writes that there is a lake at the foot of the Alps, many miles in circumference, where for almost the entire year, flowers of the sweetest scent and most excellent color can be seen around its edge, similar to the Ox-eye. This Ox-eye does not seem to be the one that the country folk call "Bull’s eye" and the "Stinking Mayweed" <note>original: *Cotulam foetidam*</note>, a meadow herb; for its flowers are white, whereas the flowers of the Ox-eye are yellow, as Dioscorides and others testify, even if the other features agree well enough. There is also another Ox-eye, of which we spoke in the section on Wild Cucumber. Dioscorides mentions that the Ox-eye is also called *Haeluron*. I read in Photius that a certain plant is called *Haelurion*; whether it is different or not is not clear. Furthermore, *Haeluros* is the animal we call a cat <note>original: *Felem*</note>, commonly referred to as *Cattus*, which poets also call *Aegiluros*. I also find in the writings of the grammarian Photius that the word *Chalcan* refers to purple dye, and also to the type of herb used to dye things purple.

---

->Annotation of MARCELLUS VERGILIUS on the same Ox-eye.<-
<note>Marcellus Vergilius (1464–1521) was an Italian humanist who translated Dioscorides.</note>

The same reason that caused the "Feverfew" <note>original: *Parthenion*</note> to be called the "Eye of the Sun"—namely, the leaves radiating around the flower and the yellow disk in the center—caused this similar plant to be named "Ox-eye" <note>original: *Buphthalmon*</note>. Indeed, the shape of the flower in both is nearly identical; only the size makes the difference. For that reason, this plant found its name from the larger eye of a larger quadruped, wishing to be called the "Ox's eye." However, one might reasonably believe it was named simply for the size of the eye, especially since the author here calls it "eye-like" <note>original Greek: ὀφθαλμοειδῆ</note>, which merely signifies the shape and appearance of an eye. Nevertheless, Pliny, in his 25th volume, chapter 8, described it in these words: "There is also the *Buphthalmos*, which is like the eyes of cattle." Following him, we have translated it as "Ox-eye."

<margin>
Otho.
,,
,,
,,
</margin>
<note>These marks likely refer to Otho Brunfels, the botanist.</note>

It appears to me to be the flower that the common people today call in German *Genstblum* <note>Goose-flower or Daisy</note>, but clearly the female variety, which we have also illustrated. For it was not possible to obtain the male variety with yellow petals on the circumference (which more closely resembles a bull's eye) at this time. Unless we wish it to be the one the same common people call "Monk's Head," or in German *Ringel bluom* <note>Marigold</note>; I see that this choice pleases others as well. Therefore, we have provided that one too. Although it would be more correct to call this one *Chrysion* or *Chrysanthemon* <note>Gold-flower</note>.

---

->SERAPION on the Ox-eye, chapter 158.<-
<note>Serapion the Younger was a 12th-century Arabic author whose "De Simplicibus" was a major medical textbook.</note>

The *Bichar* <note>the Arabic name for this plant</note> has a soft stalk and leaves similar to the leaves of Fennel <note>original: *Maratri*</note>. Its flower is lemon-colored, larger than the flower of Chamomile, and similar to the flower of the Mayweed <note>original: *Cotulae*</note>; for this reason, some call it by that name.

### It is sharper and more biting than Chamomile, and its power to dissolve [humors] is greater than that of Chamomile itself.

---

->AVICENNA, Book Two.<-
<note>Avicenna (c. 980–1037) was a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard medical text in Europe and the Islamic world for centuries.</note>

*Bichar* is the plant called *Keusen*, that is, the "Eye." Its rose <note>flower head</note> is lemon-colored and reddish, and thicker in the middle than the Chamomile flower. It is "hot" in the second degree and "dry" in the first degree.
<note>These degrees refer to the Galenic system of humors, used to determine how a plant affected the body's balance of heat and moisture.</note>

VOLUME First. Concerning Mercurialis, the sixth species of Parthenion
<note>The author is classifying this plant as a subtype of *Parthenion*, a name used in antiquity for several different plants, including pellitory-of-the-wall and feverfew.</note>
A
<note>This letter 'A' is a printer's signature, used to help binders assemble the book pages in the correct order.</note>

-># COLLECTION L.<-
<note>original: *RHAPSODIA L*. In this context, a "rhapsody" refers to a collected volume or a specific section of botanical knowledge.</note>

## NOMENCLATURE of the Herb Mercurialis.

Greek: *Parthenion* <note>original: παρθένιον</note>, *Linozostis* <note>original: λινόζωσις</note>.
Latin: *Mercurialis*, *Linozostis*, *Parthenion*, Herb of Hercules, Ointment-herb <note>original: *Vnguentaria*</note>.
German: **Mercury (Bingelkraut), Dung-weed (Scheisskraut), Manure-milt (Mistmilt), Dog-milt (Hundtsmilt), Dung-milt (Scheissmilt), Fat-mallow (Speckmalten), Lap-mallow (Schossmelden), Cow-root (Küwurz).**
<note>The German names often reflect the plant's powerful laxative effects (*Scheisskraut*) or its growth in nutrient-rich, manured soils (*Mistmilt*).</note>

---

### The History of Mercurialis according to Pliny, Book 25, Chapter 5.

*Linozostis*, or *Parthenion*, was discovered by Mercury <note>The Roman messenger god, known as Hermes to the Greeks.</note>; for this reason, many among the Greeks call it *Hermupöan* <note>meaning "Herb of Hermes"</note>. Among us Romans, everyone calls it *Mercurialis*. There are two kinds: the male and the female, the latter of which is more effective. It has a stem a cubit high <note>about 18 inches</note>, sometimes branching at the top, with leaves narrower than Basil, dense joints, many hollows at the leaf-axils, and seeds hanging from the joints. The seeds are abundant; in the male plant, they stand near the joints and are fewer, short, and twisted, whereas in the female they are loose and white. The leaves of the male are darker, and those of the female are lighter. The root is unnecessary and very thin. They grow in cultivated fields.

### On the Reason for the name "Mercurialis" by Marcello Virgilio.
<note>Marcello Virgilio Adriani (1464–1521) was a famous Florentine scholar and translator of Dioscorides.</note>

<margin>B</margin>
The herb Mercurialis immediately commends itself by its divine name, though it is otherwise a common weed, growing in almost all vineyards and fields. In some places, it is so abundant and potent that it even taints the flavor of wines with its own taste, making them unpleasant to those who drink them. Its primary and most notable natural power lies in purging the bowels, and it is accepted by everyone for medicinal use. Marcus Cato, in the chapter on Polypody <note>a type of fern</note> which we mentioned, counted this herb among those he taught the rural household to use for purging the bowels, warning that not much of it should be taken. Because this power is shared with many other plants, it does not seem that it should have been honored with a divine name for that reason alone. 

We believe that the reason for its divine name is what was handed down at the end of the chapter from the accounts of others by Dioscorides, and by Pliny in Volume 25, Chapter 5. For it was more fitting for a God to reveal something to men that was rare, unknown, and desired through all the centuries: by those who either take it badly that they are fathering more daughters and realize that the fertility of their wives in that sex will be a calamity for them, or by those who desire—with daily sacrifices and prayers—to leave behind a memory of their name, a support for their lineage, heirs for the family, and citizens for the Republic. They learned from God by what other means they could achieve this for themselves. 

<note>This refers to the ancient belief that consuming the "male" plant would help conceive a boy, and the "female" plant a girl.</note>

And so it happened that the Greeks called it *Hermou poan*, that is, the herb of Mercury, and the Latins called it *Mercurialis*. It is commonly known, as we have said, and because of the excessive loosening power it possesses, it is even now used as an insult among our people.

### On its Temperament according to Averroes, Book 5 of the *Colliget*.
<note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a 12th-century Andalusian polymath. His *Colliget* was a standard medical textbook in European universities.</note>

Mercurialis is hot and dry in the first degree <note>a classification in humoral medicine indicating a mild effect</note>. It is composed of contrary substances—that is, it is astringent, sharp, and watery. When it is fresh, it purges lightly, such that it is at the beginning of the first degree among purgative medicines. Therefore, it is given at the onset of fevers, before digestion, just as cassia fistula, tamarinds, and similar things are given. Anyone who drinks half a pound of the juice purges thick bile <note><term>choleram grossam</term>: a heavy or concentrated form of the "yellow bile" humor.</note> and phlegm. If it is boiled in wine while fresh, it consolidates large wounds and heals ulceration caused by fire burns. If its leaves are boiled in vinegar, they are very effective for ailments of the spleen. Its flower is even more effective in this regard. And from its juice is made...

<sig>z</sig>

<header>Medicines from SIMPLE HERBS</header>

A head-purger <term>original: *Caputpurgium*; a medicine intended to clear the head of excess humors through the nose or mouth</term>: and then it is very effective for long-standing fluids running to the ears and nostrils.

->ITS BENEFITS from Dioscorides<-
->book four.<-

Both [the male and female varieties] are eaten among vegetables to move the bowels.
Boiled in water, if the broth is drunk, it draws out bile and water <note>In ancient medicine, "drawing out water" refers to reducing edema or swelling</note>.
It is established that this one [the male] causes males to be conceived, and that one [the female] causes females, if they are drunk after menstruation and the crushed leaves are applied to the genitals.

->FROM PLINY.<-

Hippocrates praised Mercury-herb with wondrous acclaim, and no one among physicians knew them in this manner as he did.
He applied them to the womb with honey, or rose oil, or iris oil, or lily oil. Also for inducing menstruation and the afterbirth.
He said it performs the same by drinking or by fomentation <term>original: *fotu*; a warm, medicinal soak or compress</term>.
He dripped the juice into deaf ears and rubbed it on with old wine.
He applied the leaves to the belly, for eye-inflammations, for difficulty in urinating, and for the bladder.
He gave a decoction of it with Myrrh and Frankincense.
Indeed, to loosen the bowels, even in a fever, a handful is boiled in two sextarii <note>A Roman *sextarius* is roughly equivalent to a pint or half-liter</note> of water until reduced by half: it is drunk with salt and honey added; it is also boiled more healthfully with a pig's trotter or a chicken.

For the sake of purging, some thought both kinds should be given, or boiled with mallow.
They purge the chest and draw out bile, but they harm the stomach.

->The same is said by Oribasius, in his *Easily Procurable Remedies* [Euporista], book one.<-

->FROM GIOVANNI VIGO.<-

Mercury-herb boiled with chicken broth and taken with sugar powerfully softens a bound <note>constipated</note> stomach and empties it. A capon boiled with Mercury-herb, and its broth taken by mouth, purges raw humor and black bile <note>In the four humors theory, black bile was associated with melancholy and sluggishness</note> by softening the belly.

->FROM HIERONYMUS THE HERBALIST.<-

The water of the Mercury-herb puts out burns and soothes pains.

->NOTE.<-

It does not escape me that there are those who consider the Wound-herb, which is commonly called **Good-Henry** <note>original: **Gůtheynrich**; refers to the plant *Blitum bonus-henricus*</note>, to be another species of the Mercury-herb, equal in powers and benefits in all respects. I wanted to advise this because, as we also stated above, it is categorized by others among the Dragon-plants <term>original: *Dracontia*; a class of plants with spotted stems or snakelike roots</term>; therefore, we have placed it in both locations.

VOLUME One.

# ¶ Concerning the Seventh species of Parthenium: PELLITORY-OF-THE-WALL
->RHAPSODY 51<-

**CONCERNING** this herb, read the Corollary of Barbaro, and the dispute between Leoniceno and Collenuccio, found above in the description of the herb Feverfew <note>original: *Matricariae*; these were famous Renaissance scholars who debated the correct identification of plants mentioned in ancient texts</note>. For in that place, Pliny is explained, along with what he thought regarding Pellitory. However, that it is numbered among the species of Parthenium, everyone confirms with one voice, especially Apuleius.

->On its NAMING<-

<margin>A</margin> They call it *helxine* <note>Greek: ἑλξίνην</note> in Greek, or *parthenion* <note>Greek: παρϑένιον</note>. In Latin, it is *Parietaria* [Pellitory-of-the-wall], *Muralium* [Wall-herb], *Perdicium* [Partridge-herb], *Vicariam*, *Vitriolam*, *Parthenion*, and *Sideritim*. In German, it is called **St. Peter’s Herb** <note>original: *S. Peterskraut*</note> or **Day and Night** <note>original: *Tag vnd nacht*</note>.

->Its description from Dioscorides, book 2.<-

It has the hairy leaves of Mercury-herb, stems that are slightly reddish, and around them are rough seeds <note>original: *semina aspera*</note> that cling to clothing. It grows around towers and walls; in some places also around hedges.

### A very eloquent and noteworthy observation regarding Pellitory, by Marcello Virgilio; and therein regarding the reasoning for the name Helxine and its other species.

<margin>B</margin> **I**T WAS ONCE indicated by many names, and among them several names shared with other plants, under the title *Helxine*. Among the Greeks, the physicians of the Greeks testify to this, who say that *Helxine* was first called *Perdicium* [Partridge-herb], *Parthenium*, and *Heraclea*, and soon also *Cissampelos* [Ivy-vine]. By treating the herb of the same name in two separate chapters, and not attributing the same powers to both, they clearly seem to have established two *Helxines* under the same name but of a different nature. Besides them, Nicander also, in his *Theriaca* <note>A famous ancient poem about venomous creatures and their antidotes</note>, having first made mention of *Parthenium* and then *Helxine*, praised both against poisons. He spoke of "helxine, which some call clybatim" <note>Greek: ἑλξίνην, ἥντινα κλύβατιν καλέουσι</note>. In that passage, his commentator says that *Clybatim*, *Sideritim*, *Parthenium*, and *Perdicium* are all names for one and the same plant; and again he mentions "and indeed of Parthenium" <note>Greek: καὶ μὴν παρϑένιοιο</note>. Again, the same commentator testified that *Parthenium* is named *Helxine* and *Perdicium* by some. Among the Latins, Pliny in book 22, chapter 17, followed the Greeks with these words: "Some call *Helxine* by the name *Perdicium*, because partridges <note>Latin: *Perdices*</note> especially feed upon it; others call it *Sideritim*, and some *Parthenium*." In the face of such consistent testimony, one cannot fail to admit that *Helxine* was once called by so many names. However, one should not therefore believe that these two plants, different in their characteristics and powers, are actually one. For in shared names, there must be one plant which is indicated by that name primarily, truly, and in its own right; then, others are admitted to that name based on similarity; these, while keeping their own genus, enter into an equal partnership and community of the name only by adoption. That there are two *Helxines* of dissimilar nature is shown by their characteristics; and after the ancients, especially Paul of Aegina, acting separately and distinctly in his 6th book, describes them with these words: "Helxine: there are those who call it Perdicium, those who call it Parthenium, those who call it Sideritim, and those who call it Heraclea. Its power is to cleanse by scouring, and it is slightly cooling with a certain moisture." <note>Greek: ἑλξίνη οἳ δὲ περδίκιον... This refers to the plant's ability to "scour" or clean the skin or internal organs</note>. This is the history and medicine of the *Helxine* treated in this chapter by Dioscorides, according to Paul. Immediately after which, the same author says: "Helxine, which is called Cissampelos, has the power of dispersing" <note>Greek: ἑλξίνη καὶ κισσάμπελος διαφορητικῶς ἐστὶ δυνάμεως; "dispersing" refers to the medical ability to break up tumors or humors</note>. Of this plant, there is no history in Dioscorides. Indeed, the printed editions and most other manuscripts have a very brief history and medicine added at the end of the chapter, rather than described from the beginning, which clearly seems to have been added to this writer later. Other translators have joined it to their editions. For us, who have undertaken this work with the intention that everything in Dioscorides be restored based on the faith of the better versions, it did not please us to include those things against the oldest and best witnesses—especially since its medicine disagrees with the ancients, which Paul of Aegina said was for dispersing, but those manuscripts said was for loosening the bowels. But as for which are the *Helxines*, we admit that much: nevertheless, things that poorly suit the author and disagree with others should not be read in Dioscorides. For it could have been enough for this writer to mention this kind among the names of the other plant; or, as has happened in many other cases, this second *Helxine* might have been lost from this chapter. From these things, it is easy to reason that there are two *Helxines*. One with the leaves of the Mercury-herb, as he says here—or as Pliny says, of a mixed resemblance between Plantain and Horehound; the other of Ivy, growing in vineyards, and therefore called *Cissampelos*. The former is named so primarily and in itself; the latter is a relative to it, or at least similar; and similar, as we believe,

<header>MEDICINES of SIMPLE Substances</header>

<margin>C</margin>
...by that tenacious clinging to clothing. For this is the primary characteristic of *Helxine*, and from which its name was derived <note>The Greek name *Helxine* comes from *helko*, meaning "to draw" or "pull," because it clings to clothes</note>. After this, we must also investigate why so many other names have crept in to describe *Helxine*: not for both types, but as we believe, for the former one, which bears seeds in burr-like heads that stick to garments. There may be several reasons for its varied occurrences in different places. But as to why it was called *Perdicium* [Partridge-herb], there is no reason other than that provided by Pliny and Theophrastus: namely, because partridges, those most well-known birds, feed on its seed; they dig up the herb and roll around in it. <margin>Absyrtus the Greek.</margin> Absyrtus, a Greek author of veterinary medicine, commanded that the herb called by this name be used against coughs in beasts of burden. His words are: "the herb which the Romans call *perdicium*" <note>original Greek: βοτανήν ἢν ῥωμαῖοι περδίκιον καλοῦσι</note>. Celsus also, in the second book of his medical work, is believed to have understood this herb when he named it the "Wall herb" [*Muralem herbam*]: since it makes its birthplace on ramparts and walls. For this reason, it is still called *Parietaria* [Pellitory-of-the-wall] by many in several places. Here he also says it grows "among fences and walls" <note>original Greek: ὑποφραγμοῖο καὶ τοίχοιο</note>, that is, in stone enclosures and walls. Thus far, these names are specific to this first type of *Helxine*, assigned to it for various reasons. However, the names *Sideritis* and *Parthenion* belong properly to other plants, but have been added to this one and accepted due to some similarity. And we believe that *Helxine* was called *Sideritis* because both have leaves like Horehound [*Marrubium*]. Yet here he describes *Helxine* with the leaf of the Mercury-herb [*Mercurialis*]; others, however, and especially Pliny, describe it as having a mixed similarity between Plantain and Horehound. Both have rough leaves. For it is by this roughness alone that it holds onto clothing with a tenacious grip. Both also grow among rocks. But why it was once called *Parthenion* is not quite clear to us now. The herb properly called by this name is a relative of the Chamomile [*Anthemis*], treated in the previous volume between Chamomile and Ox-eye. That name was added to others, which are numerous in the discipline of medical materials, and accepted due to similarity. Indeed, Mugwort [*Artemisia*] is also called *Parthenion*. Furthermore, Paulus Aegineta clearly indicates that *Parthenion* is a name for *Helxine*, not a separate genus; for when he had dealt with *Helxine*, and shortly thereafter proposed *Parthenion*, he said only this: "it is spoken of under Helxine" <note>original Greek: εἴρηται ἐν τῇ ἑλξίνῃ</note>, as if *Parthenion* is nothing by itself, but one of many names for *Helxine*. This *Helxine* is commonly and widely known as *Muralis* [Wall-herb] and *Parietaria*. On the other hand, the variety called *Cissampelos* is difficult to recognize; it was named for the reason that it grows in vineyards with a leaf like Ivy [*Hedera*]: from which nature its other names were also made, *Melampelon* [Black-vine] and *Cissanthemon* [Ivy-flower]. For all these have the name of Ivy joined to them, an index of their birthplace and their leaves. We have observed in several places in this writer that types of plants are listed by him using these names, rather than the names themselves. <margin>D</margin> We believe this happened in this place: because there are those who, among these names, distinguish them separately for each kind of *Helxine*; and to distinguish them based on what has been said so far will not be difficult for readers. We will also add this: that what he says here about *Helxine* being "polyonymous," that is, having many names, pertains to that first type. For that is the one indicated by so many names.

## Its POWERS and Benefits.

The leaves have a nature that is cooling and thickening.
For this reason, when applied as a liniment, they heal "sacred fires" <note>original: *ignes sacros*; likely erysipelas or skin inflammations</note>, burns, growths <note>original: *condylomata*; warts or swellings</note>, incipient superficial abscesses [*panos*], tumors, and inflammations.
Its juice mixed with white lead is most aptly smeared on "sacred fires" and creeping ulcers. It is applied to gouty limbs [*podagris*] with goat suet or a cypress wax-salve.
Taken in a small cup [*cyatho*], it helps a chronic cough.
For tonsils swollen with inflammation, it is most usefully both gargled and applied externally.
The juice provides relief for ear pain.

### FROM APULEIUS.

Pellitory [*Parietaria*], as the Greeks say, possesses a styptic virtue: finally, it is used for similar causes as the herb Plantain [*Arnoglossos*].
The Partridge-herb [*Perdicialis*] is boiled in water, and with this same water you shall bathe the feet or knees; then apply the crushed herb itself with lard to the feet, covered with a cloth, or above the knees; it will heal wonderfully.

### FROM JOANNES VIGONIUS.

Pellitory is hot and dry in the third degree, namely the leaves. But its seed is cold and moist. Although it pleases others that it is of a cold and styptic complexion. GALEN, however, in the eighth book of *Simple Medicines*, in the chapter on *Helxine*, says its seed has the power of purging lightly.

...with a certain astringency <note>original: "stipticitate"; the quality of contracting tissues or stopping bleeding</note>, associated with coldness and moisture. Furthermore, Pellitory, heated in a pan with a little wine and a few leaves of parsley, along with watercress, and applied to the pubic area <note>original: "pectini"; referring to the region of the pubic bone</note>, most powerfully provokes urination; and when placed upon the belly in the manner already described, it removes the pain of the intestines.

Moreover, when decocted with mallows, roses, wormwood, feverfew, bran, and husked beans, then all pounded together and boiled again with thick syrup until it reaches a solid thickness—and finally administered in the manner of a plaster—it most excellently aids the tearing of muscles <note>original: "lacertorum attritionibus"; "lacerti" refers specifically to the muscles of the arms or legs</note> and the bruising of the musculature.

## ¶ On Mugwort, the Eighth Species of *Parthenion*. Rhapsody LII.

->¶ NOMENCLATURE<-

**Greek:** *Artemisia* <note>original: "ἀρτεμισια"</note>, *Anactyris* <note>original: "ἀνακτύρις"; meaning "royal"</note>, *Toxetesia* <note>original: "τοξητησια"</note>.
**Latin:** *Artemisia*. Greater Wild Thyme <note>original: "Serpillum maius"</note>. *Rapium*. Royal herb. *Valentia*. Royal pot-herb. *Parthenis* <note>meaning "virginal"</note>.
**German:** **Mugwort [Beyfuß]. Bucken. St. John’s Belt [S. Johans gürtel]. Sun-fan [Soñen wedel].**

### The History of Mugwort from Pliny, Book 25, Chapter 7.

Artemisia <note>Mugwort</note> was first discovered and shown by Artemisia, the wife of Mausolus <note>The ruler of Caria (d. 353 BCE) for whom the famous Mausoleum was built</note>; previously, it was called *Parthenis*. There are some who think *Artemisia* was named after the goddess Artemis <note>Diana</note>, because it specifically heals the ailments of women. It is a shrubby plant like wormwood, but with larger and "fat" <note>succulent or thick</note> leaves. There are two types: one with broader leaves, the other with more delicate leaves, which grows only in maritime regions. Some people in inland regions use the same name for a plant with a single stem, <margin>B</margin> very small leaves, and abundant flowers breaking forth. When the grapes ripen, it has a not unpleasant odor; some call this *Botrys* <note>original Greek: "βότρυς", meaning a cluster of grapes</note>, others *Ambrosia*. This kind grows in Cappadocia.

## ¶ On the nomenclature and origin of Mugwort by M. Vergilius <note>Marcello Virgilio Adriani (1464–1521), a scholar known for translating Dioscorides</note>. Furthermore, on its difference from Feverfew, which we placed above as the first species of *Parthenion*.

In the past, Mugwort enjoyed a great range of names and honors. It was first called *Parthenis*, that is, "virginal," because a virgin goddess—namely Artemis—gave her name to it. Soon it was called the "Royal pot-herb" <note>original Greek: "βασιλικὸν λιχάνον"</note>. Then, for the same reason, *Anactorium*, for the Greeks call kings *Anactas*. It is also called *Ephesia* after that region. Just as from its present remedy and help, it is called *Sozusa*, that is, "the Savior" or "the Healthy." The Romans, following the example of the Greeks, called it the "Royal herb"; and if it is to be accepted by resemblance, they called it the "Greater Wild Thyme." This was the nomenclature of Mugwort among the ancients. 

Among later writers, some counted Mugwort among the *Cannabiscere* <note>hemp-like plants</note>, making it a relative to that plant and indicating it by the same name. Others have testified that Mugwort is "Feverfew" [*Matricaria*], a pot-herb known to everyone. This, we believe, happened for no other reason than its double nature. For the plant which is called *Monoclonos* <note>single-stemmed</note> by this writer, or "of a single stem" by Pliny, is described as being not entirely dissimilar in shape to hemp, especially because of the unique stem it produces. Conversely, the type which is handed down by this and other authors as being shrubby in the manner of wormwood could easily be transferred to the Feverfew [*Matricaria*] of our world and our age, because of the powers it possesses. Even if the Greek history regarding Mugwort does not entirely correspond to this, nor can it be confirmed by any certain author, it should not be entirely rejected. For it is outstanding for women. I speak now of "women’s matters," which the Greeks call *gynecaeia* <note>original: "γυναικεῖα"</note>. The power of Mugwort was treated by us at greater length under the entry for Sweet Flag [*Acorus*]. It must be believed that the later name "Feverfew" [*Matricaria*] was given by later people for no other reason than its effect on the wombs <note>original: "matricibus"; the root of the name *Matricaria*</note>.

### On its Temperament.

All its species heat in the second degree and dry either in the full first degree or at the beginning of the second; they are of moderately thin parts.

# MEDICINES of Simple Substances

<margin>C</margin>
### Its Virtues and Benefits according to Dioscorides, Book 3.

When Mugwort [Artemisia] is appropriately boiled, it is used for women's exhaustion and applied to draw out the menses, to assist in labor, and to expel the placenta <note>original: "secundas"; the afterbirth</note>. It is likewise used for obstructions of the womb and for inflammations of the same. It breaks down stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> and stimulates suppressed urine. When smeared upon the pubic area, it drives forth the menses. The juice of the plant, applied to the womb with myrrh, has the same effect as a seated bath. Three drachms <note>a unit of weight, roughly 3.5 grams</note> of the foliage are taken in a drink for the sake of drawing out these same fluids.

### FROM APULEIUS.

If anyone traveling on a journey carries the "single-stalk" Mugwort herb with them in their hand, they will not feel the labor of the road. It also puts demons to flight, and when placed in the home, it blocks "evil medicines" <note>likely referring to harmful charms or poisons</note> and averts the "evil eye" of wicked men. When pounded with lard <note>original: "axungia"; pig fat used as an ointment base</note> and applied, it removes pain in the feet. Also, when crushed and reduced to a powder and given in a drink with honey-water <note>original: "aqua mulsa"</note>, it soothes the pain of the intestines.

### FROM PLATEARIUS.

Mugwort is called the "Mother of Herbs"; it is hot and dry in the fourth degree <note>the highest intensity in the humoral system of medicine</note>. Its leaves are more suitable for medical use than the roots, and green leaves are better than dried ones. It is effective against sterility caused by excess moisture; for if the sterility were caused by dryness, the herb would be harmful. These conditions can be sufficiently weighed by the constitution of the women—namely, whether she is stout or thin. It is given as an electuary <note>a medicinal paste made with honey or sugar</note> with powdered bistort, nutmeg, and sugar. However, it is more beneficial if the patient is bathed in water in which Mugwort and laurel leaves have been cooked. To provoke the menses, let a pessary be made from it, or a decoction.

<margin>D</margin> Against tenesmus <note>original: "tenasmonem"; the distressing and constant urge to evacuate the bowels</note>, let the patient receive the smoke of resin <note>original: "colophoniae"</note> placed upon coals through the anus; then let the physician heat Mugwort upon a roof-tile, and once heated, let it be placed upon a millstone, and let the sick person sit upon it. This is a proven remedy. Against the glands <note>likely hemorrhoids or abscesses</note> that arise near the anus, let a small incision <note>original: "scarificatio"</note> first be made around them; afterward, let the powder of Mugwort and Horehound [Marrubium] be applied. Against a migraine, let some opiate be given with warm water, or with wine from a decoction of Mugwort.

### FROM GIOVANNI DI VIGO.

Mugwort is of a hot and dry temperament around the third degree. Its power is to comfort the "nervous parts" <note>original: "loca nervosa"; referring to tendons, ligaments, or the nervous system</note>. When boiled with wine and pain-relieving substances <note>original: "anodinis"</note> and administered in the form of an epithem <note>a liquid poultice or compress</note> with a sponge, or used as a wash made from its decoction as described above, it most powerfully comforts the nervous parts with a certain soothing effect. It also works wonderfully for tenesmus caused by cold, in this manner: Take powdered resin, with cypress nut, and a little frankincense; then place the powder upon glowing coals and receive the smoke. Afterward, have a proper quantity of Mugwort, fresh and heated on a tile, having first been sprinkled with astringent <note>original: "stiptico"</note> wine; let the patient sit upon this, because it wonderfully soothes the tenesmus, and it is a tested medicine.

### FROM HIERONYMUS THE HERBALIST.

Mugwort water induces sleep. Applied as an ointment, it makes the beard grow. It wipes away "moths of the head" <note>original: "tineas"; referring to scalp conditions like ringworm or scabs</note>. It expels jaundice. It cures the beginning stages of dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note>. It comforts the stomach and the chest. Applied as a rub, it cools weariness and exhausted limbs. Taken as a drink at a weight of 1 ounce, it accelerates childbirth. Taken at a weight of 3 ounces, it expels a dead fetus. It also represses and drives away "evil accidents" <note>complications</note>, tumors, and other things that usually happen to women around their private parts. It mitigates a cough when drunk morning and evening. It draws out urine and stones. It opens obstructed kidneys. It is also a unique antidote against poisons.

### CONTENTS of the following
### Appendix.

**On the use and administration of <term>Simples</term>.** <note>original: "Simplicium." A "simple" is a medicinal herb or plant used on its own, as opposed to a "compound" medicine made of many ingredients.</note>
Those who first wrote on the use of herbs, and their discovery. Concerning ancient Medicine. And why their remedies are practiced less today.
**Praise of Agriculture.**
The study of agriculture among the <term>Ancients</term>. <note>original: "Veteres," referring to the Greek and Roman authorities.</note>
Illustrious cultivators of fields and gardens in Rome.
Praise of farmers, and what must be observed in preparing the field.
**The care of Gardens.**
The method of watering gardens, and which things fare better when transplanted. Concerning the juices and flavors of garden plants.
**On the diseases of gardens, and remedies regarding ants and gnats.**
How the qualities of herbs are to be investigated from their color, scent, and juices.
At which times herbs are especially to be gathered.
**On the various differences between herbs.**
Differences of seeds, juices, scents, flavors, trees, flowers, etc.
Differences of roots.
Differences and types of grapevines.
Classes of temperaments.
The <term>degrees</term> of herbs. <note>Medicinal plants were classified by "degrees" (1st through 4th) of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness.</note>
Various operations and effects of herbs.
**Table of medicines and venomous animals.**
Table of edibles.
Three tables of <term>cathartics</term>. <note>Medicines used to purge the bowels.</note>
Table of evacuants.
Table of restoratives. <note>original: "Confortatiuorum," medicines intended to strengthen the heart or spirit.</note>
Table of digestives.
Table of those things which are suitable for individual body parts.
**On the division of Humors and Qualities, Table 1.** <note>The four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—were believed to control human health and temperament.</note>
Table of Natural Things.

## On the use and administration of <term>Simples</term>, by the same
### OTTO BRUNFELS.

<margin>A</margin>
Since every discipline consists primarily of three things—namely, instruction, use, and imitation—this is especially true in the medical art. Indeed, the practical use of things is so vital that if you do not know how to handle and apply what you have learned with much sweat, you will not only fail to produce any fruit, but you will even err to the peril of many. Therefore, I believe I am doing something worthwhile if, after providing the identification and powers of herbs, I also prescribe some method for them: specifically, what aids those who are to administer them to the suffering should rely upon, and what path they should follow. For we see that even great physicians stumble here—to say nothing of <term>quacks</term> <note>original: "agyrtas," referring to traveling herbalists or street healers of low reputation</note> and <term>empirics</term> <note>Healers who relied solely on experience rather than theoretical medical education</note>, let alone the common folk who have no knowledge of these matters. When these people occasionally attack diseases with simple medicines, they achieve so little that they actually make the diseases worse at great cost to the patients, rendering them hopeless and incurable. 

And I do not know if there is any other more destructive plague in medicine than this: that with the reasoning of philosophy and its first elements ignored, certain fools and "Thessalian asses" <note>An ancient proverbial expression for a person who is both stupid and stubborn</note> offer any drink to anyone, for any reason, with no judgment applied. They fail to consider the circumstances: which sex, what time of year, what age, in what location, and for which specific disease each remedy should be administered. The result is that they not only fail to achieve the desired effects, but they even expose the art of medicine itself to ridicule. I have no doubt that all the current contempt for medicine by "Simples" crept in because, when results did not immediately satisfy the stupidity of these foolish men, they blamed the "vanity" of science and nature rather than their own ignorance. Indeed, it might have been better if no herbals had been written at all until now, since they have led so many to their end. It is important, therefore, to contemplate the effects of Simple things just as one does with <term>Compound</term> drugs: not only what the herb itself promises in a book, but also at what time it was cultivated, in what place it grew, when it was collected, how it was preserved, how much strength it has when green and succulent versus when dried and parched, what its <term>temperament</term> is <note>The balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities</note>, and in what proportion it should be administered. 

<margin>B</margin>
Although the books of physicians are full of these matters, I shall state each point briefly, so that whoever reads our work may be reminded of almost everything that others pursue in long-winded commentaries. This is done in a new style of writing, specifically through tables. This method, besides being exceedingly useful, is also succinct and very pleasing; consequently, it is more easily remembered. However, before we present these tables, we shall first set forth a few things from Pliny, Dioscorides, Theophrastus, Varro, and Columella regarding rural matters and the cultivation of gardens. For all these things prepare the way for an exact knowledge of herbs. Although these things are well known to learned Doctors, they are a significant help to those who are constrained by a lack of books. Otherwise, there would have been no need to cite authors at all in this entire work, since I have transcribed everything from other authors. As I have warned several times before, and now testify again, I prefer to candidly admit whose work I have benefited from, rather than to transcribe authors word-for-word in my own "scribbling" style without naming them. Yet today, some do exactly that; by suppressing the glory of the ancients (who nevertheless wrote far better and more learnedly) and making the labors of others their own, they are called the "lights of Germany." I too could have attempted some tragic deception of this kind, were it not the mark of a base mind and an unhappy talent—as Pliny says—to prefer being caught in a theft than to repay a loan, especially when the principal grows from interest. But leaving contention aside, let us proceed to our <term>Isagoge</term> <note>original: "Isagogen," a Greek term for an introductory manual or primer</note>.

OUR people [the Romans] celebrated this study less than was fitting, though they were most greedy for all useful things and virtues. The first, and for a long time the only one, was Marcus Cato, the teacher of all good arts, who touched upon it only briefly. Even the medicines for oxen were not omitted by him. After him, one of the illustrious men, C. Valgius—a man of respected erudition—attempted it in an unfinished volume dedicated to the Divine Augustus. He even began a religious preface, praying that the majesty of that prince might always heal all human ills. Before him, as far as I have found, only Pompeius Lenaeus (a freedman of Pompey the Great) had composed a work among us, at which time I notice this science first reached our people. For...

# A P P E N D I X

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Mithridates</margin>
¶ Mithridates, the greatest of the kings of his age, whom Pompey <note>Pompey the Great, the Roman general who defeated Mithridates in 66 BCE.</note> defeated, is understood—through evidence as much as by fame—to have been the most diligent seeker of life among all who were born before him. He alone devised the practice of drinking poison every day, having first taken remedies, so that by the habit itself the poison would become harmless. He was the first to discover types of <term>antidotes</term>, one of which still retains his name. They say it was his invention to mix the blood of Pontic ducks into antidotes because they lived on poisonous food. There exist volumes composed for him by Asclepiades, a man famous in the medical art, who, when summoned from the city of Rome, sent these instructions to the king instead. It is certain that Mithridates alone among mortals spoke twenty-two languages; during the fifty-six years of his reign, he never addressed any man from the subject nations through an interpreter. Therefore, being uniquely curious about medicine alongside his other great talents, he sought out individual secrets from the subjects who inhabited a large part of the world, leaving behind a chest of these commentaries, specimens, and their effects in his private archives. When Pompey gained possession of all the royal plunder, he ordered his <term>freedman</term> <note>A former slave who had been granted his freedom; Lenaeus was a noted scholar in Pompey's household.</note> Lenaeus, a man most learned in the grammatical art, to translate these into our language <note>original: "sermone nostro" – meaning Latin.</note>. Thus, that victory benefited human life no less than it benefited the Republic. Besides these, the Greek authors have recorded medical matters, whom we have mentioned in their proper places.

<margin>Euax</margin>
Among these was Euax, the King of the Arabs, who wrote to Nero regarding the effects of <term>simples</term> <note>Medicinal plants used on their own, rather than as part of a complex mixture.</note>. Also Crateias, Dionysius, and Metrodorus, who used a most charming method, though one through which little else is understood than the difficulty of the subject. For they painted likenesses of the herbs and wrote their effects underneath. However, a picture is deceptive because of the vast number of colors, especially when attempting to rival nature; furthermore, the varying skill of those who copy the drawings causes much degeneration from the original. Moreover, it is not enough to paint a plant in only one stage of its life, since the appearance of the year changes with fourfold variety. For this reason, other authors described them in words. Some, having indicated the likeness, satisfied themselves with providing only the names, as it seemed sufficient to demonstrate the powers and force of the plant to those willing to seek them out. Nor is this difficult to learn.

<margin>Antonius Castor</margin>
It was our good fortune, with a very few exceptions, to contemplate the rest of these plants through the knowledge of Antonius Castor. He held the highest authority in that art in our age. We visited his small garden, in which he nurtured a great many plants. He had passed his hundredth year of age, having experienced no bodily ailment, and neither his memory nor his vigor were shaken by his years. Nothing else will be found that antiquity admired more. A method was discovered long ago for predicting the hours—not only the days and nights—of the eclipses of the sun and moon. Yet, a persistent belief remains among a large part of the common people that this is compelled by sorcery and herbs, and that the knowledge of women prevails in this matter. Indeed, have not Medea of Colchis and others filled the world with fables, and especially the Italian Circe, who was even numbered among the gods?

<margin>D</margin>
From this, I believe, arose the report by Aeschylus (one of the most ancient in the poetic art) that Italy was filled with the power of herbs. Many cite the fields of Circeii, where Circe lived, as a great piece of evidence that still endures among the Marsi <note>An ancient Italian people famed for their skill as snake-charmers and healers.</note>, who are said to be descended from her son and are known to be tamers of serpents.

<margin>Homer</margin>
Homer, the first parent of all learning and antiquity, while admiring Circe in many other ways, attributed the glory of herbs to Egypt—even at a time when that land was being watered by the Nile, before it was formed by the river's silt. He recounts that many Egyptian herbs were given to Helen by the wife of the king, as well as that noble <term>Nepenthes</term> <note>original: "Nepenthes," a legendary medicine used to banish grief and anger.</note>, which brings the forgetting of sadness and anger, and which Helen was to offer to all mortals to drink. However, the first of all whom memory records to have published anything more curiously regarding these herbs was Orpheus. After him, Musaeus and Hesiod—we have already mentioned how much they admired the herb <term>Polion</term> <note>A Mediterranean herb, possibly *Teucrium polium*, believed to have magical or protective properties.</note>. Orpheus and Hesiod recommended <term>fumigations</term> <note>The use of smoke from burning herbs for medicinal or ritual purification.</note>. Homer also celebrates other herbs by name, which we shall speak of in their own places. After him, Pythagoras, famous for his wisdom, was the first to compose a volume on their effects, assigning their discovery and origin to Apollo, Aesculapius, and the immortal gods in general. Democritus also composed works, both of them having traveled through Persia, Arabia, Ethiopia, and especially Egypt.

<margin>The incredible power of herbs</margin>
Indeed, antiquity was so awestruck by these things that it even affirmed things incredible to say. Xanthus, an author of histories, recorded in his first book that a killed dragon cub <note>In this context, "draco" or dragon often refers to a large serpent.</note> was recalled to life by its parent using a herb which he calls *Balin*; he also records that by the same herb, Tillon, whom the dragon had killed, was restored to health. Juba also records that a man in Arabia was recalled to life by a herb. Democritus said, and Theophrastus believed, that there is a herb such that if a wedge driven into a tree by shepherds is touched by it (brought by the bird we mentioned), the wedge would jump out. Even if these stories lack credibility, they fill us with wonder and force us to confess that much truth remains hidden. Hence, I see that many think nothing can be achieved by the power of herbs, but rather that the powers of most are simply unknown. Among their number was Herophilus, famous in medicine, who is said to have remarked that some herbs might even be beneficial just by being trodden upon. It has certainly been observed that wounds and diseases are inflamed by the arrival of those who have traveled on foot. This was the ancient medicine, which migrated entirely into the Greek languages. 

But why do more discoveries not arise now? Unless it is because only the rustic and those ignorant of letters experience them, as they are the only ones living among the plants. Furthermore, there is a lack of concern for searching because of the crowd of doctors available. Many things have been discovered that lack names, like the one we mentioned for the care of crops, which we know protects the grain if buried in the corners of the field so that no bird enters. The most shameful cause of this scarcity is that even those who know will not show others, as if what they have passed on to others would then be lost to themselves. Added to this is the uncertain nature of discovery. For even among things already found, some causes were discovered by man, while others (to speak truly) were discovered by God. Until these years, the bite of a mad <note>The text ends mid-sentence at "rabidi," likely referring to a mad dog or rabies.</note>

<margin>The Wild Rose</margin>
Recently, the mother of a soldier serving in the praetorian guard <note>The elite unit of the Roman Imperial Army.</note> saw in a dream that she should send her son a drink made of the root of the wild rose (which they call *cynorrhodos* <note>original: "cynorrhodon". From the Greek for "dog-rose," as it was believed to cure rabies.</note>), which she had been charmed by the sight of in a thicket the day before. This happened in Lusitania [modern Portugal], in the part closest to Spain. It happened by chance that while the soldier, from the bite of a dog, was beginning to fear water, a letter arrived from his mother begging him to obey this religious vision. He was saved beyond all hope, and so was anyone else who tried a similar remedy later. Previously, according to authors, the only medicine from the wild rose was the ash of the little sponges <note>original: "spongiolae". These are mossy galls caused by wasps, often called "Robin's pincushion".</note> that grow in the middle of its thorns, mixed with honey to treat hair loss. In the same province, 
<margin>Dragon-herb</margin>
I learned that in the field of a host, a plant called *dracunculus* <note>original: "dracunculus". Likely the Dragon Arum (*Dracunculus vulgaris*), known for its mottled, snake-like stem.</note> had recently been found. It has a stem the thickness of a thumb, with multi-colored spots like a viper's, which they said was a remedy against all bites. There is another of the same name which we mentioned in the previous volume, but this one has a different shape and another wonder: it comes out of the earth at the first molting of serpents, reaching nearly two feet in height, and hides itself in the earth again when they do. While it is hidden, no serpent appears at all; this alone would be a helpful gift of nature, if it only warned us and showed the time of danger.

### ¶ Another praise of herbs, from the same Pliny, Book Twenty-Seven, Chapter One.

My admiration for antiquity certainly grows through this very treatment. The more plants remain to be discussed, the more I am moved to adore the care of the ancients in discovering them and their kindness in passing them down. Without a doubt, the generosity of Nature herself could seem surpassed in this way, if it were an invention of human labor. But now it is clear that it was a work of the gods, or certainly divine, even when a human discovered it; and that the mother of all [Nature] gave birth to these and showed them, with no greater miracle of life, if we wish to admit the truth. The Scythian herb from the Maeotian marshes <note>The Sea of Azov region.</note>, and *Euphorbia* <note>Spurge.</note> from Mount Atlas beyond the Pillars of Hercules [Gibraltar], and in another part, the British herb from the islands of the Ocean placed outside the lands at the very edge of Nature's reach; likewise the Ethiopian herb from the region scorched by the stars—these and others are carried from here and there for human health throughout the whole world. By the immense majesty of the Roman peace <note>original: "Romanę pacis". The *Pax Romana*, a long period of relative peace and stability across the Roman Empire that facilitated the exchange of knowledge and goods.</note>, not only do men from different lands and nations show these to one another, but even the mountains, the peaks reaching into the clouds, the pastures of the flocks, and the herbs themselves are displayed in turn. I pray that this gift of the gods may be eternal. Indeed, the Romans seem to have given a second light to human affairs.

### ¶ ON THE PRAISE OF AGRICULTURE, FROM MARCUS CATO at the beginning of his work.

<margin>
B
,,
,,
</margin>
It is sometimes better to seek wealth for the people through trade, if it were not so dangerous; and likewise to lend money at interest, if it were so honorable. For our ancestors held it thus, and so placed it in the laws, that a thief should be condemned to pay double, but a usurer fourfold. From this, one can judge how much worse a citizen they considered a usurer to be than a thief. And when they praised a good man, they praised him thus: as a "good farmer" and a "good husbandman." He who was praised in this way was thought to be most amply praised. I consider a merchant to be energetic and eager to seek profit, but, as I said above, it is a dangerous and calamitous life. But from farmers, the bravest men and the most energetic soldiers are born; from them comes a gain that is most pious and stable, least liable to envy, and those occupied in that pursuit are least likely to think evil thoughts.

### ¶ That Agriculture was the greatest pursuit of the ancients, and concerning the singular diligence of gardens, from Pliny, Book 18, Chapter 1.

Next follows the nature of crops, gardens, and flowers, and whatever other things besides trees or shrubs come forth from the kind earth, simply through the immense contemplation of herbs—if anyone should estimate their variety, number, flowers, scents, colors, juices, and the powers which she brings forth for the sake of human health or pleasure. In this part, it is pleasing first of all to act as a protector for the Earth and to stand by the parent of all things, even though she was defended at the beginning of this work. However, since the material itself inwardly sparks a reflection on that same parent and her harms, we press charges against her for our own crimes and attribute our own fault to her. She brought forth poisons, but who discovered them except man? It is enough for birds and wild beasts to beware and flee from them. And while elephants sharpen and file their horns against trees, and the rhinoceros against hard rock, and boars sharpen the daggers <note>original: "sicas". Short, curved daggers.</note> of their teeth—and while animals know how to prepare themselves to do harm—which of them, except man, dips his weapons in poison? We both...

<margin>C</margin>
...we smear our arrows with poison, and we give to iron itself something more harmful than the blade. We even infect the rivers and the very elements of nature. The very air we breathe, we turn toward our own destruction. Nor should we think that nature's secrets are hidden from the animals; indeed, we have already pointed out those creatures which prepare themselves against combat with serpents, and those which devise remedies for healing themselves after a battle. No animal fights with a poison that is not its own, except for man. Let us, therefore, confess our fault, for we are not even content with the poisons that grow naturally: for how many more types of them are manufactured by human hands? What then? Are not some men even born to be poisons? The dark tongue of such men flickers like a serpent's; their soul's rot burns whatever it touches, finding fault with everything, like birds of ill omen. They envy the darkness and the quiet of the very nights with their moaning (which is their only voice), so that like ill-omened creatures, they prevent others from acting or being useful in life. They know no other reward for their loathsome spirit than to hate all things. But even in this, the same majesty of nature has produced so many more good and worthy men, just as she is more fertile in those things which help and nourish us. Out of respect and joy for these good men, let us also—leaving behind those crowds of men agitated by their own heat—proceed to cultivate life, and do so all the more constantly as the gratitude for our labor and fame is more greatly sought. Indeed, our discourse concerns the countryside and rustic practices, things which held the greatest life and honor among the ancients.

## Regarding those who were illustrious in the care of fields and
## gardens in Rome, from Pliny's
## eighteenth book,
## chapter three.

**WHAT WAS** the cause of such great abundance back then? In those days, the fields were cultivated by the hands of the Emperors themselves <note>Pliny uses "Emperors" or "Commanders" (Imperatores) to refer to the great leaders of the early Roman Republic.</note>—as it is right to believe—the earth rejoicing under a laurel-decked plowshare and a triumphal plowman. Either those men handled seeds with the same care they used in war, and laid out their fields with the same diligence they used for military camps, or perhaps all things grow more happily under honest hands, because they are also done more attentively. When honors were granted to Serranus, they found him sowing, which is where his surname comes from <note>Serranus is derived from the Latin *serere*, meaning "to sow."</note>. While Cincinnatus was plowing his four acres on the Vatican—which are called the Quintian Meadows—a messenger brought him the news of his appointment to the Dictatorship; and indeed (as Norbanus relates), his mouth was still bare and covered in dust. To him the messenger said, "Cover your body, so that I may deliver the mandates of the Senate and the Roman people." In those days, even the messengers were of such a kind, given that very name <note>original: "viator". Literally "traveler" or "wayfarer," these were official attendants who summoned senators from their country estates.</note> because they frequently summoned the Senate and its leaders from the fields. <margin>D</margin> But now, those same fields are worked by feet in shackles, by hands that are condemned, and by faces that are branded <note>original: "inscripti uultus". Referring to the practice of branding the foreheads of slaves who had attempted to escape.</note>. Yet the earth is not deaf; she is called our parent, and she herself is said to be cultivated, taking honor from it. Thus, it is believed that now she produces her bounty unwillingly and with indignation. We wonder why the profit from slave-prisons <note>original: "ergastulorum". These were private prisons on Roman estates where slaves worked in chains.</note> is not the same as it was from Emperors. Therefore, giving instruction on the cultivation of the field was a primary concern even among foreign nations. Indeed, kings have done so, such as Hiero, Philometor, Attalus, and Archelaus; as well as generals like Xenophon, and even Mago the Carthaginian. Our Senate attributed such great honor to Mago that, after the capture of Carthage, when they gave the libraries away to the minor kings of Africa, they decreed that his twenty-eight volumes <note>original: "duodeteriginta uolumina". Mago’s work was considered the "Bible" of ancient agriculture.</note> alone should be translated into the Latin language (although Marcus Cato had already composed his own precepts), and the task was given to those skilled in the Punic tongue. In this task, Decimus Silanus, a man of a most illustrious family and composed wisdom, surpassed all others. We follow those whom we have listed in this volume, not forgetting to name Marcus Varro, who, while in the eighty-first year of his life, thought it necessary to set down his knowledge on this subject.

## Praise of Farmers, and what things must be observed in
## preparing a field, from Pliny's 18th book,
## chapter five.

<margin>,,</margin>
<margin>,,</margin>
**THE BRAVEST** men and the most energetic soldiers are born from farmers, and they think the least evil thoughts. Do not buy an estate greedily. In rural matters, do not spare labor, and in buying a field, spare it even less. One always regrets a bad purchase. For those about to prepare a field, it is necessary above all to look at the force of the waters and the neighbors. Each of these has great and clear interpretations. Cato orders that among neighbors, one should further estimate how they "shine." "In a good region," he says, "things shine well." The famous Attilius Regulus, twice consul during the Punic War, used to say that one should neither buy an unhealthy field in the most fertile places, nor a healthy one in exhausted soil. The healthiness of a place is not always revealed by the complexion of the inhabitants, because those who are accustomed to it can endure in pestilential spots. Furthermore, some places are healthy during certain parts of the year, but nothing is truly healthy unless it is healthy all year round. A field is bad when the owner must wrestle with it. Cato orders that among the first things to be seen is whether the soil is strong in its own merit and in its position. See that there is a supply of laborers nearby and a strong town; that there is transport by ships or roads; and that it is well-built and cultivated. I see that many are deceived in this. For they think the laziness of the previous owner will be to the buyer's advantage. Nothing is more ruinous than a deserted field. Therefore, Cato says it is better to buy from a good owner, and that the discipline of others should not be rashly despised; for a field is like a man: no matter how profitable it may be...

-># APPENDIX<-

A 3
<meta>catchword: perspective</meta>

<margin>A</margin>
...though it may be costly, not much remains. That man <note>Cato the Elder</note> judges the vineyard to be the most profitable part of a farm; and not without reason, since above all things he took care to account for the expenses. Next, he favors irrigated gardens; and this is not incorrectly judged, provided they are near a town. Then come the meadows, which the ancients called "ready lands" <note>original: "parata"</note>. The same Cato, when asked what was the most certain source of gain, replied: "To feed cattle well." What was next? "To feed them moderately well." The point of all his observation was that a crop should be most approved when it can be produced with the least expense. This is decided differently in different places depending on the opportunities of the location. To this same point belongs his saying that a farmer ought to be a seller rather than a buyer. A farm should be acquired in one’s youth without hesitation, but one should not build upon it until the field is fully planted. Even then, one should build only with hesitation; it is best, as the common saying goes, "to enjoy another man’s madness" <note>This refers to buying a lavish estate that someone else spent a fortune building and then went bankrupt over</note>, provided that the maintenance of the villas is not a burden. Nevertheless, they say truly that he who lives well visits his fields often; and that the master's presence <note>original: "fontem," likely a variant of "frontem" (forehead/face), meaning the master’s gaze or face is more useful than the back of his head</note> is more profitable than the back of his head.

### On the care of gardens, according to other teachings from Pliny, Book 19, Chapter 4.

From these matters, it remains to return to the care of gardens, a subject noteworthy by its very nature. Antiquity admired nothing more than the gardens of the Hesperides <note>The mythical garden of golden apples</note>, and those of the kings Adonis and Alcinous, as well as the hanging gardens, whether they were made by Semiramis or the Assyrian king Cyrus, whose works we shall discuss in another volume. Indeed, the Roman kings themselves cultivated the earth. For even Tarquin the Proud sent back that cruel and bloody message <note>The story of Tarquin striking the tallest poppies to signal the execution of leaders</note> from his garden. In the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law</note> of our laws, the word "villa" is never used; it is always "garden" <note>hortus</note> in that sense, and the word for "garden" refers to the hereditary estate. This matter was accompanied by a certain religious awe: we see gardens and doorways dedicated specifically as protections against the fascinations of the envious. For a remedy, statues of Saturn are used, although Plautus assigns gardens to the protection of Venus. Nowadays, under the name of "gardens," people possess luxuries, fields, and villas within the city itself. Epicurus, the master of gardens, first instituted this at Athens. Until his time, it had not been the custom to have rural estates in towns. In Rome, the garden was by itself the poor man’s field. From the garden came the market-goods for the common people—and how much more innocent a diet that was! For I believe it is better to be submerged in the depths and to seek out types of oysters through shipwreck, or to seek birds beyond the Phasis river <note>Modern Rioni River, famous for pheasants</note>, which are safe due to fabled terrors and thus more precious. Others hunt in the tombs of Numidia and Ethiopia, or fight with wild beasts, desiring to be eaten by that which another man eats. But by Hercules, what things these are, and how ready for pleasure and satiety they would be, if the same indignation did not meet us everywhere? It might be bearable that exquisite fruits are born—some for flavor, others for size, others for their monstrous shape—which are forbidden to the poor; or that wines are aged and "castrated" <note>original: "castrari," meaning to filter wine through linen to remove its strength/body</note> by strainers; and that no one's life is long enough that he does not drink wine born before him. From the grains, too, luxury has devised a certain nourishment, living only on the "marrow" of them <note>The finest white flour</note>, and on the works and engravings of bakeries, some eating the bread of the nobles and others that of the commoners, with the price of grain descending through so many types even to the lowest plebeians. Has a distinction even been found among herbs? Wealth has created a difference in food, even for a single penny's worth. Even among these, they deny that certain plants grow for the common tribes, and the stalks <note>cabbage or kale</note> are so fattened that a poor man’s table cannot hold them. Nature had made wild asparagus <note>original: "corrudas"</note> so that anyone might harvest them anywhere. But look! Now we see "fattened" asparagus. And Ravenna pays back three pounds' weight for one. Alas, the prodigies of the stomach! It would be a wonder if cattle were not allowed to eat thistles, yet the common people are not allowed. Even waters are separated. The very elements of nature are divided by money. These people drink snow, those drink ice, and they turn the punishments of the mountains into a pleasure for the throat. Coldness is preserved for the summer heats, and it is devised so that snow may stay cold in months not its own. They boil some waters, which they then soon turn into winter-chill. Nothing, therefore, pleases man in the way that nature intended. Shall even a herb be born only for the wealthy? Will no one look back at the Sacred and Aventine hills, and the secessions of the angry plebeians? For death will certainly make equal those whom money has placed above others. And so, by Hercules, no tax of the market was greater in ROME than the outcry of the plebeians accusing all the leaders, until the tax on this merchandise was remitted; it was found that the census was not more profitably or safely held, nor with less right of fortune, than when that payment was believed to be the poor man’s tax. The garden is a guarantor in the soil; it pays its return under the open sky, rejoicing in the surface of the earth and any heaven above. CATO praises the stalks <note>cabbages</note> of the gardens. From this, the ancient farmers were first judged; they immediately formed the judgment that a mistress of the house <note>original: "matremfamilias"</note> was worthless (for this was said to be the woman's care) where the garden was neglected. For then one must live from the meat-rack or the market; and they did not approve of stalks as much as we do now, condemning side-dishes <note>pulmentaria</note> that required another side-dish to be palatable. That was to spare the oil. For cravings for meat were even considered a cause for reproach. Gardens were most pleasing because they did not require fire and they saved on wood. It was a thing ready and always prepared, which is why they were called <term>acetaria</term> <note>Salads served with vinegar (acetum)</note>; they are easy to digest, not burdening the senses with food, and they least excite a craving for bread. The part of them pertaining to seasonings admits that resourcefulness used to be found at home; Indian pepper was not sought, nor those things we seek from across the seas. Now, even the urban plebeians, in their windows, provide a daily countryside to their eyes with the image of gardens, before the <note>Text cuts off</note> view is blocked...
