# APPENDIX

<margin>C</margin> In many cases, the cruelest necessity of the masses has gathered together an innumerable variety of plants. For this reason, let these plants also receive some honor, lest their commonness strip away their authority—especially since we see that even the surnames of the nobility were born from them. For example, the Valerius family was not ashamed to be called "the Lettuce-men" <note>original: "Lactucinos," a branch of the Valerian clan named after *lactuca* (lettuce)</note>. May some favor fall upon our work and care, following Virgil’s own admission that it is difficult to bestow the honor of fine words upon such humble things. There is no doubt that gardens should be joined to the villa, and they must especially be kept well-watered if a flowing stream is available. If not, they must be irrigated by water from a well using a pole-and-bucket <note>original: "pertica," a simple lever system</note>, pneumatic machines, or a "swipe" <note>original: "tollenonum," a counterweighted sweep used to lift water</note>. The soil should be broken up starting with the west wind <note>the *Favonius*, marking the start of spring</note>; it must be prepared for autumn after fourteen days and turned over again before the winter solstice. It is considered a fair day's work to spade eight *iugera* <note>about 5 acres</note> of land. Manure should be mixed with the earth to a depth of three feet and divided into garden beds. These beds should be surrounded by raised, rounded borders, with individual paths and furrows between them to allow both access for the gardener and a path for the flowing water.

In these gardens, some plants are valued for their bulbs, others for their heads, some for their stalks, others for their leaves, and some for both. Some are prized for their seeds, others for their bark, some for their skin or cartilage, others for their flesh, and still others for their fleshy layers. The fruit of some grows in the earth, others outside of it, and some only outside. Certain plants lie flat as they grow, such as gourds and cucumbers. These same plants can also hang, even though they are much heavier than the fruits produced on trees. However, the cucumber is made of a cartilaginous substance. In this plant alone, the rind turns into a wood-like texture upon ripening. Radishes, navews, and turnips are hidden in the earth, as are—in a different manner—elecampane, skirret, and parsnips. Some we call "cane-like" <note>original: "ferulacea"</note>, such as dill and mallows. Indeed, authors report that in Arabia, mallows become tree-like in the seventh month, providing wood for walking sticks immediately. There is also a mallow tree in the estuary of the town of Lixus in Mauretania, where the Gardens of the Hesperides <note>The legendary garden of Hera where golden apples grew</note> are said to have been. It is 200 paces from the ocean, near the shrine of Hercules, which they say was ancient even to the people of Gades <note>modern Cadiz</note>. The tree itself is 20 feet high and so thick that no one can wrap their arms around it. Hemp is considered to be of a similar kind. We shall also call some things "fleshy," such as the sponges <note>likely referring to puffballs or similar fungi</note> that grow in the moisture of meadows. We have already spoken of the toughness of mushrooms within the context of the nature of wood and trees, and of another kind of truffle just a moment ago.

->¶ The method for watering gardens, and which plants<-
->become better when transplanted. Also, concerning<-
->the juices and flavors of garden plants,<-
->from Pliny, Book 19, Chapter 12.<-

<margin>D</margin> The hours for watering these plants are morning and evening, so that the water does not become scorched by the sun. For basil <note>original: "ocimo"</note> alone, noon is also acceptable. It is thought that seeds burst forth most quickly if they are sprinkled with boiling water at the very beginning. Moreover, all plants become better and larger when transplanted, especially leeks and navews. There is also a medicinal quality in transplanting; plants cease to feel injuries, as is the case with chives, leeks, radishes, celery, lettuce, turnips, and cucumbers. However, almost all wild varieties have smaller leaves and stalks but sharper juices—such as savory, oregano, and rue. Only wild dock <note>original: "lapathum"</note> is better than its cultivated counterpart. This unplanted variety is called *rumex* (sorrel), and it grows very vigorously. It is said that once planted, it lasts forever and is never spoiled, especially in soil near water. Its use in food with barley groats <note>original: "ptisana"</note> provides a lighter and more pleasant flavor. The wild variety is useful for many medicines. Indeed, care has omitted nothing; I have even found it recorded in verse that if seeds of leeks, rocket, lettuce, celery, endive, and watercress are tucked into individual hollowed-out pieces of goat dung and planted, they thrive marvelously. Wild plants are understood to be drier and more pungent than cultivated ones. For we must also speak of the differences in juices and flavors, which are perhaps even greater in these plants than in orchard fruits. Savory, oregano, watercress, and mustard are pungent. Wormwood and centaury are bitter. Cucumbers, gourds, and lettuce are watery. Savory alone is purely sharp. Celery, dill, and fennel are both sharp and aromatic. A purely salty flavor is not found in growing plants; otherwise, salt sits on the surface like dust, and only in circles of water—reminding us that the vanity of life is often a mere persuasion. All-heal <note>original: "Panax"</note> gives the flavor of pepper, and even more so does "pepperwort" <note>original: "siliquastrum"</note>, which takes its name from this fact. *Libanotis* <note>rosemary</note> has the scent of frankincense, and *myrrhis* the scent of myrrh. We have already spoken abundantly of all-heal. *Libanotis* is sown from seed in damp, thin, and dewy places. It has a root like alexanders, which is indistinguishable from frankincense. Its use after one year is very healthy for the stomach. Some call it by another name: rosemary. The vegetable "myrrh-chervil" <note>original: "smyrnium"</note> is sown in the same places and tastes of myrrh at the root. The same is true for the sowing of pepperwort. The remaining plants differ from others in scent and flavor, such as dill. So great is the diversity and power of these plants that not only is one thing changed by another, but a scent can even be entirely removed. The smell of celery is removed from cooked dishes by vinegar, but the same celery in bags in a cellar can give a heavy scent to wine. Let this be enough said of garden plants for the sake of food alone. The greatest work of nature remains within them, for so far we have only treated their growth and certain generalities. The true nature of each can only be known through its medicinal effect—a vast and hidden work of the divine, than which no greater can be found. Reason dictated that we should not weave this into every single entry, as the desire for healing belongs to others; it would have led to long delays for both topics had we mixed them. Now each shall stand in its own section, and they can be joined by those who wish to do so.

### ¶ Concerning the diseases of gardens, and remedies regarding ants and gnats, from Pliny, book 19, chapter ten.

<margin>Sabinus Tiro <note>A writer on gardening and a contemporary of Maecenas; he is often cited by Pliny.</note></margin>
Garden plants also experience diseases, just like the other crops of the earth. For instance, Basil <note>original: "Ocimum"</note> kills itself, and it regularly degenerates into Wild Thyme, just as Water-mint turns into Calamint. From the seed of old Cabbage, Turnips are produced. In turn, Cumin is killed from the bottom of its stalk unless it is kept clean. It has a single stalk and a root similar to a bulb, growing only in thin soil. Otherwise, the specific disease of Cumin is the "scab" <note>original: "scabies," likely a fungal blight</note>. Basil also turns pale under the rising of the Dog Star <note>The "Canis ortu" refers to the hottest days of summer (July/August), associated with Sirius.</note>. Indeed, all things turn yellow at the approach of a menstruating woman. Certain types of small beasts also breed within them: gnats in turnips, caterpillars <note>original: "erucae"</note> and little worms in radishes. The same happens to lettuce and greens. In both of these, slugs and snails are also found. Furthermore, there are certain animals that are very easily caught if dung is thrown down, as they hide themselves in it. Sabinus Tiro, in the book *On Gardening* <note>original: "cepuricon," from the Greek *kepourika*</note> which he dedicated to Maecenas, claims that it is not helpful for Rue, Wild Savory <note>original: "cunila"</note>, Mint, or Basil to be touched by iron. He also showed a remedy against ants—not the least destruction of gardens if they are not well-watered—by blocking their holes with sea-ooze or ash. However, they are most effectively killed by the Heliotrope herb. Some also think that water in which raw brick has been dissolved is hostile to them. The "medicines" for Turnips are to sow bitter-vetch <note>original: "siliquas," likely *Vicia ervilia*</note> along with them, just as one sows chickpeas with greens. This keeps away the caterpillars. If these pests have already been born through neglect, the remedy is to sprinkle a decoction of wormwood juice or "houseleek" <note>original: "sedi," also called *aizoum*</note>, a type of herb we have already described. They say that if the seed of greens is soaked in its juice before being sown, the greens will not be liable to any animals. In general, however, caterpillars will not appear if the skull bones of a female horse <note>original: "equino genere foeminae duntaxat"</note> are placed on a stake in the garden. They also say that a river crab hung in the middle of the garden helps against caterpillars and blight. There are those who touch the things they do not want to be liable to these pests with blood-red twigs. Gnats also infest gardens, especially well-watered ones if there are some small trees present.
->These are driven away by burning galbanum.<-

### ¶ Concerning the investigation of the qualities of herbs by their color, scent, and juices, from Pliny’s book 21, chapter seven.

In the times of the Trojans, this study was already held in honor. Indeed, Homer praises these three flowers: the lotus, the saffron-crocus, and the hyacinth. However, the difference in all perfumes, and even herbs, lies in their color, scent, and juice. In scented things, the flavor is rarely anything but bitter; conversely, sweet things are rarely scented. Thus, wines are more scented than grape-musts, and all wild things are more scented than the tasteless ones. The scent of some is sweeter from a distance, but grows dull when moved closer, such as the violet. A fresh rose smells from a distance, but a dry one must be closer. All scents are sharper in the springtime and in the mornings. As the day turns toward the midday hours, the scent grows dull. New growth is also less scented than old. Yet, the sharpest scent of all occurs in midsummer. Roses and saffron are more scented when gathered on clear days, and all things are more scented in hot climates than in cold ones. However, in Egypt, flowers have very little scent because the air is foggy and dewy from the Nile river. Some scents have a heaviness within their sweetness. Some do not smell when green because of excessive moisture, such as the "ox-horn" <note>original: "buceros," a Greek-derived name for Fenugreek</note>, which is Fenugreek. <margin>Buceros, Fenugreek.</margin> Not everyone has a sharp scent without juice, such as the violet, the rose, and saffron. But of those sharp things that lack juice, the scent of all of them is heavy, as in both kinds of lily. Southernwood and Marjoram have sharp scents. In some, only the flower is pleasant, while the remaining parts are inert, such as the violet and the rose. Of garden plants, the most scented are those that are dry, such as rue, mint, celery, and those that grow in dry places. Some are more scented with age, such as quinces; and the same are more scented when picked than on their own roots. Some do not smell unless broken or rubbed. Others do not smell unless the bark is removed. Some, however, only smell when burned, such as frankincense and myrrh. All crushed flowers are more bitter than untouched ones. Some dry ones hold their scent for a long time, such as melilot. Certain plants make the very place they grow more scented, such as the iris—indeed, even the whole tree whose roots it touches. The *Hesperis* <note>Night-scented stock</note> smells more at night, which is how its name was found <note>from the Greek *hesperos*, meaning evening</note>. None of the animals are scented, unless something is said of panthers, if we believe it.

### ¶ At what times herbs are especially to be gathered, from the prologue of DIOSCORIDES.

Truly, one must first take care that each thing is both harvested and stored away at its proper time. For if they are picked or stored out of season, they perform their function either not at all or in a vanishing way. Indeed, they should be harvested during a clear state of the sky. It matters greatly during the gathering if there are either droughts or hostile rains; just as it matters whether the places in which they come forth are sloping, exposed to the winds, well-ventilated, cold, and lacking in water.

# A P P E N D I X
A
B

For in these places <note>referring to mountainous or wild areas mentioned previously</note> their medicinal powers are understood to be far stronger. Conversely, those plants which spring up in flat, moist, and shaded areas, or in other places sheltered from the wind, mostly degenerate and are less potent in their strength. This is even more the case if they are not gathered at the most opportune hours, or if they have withered through weakness. Nor should it be ignored that plants may reach maturity earlier or more quickly due to the early or late nature of a location or the mildness of the year. Some, by their own power, bloom and produce leaves in winter, and certain ones bear flowers twice a year. Therefore, for whoever intends to achieve expertise in these matters, it is necessary to be present when they first sprout from the soil, when they are mature, and when they are aging. For he who has only stood by a budding herb cannot recognize it when it is full-grown; nor will he who has only inspected the adult plant know it when it is newly erupting. Thus it happens that, because of the changed appearance of the leaves, the height of the stalks, and the size of the flowers and seeds, some who have not previously observed these variations of age fall into great error. This is the same cause that deceived several writers who deny that certain herbs—for example, Grass <note>original: "Gramen"</note>, Cinquefoil <note>original: "Quinquefolium"</note>, and Coltsfoot <note>original: "Tussilaginem"</note>—send forth a flower, fruit, or stalk. Therefore, he who goes more often to look at the herbs and their habitats will most surely obtain knowledge of them.

It is also useful to know that among herbaceous medicines, only the types of Hellebore <note>original: "Veratri"</note>—I mean the black and the white—endure for many years; the rest are useless after three years. However, those which abound in branches, such as Topped Lavender <note>original: "Stichas"</note>, Germander <note>original: "Trixago"</note>, Hullwort <note>original: "Polium"</note>, Southernwood <note>original: "Abrotonum"</note>, Sea Wormwood <note>original: "Seriphū"</note>, Wormwood <note>original: "Absinthium"</note>, Hyssop <note>original: "Hyssopum"</note>, and others of that kind pregnant with seed, should be harvested. Flowers should also be gathered before they fall off of their own accord. It is necessary that fruits be shaken out when ripe, and seeds gathered when they begin to dry, before they drop away. The juice of herbs and leaves ought to be drawn out while the stalks are still budding. Milk and "tears" <note>sap or resin</note> should be collected by cutting the stalk during its growth. It is proper to remove roots and gums, or barks, for storage when the herbs are stripped of their leaves. They are also dried after being cleaned right there, in places that do not smell of moisture; but those covered in mud or dust ought to be washed with water. Flowers and all things that exhale a pleasant scent should be stored in small boxes made of lime-wood <note>original: "arculis tiliaceis"</note> that are not covered with any mold. Sometimes seeds are aptly wrapped in paper or leaves so that they may last. For liquid medicines, a denser material is suitable, such as silver, glass, or horn. Earthenware is also adapted for use, provided it is not porous, as is wood, especially that made from boxwood. However, bronze vessels are used for liquid eye medicines which are composed of vinegar, liquid pitch, or cedar oil. It is proper for fat and marrow to be stored in tin vessels.

<meta>This page continues the botanical classification system, moving from the general growth conditions described on the previous page into a formal taxonomy of plant types—trees, shrubs, and herbs—based on the works of ancient authorities like Theophrastus. It organizes plants by their physical structures, habitats, and internal components.</meta>

# A P P E N D I X.

A **TREE** <note>original: "ARBOR"</note> is that which rises from a root with a single trunk <note>original: "caudice"</note>, and is branched, knotty, full of twigs, or is not easily broken apart, such as the Olive, the Vine, and the Fig.
A **SHRUB** <note>original: "Frutex"</note> is that which raises itself from a root with multiple trunks and branches, such as the bramble or the buckthorn <note>original: "paliurus"</note>.
An **HERB** <note>original: "Herba"</note> is that which comes forth from a root with leaves but without a trunk, and bears its seed on a stalk, such as grains and vegetables.

In some, there is also a pit or stone <note>original: "nucleus"</note>.

## ¶ On the distinction of SEEDS.
The last thing in all plants is the seed; this contains within it moisture and innate heat, which, when they cease to be, the seed is left infertile.
In some, the seed lies directly beneath the surrounding cover, such as:
The Palm and the Almond.
Some are covered by flesh.
Some are in pods <note>original: "siliquis"</note>.
Others are in small vessels, such as the Poppy.
Some are in husks <note>original: "folliculis"</note>.
Others lie naked, such as Dill, Coriander, Cumin, and Fennel.
No tree has a naked seed, but it is either covered by flesh, or skin, or a crusty shell, like the acorn.
No tree seed is contained in a vessel <note>referring to a seed capsule or pod</note>.

### ¶ Another difference of TREES.

Certain trees are perpetually fruit-bearing, such as the Assyrian Apple, which others call the Median Apple <note>the Citron</note>; it bears fruit at all hours, with some falling, others ripening, and others still growing beneath. Pliny, Book 12, Chapter 3.

### ¶ Another difference.

Certain trees even clothe their own peoples, such as the Silk-cotton trees <note>original: "Gossampini"</note>. Pliny, Book 12, Chapter 11.
Certain ones are said to "sleep" by the inhabitants.
For some, the leaves never fall, because they are moistened by cold springs and rains, as on the island of Tylos <note>modern-day Bahrain</note>.
In those where the bark is powerful, the trunk remains without flavor, as with wood-cinnamon <note>original: "Xilocinnamum"</note>—that is, the wood of the cinnamon—which is held in low esteem because of the sharp pungency of wild marjoram. On the contrary, the bark is highly prized.
->A Miracle<-
A certain tree is said to be in Chora, one belonging to the Syagri <note>a people of the Arabian peninsula</note>. Pliny says we have heard a wonder about it: that like the Phoenix bird—which is thought to have taken its name from this palm <note>Greek "phoinix" means both palm and phoenix</note>—it dies and is reborn from itself as it was before, full of fruit. Pliny, Book 13, Chapter 4.

### ¶ Another difference: The fruits of certain trees are known, while the trees themselves are unknown.

What the appearance of the Frankincense-bearing tree <note>original: "thuriferae"</note> might be is not yet certain. For Pliny says we have conducted affairs in Arabia, and Roman arms have penetrated a great part of it. Even Gaius Caesar, son of Augustus, sought glory there, yet from him, as far as I know, no Latin description of those trees has been handed down. The accounts of the Greeks vary. Some have reported it has a leaf like a pear, but smaller and of a grassy color. Others say it is like the Mastic tree, with a small shrubby leaf. Some say it is the Terebinth; and this was seen by King Antigonus when a branch was brought to him. King Juba, in those volumes he wrote to Gaius Caesar, son of Augustus, when he was burning with the fame of Arabia, reports that it has a twisted trunk, branches like a maple (especially the Pontic variety), and emits a sap like almond milk; such trees appear in Carmania and were sown in Egypt through the zeal of the reigning Ptolemies. It is certain that the bark is like that of a laurel. Some have said the leaf is similar. And so on in the following parts of Book 12, Chapter 13.

...if God permits. The Ethiopians understand this to be Jupiter. They call him Assabinus <note>Assabinus was a South Arabian and Ethiopian deity, often identified by Roman writers with Jupiter or Dionysus</note>. Forgiveness for harvesting is obtained through the entrails of 44 oxen, goats, and rams. However, it is not permitted before sunrise or after sunset. The priest divides the branches with a spear and sets aside a portion for the god; the merchant stores the rest in wicker baskets. Whatever falls to the Sun is left behind and spontaneously catches fire. Pliny, Book 12, Chapter 19.

Trees and plants also sometimes "abort" <note>fail to reach maturity or bear fruit</note>. We have also found abortions of trees; this happens both from the manner of bearing and from the manner of pruning. Pliny, Book 12, Chapter 2.

### ¶ Another distinction of Roots.
#### OF PLANTS

Some float upon the waters in the manner of duckweed, entirely without any root at all. Such is Malabathrum <note>Cinnamon leaf</note>, the leaf of the Indian Nard, which Dioscorides mentions in his first book.

Some have knotted roots, such as types of Satyrion <note>an orchid</note>, Birthwort <note>original: "Aristolochię"</note>, and all types of bulbs.

Some have tender roots, such as Basil <note>original: "Ozymon"</note>.

Some have very fat roots, such as Asphodel and the Seal of Mary <note>original: "Sigillum Mariæ," likely referring to Black Bryony or Solomon's Seal</note>.

Some have roots that appear almost cut off in the center, such as Valerian and the plant called Devil’s Bit <note>original: "Morsus diaboli," so named because the root ends abruptly as if bitten off</note>.

Some are hairy <note>original: "comatas," literally "maned"</note>.

Some are divided <note>original: "sectas"</note>.

Some are tucked up and short.

Some are immoderately long, of the kind Pliny mentions regarding the Moly <note>a mythical herb with a black root and white flower</note>; he had this brought to him from Campania, dug up over several days from among rocky difficulties, with a root 25 feet long—and even then it was not whole, but broken off. See Pliny, Book 25, Chapter 4.

Read the same distinction regarding trees in Theophrastus, Chapter 7, Book 3.

Some have infinite knots, such as the Wart-wort <note>original: "uerrucaria"</note>.

Some have twisted roots, such as Snakeweed <note>original: "Colubrina"</note> and Tormentil.

Some have only a sharp little root, entirely without any hairs.

Some have white roots, some black, some red, some grain-colored, some yellowish-brown, and some green.

### ¶ Distinction by duration.
#### OF PLANTS

Some last for many years, such as Hellebore <note>original: "Veratrum"</note>, whether the black or the white variety.

Some for two, three, or five years. Squirting Cucumber <note>original: "Elaterium"</note> lasts for a very long time. The Black Chameleon plant lasts 40 years, Centaury no more than 12. Sulfur-wort <note>original: "Peucedanum"</note> and Birthwort last 5 or 6. The wild vine lasts one year if it is kept in the shade.

### ¶ Other distinctions of Plants.

Some are wild, which thrive nowhere better than in the fields, such as Broom <note>original: "Genistę"</note>, Tamarisk <note>original: "Myricę"</note>, and others of that kind.

Some are garden plants, such as Hyssop and Wormwood <note>original: "Absinthiū"</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Some are for crowns <note>coronary plants used for garlands</note>, such as Roses, Lilies, and Everlasting <note>original: "Heliochrysos"</note>. Others are not for crowns.

### ¶ Another distinction from taste
#### OF PLANTS.

Some are in taste:

| | | |
|----------|----------|----------|
| Sweet | Tasteless | |
| Salty | Sour | Bitter |
| Styptic <note>Astringent, causing tissues to contract</note> | Sharp <note>Pungent</note> | Pontic <note>A harsh, tart flavor</note> |

### ¶ Another from the quality of Plants. For they:

| | |
|----------|----------|
| Cool down | Cut <note>Break down thick fluids</note> |
| Dry out | Divide |
| Heat up | Refine <note>original: "Subtiliant"</note> |
| Moisten | Open |
| Glue together | Kill |
| Constrict | Cleanse |
| Impel | Expel |
| Thicken | Cause to rot |

But which ones are of this kind are reviewed below in the "Classes of Temperaments."

### ¶ Another distinction concerning odor
#### OF PLANTS.

Some, because excessive moisture dulls the scent, remain without odor until that moisture is released. Others, on the contrary, have no scent when dry but give off a great odor when green. Some, whether fresh or dry, always breathe out their own proper scent.

<margin>B</margin>
### ¶ On the distinctions of Vines.

The types of vines are multiplied and differ in size, color, tastes, and their berries. For:
> They shine with a purple color.
> They glow rosy, and shine green.
> There are white and black ones, but these are common.
> The "Bumasti" <note>original: "bumasti," meaning "cow-breast" in Greek</note> swell in the manner of breasts.
> Some stretch out with very long finger-like berries <note>original: "dactyli"</note>.
> Others last through the winter, hanging from a knotted ceiling-hook.
> Some are preserved in their own spirit, enclosed in earthenware pots and then in jars, packed with grape-skins poured around them.

To others, the smoke of the forge brings grace—as it does to wines; the authority of Tiberius Caesar gave these vines special glory in the kilns of Africa.

### ¶ On the various types of Vines.

<margin>Pliny, Book 14, Chapter 2.</margin>
Pliny says that Democritus alone thought the types of vines could be counted, claiming to know all those of Greece. Others have handed down that they are innumerable and infinite; this will appear more true from the wines themselves. Indeed, not all can be named, since they are nearly as many as the wines.

Therefore, the Vines are:
Aminean <note>A high-quality Roman vine</note>, and of these some are called:
-> German <-
-> Twin <-
-> Woolly <-
Nomentane: which are also called Reddish.

Some come forth from seed, as do almost the greatest part.

Of these, some are procreated from the seed of a union, others are produced from the earth without any seed at all: Theophrastus, *On the Causes of Plants*, Book 1, Chapter 1.

### ¶ O B S E R V A T I O N.
All those trees which are common to both mountains and plains grow larger and more beautiful to the sight in the plains, but are better for use in both their timber and fruit in the mountains; Pears and Apples being the exceptions.

### ¶ Another distinction regarding the flowering of trees.
Some flower abundantly.
Some very little.
Others are entirely without any flower.
Some flower but do not bear fruit, such as the second species of Juniper.
Some flower very little and show fruit immediately.
For some the buds come forth soon,
For others, more slowly.

Others when mature, such as:

| | |
|---|---|

Some immediately at the start of Spring, such as:

| | |
|---|---|
| Wild Fig | Hawthorn |
| Phillyrea | Turpentine Tree |
| Christ’s Thorn | Chestnut |
| Walnut | |

Others later, such as the Apple.
The latest of all are the Cork-oak, the Whitebeam, the Quadratoria <note>A term for a specific square-cut timber tree, likely a type of Oak or Box.</note>, the Thuya, and the Yew.

### ¶ Another distinction regarding the fruiting of trees.
Trees also vary in the production of their fruit; for some fruit around the summer solstice, such as Dogwoods. Some around the wheat harvest, such as the Turpentine tree. Some in summer, such as the Ash and Maple. Some in autumn, such as the Walnut and types of Pears. Around the setting of the Pleiades <note>original: "vergiliarum occasu." The setting of this star cluster in late autumn was a vital agricultural marker for the Greeks and Romans.</note>, such as the Chestnut and Oak. Some after the setting of the Pleiades, such as the Phillyrea, Holm Oak, Christ’s Thorn, and Hawthorn. Some at the beginning of winter, such as the Nut-tree. Some at the first frosts, such as the Apple. Of all trees, the Juniper, Celastrus, and Holm Oak finish their fruits the latest.

More on this in Theophrastus, Book 3, Chapters 8 and 6.

<meta>This page transitions from the botanical classification of plants (vines, trees, and habitats) to a pharmaceutical appendix. It lists substances—herbs, minerals, and animal products—categorized by their "temperament" or "complexion" (Hot, Cold, Moist, Dry) and the intensity of these qualities measured in four degrees, following the classical medical tradition of Galen and Avicenna.</meta>

### A

**Common Wormwood** <note>original: "Absinthium commune"</note> is hot in the first degree, dry in the second or third, but its juice is hotter.
**Southernwood** <note>original: "Abrotanum"</note> is hot in the third degree, dry in the second.
**Avicenna** <note>The 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina, a primary authority for this text.</note> says it is hot and dry in the second degree.
**Sorrel** <note>original: "Acetosa"</note> is cold in the first degree (others say the third), dry in the second.
**Acacia** is cold in the second degree, dry in the third or second.
**Sweet Flag** <note>original: "Acorus"</note> is hot and dry in the second degree.
**Agaric** <note>original: "Agaricus"; a medicinal fungus from larch trees.</note> is hot in the first degree, dry in the second.

**Vinegar** <note>original: "Acetum"</note> is cold and dry.
**Cultivated Garlic** <note>original: "Allium domesticum"</note> is hot and dry in the third degree.

**Aloe** is hot at the beginning of the second degree, dry in the third.
**Winter Cherry** <note>original: "Alkekengi"</note> is cold and dry in the second degree.
**Marshmallow** <note>original: "Althea"</note> is hot and moist in the first degree.
**Bishop’s Weed** <note>original: "Ameos"</note> is hot and dry in the third degree.
**Amomum** <note>An aromatic spice related to cardamom.</note> is hot and dry in the third degree. **Avicenna** says hot and dry in the second.
**Sweet Almond** <note>original: "Amigdala dulcis"</note> is hot and moist in the first degree.
**Ambergris** <note>original: "Ambra"</note> is hot in the second degree, dry in the first.

**Dill** <note>original: "Anetum"</note> is hot in the third degree, dry at the start of the second.
**Anise** <note>original: "Anisum"</note> is hot and dry in the third degree.
**Watermelon** <note>original: "Anguria"</note> is cold and moist in the second degree; its seed is cold and dry in the first.
**Whey** <note>original: "Aqua lactis"; literally "water of milk."</note> is cold and moist in the first degree.
**Cultivated Hazelnuts** <note>original: "Avellanæ domesticæ"</note> are hot and dry in the first degree; and roasted <note>original: "assatæ"</note> ones are drier.
**Rosemary Flower** <note>original: "Anthos"</note> is hot and dry in the third degree.
**Cultivated Celery** <note>original: "Apium domesticum"</note> is hot at the beginning of the third degree, dry in the middle of the third.
**Gum Ammoniac** <note>original: "Armoniacum"</note> is hot in the third degree, dry in the second.
**Arsenic** <note>original: "Arsenicum"</note> is hot in the third degree, dry in the second.
**Mugwort** <note>original: "Arthemisia"</note> is hot and dry in the second degree.
**Birthwort** <note>original: "Aristologia"</note> is hot in the first degree, dry in the second.
**The Whole Orange** <note>original: "Arancia tota"</note> is cold and moist at the start of the first degree.
**Orange Peel** <note>original: "Arantiæ cortex"</note> is hot and dry in the second degree.
**Orange Acidity** <note>The juice.</note> is cold and moist in the second degree.
**Asafoetida** <note>A pungent resin.</note> is hot and dry in the third degree.
**Asarabacca** <note>original: "Asara baccara"</note> is hot and dry in the third degree.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical appendix of medicinal substances, specifically concluding the letters H and Y, and covering the entire letter Z. It then transitions into a thematic reorganization of the substances based on their Galenic "complexion"—grouping them by their primary qualities of heat and dryness in specific degrees.</meta>

->A P P E N D I X.<-

**St. John’s Wort** <note>original: "Hypericon"</note> is hot and dry in the third degree.
**Hyssop herb** <note>original: "Hysopus herba"</note> is hot and dry in the third degree.
**Moist hyssop** <note>original: "Hysopus humida"</note> is hot in the first degree and moist in the second.

### Z

**Ginger** <note>original: "Zinziber"</note> is hot in the second degree and moist in the first; this applies when it is **fresh**, because when it is **dried** it is dry in the first degree.
**Zedoary** <note>original: "Zedoaria"; a root related to ginger used to treat digestive issues</note> is hot in the third degree and dry in the second.
**Red sugar of one boiling** <note>original: "Zuccarum ru. unius decoctionis"; raw or minimally refined sugar</note> is hot.
**Sugar of two boilings** is hot in the middle of the first degree.
**Sugar of three boilings** is **temperate**; and **Avicenna** <note>the influential 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> says it is "colder," meaning less hot, because through the process of boiling, the thin, hot, fiery parts are consumed.
The more that **sugar** is aged, the more it is dried out; thus it is called "dry" in comparison to new sugar.
**Penidium sugar** <note>original: "Zuccarum penidij"; a form of clarified sugar or barley sugar often used for coughs</note> is hot and moist in the first degree.

## ¶ Hot in the first degree: dry in the same, or in the second.

**Wormwood** <note>original: "Abfinthium"</note> is hot in the first degree and dry in the second or third; its juice is hotter.
**Agaric** <note>original: "Agaricus"; a medicinal fungus, usually the larch polypore, used as a purgative</note> is hot in the first degree and dry in the second.
**Birthwort** <note>original: "Ariftolochia"</note> is hot in the first degree and dry in the second.
**Laurel berry** <note>original: "Bacca lauri"</note> is hot and dry.
**Betony** <note>original: "Betonica"</note> is hot and dry in the first degree.
**Colophony** <note>original: "Colofonia"; a form of pine resin or rosin</note> is less hot and more dry, specifically in relative terms.
**Marigold** <note>original: "Calendula"</note> is hot and dry.
**Cabbage** <note>original: "Caulis"</note> is hot in the first degree and dry in the second.
**Greater cardamom** <note>original: "Cardamomum maius"</note> is hot and dry in the first degree.
**Chamomile** <note>original: "Camomilla"</note> is hot and dry in the first degree.
**Citron peel** <note>original: "Citri cortex"</note> is hot in the first degree and dry in the second, or equal.

<meta>This page concludes the dietary guidelines and transitions into an extensive toxicological and nutritional catalog. It provides a list of poisonous substances—ranging from plants and minerals to animals—before concluding with a hierarchy of foods based on their nutritional value and their effect on the body's humors.</meta>

->A P P E N D I X.<-

<margin>C</margin> Milk and fresh cheese are beneficial if they are well digested. A sign of good digestion is if they do not cause acidic or smoky belching, nor weigh down the chest or the stomach.
White wine, clear, light, fragrant, and leaning toward tartness rather than sweetness, should be taken moderately diluted in the summer.
Oven-baked bread.
Well-leavened.
All preserved or pickled foods are harmful, especially those made with honey.
Certain things are beneficial when prepared with sugar, such as plums, gourds, chicory, and quinces, provided they are prepared without "hot" spices.
Broths and boiled foods are better than roasted or fried foods.

<summary>This page lists herbal and mineral remedies for gynecological and proctological conditions, ranging from menstrual regulation to the treatment of "uterine suffocation" and the expulsion of the afterbirth. It reflects the early modern medical practice of using sympathetic and antipathetic odors to influence the movement of the womb.</summary>

### ¶ T A B L E &nbsp; I. On the division of Humors and Qualities.

A **HUMOR** is any fluid body that is primarily converted into nourishment.
Of these, some are called Primary, and some are called Secondary.

->The four P R I M A R Y humors:<-

Blood.
Phlegm.
*
<column-break/>
* Choler <note>Yellow bile.</note>
Melancholy <note>Black bile.</note>

**B L O O D**
**Natural**, namely, when the color is red, pure, without a bad odor, and for the most part sweet. **Unnatural**: First, if by its nature—its "complexion" and quality—it has been altered by heat. Second, when some other corrupt humor has been commingled with it.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the practical lists of medicinal plants seen on the previous page to the theoretical underpinnings of Galenic medicine. Having listed substances suitable for various organs, the text now explains the nature of the four humors—the vital fluids (Blood, Phlegm, Yellow Bile, and Black Bile) believed to govern health and temperament.</meta>

<header>A P P E N D I X.</header>
<sig>F 3</sig>

->And this happens in two ways.<-
Specifically, when a humor coming from the outside penetrates the blood and corrupts it.
Or if such a humor is generated within the blood itself, namely by some imbalance <note>original: "intemperie"; refers to a lack of proper proportion between the primary qualities of hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>.

# PHLEGM
<term>Natural Phlegm<note>original: "Phlegma Naturale"; in Galenic medicine, phlegm is cold and moist, associated with winter and the brain.</note></term>, which although not active at the moment, is nevertheless suited to become blood in time. For Phlegm is simply blood that has not been <term>properly cooked<note>original: "probe percoctus"; refers to the process of "coction" or metabolic digestion by which the body transforms food into humors.</note></term>.

### The body requires this Phlegm for a twofold reason.

**By Necessity.** First, when blood is lacking in the limbs, the natural virtues act upon the phlegm to convert it into blood, so that it may nourish them once more. Second, for when it is mixed with the blood, it makes the blood somewhat suitable for restoring and fortifying the parts of the body that have a phlegmatic temperament.
**By Utility.** Namely, so that the power of the limbs, and the limbs themselves which must be restored, may be made more agile—specifically by moistening them, so that the joints do not become dried out due to constant motion.

## Non-natural Phlegm,
<margin>1</margin> Which is either of a different substance, for example, <term>mucilaginous<note>original: "mucilaginosum"; thick and slimy like mucus.</note></term>, though not clearly of a different essence to the senses.
**Raw Phlegm**, equal in substance but different in its true nature.
**Subtle Phlegm**, or very watery.
**Gypsum-like Phlegm**, which is very thick, and whose thin part is capable of being dissolved.
**Glassy Phlegm**, the worst of all, similar to thick and molten glass.
<margin>2</margin> Or it is of a foreign taste and corrupted from natural phlegm, and this exists in a fourfold distinction.
<margin>1</margin> For it is either **Salty**.
This is sharper, drier, and lighter than all others.
<margin>2</margin> Or **Sour**, and this comes from:
A foreign substance, and sour <term>melancholy<note>original: "melancholia"; black bile.</note></term> mixed with it.
The boiling of itself: as in sweet phlegm, and in other juicy humors, which first boil and then turn sour.
<margin>3</margin> Or **Pungent**, and this happens:
From something external, such as pungent melancholy mixed with it.
From itself: because it has been so intensely chilled that it has turned into pungency.
<margin>4</margin> Or **Tasteless**,
With which natural blood is mixed, and which is felt in <term>rheumatisms<note>original: "rheumatismis"; in this period, it refers to the "downward flow" of watery humors, not just joint pain.</note></term>.

# CHOLERA
<note>original: "CHOLERA"; refers to Yellow Bile, the humor associated with fire, summer, and a hot, dry temperament.</note>
**NATURAL**, is the foam of the blood:

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> its color is red and clear, and it is itself light and sharp. It is divided into two parts:
Either it is mixed with the blood. And this is for a twofold reason. **Necessity:** so that it may nourish the choleric limbs, namely, the lungs. **Utility:** because it thins the blood and makes it penetrate to the internal parts.
Or it flows to the <term>gallbladder<note>original: "fellis schistim"; the vessel or sac of the bile.</note></term>. And that is for a twofold reason. **Necessity:** either because it cleanses the whole body, or because it nourishes the gallbladder itself.
**Utility:** this is because it washes and purges the intestines, and because it pricks the muscles of the anus to expel the body's superfluities <note>waste products</note>.

## Unnatural Cholera occurs when

Something else foreign is mixed into its substance.
And so it is either "famous" or "known": where that which is mixed in is foreign by way of phlegm. And from this is generated:
->Cholera<-
**Citrine (Lemon-colored):** because the mixed phlegm is thin.
**Vitelline (Yolk-like):** where the phlegm is thick.
Or when the substance is vitiated <note>corrupted</note> within itself. And it becomes:
**Of lesser fame:** which is also called **Adust** <note>burnt</note> Cholera, with which melancholy is mixed. And this is generated in two ways.
First, when Cholera is burnt within itself, or an ashiness occurs in it: which is worse.
Second, if melancholy has been burnt from the outside and is mixed with it.
<margin>B</margin> When the thin part in the blood is burnt, the thickness of which is **Black Cholera**, and it is generated mostly in the <term>liver<note>original: "epate"</note></term>.
Another type, whose generation is in the stomach, arising from the generation of <term>bad chyme<note>original: "mali chimi"; partially digested food.</note></term>. And so it becomes:
**Leek-green (Prassiva)**, which seems to be made from the mixing of yolk-like bile.
**Verdigris-like (Eruginosa)**, which is like the rust of copper.

# MELANCHOLY.
<note>original: "MELANCHOLIA"; refers to Black Bile, the humor associated with earth, autumn, and a cold, dry temperament.</note>
**Natural**, is the dregs, turbulence, and excess of good blood: its taste exists between sweetness and pungency. And this flows with the blood for a twofold reason: **Necessity**, to prepare blood that can nourish the melancholic limbs, such as the bones. **Utility**, so that it may restrain the blood and thicken it.
Or it flows to the <term>spleen<note>original: "lienam"</note></term>. And this in two ways:
->Either for the sake of<-
**Necessity:** so that it may cleanse the whole body from this excess, or so that it may nourish the spleen.
**Utility:** because it binds and strengthens the mouth of the stomach, and excites the desire of hunger.
**NON-Natural Melancholy**, adust and ashy: is produced in four ways, namely from the ashes of:
->Cholera<-
->Phlegm<-
->Melancholy<-
->Blood.<-

It explains how these fluids serve the body through "necessity" (nourishment) and "utility" (mechanical function like joint lubrication or digestion).</summary>

### Now, for the secondary humors

Blood
Yellow Bile <note>original: "Cholera"</note>
Phlegm
Black Bile <note>original: "Melancholia"</note>

**The Unnamed Humor** <note>original: "Innominatus"</note>, which is more solid in the openings of the ex-

### TABLE II. Concerning the Natural Things.
The "Natural Things" <note>original: "Res naturales"; these are the seven factors that constitute the physical body and its health.</note> are seven, namely:

| | |
|---|---|
| 1 Elements | 2 Complexions <note>Or "Temperaments"</note> |
| 3 Humors | 4 Members <note>Body parts or organs</note> |
| 5 Virtues <note>Vital powers or faculties</note> | 6 Spirits <note>Vital breaths</note> |
| 7 Operations <note>Functions or activities</note> | |

### 1 ELEMENTS
**The Natural Elements are:** Fire. Air. Water. Earth.
**The Medicinal Elements are:** Male seed. Female seed, and menstrual blood. These are considered in the context of hereditary diseases, namely: The Stone <note>original: "Calculo"; kidney or bladder stones</note>, Leprosy, Gout <note>original: "Podagra"</note>, and Epilepsy. For there is one method of curing them when they take their origin from birth or from the very beginnings of generation, and quite another when they arise from other causes.

### 2 COMPLEXIONS <note>Or "Temperaments"</note>
<margin>D</margin> ->Simple<-

| | |
|---|---|
| 1 Hot | 2 Moist |
| 3 Cold | 4 Dry |

->Composite<-
Hot and moist.
Hot and dry.
Cold and moist.
Cold and dry.

And they are equal <note>in balance</note> in their:
Quality
Quantity
Species.

These are recognized by:
| | |
|---|---|
| Age | Sex |
| Form | Appearance |
| Character | Habits |

And by Medical Skill.

->They are specifically considered as follows:<-
Whether they are tempered <note>balanced</note> or distempered <note>imbalanced</note>.
Whether they have fallen away from a healthy balance uniformly in the whole body, or only in a specific part.
Whether they are simple or composite.
Whether they are sanguine, choleric, phlegmatic, or melancholic.
Whether they have fallen far, or only a little, from a healthy balance.

### 3 HUMORS
Regarding these, we first consider their substance, which depends on:
Their matter and their disposition. *

<column-break/>

-tremities of the small veins, and is contained within similar, neighboring members that absorb it.

**Dew** <note>original: "Ros"</note>, is the humor passing through all simple members, like a dew that is ready to be converted into nourishment.

**Exchange** <note>original: "Cambium"; so named by the "barbarians," or non-Classical medieval authors</note>, is the humor that was coagulated shortly before, so that it may be received into the place of that which has been dissolved <note>used up by the body</note>.

**Glue** <note>original: "Gluten"</note>, is the humor that exists deep within the simple members from the very beginning of birth.

* Also by the Agent—that is, the power of the humor itself within the member,
By the celestial aspect <note>astrological influences</note>,
And by the judgment of the nourishment consumed.

By Medical Skill, we consider:
| | | |
|---|---|---|
| From what | Place | they were generated. |
| | Time | |

Secondly, we consider the humor's:
| | |
|---|---|
| Viscosity | Thickness |
| Fineness | Fluidity |

Its consistency, especially in "flux of the belly" <note>diarrhea</note>.
The time in which they are generated.
Likewise, the location.
The movement and rest of the humors, whether in a state of "flux" <note>flowing</note> or ready to flow, as in paralysis and catarrh.
And the mobility in "acute" humors, whose fury we fear.

So that the Physician does not waver in:
Diverting them
Digesting them
Maturing them
Evacuating them.

It also categorizes the body's organs into "principal" organs like the heart and liver versus "ignoble" extremities like the hands and feet.</summary>

**The Rational**
**The Memory**
**The Motive Faculty of the Will**, which moves the limbs through the
**Nerves** proceeding to the spinal cord.

**The Sensory Faculty**, whose organs are:

### III Accidents of DISEASE,
->OF WHICH<- <note>In early medicine, "accidents" are the symptoms or complications that follow a disease but are not the disease itself.</note>
Some are prevening, such as shivering in a fever.
Some are concomitant, such as a headache during a fever.
Some are subsequent, such as a prolonged loss of appetite.
Some are true: which depend on the sickness itself, and are removed when it is removed.
Some are descending from things other than the disease and its cause, such as colic pain during a fever.
Some are strong, such as those drawing the entire focus of care to themselves.
Some do not draw care to themselves, at least not significantly, or differ from the care suited to the disease.
Some are apt to draw other accidents to themselves, or induce diseases, such as burning urine causing an irritation of the bladder.

## ❡ T A B L E VI. On the Temperament of Bodies.

**Signs of a hot body.**
It grows and increases easily.
It is warm to the touch.
Slender, and worn away by thinness.
Veins are wide and swollen.
Movement is swift.
A stubborn character.
Moderate sleep, a fast pulse.
Hair is abundant, curly, and black.
Color is ruddy, or a dark red.

**Signs of a cold body.**
It matures slowly.
A dull character.
Pulse is slow and small.
Breathing is faint.
Somewhat cold to the touch.

Sleepiness.

Soft to the touch.
Softish flesh.

Hidden bones <note>Meaning the bones are well-covered by flesh or fat.</note>.

# A P P E N D I X

<margin>C</margin>
¶ **There are also diseases**
->**Intermittent**<-
Daily fever — Tertian fever <note>Fever recurring every third day.</note>
Quartan — Quintan.
->**Continuous**<-
Semi-tertian — Typhoid-like <note>original: "τυφῶδες," meaning a burning or smoky fever</note>, that is, burning.
->**Acute**<-
Brain fever <note>original: "Phrenitis"</note> — Lethargy
Pleurisy — Pneumonia.
->**Peracute**<-
Severe quinsy <note>original: "Synanche"</note> — Dog-quinsy <note>original: "Cynanche," both referring to severe throat inflammations that threaten suffocation.</note> — Apoplexy.
->**Acute & Continuous**<-
Burning fevers — Brain fevers — Pleurisies
Certain ones are acute and not continuous.
Certain ones are neither acute nor continuous, such as long-lasting diseases.
Certain ones are common <note>original: "uulgares," meaning epidemic</note>, which at certain times invade many mortals in the same place.
Hippocrates identifies 9 differences: namely, acute, peracute <note>very sharp/sudden</note>, malignant, long, medium, destructive, mild, dangerous, and least dangerous.
A peracute disease is one where the force and appearance <note>original: "phantasia"</note> are greater and more difficult than an acute one, which usually reaches its turning point <note>original: "indicationem"</note> on the seventh day.
A malignant disease is one which is greatest in force and difficult, but weak in its presentation, having no certain time for its turning point.
A long disease is one which is judged for better or worse over months or years, or even ends with the man's death.
<margin>D</margin>
A medium disease is one which is between long and acute, participating in both, and is judged on the 20th or 30th day.
A destructive disease, or a lethal one, is one which always turns for the worse.
A mild disease is one which by no means carries off the man.
A dangerous disease is one that tends equally toward health and destruction. It is also called a doubtful disease.
A least dangerous disease is one which always foretells future health as far as it is able, and it has this in common with the mild disease.
¶ Every disease is recognized either from:
Substantially inherent traits, as if something in the composition of the members is in excess, or is missing, or is out of its proper place, — Or from
Impaired function of a limb, — Or from
A quality changed by things leaving the body according to the seasons of the year.

¶ **They are transformed into other diseases**

| :--- | :--- |
| Disease of the sides <note>Pleurisy</note> | Into burning fever. |
| Agitation of the mind | Into a defect of the lung |
| Defect of the lung | Into burning fever. |
| Straining <note>original: "Tineſmos"</note> | Into difficulty of the intestines: |
| <gloss>In the intestines: sometimes into dysentery,</gloss> | |
| Difficulty of the intestines. | Into lightness of the intestines, or lientery <note>A form of diarrhea where food is passed undigested.</note>, |
| Lientery | Into dropsy <note>Edema or swelling.</note>. |
| White phlegm | Into dropsy. |

## On the Causes of Diseases,
### T A B L E VIII.

Certain causes are called
**Procatartic** <note>The triggering or external causes.</note>, which, once they have created the adverse health, are separated from it, such as a biting dog or a stinging scorpion.
**Conjoined**, which are present when the effects are present; when they cease, the effects also cease, such as a stone in the bladder or a growth <note>original: "unguis," literally a nail or claw</note> in the eye.
**Preceding**, which are prepared and aided by the procatartic cause.
**Perfect**, which achieve the same end within themselves.
**Concauses**, which produce an equal effect alongside others.
**Co-helper causes**, which cannot produce a disease by their own power, but can with the help of another.
**Manifest**, whichever are detected by themselves and perform some effect.
**Non-manifest**, whichever are not at all detected by themselves. <meta>catchword: (duntur.</meta>
**Obscure**, which are detected neither by themselves nor by others.
**Obscure for a time**, which are unknown for a while, but can again fall under the senses.
Furthermore, all diseases occur either:
**From those things which are in the body, such as**
Bile — Phlegm — Melancholy.
Abundance and corruption of the blood.
**Or from those things which are outside the body, such as**
Labors — Wounds
External heat — Cold
Dryness — Moisture.

## C A N O N E S <note>General rules or principles of medicine.</note>

Once the cause is known, it is removed first.
Then universal remedies are applied.
Finally, particular ones, according to the requirements of the disease.
Contraries are generally cured by contraries.
And likes provide aid to likes.
Yet excess must be avoided in all things, but especially in those that repel <note>original: "repercuſſiuis," medicines meant to drive back humors.</note>.

# A P P E N D I X

¶ **Likewise, all diseases**
->**Hot [diseases] happen either**<-
From food, otherwise prone to exciting heat.
From increased heat. Because of putrefaction <note>The breakdown of humors, which was thought to generate heat.</note>.
Because of proximity to a hotter body.
From blockage <note>original: "obstipatione," referring to a clogging of the body's pores or vessels</note>.
->**Cold [diseases]**<-
From proximity to cold things.
From the quality and quantity of food and drink.
From constipation. From excessive porosity <note>original: "raritate," meaning the body is too "thin" or open, allowing heat to escape.</note>.
From leisure. From immoderate movement.
->**Dry [diseases]**<-
From much perspiration and little nutrition.
From dry foods. From anxiety.
From wakefulness. From immoderate studies.
From the surrounding dry air.
From baths and waters of Nitre, Sulfur, Alum, and Bitumen.
From drying medicines.
->**Moist [diseases]**<-
From moist foods. From too much drink.
From a soft upbringing. From leisure and tranquility.
From frequent dwelling in sweet-water baths.
From idleness. From a moist constitution of the weather.
From rains.
From medicines which cause moistening.

### ¶ Table IX. On the differences of Pulses.

THE PULSE is the much-extended depth, length, and breadth of the artery.
**Small** pulse, which is the opposite of the large.
**Moderate**, participating in both.
**Full**, which is intermediate, falling under the touch as if the casing of the artery seems more corporeal: especially when its inner part is entirely more moist and thicker to the grasp.
**Hard**, when the artery seems and is felt to be sinewy and hard, and then a powerful spirit <note>The "vital spirit" believed to flow through the arteries.</note> is underneath, as if the struck part retains the blow.
**Soft**, which is the opposite of the hard, weakly striking an unresisting artery: whose spirit is dissolved and mild.
**Moist**, is indeed soft, since in it a gentler and more placid substance renders a certain thinner moisture.
**Dry**, in which the moisture seems to have been consumed.
**Vehement**, which makes a violent stroke.
**Weak**, which makes a feeble stroke.
**Moderate**, which maintains a proportion to both.
**Dense**, or frequent, which does not have a long elevation or compression.
**Trembling**, which does not have an equal stroke.
**Oblique**, which does not depart from the straight position of the artery.
**Unequal**, which rises higher according to some part, and frequently falls away, the vessel being inflated and weakened.
**Intermittent**, which fails not only for two, but for three or more strokes, causing a distraction

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
of one, or two, or even more.
**Failing**, in which the artery remains immobile not only for two, but for three or more strokes.
**Intervening**, when after two strokes the motion follows its own order, but a middle stroke falls out between them.
**Leaping**, that is, goat-like <note>original: "caprifans," a pulse that jerks or leaps like a goat.</note>, when the artery is thought to leap, and is immediately carried to another motion before it has the appearance of compression.
**Recurring**, which as much as it exceeds in magnitude or vehemence, so much does it return back in others.
**Ant-like**, which is small, empty and frequent, and weak: this usually demonstrates extreme danger and death <note>original: "formicans," a tiny, crawling pulse resembling the movement of an ant.</note>.
**Very full**, holds the vessel strongly.
**Thin**, subtly.
**Average**, moderately; do not take your fingers away until it has struck a hundred times.

->¶ **Significations.**<-
->**The Pulse**<-

In the beginning weak, the same becoming more intense: good.
From the first strong, then more relaxed: bad.
**Strong**, a strong Heart.
**Weak**, a weak Heart.
**Fast** in a healthy person: health.
**Small** in a healthy person: weakness of the chest and the area around the heart <note>original: "pręcordiorū"</note>: in a sick person: the end of life.
**Small and fast** in a healthy person: anger, bile.
<margin>B</margin>
In a sick person: overflowing heat.
**Slow** in a healthy person: coldness.
**In a sick person**: dryness.
**Infrequent**, a failing of the vital power <note>original: "uirtutis"</note>.
**Slow** also: a failing of heat.
Seek the rest from Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note>, in his book on Pulses.

---

## TABLE X. On the judgments of Urines.

->¶ **How it should be collected, and what should be observed before judgment.**<-

Let it be collected when digestion <note>original: "concoctione"</note> is complete.
It should not sit for more than six hours.
The whole should be received, and not just a part.
Judgment should not be pronounced upon it unless it has been rendered quite still.

->¶ **Things that hinder judgment**<-

Frequent movement. A dark place.
A place that is too transparent <note>Too much light causing glare.</note>.
A green flask <note>original: "matula"</note>, one wide at the bottom, or too narrow, or solar rays.

->¶ **Liquids similar to Urine.**<-

Mead <note>original: "Hydromel," honey and water.</note>.
Syrup of vinegar.
Honey water. Water tinted with saffron.

**In Summer**
Golden or saffron-colored, of a middling substance.
**The Sediment** <note>original: "Hypostasi"</note>
Light, white, and even.

Corresponding to the proportions of the season, tending toward whiteness.

In a larger quantity.
Containing more undigested matter.

### ¶ Judgment based on the disposition of the "non-naturals."
<note>In Galenic medicine, "non-naturals" are external factors that affect health, such as sleep, diet, and exercise.</note>
->U R I N E<-
**In the sleepy**
White and thick,
with many undigested contents.
**In those excessively wakeful**
Thin,
Turning from white to watery, then to golden,
oil-like, black, or scorched.
**In the fasting**
Flaming, saffron-colored, and thin.
**In those oppressed by hunger**
Thin and white, without sediment.

### ¶ On judgment based on abundance and quantity.
->Much urine in the healthy<-
From excessive drinking of thin wine.
From rare or moderate bowel movements.
From the excessive use of diuretics.
->Much urine in the sick,<-
The disease of diabetes <note>original: "Passionem diabetis"</note>, or the wasting away of the body.
The evacuation of superfluous fluids.
The determination of an illness, or a crisis resulting from dropsy <note>original: "hydrope," an old term for swelling or edema.</note>.
**Much urine in acute fevers**
Either the resolution of the fever.
Or the conversion into a Hectic fever <note>A persistent, wasting fever often associated with consumption.</note>.
Or a spasm.
**If it should be**
Flaming,
Slightly saffron, tinted, and with bad contents, it is
not to be praised.
->Little U R I N E<-
A drier diet.
The use of sticky <note>original: "glutinosorum"</note> foods.
Obstructions <note>original: "Opilationes," specifically blockages in the vessels or organs.</note>, or excessive bowel movements.
Sometimes an intense fever.
Injury to the urinary organs.

### ¶ On the significations of the substance of Urines.
<note>"Substance" refers to the viscosity or thickness of the fluid.</note>
->U R I N E<-

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
**Subtle or Thin**
Signifies coldness and dryness.
A dry humor.
A lack of digestion <note>original: "concoctionis"</note>.
Obstruction of the liver.
A failure of the attractive and expulsive powers.
**Gross or Thick**
A hot and moist temperament.
Strong, moist digestion.
Humors mixed with phlegm and blood.
**Middling**
A temperate constitution.
Complete digestion.
A balance of all humors.

### ¶ On the significations of transparent Urine.
->U R I N E<-
**Transparent**
White and thick.
Crude, thick phlegm, and the sicknesses
arising from it, such as Epilepsy, etc.
With a tint, it signifies "egg-yolk" bile <note>original: "Choleram uitellinam," a specific type of yellow bile compared to the color of egg yolks.</note>.
However, it always signifies a lack of digestion,
whether it is thin or thick.
With a diversity of colors, it signifies scorching and internal heat.
With bran-like scales <note>original: "furfuribus," meaning flaky sediment.</note>, if the illness is not in the urinary tract, it signifies the liquefaction of phlegm.
<margin>B</margin>
**Turbid or Turbulent**, signifies a multitude of humors which are
expelled by nature; likewise, the labor of nature in
separating and expelling them.
**Turbid in acute fevers**
A "boiling" of the humors.
Liquefaction <note>The breakdown of body tissues or humors.</note>.
**Persistently turbulent**, signifies a long illness and
imperfect digestion.
**Remaining transparent and watery**, signifies a lack
of digestion.
**Urine passed clear that becomes turbid**, or that which is
**turbid and becomes clear**, signifies that the matter is beginning
to overcome the disease, though not perfectly.
**That which is least transparent**, like clear water,
nor turbid like that of beasts of burden <note>original: "subiugalium," referring to the cloudy urine of yoked animals like oxen.</note>, but
staying in the middle, portends health.

### ¶ On the significations of the odor of Urine.
->U R I N E<-
**Lacking odor**
Rawness of the humors.
A cold temperament.
In acute cases, it signifies death.
**Stinking**
With signs of good digestion and scales, it signifies
the itch <note>original: "scabiem."</note>.
With pus <note>original: "sanie."</note>, it signifies an ulcer.
Without digestion, an abscess <note>original: "apostema."</note> in the urinary tract.

<margin>C</margin> In acute cases, there is danger.
**Sweetness** indicates a dominance of uncorrupted blood.
**Bitterness** indicates a dominance of choler <note>Yellow bile, associated with heat and fire.</note>.
**Acridity** indicates madness or melancholy.
**In the healthy**, it suggests a future fever or the body’s attempt at expulsion.

->Acrid<-
Indicates the putrefaction of the humors.

### ¶ Prognosis from white color.

->White urine<-
->Dominance of cold.<-
**Crystalline**
->Weakness of digestion.<-
**Mucilaginous**, indicates a dominance of phlegm and its thick abundance.
**Oily**, or pearlish, indicates liquefaction <note>The medical theory that the body’s fat or substance is "melting" into the urine due to disease.</note>.
**Fungal**
Pus, Phlegm, or Stones.
**In acute fevers**, or if it appears milky after a colored state, it signifies that the choleric part has diverted to other places rather than through the urinary passages; it therefore signifies a future frenzy <note>original: "phrenitim," a brain fever or delirium</note> or a rheum <note>discharge</note> of the head.
**In a continuous fever** without a flux <note>discharge/flow</note>, in a frenzy, or in any other abscess, it signifies a change into a quartan fever <note>A fever that recurs every four days, often associated with malaria.</note>.

<margin>D</margin> ->In jaundice<-
Weakness of the liver's color.
Labor of the expulsive faculty.
Future dropsy <note>original: "hydropem," swelling caused by excess fluid.</note>.
**In the healthy and persisting**, it indicates a lack of concoction <note>The "cooking" or processing of humors by the body's heat.</note>.
**Luminous and plentiful**, in the healthy, it indicates thick and viscous humors.
**Thin and clear**, indicates melancholic humors.
**In the beginning of a fever**, if it then turns black, it indicates the expulsion of humors through the urinary paths.
**Milky**, similar to whey, signifies death or consumption <note>original: "phthisim," a wasting disease like tuberculosis.</note>.

### ¶ Meanings of Citrine (Yellow).

->Citrine urine,<-
**Pale**, indicates imperfect digestion.
**Yellow**, indicates the beginning of digestion.
**Intensely citrine**, indicates perfect digestion.
**Golden**, indicates a balanced temperament of digestion.
**Fiery and thin**, indicates an acute fever.

### ¶ Judgments of Red.

->Red urine<-
**Bloody in acute cases**, indicates repletion <note>An overfullness of the vessels</note>, and especially of the blood.
Provided there is no rupture of a vein.
**The same if thin**, indicates a flow of humors to "suffocating" places <note>Likely referring to the chest or throat</note>, if it is passed little by little.
**The same if thick**, and then thin, indicates a relapse.
**In jaundice**, if moderately red, it indicates heat of the liver and its "suffocation," and future dropsy.
**Intense red in the healthy**, indicates hunger or a "burning" in the stomach.
**In pain of the kidneys**, it indicates an abscess of the same.

<column-break/>

**In frequent headache**, it indicates future mania.
**Turbid**, indicates weakness of the liver.

### ¶ On the meanings of green.

->Green urine,<-
**Supreme coldness**, especially if it is quite thin.
**Thick**, also signifies cold.
**Leek-green**, indicates adustion <note>original: "adustionem," the "burning" or scorching of humors through excessive heat.</note>.
**Thick**, indicates the drinking of poison.
The same is noted of **verdigris** <note>A bright green color, here associated with copper-like bile.</note>.

### ¶ On the meanings of Black.

->Black urine<-
**Proceeding from saffron-color**, indicates the thickness of choler.
**Proceeding from dark brown**, indicates a dominance of black bile.
**From green**, indicates "burnt" choler.
**If preceded by green or livid color**, indicates a dominance of cold.
**If preceded by red or citrine**, with a dissolution of strength, it indicates the death of the natural color.
**In the beginning of a fever**, it indicates the worsening of the disease and a failure of natural heat.
**At the end of a melancholic sickness**, it indicates the termination of the illness, if it was previously thick and watery.
**In acute cases**, if good signs did not precede it, it indicates "burning" and death.
**Or dark red**, if not caused by drinking red wine, it sometimes indicates:
Heat and intensity in the kidneys.
**In the elderly and women**, it indicates a failure of natural heat.

### ¶ Meanings of Oil-like urine.

->Oil-like urine<-
**Transparent like oil**
Consumption
Liquefaction
A critical expulsion <note>A "crisis" or turning point in a disease.</note>.
**Scant and stinking**, signifies supreme consumption <note>Wasting away of the body.</note>.
->Like the washing of meat<-
Consumption
Destruction of the liver.
Dropsy.
->If it becomes so after being black<-
->and there is relief<-
The cleansing of "burnt" humors.
**If it appears on the fourth day** in very acute cases, it signifies death on the seventh day.
->Simple<-
A preparation for consumption.
Wasting.
**In color and substance**, indicates a liquefaction of the kidneys or consumption.
**In "canine" colors** <note>Likely referring to a pale, bone-white or yellowish-grey color.</note>, it indicates the "burning" of both types of choler.

¶ **Judgment on the sediment.** <note>original: "hypostasi," the sediment that settles at the bottom of a urine glass.</note>
->Natural sediment should be:<-

| | |
|---|---|
| White | Moderate in substance |
| In an equal mixture of parts. | |
| Continuous | Appearing quickly |
| Long-lasting | Residing at the bottom. |
| Round | Shaped like a pine-nut. |

->Sediment<-

| | |
|---|---|
| White and mucilaginous, | signifies rawness <note>undigested humors</note> and a mixture of oiliness. |
| Black, | signifies the same as black urine <note>often associated with extreme "burning" of the humors or death</note>. |
| Green, | the same as green urine. |
| Citron-yellow, | signifies most burning heat. |
| Red, | signifies an abundance of blood. |

¶ **Concerning the Circles.** <note>The "circulus" refers to the ring or crown formed at the top of the urine where it touches the glass.</note>
->The Circle<-

| | |
|---|---|
| Foamy | Disturbance of the internal senses. |
| | Viscous <note>sticky or thick</note> humors. |
| | Windiness <note>gas</note> in the ventricles of the brain. |
| Leaden-colored, | signifies epilepsy. |
| Green, | signifies melancholy <note>the humor of black bile</note>. |
| Red, | signifies a flux of blood. |
| Trembling, | signifies paralysis and spasms caused by fullness <note>over-abundance of humors</note>. |

¶ **Concerning the meanings of foam.**
->Foamy urine<-
->Black, citron, or reddish-brown<-

| | |
|---|---|
| Jaundice | Suffering of the spleen. |
| Windiness with viscosity. | |

If it persists, it signifies a blockage <note>original: "opilationem"</note>; especially if the bubbles are large, it signifies winds in the urinary passages, raw phlegm, or an abundance of kidney disease <note>original: "Nephritim"</note>.

Granular foam signifies catarrh <note>a flow of mucus</note>; and if they float on the surface, they signify that the matter does not descend to the lower parts.

When in the middle region, it signifies matter dripping to the chest; but in the bottom, it signifies it is falling to the joints.

If it is halfway between bubbles and grains, it signifies heat, or a weakness of heat.

¶ **Concerning Scales.**
->Scales in the urine<-

Red scales signify an ailment of the kidneys.
White scales signify a suffering of the bladder.
Dark, obscure scales like those of fish signify the ultimate dissolution <note>the "melting" or breaking down of the body's substance</note>.

¶ **Concerning Bran-like flakes.** <note>original: "Furfuribus," small flakes resembling bran or dandruff.</note>
->Bran in the urine<-

With an itching of the head of the penis and with rot, it signifies a scabies <note>skin-like irritation or sores</note> in the bladder.

Without stench or rot, but with difficulty in urinating and weakness, it signifies a dissolution of the body, especially if the flakes are dark.

If they are large like crushed grain:
White flakes signify burning in the bladder.
Black flakes signify burning in the spleen.

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin>
Red flakes signify a burning of the blood.

->Fleshy urine,<-
Signifies a dissolution <note>decay or wasting</note> of the liver.

->Oily urine, in which sediment floats on top.<-
If there is much of it, it signifies the dissolution of body fat.
Citron-colored, signifies the dissolution of old fat.
A small amount signifies the dissolution of the kidneys.

->Purulent urine <note>original: "Saniosa," containing pus or bloody discharge</note><-
Signifies the eruption of an ulcer, if pain preceded it.

->Full of small bits<-
Signifies weakness of the digestive faculty.
A rupture of the mesenteric veins, or from the consumption of milk or cheese.

->Sandy urine<-
Signifies a stone in the kidneys or bladder, or a dissolution of the same.
If the "sand" does not reside at the bottom and tends toward redness, it signifies a burning of the liver; if citron-colored, a burning of the spleen.

->Mucilaginous<-
Signifies an exuberance of thick humors.
A cold complexion.
A crisis of sciatica and the joints.

If hairs float in it,
It signifies the consolidation of hidden heat, from the color acting upon it, in the kidneys.

->Fermented,<- <note>looking yeasty or bubbly like leaven</note>
Signifies weakness of the stomach.
Bad digestion.
The constant use of dairy products.

<margin>B</margin>
->Ash-colored<-
Signifies burnt phlegm and the long duration of a foreign heat <note>a fever caused by external factors or unnatural humors</note>.

->Bloody<-
Signifies weakness of the liver.
A wound in the urinary passages.
A breach of continuity in the bladder, if there is a little.
If there is much, a breach in the spleen.
What kind it is—that is, if something floats in it like a small skin, or a full bladder, or similar to an egg—signifies:
Raw, viscous phlegm.
Glassy, mucilaginous phlegm, or winds.
The opening of the urinary passages.

->Calculous <note>Stony</note><-
Signifies a stone is present, or viscous phlegm in the urinary passages.
Strong heat in those same places.

->Spermatic<-
If the sperm is divided and intermittent, it signifies that sexual intercourse preceded it, or a nocturnal emission of seed.
If it is spherical and truncated, it signifies abstinence from intercourse, or nocturnal pollution.
And if this happens many times, it signifies an incontinence of the seed, or a paralysis of the genital members.
